Ask your parent to write a late note for school
Text your friend to say you are going to be late again
payload.explanation: Cutting non-essential steps when you have pressed snooze too many times is the quickest way to recover lost time.

payload.snippet: Your school uniform shirt is creased badly and the iron is already hot but you are running short on time.

Wear the creased shirt and hope no one notices
Switch to a different shirt that is not part of the uniform
Ask your parent to iron it while you eat breakfast slowly
payload.explanation: A quick iron of the visible areas is the fastest fix that makes the biggest difference to appearance.

payload.snippet: The bathroom is occupied by your sibling and you have ten minutes before you need to leave.
options: Do what you can at the kitchen sink while you wait
Bang on the door repeatedly until they come out
Wait at the bathroom door doing nothing
Skip washing completely today
payload.explanation: Using an alternative space keeps your routine moving without creating conflict.

payload.snippet: You realise you have not done part of your homework while eating breakfast before school.
options: Pack the homework and do the missing part in the form room before registration
Stay home until it is done
Submit what you have and tell the teacher at the start of class
Copy a friend's work on the bus
payload.explanation: Arriving early to form room to finish homework is honest and still gets it submitted on time.

payload.snippet: It is the first cold morning of the autumn and you cannot find your school coat anywhere.

Go without any coat in the cold
Turn the house upside down and miss school
Ask your parent to drive you because of the coat

payload.snippet: Your packed lunch fell off the counter and everything has spilled on the kitchen floor.

Leave the mess and go to school without lunch
Cry and refuse to go to school
Ask your parent to bring lunch to school later

payload.snippet: You feel very tired this morning because you stayed up too late last night.
options: Get up, eat breakfast, and walk to school briskly to wake up naturally
Stay home because you are tired
Text your friend to say you cannot cope today
Go back to sleep after breakfast

payload.snippet: Your bus pass is missing and you are not sure if you have enough change for the fare.

Refuse to get on the bus without the pass
Ask a stranger on the bus to pay for you
Walk home instead of going to school
payload.explanation: Counting change and resolving the pass issue later is the practical split — today's journey and tonight's search are separate problems.

payload.snippet: Your younger sibling is refusing to eat breakfast and it is making the whole family late this morning.

Argue with your sibling to make them eat faster
Skip your own breakfast to wait for your sibling
Start crying because the routine is broken
payload.explanation: Handing the sibling issue to a parent and focusing on your own readiness is the most productive split of effort.

payload.snippet: You cannot remember if you have PE today and your kit is not in your bag.

Leave the kit and hope you do not have PE
Text a friend to ask while you wait for the answer
Tell the teacher you forgot and accept the consequence

payload.snippet: You woke up fifteen minutes before the bus with wet hair because you showered the night before and it has dried awkwardly.
options: Style it as quickly as possible and accept that it will not be perfect today
Stay home because your hair looks bad
Shower again and miss the bus
Blow dry it completely and skip breakfast to make up the time
payload.explanation: Accepting a less-than-perfect hair day is the correct morning tradeoff when time is short.

payload.snippet: The cereal box is empty and it is the only breakfast food you normally eat.

Skip breakfast because your preferred food is gone
Wait for your parent to buy more cereal before eating
Go to school hungry and ask a friend for food
payload.explanation: Any breakfast is better than no breakfast — checking for alternatives takes fifteen seconds.

payload.snippet: Your school has sent a reminder that it is non-uniform day today and you completely forgot until this morning.
options: Choose an appropriate outfit quickly from what is in your wardrobe
Wear your uniform and explain you forgot
Stay at home because you have nothing to wear
Text the school to ask if you can wear uniform instead
payload.explanation: A quick wardrobe decision is the correct response to a forgotten non-uniform day — uniform is always a fallback anyway.

payload.snippet: You cannot remember whether you locked the front door after leaving and you are already five minutes into the walk to school.
options: Text a parent to check or turn back only if no one is home to confirm
Turn back regardless to check even though you will be late
Keep walking and worry about it all morning
Assume it is fine because you usually lock it
payload.explanation: A text or call check takes ten seconds and confirms the answer without necessarily requiring you to turn back.

payload.snippet: The morning news is reporting heavy traffic on the road your parent drives you to school on.

Wait until you are stuck in traffic to mention it
Ask your parent to drive a different way without explaining why
Take the bus instead without telling your parent
payload.explanation: Early information allows a route decision before the car has moved — announcing it in traffic is too late.

payload.snippet: You feel a sore throat coming on but it is a normal school day and you have no temperature.

Refuse to go to school because of a sore throat
Take cold medicine from the cabinet without telling your parent
Ask your teacher to send you home when you arrive
payload.explanation: A sore throat without a temperature is not normally a reason to miss school — monitoring it is the right response.

payload.snippet: Your water bottle is empty and you forgot to refill it last night before bed.

Go to school without a water bottle
Buy a bottle of water on the way which costs money every day
Wait until school and use the water fountain all day
payload.explanation: Filling it quickly at home is both free and faster than any alternative.

payload.snippet: You and your sibling both need help from your parent at the same time and your parent is getting the baby ready.
options: Deal with what you can yourself and wait for a genuine blockage
Demand your parent helps you first
Give up on your morning routine entirely
Wake the other parent to get both children sorted at once
payload.explanation: Handling what you can independently before asking for help reduces the morning bottleneck.

payload.snippet: The school gate opens at 8:45 and you arrived early at 8:30 and there is nowhere to wait under cover in the rain.

Go home and come back at 8:45
Knock on the school door and demand early entry
payload.explanation: Using nearby shelter is the obvious and free solution to waiting in the rain.

payload.snippet: You have a maths test first period and you realise you left your revision notes at school yesterday.

Ring the school to ask if someone can read you the notes
Blame the teacher for not letting you take notes home
payload.explanation: A quick mental review of what you already know is productive in the time available — the notes are gone and the test is not.

payload.snippet: Leo's mum packed a sandwich but he does not like it.

refuses to eat at all
demands a new one now

payload.snippet: Kai forgot to put his lunch in his bag before school.

steals another child's food
calls home to complain

payload.snippet: Nina finds her apple has a small brown bruise on one side.
options: eats around the bruise
throws the whole apple away
refuses to eat any fruit
cries about her ruined lunch
payload.explanation: A small bruise does not make an apple unsafe — you can eat around it.

payload.snippet: Tom's soup spilled inside his bag on the way to school.

hides the bag and says nothing
blames the soup flask brand
goes home early for a clean bag

payload.snippet: Ava forgot to bring her water bottle to school today.

refuses to eat anything at all

cries until a teacher gives her one
payload.explanation: Drinking from a water fountain is the simple solution to a forgotten bottle.

payload.snippet: Ben's sandwich has mustard but he asked his mum for none.

throws the whole sandwich away
demands his mum bring a new one
goes home for the day
payload.explanation: Scraping off the unwanted topping is a practical fix.

payload.snippet: Grace packed cold leftover pasta and hopes it still tastes nice.
options: eats it cold without complaining
demands the teacher warm it up
throws it all away uneaten
trades her whole lunch away
payload.explanation: Eating cold leftovers is perfectly fine and wastes nothing.

payload.snippet: Max is sitting next to someone whose lunch smells very strong.

tells them their food smells awful
holds his nose loudly all lunch
refuses to eat his own food
payload.explanation: Quietly moving is the polite way to handle a strong smell.

payload.snippet: Lily dropped her fork and it now has dirt on it.
options: gets a clean fork from the counter
uses the dirty fork anyway
eats everything with only her hands
refuses to eat at all
payload.explanation: Getting a clean fork is the hygienic and sensible solution.

payload.snippet: Zoe's sandwich bag is very tricky and hard to open today.
options: asks a friend to help her
gives up eating and goes hungry
rips the whole bag apart
asks the teacher to open it
payload.explanation: Asking a friend for help is friendly and solves the problem quickly.

payload.snippet: Sam brought a delicious-smelling lunch and his friends are curious.
options: shares a little bite with friends
hides it under the table secretly
eats it very quickly to avoid sharing
tells his friends not to look
payload.explanation: Sharing a small taste is a kind and social thing to do at lunch.

payload.snippet: Finn's lunchbox has his name on it but someone else picked it up.
options: tells a teacher what happened
takes another child's lunchbox
goes hungry and says nothing
shouts at the other child
payload.explanation: Telling a teacher is the right and calm way to sort out a mix-up.

payload.snippet: Ruby's mum wrote a little note inside her lunchbox today.

throws the note away unread
feels embarrassed and hides it
tells everyone her mum is silly
payload.explanation: A loving note from a parent is something to appreciate and enjoy.

payload.snippet: Owen opens his crisps and finds they are stale from a tiny hole.

throws the entire lunchbox away
demands the school give him new crisps
cries about his ruined snack
payload.explanation: Stale crisps from a small hole are still safe to eat even if less nice.

payload.snippet: Sophie spills her juice box all over the lunch table.
options: gets paper towels to wipe it up
walks away and leaves the mess
blames her friend for bumping her
pretends the spill did not happen
payload.explanation: Cleaning up your own spill is the responsible thing to do.

payload.snippet: Jake finds his crackers crumbled into pieces inside his lunchbox.
options: eats the crumbled pieces from the box
refuses to eat anything not whole
demands his mum bring new crackers
throws away all his food
payload.explanation: Crumbled crackers are still fine to eat — shape does not matter.

payload.snippet: Chloe is very hungry but only brought a very small snack today.

takes food off another child's tray
tells the teacher she is starving
refuses to eat the small snack
payload.explanation: Eating what you have and waiting until home is the right response.

payload.snippet: Ethan's mum packed a brand new food he has never tried before.

demands his mum never pack new food
refuses it loudly in front of class
payload.explanation: Trying a small bite before deciding is the fair and adventurous thing to do.

payload.snippet: Isla forgot to pack her dessert even though she made it last night.

takes someone else's dessert instead
refuses to eat her main lunch at all

payload.snippet: Leo gets on the school bus and his usual seat is already taken by someone else.

refuses to ride the bus and calls his mum

waits for someone else to deal with the fallen bag
payload.explanation: Apologising and checking on the person shows responsibility and care.

payload.snippet: Kai lost his bus pass and the driver says he cannot ride without it.

pushes past the driver and gets on anyway
pretends to look for it and sneaks on
cries loudly until the driver lets him on
payload.explanation: Honest communication with the driver is the right response when you have lost your pass.

payload.snippet: Nina is sitting next to someone who smells strongly of something unpleasant.

payload.explanation: Staying quiet and respectful is the polite response in a sensitive situation.

payload.snippet: Tom is not sure which stop to get off at because the route changed today.

stays on the bus all the way to the final stop
calls his mum in a panic while the bus is still moving
payload.explanation: Asking the driver is the safest and most sensible option when unsure.

payload.snippet: Ava's bus arrives but the queue is long and she might not get on this one.

payload.explanation: Swans are protective and can be aggressive — slowly backing away is the safest response.

payload.snippet: Ava sees a fox sitting in her garden in the middle of the day looking very still and unwell.
options: tells an adult straight away who can call a wildlife rescue organisation
tries to pick the fox up to take it to the vet herself
shouts at the fox to see if it reacts to noise normally
gives the fox food and water and waits to see if it recovers
payload.explanation: A fox out in daytime acting unusually could be sick — adults and wildlife rescues know the right steps.

payload.snippet: Ben is at the beach when a seagull swoops down very low and snatches food right from his hand.
options: stays calm and does not chase the seagull or wave food around
chases the seagull along the beach shouting
throws his remaining food at other seagulls in retaliation
holds his remaining food very high in the air while walking
payload.explanation: Staying calm and keeping food covered or out of reach prevents further seagull swoops.

payload.snippet: Grace finds a toad in the garden that is struggling to move and looking very dry.
options: calls an adult to help and keeps the garden hose available to gently moisten it
picks it up and runs it under the cold tap forcefully
puts it in a jar with no air holes to carry it to the vet
leaves it and assumes it will be fine without any help
payload.explanation: Toads can dry out in heat — keeping them moist while an adult calls for advice is the correct response.

payload.snippet: Max is on a countryside walk when a herd of cows with calves starts moving toward him and his family.
options: stays calm, moves to the edge of the field, and climbs over the fence if they get too close
runs at full speed directly across the middle of the field
tries to pet the nearest calf to show the cows he means no harm
waves his arms and jacket to try to stop the cows coming toward them
payload.explanation: Moving to the fence edge and exiting if necessary is the safest response to cows with calves.

payload.snippet: Lily discovers a hedgehog curled up in a pile of leaves she was about to rake away.
options: gently puts the leaves back and tells an adult so they can move the pile safely later
pulls the hedgehog out of the leaves to look at it up close
pours water on the leaves to wake the hedgehog up
removes all the leaves anyway since the hedgehog can find another place
payload.explanation: Hedgehogs hibernate and nest in leaves — protecting the pile and seeking adult help is kind and correct.

payload.snippet: Zoe is at the pet shop when a hamster in a tank bites her finger as she reaches in.
options: removes her finger calmly and asks the shop assistant for help
jabs her finger back in and tries again immediately
drops the tank lid to stop the hamster from getting out
shouts loudly and tells everyone in the shop the hamster is dangerous
payload.explanation: Calmly removing the finger and getting help is the right response — bites can happen when animals feel threatened.

payload.snippet: Sam is walking near a pond when he hears a loud hissing sound from some tall reeds nearby.
options: stops immediately and steps back from the reeds cautiously
pushes the reeds aside to find out what is making the noise
throws a stone into the reeds to scare whatever is there away
calls out loudly to see if a person made the noise
payload.explanation: Stopping and stepping back is the correct caution response when you hear an unexpected animal sound from cover.

payload.snippet: Finn sees a wasp flying around his food at a picnic table.
options: covers the food and moves calmly away from the wasp
swats at the wasp hard with a newspaper
blows air at the wasp repeatedly to drive it away
tries to squash the wasp under his cup
payload.explanation: Covering food and moving calmly is the safest response — wasps only sting when threatened.

payload.snippet: Ruby is visiting a farm when she finds a newborn lamb that seems to have wandered away from its mother.
options: tells the farmer immediately and stays nearby without touching the lamb
picks the lamb up and tries to return it to the flock herself
bottle-feeds the lamb with water from her drinks bottle
calls the lamb's name to see if its mother comes running
payload.explanation: Telling the farmer immediately is the right action — farmers know how to reunite separated lambs safely.

payload.snippet: Owen is on holiday when he notices a jellyfish on the beach near where children are playing.
options: tells a lifeguard or beach supervisor about the jellyfish straightaway
picks up the jellyfish to move it away from the children
throws sand on the jellyfish to bury it quickly
tells the children it is dead and completely safe to touch
payload.explanation: Telling a lifeguard ensures the correct hazard warning is given and no one is injured.

payload.snippet: Sophie finds a mouse in the kitchen of her house that is running along the back of the cupboards.
options: tells a parent or adult who can contact pest control
tries to catch the mouse using a bowl from the kitchen
pours bleach near the cupboards to drive it away
feeds the mouse to encourage it to stay in one place
payload.explanation: Telling an adult who can contact pest control is the responsible and humane action.

payload.snippet: Jake is in the garden when a bee lands on his arm and stays there without stinging.
options: stays completely still and waits patiently for the bee to fly away on its own
shakes his arm hard to make the bee fly off immediately
tries to flick the bee off quickly with his other hand
calls for help loudly even though the bee is not stinging him
payload.explanation: Staying still is the safest response — bees are harmless when resting and will leave on their own.

payload.snippet: Chloe sees a seagull trapped in a plastic net near the seafront and it cannot free itself.
options: finds a nearby adult and tells them so a wildlife rescue can be called
tries to cut the net herself using scissors from a nearby shop
shouts at the seagull to encourage it to struggle free faster
picks the seagull up to try to unwrap the net herself
payload.explanation: Finding an adult and calling a wildlife rescue is the safest and most effective action.

payload.snippet: Ethan sees a large dog tied up outside a shop that starts growling as he walks past.
options: crosses to the other side of the pavement giving the dog plenty of space
stops and stares at the dog trying to decide if it is dangerous
tries to calm the dog by reaching out his hand for it to sniff
makes loud noises to see whether the growling gets worse or stops
payload.explanation: Crossing to give the dog space is the safe and sensible response to a growling restrained dog.

payload.snippet: Isla finds a slow worm in her garden curled up under a piece of wood.
options: gently replaces the wood and leaves the slow worm alone
picks it up thinking it is a worm and it will not mind
shows all her friends by lifting the wood repeatedly
pours water on it to make it move so she can see it better
payload.explanation: Slow worms are protected reptiles — leaving them undisturbed under their refuge is the correct and legal response.

payload.snippet: Leo is building a tall tower but it falls over every time he adds a new layer.
options: makes the base much wider and uses heavier blocks at the bottom
keeps building it taller until it somehow stays up on its own
uses tape to stick the blocks together so they cannot fall
gives up and knocks down everyone else's tower in frustration
payload.explanation: A wider, heavier base is the engineering solution to a toppling tower.

payload.snippet: Mia wants to build a birdhouse but has never used a hammer or nails before.
options: asks an adult to supervise and teach her before she begins
hammers nails in by herself without any guidance or safety check
uses the hammer as a bat to play a game instead
draws a birdhouse on cardboard since it is much safer and easier
payload.explanation: Getting adult supervision when using tools for the first time is both safe and a great way to learn.

payload.snippet: Kai's team is building a model bridge and his partner wants to do it completely differently from him.
options: discusses the two ideas and tries combining the best parts of each
ignores his partner and builds his own version on the side
gives in completely and lets his partner do it all themselves
argues until the teacher makes them split into separate teams
payload.explanation: Discussing and combining ideas produces a better result and teaches collaboration.

payload.snippet: Nina is following instructions to build a shelf but finds the booklet is in another language.
options: looks up pictures in the booklet and figures out the steps from the diagrams
throws the instructions away and guesses every single step
gives up and asks her parents to pay someone else to do it
calls the customer service number on the booklet for help
payload.explanation: Using the diagrams when the written instructions are unclear is a smart problem-solving approach.

payload.snippet: Tom has cut a plank of wood two centimetres too short for his project and cannot undo the cut.
options: measures and cuts another piece to the correct length instead
glues the two cut pieces back together and hopes it holds
tries to stretch the wood to the right length by pulling hard
uses the short piece anyway and pretends the measurements were flexible
payload.explanation: Cutting a new piece to the right length is the correct response to a measurement error.

payload.snippet: Ava is building a model using air-drying clay but it has cracked in several places while still soft.
options: smooths more water and clay over the cracks gently with her fingers
leaves the model as it is hoping the cracks close up when it dries
throws the cracked clay away and starts from scratch entirely
bakes the clay in the oven to see if it helps
payload.explanation: Smoothing water and clay into soft cracks repairs them before drying is complete.

payload.snippet: Ben is helping paint a fence when the paint keeps dripping down onto the path below.
options: puts newspaper or a dust sheet down on the path below first
paints faster so less paint has time to drip onto the path
wipes each drip as it forms which takes a very long time
stops painting the bottom third of the fence where drips mostly occur
payload.explanation: Laying a dust sheet or newspaper prevents paint dripping onto surfaces below.

payload.snippet: Grace discovers her team built the wrong wall in the wrong place during a school project.
options: tells the teacher and asks whether the wall can be moved or changed
says nothing and hopes the teacher does not notice during marking
tears the wall down and rebuilds it without telling anyone what happened
convinces her team the wrong position was actually the plan all along
payload.explanation: Telling the teacher promptly allows the problem to be fixed properly.

payload.snippet: Max is mixing cement for a small garden project but it is coming out too runny and liquid.
options: adds more dry cement powder to thicken the mixture to the right consistency
keeps adding water to the mix hoping the runny cement will firm up
leaves the liquid cement to dry and uses it next time
pours the runny cement out and starts the whole mixture from scratch
payload.explanation: Adding more dry powder is the correct way to thicken an overly runny cement mix.

payload.snippet: Lily is building a den in the garden and wants to use a large sheet of glass she found in the shed.
options: leaves the glass in the shed and finds a safe alternative material
carries the glass outside carefully and leans it against the fence
drills holes in the glass herself to attach it to the structure
smashes the glass into smaller pieces since it is too big to use as is
payload.explanation: Glass is a dangerous building material for a den — finding a safe alternative is the right decision.

payload.snippet: Zoe notices a very big crack forming in the wall of the outdoor classroom at school.
options: tells a teacher about the crack immediately
puts a poster over the crack so it cannot be seen by anyone
pokes a stick into the crack to see how deep it goes
uses filler from the art room to seal the crack herself
payload.explanation: Reporting a structural crack to a teacher immediately is the safe and correct action.

payload.snippet: Sam's team is building a model tower in class and his teammate keeps adding pieces that make it less stable.
options: explains politely to his teammate why those pieces are weakening the structure
takes the pieces off silently while his teammate is not watching
lets the tower fall over so the teacher sees what his teammate did wrong
tells the teacher his teammate is ruining the project
payload.explanation: Explaining politely why certain pieces weaken the design is the collaborative and educational approach.

payload.snippet: Finn is helping his dad build a garden shed when he sees his dad start to skip an important step in the instructions.
options: mentions it to his dad calmly and asks if they should follow the step
stays silent since it is his dad's shed and his dad knows best
follows the instructions himself on the next panel without telling his dad
reads out all the skipped steps loudly until his dad agrees to do them
payload.explanation: Mentioning the skipped step calmly allows his dad to decide with full information.

payload.snippet: Ruby is painting a mural on a school wall and runs out of the specific red paint halfway through.
options: tells the art teacher and asks what to do before continuing
mixes other colours together hoping to create a matching red shade
leaves the mural unfinished since she cannot continue without that colour
uses a completely different colour for the remaining section of the mural
payload.explanation: Telling the teacher ensures the correct paint can be obtained before the mural is compromised.

payload.snippet: Owen is assembling flat-pack furniture and has several screws left over after finishing.
options: checks the instructions to see whether the extra screws are spares or were forgotten
assumes leftover screws are just extras and leaves the furniture as it is
unscrews everything and starts completely from scratch to find where they go
throws the leftover screws away since the furniture seems solid enough
payload.explanation: Checking the instructions is the only reliable way to know whether remaining screws are spares or missing.

payload.snippet: Sophie needs to cut a piece of wood for her project but the only saw available is a large sharp one.
options: asks a supervising adult to cut the wood for her using the large saw
cuts the wood herself since the project needs to be done soon
uses a blunt kitchen knife which is safer than the large sharp saw
finds a different piece of wood that does not need to be cut
payload.explanation: Asking an adult to operate a large sharp saw is the correct safety decision.

payload.snippet: Jake is working on a group construction project when one team member does no work and keeps distracting the others.
options: calmly asks the team member to take on a specific part of the task
does all the work himself while complaining to the rest of the team
tells the teacher immediately without first trying to involve the team member
stops working himself since it is unfair that only some people are contributing
payload.explanation: Assigning the team member a specific role is the constructive solution before escalating to the teacher.

payload.snippet: Chloe is building a model volcano and the baking soda and vinegar reaction is much less dramatic than expected.
options: checks the amounts in the recipe and adjusts the quantities
adds washing-up liquid and food dye hoping to make it more dramatic
declares the experiment a complete failure and refuses to present it
waits longer for the reaction to intensify but adds nothing new
payload.explanation: Checking and adjusting the quantities based on the recipe is the scientific approach.

payload.snippet: Ethan is designing a building on a computer program and accidentally deletes a large section of his work.
options: uses the undo function to recover the deleted section
closes the program without saving hoping the deleted section reappears
starts the whole design completely from scratch in a new file
shouts at the computer for making him lose his work
payload.explanation: The undo function (Ctrl+Z) is the immediate and correct response to an accidental deletion.

payload.snippet: Isla is helping repair a fence when the post she is supposed to nail her planks to is soft and rotten.
options: tells the adult in charge that the post is rotten and cannot hold nails safely
nails the planks in anyway and hopes the soft wood holds them
uses more nails than usual to compensate for the soft wood
cuts the rotten part off the post and nails higher up instead
payload.explanation: Reporting rotten wood to the adult in charge ensures the fence is repaired properly and safely.

payload.snippet: Leo takes a library book home but spills juice all over the pages.
options: tells the librarian honestly when he returns it
hides it and hopes the librarian does not notice
pretends it arrived damaged from the library
buys a replacement copy without saying anything
payload.explanation: Telling the librarian honestly is the right thing to do — libraries can assess and deal with damage properly.

payload.snippet: Mia is in the middle of reading when her little sibling tears out an important page.
options: tells an adult calmly and shows them what happened
shouts at her sibling until they cry
tears out more pages in anger
throws the whole book away
payload.explanation: Telling an adult calmly means the book can be repaired and the situation handled fairly.

payload.snippet: Kai discovers his favourite book is available to borrow from the library for free.
options: borrows it from the library
asks his parents to buy it from a shop instead
photocopies the whole book to keep
just reads it in the library without borrowing it
payload.explanation: Borrowing from the library is free and exactly what libraries are there for.

payload.snippet: Nina reads a story about a character who looks and lives just like her.
options: feels happy to be represented in a story
says books about her own life are boring
tells everyone the book is unrealistic
skips those pages since she already knows what life is like
payload.explanation: Seeing yourself in stories is valuable and important — it is worth celebrating.

payload.snippet: Tom is reading at night and his torch suddenly runs out of battery.
options: saves his page and goes to sleep
reads in complete darkness squinting hard
wakes his parents up for batteries immediately
reads sections aloud from memory for the rest of the night
payload.explanation: Saving your page and sleeping is the sensible and healthy response to a flat torch.

payload.snippet: Ava writes a book review for school but is not sure what she wants to say.
options: writes what she honestly thought about the book
copies sentences from someone else's review
says it was wonderful even though she did not enjoy it
refuses to write any review at all and says she forgot
payload.explanation: Honest personal responses to books are what makes book reviews meaningful.

payload.snippet: Ben picks up a book that is written entirely in a language he does not know.
options: looks at the pictures to guess what the story might be about
makes up completely different words for every page
throws it down immediately and walks away
reads nonsense words aloud while turning pages
payload.explanation: Using pictures to guess a story's meaning is a creative and valid reading strategy.

payload.snippet: Grace's class has to read silently but she finds it very hard to concentrate today.
options: takes a slow breath and refocuses on her page
starts talking out loud in the middle of class
gets up and walks around the classroom
taps on her desk to make a rhythm to help her
payload.explanation: Taking a slow breath to refocus is a self-regulation technique that helps with concentration.

payload.snippet: Max has to read a book for a project but finds the topic very boring from the first page.
options: reads a few more pages to give it a fair chance
stops reading after the first page and makes up a review
tells the teacher the book is terrible and he wants a different one
reads only the last page and guesses the rest for his project
payload.explanation: Giving a book a fair chance by reading further before judging it is the mature approach.

payload.snippet: Lily reads the final chapter of her book before reading the middle by accident.
options: reads the middle chapters anyway since they still add to the story
refuses to continue reading since the ending is already known
immediately tells all her friends the ending before they finish it
reads the book backwards from the end chapter to the beginning
payload.explanation: Knowing the ending does not remove the value of the journey — reading the middle still matters.

payload.snippet: Zoe brings her own book to story time but the teacher reads a different one.
options: listens to the teacher's chosen story attentively
reads her own book secretly under the desk
asks loudly why her book was not chosen
puts her book on the teacher's desk hoping the teacher will read it next
payload.explanation: Listening to the teacher's story is respectful and may introduce you to a book you would enjoy.

payload.snippet: Sam is at story time when one child keeps talking loudly over the story being read.
options: listens carefully without joining the disruption
shouts at the child to be quiet immediately
starts talking too so everyone is equally noisy
loudly points at the child and tells the teacher to stop the story
payload.explanation: Staying focused on the story without reacting to disruption is the mature response.

payload.snippet: Finn writes a story for class and his best friend tells him it is the best in the whole class.
options: thanks his friend and feels genuinely proud of his work
insists his story is not actually that good to seem modest
demands the teacher confirm in front of everyone that it is the best
lets his friend copy the same idea for their own story assignment
payload.explanation: Accepting a genuine compliment with gratitude and pride is healthy and appropriate.

payload.snippet: Ruby reads a story where the main character makes a really bad decision.
options: thinks about what she would have done differently
throws the book because she is upset with the character
says the whole story is bad because the character was wrong
tells the teacher the book should be banned from the class
payload.explanation: Thinking critically about characters' decisions develops empathy and judgment.

payload.snippet: Owen is halfway through a great book when he loses it completely.
options: searches his home carefully before doing anything else
gives up and decides he will never know the ending
pretends to his class he already read the whole ending
borrows the same book from the library to skip to where he was
payload.explanation: Searching carefully is the first and most logical response to a missing book.

payload.snippet: Sophie reads a story so funny it makes her laugh out loud in the library.
options: laughs quietly with her hand over her mouth
reads the funny part again at full volume for everyone
keeps laughing loudly ignoring the people around her
tells the librarian the book is inappropriate because it made her laugh
payload.explanation: Laughing quietly and covering your mouth respects the quiet environment of a library.

payload.snippet: Jake is asked to read aloud in class but feels very nervous about it.
options: takes a breath and reads at his own steady pace
refuses completely to read aloud in front of everyone
reads so quietly that no one can hear what he is saying
asks his friend to stand up and read it for him instead
payload.explanation: Taking a breath and reading steadily is a brave and effective way to manage reading nerves.

payload.snippet: Chloe starts a book and realises within a few pages it is too hard for her level right now.
options: finds a slightly easier book to build her skills first
says she hates all books and reading is pointless
pretends she read it and makes up a summary
gives up reading completely for a whole month
payload.explanation: Finding a book at the right level allows you to build confidence before trying harder books.

payload.snippet: Ethan wants to read a very long book but can only manage a few pages each evening.
options: reads a bit each day until he finishes the whole book
stays up all night to finish it as fast as possible
skips several chapters to reach the ending sooner
gives up since it will take too long to ever finish it
payload.explanation: Reading a little each day is a sustainable habit that gets even the longest book finished.

payload.snippet: Isla finds a library book on the shelf with a very torn and damaged cover.
options: tells the librarian about the damage before borrowing the book
hides it back on the shelf so it is not her problem
borrows it and tears it a little more by accident at home
takes it home to try to fix it herself without telling anyone
payload.explanation: Telling the librarian about existing damage before borrowing protects you from being blamed for it.

payload.snippet: Leo is swimming in the sea when he realises he has drifted quite far from the shore.
options: swims calmly parallel to the shore and then back in
swims directly toward the shore using all his energy
calls for help while treading water in place
dives under the waves and swims as fast as he can straight back
payload.explanation: Swimming parallel to shore first is correct for escaping a current — swimming directly back exhausts you against the pull.

payload.snippet: Mia falls into the deep end of the pool even though she cannot swim confidently.
options: floats on her back and calls for help calmly
panics and thrashes around in the water wildly
tries to swim to the edge using all her strength
holds her breath and sinks to the bottom to push off
payload.explanation: Floating on your back and calling for help conserves energy and keeps you safe.

payload.snippet: Kai is playing with a hosepipe in the garden when it accidentally sprays into his baby sibling's face.
options: turns off the water immediately and checks his sibling is okay
laughs and sprays them again to see the reaction
drops the hosepipe and runs inside to hide
blames the hosepipe for pointing the wrong way
payload.explanation: Turning off the water and checking on his sibling shows responsibility and care.

payload.snippet: Nina is at a water park when she gets too cold in the water and starts shivering.
options: gets out, wraps in a towel, and warms up before going back in
stays in the water since swimming will warm her up eventually
goes into the wave pool since the waves will warm her up
jumps into an outdoor jacuzzi without checking the temperature first
payload.explanation: Getting out and warming up properly is the safest response to feeling too cold in water.

payload.snippet: Tom wants to jump off a high diving board at the pool but has never done it before.
options: tries the smallest board first to build confidence gradually
runs at the highest board and jumps before he can change his mind
watches others jump and decides it is not for him today
tells others watching that he will definitely do it but then does not
payload.explanation: Starting on a smaller board builds confidence safely — both trying the small one or deciding not to jump are valid choices.

payload.snippet: Ava is helping at a water safety lesson when she sees a younger child run toward the pool.
options: steps in front of the child and reminds them calmly to walk
shouts at the child to stop immediately
chases after the child at a run herself
lets the instructor deal with it since it is their class
payload.explanation: Stepping in front calmly and reminding the child protects them and models correct poolside behaviour.

payload.snippet: Ben is playing in the river with friends when he notices his friend has got stuck in some reeds near the bank.
options: reaches his friend something to hold onto and calls for help
jumps into the river to swim to his friend
shouts instructions to his friend about how to free themselves
calls for help and then tries to reach with a stick or clothing
payload.explanation: Reaching something for them to hold and calling for help is the correct water rescue response — jumping in often results in two people in difficulty.

payload.snippet: Grace finds a very young child playing alone near a deep pond in the park.
options: stays near the child and looks for a parent or adult immediately
takes the child's hand and leads them away from the pond herself
calls the child's name loudly to try to find the parent
sits far away and watches to make sure the child does not fall in
payload.explanation: Staying near the child to ensure safety while finding an adult is the most protective action.

payload.snippet: Max is in a kayak on a calm lake when his kayak tips over and he goes into the water.
options: stays calm, holds onto the kayak, and waits for the instructor's help
swims away from the kayak toward the nearest shore as fast as possible
tries to flip the kayak back upright while treading water
shouts for help while swimming away from the kayak
payload.explanation: Staying with the kayak and waiting for the instructor is the correct capsize response — the kayak provides flotation.

payload.snippet: Lily is at a water park when she realises her phone is in her pocket just before going down a waterslide.
options: steps out of the queue to leave her phone somewhere safe first
keeps the phone in her pocket and hopes it survives the water
throws the phone onto the grass and hopes someone does not take it
goes down the slide as planned and buys a new phone if needed
payload.explanation: Stepping out to secure the phone before the slide is the only sensible option.

payload.snippet: Zoe is learning to swim but keeps swallowing water each time she tries to breathe.
options: asks the instructor to show her the correct head position for breathing
gives up swimming since swallowing water means she is not ready
swims with her mouth closed and just holds her breath the whole time
swims faster so she has less time to swallow water
payload.explanation: Asking the instructor for help with breathing technique is the correct learning approach.

payload.snippet: Sam is snorkelling when he sees what looks like a rare fish and wants to touch it.
options: watches it from a safe distance without touching anything
reaches out to touch it gently since touching one fish seems harmless
chases it to get a closer look for a longer time
catches it in his hands to show other snorkellers
payload.explanation: Never touching marine creatures while snorkelling protects both the creature and the snorkeller.

payload.snippet: Finn is at the beach when a warning flag goes up indicating strong currents and no swimming.
options: gets out of the water and stays on the beach
ignores the flag and swims faster to stay in one place against the current
waits to see if other swimmers get out before deciding what to do
moves to a different part of the beach and swims there instead
payload.explanation: Getting out immediately when a warning flag is raised is the correct response to beach safety signals.

payload.snippet: Ruby's little sibling has taken off their armbands at the pool without any adult knowing.
options: puts the armbands back on and tells a pool supervisor immediately
lets the sibling swim without armbands since the pool has lifeguards watching
holds the sibling's hand in the water to keep them safe herself
shouts at her sibling for taking the armbands off in front of everyone
payload.explanation: Replacing the armbands and alerting a supervisor is the correct protective action for a non-swimmer in deep water.

payload.snippet: Owen is at a pool party and a friend challenges him to hold his breath underwater for as long as possible.
options: declines the challenge and explains that breath-holding games in water are dangerous
takes the challenge since the pool is safe and lifeguards are watching
holds his breath only for a short count before coming up for air
agrees but asks the lifeguard to watch and intervene if needed
payload.explanation: Breath-holding challenges in water are genuinely dangerous — declining is the correct response regardless of supervision.

payload.snippet: Sophie is learning front crawl but finds she keeps sinking at the legs.
options: asks the instructor for help with her leg kick technique
switches to breaststroke which is much easier for keeping legs up
adds floats between her legs to stop them sinking and uses them permanently
swims with her head up higher hoping her legs naturally rise
payload.explanation: Asking the instructor to diagnose and correct the leg position is the most effective learning approach.

payload.snippet: Jake is at the beach when he wants to swim but the lifeguard tells him the sea is too rough today.
options: stays out of the water and finds another activity
swims anyway since he is a strong swimmer and the waves look manageable
walks along the shore to a different part of the beach to try there
asks his parents if they think the lifeguard is right
payload.explanation: Following lifeguard advice is mandatory — they have authority over sea safety and their judgment must be respected.

payload.snippet: Chloe is in a rowing boat on a lake when her oar slips and falls into the water.
options: uses the remaining oar to paddle back to shore using a paddling motion
jumps into the lake to retrieve the dropped oar quickly
stands up in the boat and leans over to reach the oar from above
sits still and waits for someone passing to help her
payload.explanation: Using the remaining oar to paddle back is the safest response — standing in a rowing boat causes it to rock dangerously.

payload.snippet: Ethan is in a paddling pool when he starts to feel dizzy from the heat outside.
options: gets out of the pool and moves to a shaded area to cool down
stays in the pool since the water is cool and will help his dizziness
drinks some pool water since he is feeling dehydrated
closes his eyes and floats on his back until the dizziness passes
payload.explanation: Getting out and moving to shade is the correct response to heat dizziness — dehydration needs water to drink, not pool water.

payload.snippet: Isla is at a swimming lesson and the teacher asks the class to jump from the pool edge but she is frightened.
options: tells the teacher she is not ready and asks to watch first
jumps in because everyone else is doing it even though she is scared
refuses without explanation and walks to the changing rooms
tells her friends she does not want to jump but pretends to the teacher she does
payload.explanation: Telling the teacher she is not ready is honest and allows the teacher to support her gradually.

payload.snippet: Tom steps outside and feels the icy air hit his face right away.
options: He goes back for his hat and scarf.
He stays out and plays for hours.
He takes off his coat quickly.
He runs to the park barefoot.
payload.explanation: Icy air is a sign he needs more warm clothing.

payload.snippet: Lily's fingers turn red and stiff while building a snowman.
options: She goes inside to warm them up.
She keeps building until it is done.
She packs snow harder with her palms.
She dips her hands in cold water.
payload.explanation: Red stiff fingers are a sign of cold injury risk — she must warm up.

payload.snippet: A heavy overnight snowfall blocks the family's front path completely.
options: Dad clears it with a shovel before work.
Mum drives across the lawn instead.
They all climb out the back window.
Dad waits for it to melt on its own.
payload.explanation: Shovelling is the standard way to clear a blocked path safely.

payload.snippet: Sam tries to walk to school but the pavements are sheets of ice.
options: He takes very small careful steps.
He runs full speed so he gets there faster.
He skates on his shoes like a fun game.
He closes his eyes and walks straight ahead.
payload.explanation: Small careful steps reduce the chance of slipping on ice.

payload.snippet: The bird feeder in the garden is buried under a thick layer of snow.
options: She clears it so the birds can eat.
She leaves it and the birds will find it.
She fills it with snowballs instead.
She moves the feeder under her bed.
payload.explanation: Clearing snow from feeders keeps birds fed in winter.

payload.snippet: Jack builds a snowman but the snow keeps crumbling and falling apart.
options: He packs the snow tighter between his hands.
He adds water from the hose to the snow.
He gives up and makes a sandcastle instead.
He uses mud to glue the snowballs together.
payload.explanation: Packing snow firmly makes it stick together for a better snowman.

payload.snippet: The sledge goes very fast down the hill and heads toward a fence.
options: He steers it sideways to slow down and stop.
He jumps off at full speed to stop faster.
He screams and closes his eyes tight.
He waits for the fence to stop the sledge.
payload.explanation: Steering sideways is the safe way to slow a sledge on a slope.

payload.snippet: Anna's boots are soaked through after playing in slush for an hour.
options: She changes into dry socks and boots.
She keeps wearing them and hopes they dry.
She stuffs newspaper in and goes back out.
She puts them in the fridge to keep them cold.
payload.explanation: Wet feet get cold fast — dry socks and boots are needed.

payload.snippet: The school heating breaks and the classroom becomes very cold.
options: The teacher asks children to keep their coats on.
The teacher opens all the windows to help.
The teacher sends everyone outside to warm up.
The teacher turns the air conditioning on high.
payload.explanation: Keeping coats on indoors traps body heat when heating fails.

payload.snippet: Ben and his dad want to drive to grandma's but the road is icy.
options: Dad waits for the gritters to treat the road first.
Dad drives very fast to get over the ice quick.
Dad turns the wipers on and sets off straight away.
Dad sends Ben on foot while he waits at home.
payload.explanation: Gritted roads are much safer to drive on in icy conditions.

payload.snippet: The snowball she throws hits a passing stranger on the back of the head.
options: She says sorry and checks they are okay.
She pretends it was someone else and walks off.
She runs home as fast as she can.
She throws another one and shouts it was an accident.
payload.explanation: Apologising and checking for injury is the right response.

payload.snippet: Ice on the school steps has made two children fall already this morning.
options: The caretaker spreads salt on the steps.
The caretaker paints the steps bright yellow.
The caretaker puts a carpet over the steps.
The caretaker closes the school for the day.
payload.explanation: Salt lowers the freezing point of water and melts ice on steps.

payload.snippet: Maya skates near the edge of the frozen pond where the ice is thin.
options: An adult calls her back to the middle.
She moves faster to test the ice at the edge.
She stamps hard to see if it cracks.
She walks off the pond to explore the bank.
payload.explanation: Ice is thinner and less safe near the edges of a pond.

payload.snippet: Oliver leaves his gloves at school and walks home in freezing weather.
options: He tucks his hands into his sleeves to stay warm.
He waves his arms to warm them up as he runs.
He holds his ears instead of his hands.
He texts a friend to bring spare gloves quickly.
payload.explanation: Tucking hands into sleeves traps body heat when gloves are missing.

payload.snippet: A thick layer of snow weighs down a branch above the garden path.
options: Dad knocks the snow off the branch with a broom.
Dad ties the branch up with string so it holds.
Dad walks under the branch very quickly.
Dad saws the whole tree down to be safe.
payload.explanation: Removing heavy snow prevents branches breaking under the weight.

payload.snippet: She decorates the snowman with a carrot nose but the dog takes it.
options: She finds another carrot inside and replaces it.
She puts the snowman in the garage for safety.
She shouts at the dog until it brings it back.
She uses a stick and pretends it is a nose.
payload.explanation: Replacing the carrot is the simple fix to the dog's mischief.

payload.snippet: Heavy snow is forecast and the family has no food in the house.
options: They shop for bread and groceries before it arrives.
They order food online and hope the driver gets through.
They wait until the snow comes and then decide.
They ask a neighbour to share their food with them.
payload.explanation: Stocking up before a storm prevents being stranded without food.

payload.snippet: Jake's hat blows off into a frozen puddle on the way to school.
options: He fishes it out and wrings it as dry as he can.
He leaves it there and carries on bareheaded.
He stamps on the puddle to crack the ice for the hat.
He takes off his coat to use as a hat instead.
payload.explanation: Retrieving and wringing the hat keeps him warmer than going without.

payload.snippet: The heating oil runs out on the coldest night of winter.
options: Mum calls the supplier for an emergency delivery.
Mum burns old newspapers in the living room fireplace.
Mum turns the gas cooker on to heat the kitchen.
Mum waits until morning and calls a regular order in.
payload.explanation: Emergency fuel deliveries are the safe solution for urgent heating failures.

payload.snippet: Clara's snowman is almost finished but she has no buttons for the eyes.
options: She uses two small stones from the garden path.
She draws eyes on with a permanent marker.
She leaves the snowman without eyes at all.
She goes to the shop and buys buttons right away.
payload.explanation: Using stones from the garden is a simple creative fix.

payload.snippet: Lily forgot to put sunscreen on and has been in the sun for two hours at the beach.
options: She goes to a shaded area and applies sunscreen before going back out.
She stays in the sun and promises to apply cream at lunchtime.
She covers herself in wet sand to block the UV rays.
She keeps her eyes shut so the sun cannot reach her face.
payload.explanation: Immediate shade and sunscreen prevents further UV damage to unprotected skin.

payload.snippet: Sam notices the dog is lying on its side in the sun and breathing very fast despite a bowl of water nearby.
options: He moves the dog to shade, wets its paws and belly, and tells an adult immediately.
He fills the water bowl again and leaves the dog to rest in the sun.
He puts a blanket over the dog to stop the heat getting to it.
He gives the dog an ice cube to lick and fans it with a magazine.
payload.explanation: Fast breathing in the sun signals heat stroke — shade, cooling, and adult help are urgent.

payload.snippet: Tom is riding his bike in summer heat and starts feeling dizzy and has a headache halfway through his ride.
options: He stops in the shade, drinks water slowly, and rests until he feels better.
He speeds up to finish the ride before he feels any worse.
He calls his friend to race him to the finish to take his mind off it.
He eats a big snack from his bag and carries on cycling normally.
payload.explanation: Dizziness and headache during heat are signs of heat exhaustion — stop, cool, hydrate.

payload.snippet: Anna is at a summer fair when she notices a toddler sitting alone in a pushchair in full sun near a closed stall with no adult visible.
options: She stays near the child, shades it with her hat, and tells a fair organiser immediately.
She pushes the pushchair herself to a shaded spot to be helpful.
She gives the toddler her water bottle and waits for the parent to return.
She takes a photo and posts it online asking if anyone recognises the child.
payload.explanation: Shading the child without moving the pushchair and alerting fair staff is the correct safeguarding response.

payload.snippet: The family is hiking in the hills on the hottest day of the year and they have drunk all their water with two kilometres still to go.
options: They find shade to rest, ration any remaining damp snacks, and use the hiking app to find the shortest route to a water source.
They run the final stretch to get it over with before they get more dehydrated.
They drink from a clear-looking stream they spot by the path.
They split up so the fastest hiker can run ahead and bring water back.
payload.explanation: Rest in shade and find a reliable water source — do not run, do not drink from streams.

payload.snippet: Jake's phone overheats and shuts down at the beach just after he has been given a meeting point to find his family.
options: He remembers the landmark his parents mentioned and walks there calmly.
He asks a stranger to use their phone and walks off with it to find signal.
He runs along the beach in the sun calling his family's names.
He sits and waits next to a lifeguard station for his family to find him.
payload.explanation: Remembering the agreed landmark and walking there calmly is the correct separated-at-beach response.

payload.snippet: Clara's pet rabbit is in an outdoor hutch and the temperature is forecast to reach thirty-eight degrees today.
options: She moves the hutch to a shaded corner, puts a frozen water bottle inside for the rabbit to lean against, and checks it every hour.
She leaves the hutch in the sun so the rabbit gets natural light during the day.
She puts ice directly in the rabbit's water bowl and leaves it for the afternoon.
She brings the rabbit inside but leaves it in a room with no windows to keep it calm.
payload.explanation: Shade, a gradual cooling aid, and frequent checks protect a rabbit in extreme summer heat.

payload.snippet: Ben is playing football in the midday heat and a teammate collapses on the ground and is unresponsive.
options: He calls for the coach immediately, gets the first-aid kit, and checks for breathing while someone calls 999.
He pours cold water over the teammate and asks him to sit up slowly.
He drags the teammate to the shade at the touchline and loosens his shirt.
He waves to get the referee's attention and points at the teammate on the ground.
payload.explanation: An unresponsive person is a 999 emergency — check breathing and get adult/coach immediately.

payload.snippet: Maya is playing outside and a bee flies into her open fizzy drink can without her noticing.
options: She checks her drink by looking inside before each sip going forward.
She tips the can upside down to empty it and then refills it from the bottle.
She puts her thumb over the can hole so nothing can get in while she plays.
She gives the drink to her friend and gets a fresh one from the cool box.
payload.explanation: Checking inside cans before each sip prevents accidentally swallowing a stinging insect.

payload.snippet: Oliver is at a summer barbecue when he sees a young child reaching toward the hot grill while adults are busy chatting.
options: He steps between the child and the grill and calls out to the nearest adult.
He shouts at the child loudly to make them freeze where they are.
He grabs the grill lid and slams it shut so the child cannot reach the food.
He takes a photo and waits to see if the adults notice on their own.
payload.explanation: Physically blocking access and alerting an adult is the fastest safe response to a child near a hot grill.

payload.snippet: The tent zip breaks on the first night of a camping trip, leaving the door open to mosquitoes all night.
options: She tucks her sheet tightly around herself and applies insect repellent before sleeping.
She sleeps outside the tent as the mosquitoes are already inside anyway.
She burns a candle inside the tent to keep the mosquitoes away.
She fills the tent opening with her backpack and hopes the mosquitoes leave.
payload.explanation: Insect repellent and covering exposed skin reduces bites when a tent zip fails.

payload.snippet: Tom's ice lolly wrapper blows off on a beach walk and lands in the shallow sea before he can grab it.
options: He wades in, retrieves it, and puts it in his pocket to find a bin.
He watches it float away and decides it is too late to do anything.
He asks the lifeguard to fish it out on his next patrol.
He covers it with sand so it does not blow away to a worse place.
payload.explanation: Retrieving litter from the sea protects marine wildlife — it is his responsibility.

payload.snippet: Anna applies factor fifty sunscreen but still gets a red burn on her shoulders after six hours at the outdoor festival.
options: She covers her shoulders with a light shirt and reapplies cream every two hours.
She wipes off the old cream and applies a fresh, thick layer all at once.
She decides factor fifty is not working and switches to factor fifteen instead.
She sits in the shade for the rest of the festival and skips the music stages.
payload.explanation: Reapplication every two hours and covering shoulders prevents further burning even with high-factor cream.

payload.snippet: Jake's sister has a wasp sting on her hand that is already swelling, and she begins to say her throat feels tight.
options: He calls 999 immediately and tells them his sister has been stung and has throat tightening.
He puts ice on the sting and asks her to drink water to calm the reaction.
He removes the sting with tweezers and applies antihistamine cream from the first-aid kit.
He calls their mum and puts the phone on speaker while he waits for her instructions.
payload.explanation: Throat tightening after a sting signals anaphylaxis — 999 is the only correct immediate response.

payload.snippet: Clara is picking strawberries in the garden when she accidentally kneels on a wasp nest hidden in the grass. Wasps begin swarming around her legs.
options: She moves calmly away from the nest without swatting and goes inside immediately.
She swats the wasps away firmly and runs straight to the garden hose.
She freezes completely still and waits for the wasps to lose interest.
She pulls up the nest with gardening gloves to move it away from the path.
payload.explanation: Moving calmly without swatting is the correct response to accidental wasp nest disturbance.

payload.snippet: The outdoor swimming pool closes early due to thunder being heard in the distance on an otherwise sunny afternoon.
options: Ben thanks the lifeguards and waits in the changing rooms until the storm passes.
Ben stays in the pool for a few more minutes as the thunder is very distant.
Ben says the thunder is too far away to matter and keeps swimming.
Ben moves to the outdoor sun loungers so the pool staff can clear it.
payload.explanation: Lightning is a life-safety risk near water — exiting immediately and waiting inside is correct.

payload.snippet: Maya's sunglasses break at the seaside and she has no spare pair for the walk back along the bright reflective beach.
options: She pulls her hat brim low and looks down at the sand as she walks.
She holds her hands over her eyes like binoculars for the whole walk.
She takes the long route through the town to avoid the bright beach stretch.
She stares straight ahead and squints tightly to protect her eyes naturally.
payload.explanation: A low hat brim reduces glare on the eyes without needing sunglasses.

payload.snippet: Oliver and his friends find a shallow tidal rock pool and want to take a crab home in a bucket.
options: He suggests they observe the crab and then put it back exactly where they found it.
He carefully places the crab in the bucket with sea water and takes it home.
He puts the crab in the bucket to show his parents and returns it tomorrow.
He moves the crab to a bigger rock pool so it has more space to explore.
payload.explanation: Rock-pool creatures should be observed and returned to their original habitat.

payload.snippet: The outdoor school sports day is moved up a week and the forecast shows thirty-five degrees on race day.
options: The teacher has children run in short heats with long water breaks and shade between each race.
The teacher keeps the full programme but extends the lunch break by fifteen minutes.
The teacher moves all running events to the afternoon when children have had time to eat.
The teacher cancels the parent seating area so children can use the grandstand shade instead.
payload.explanation: Short heats with water and shade breaks reduces heat illness risk on a very hot sports day.

payload.snippet: A sudden thunderstorm arrives while the family is swimming in the sea and the beach lifeguard starts blowing a whistle.
options: They come out of the sea immediately and move well away from the shoreline.
They swim faster toward the shallows and wait for the storm to pass.
They go to the water's edge and watch the storm from there.
They stay in the sea because the water is warm and it is only light rain.
payload.explanation: Exiting the sea immediately when a lifeguard signals is mandatory — lightning and water are deadly.

payload.snippet: Tom forgot to bring his umbrella and a heavy shower starts on his walk home from school.
options: He takes shelter under a shop awning until the shower passes.
He runs home as fast as he can through the pouring rain.
He asks a stranger for their umbrella and walks home.
He finds a plastic bag and holds it over his head the whole way.
payload.explanation: Taking shelter under an awning keeps him dry without running in the rain.

payload.snippet: Lily has left her library book outside on the garden table and notices it is starting to rain.
options: She rushes outside and brings the book indoors immediately.
She calls out to her brother to cover the book with a leaf.
She leaves the book outside and hopes the rain stops quickly.
She puts a flowerpot on top so the book does not blow away.
payload.explanation: Bringing the book inside prevents water damage to the library's property.

payload.snippet: Sam is cycling home when rain begins and the road becomes slick. He notices his brakes feel spongy and slow.
options: He slows right down, brakes gently and early, and takes extra care at every junction.
He leans into bends faster to get home before his tyres get worse.
He pedals harder to stay ahead of the wet patches on the road.
He rides on the pavement where the surface is less wet and safer.
payload.explanation: Wet roads reduce braking grip — slowing down and braking gently prevents skidding.

payload.snippet: Anna is playing outside when lightning flashes. She counts to three and then hears the thunder — the storm is close.
options: She goes inside immediately and stays away from windows.
She stays under the tall oak tree because its leaves keep her dry.
She continues playing as the thunder sounds far away still.
She runs to the metal climbing frame to get a better look at the sky.
payload.explanation: Lightning under three seconds away is extremely close — go indoors immediately.

payload.snippet: Jack left his shoes by the back door and rain has blown in and soaked them through overnight.
options: He stuffs them loosely with newspaper and lets them dry at room temperature.
He puts them directly on top of the radiator to dry them as fast as possible.
He pours hot water inside each shoe to wash out the mud and then dries them.
He puts them in the tumble dryer on high heat to get them dry quickly.
payload.explanation: Newspaper absorbs moisture and room-temperature drying preserves the shoe's shape.

payload.snippet: Maya's mum has washed all the laundry and hung it outside to dry. Dark clouds roll in mid-afternoon.
options: Maya brings all the laundry in before the rain arrives.
Maya leaves it outside hoping the wind will dry it fast enough.
Maya texts her mum and waits for instructions before touching the laundry.
Maya covers it with a plastic sheet and hopes the rain does not soak through.
payload.explanation: Bringing laundry in before rain avoids the work of washing it all over again.

payload.snippet: Oliver is hiking in the hills when persistent drizzle turns into a heavy downpour. His map is already wet and starting to tear at the fold lines.
options: He slips the map into a plastic bag from his pack to protect it from further damage.
He folds the map tightly and tucks it into his waistband to keep it drier.
He takes a photo of the map on his phone and throws the wet original away.
He asks a passing walker if he can share their map for the rest of the walk.
payload.explanation: A plastic bag protects a wet map from tearing and keeps remaining sections readable.

payload.snippet: Clara is walking to a birthday party in new white trainers when it begins to rain heavily. Muddy water splashes from passing cars onto her feet.
options: She keeps to the pavement well away from the kerb and walks steadily to the party.
She walks in the road where there is no kerb to keep her shoes clean.
She removes her trainers and carries them to keep them clean and dry.
She turns back and goes home to change before the party starts.
payload.explanation: Keeping away from the kerb reduces splash from passing vehicles in the rain.

payload.snippet: Ben's football match continues despite heavy rain. The pitch becomes very wet and the ball starts bouncing unpredictably in standing water.
options: He adjusts his footing, slows his running speed, and shortens his passes to keep control.
He kicks the ball harder to get it through the puddles more effectively.
He asks the referee to stop the game so the water can drain naturally.
He runs at the same pace as normal and focuses on staying ahead of the ball.
payload.explanation: Adapting footwork and shortening passes is the correct technique for wet-pitch football.

payload.snippet: Tom's younger sibling is scared of the thunder and hides crying under the duvet during a storm at night.
options: Tom sits with his sibling, explains that thunder cannot hurt them, and reads a story until the storm passes.
Tom tells his sibling the storm is miles away and they should go back to sleep.
Tom turns all the lights off so his sibling cannot see the lightning through the curtains.
Tom opens the curtains so his sibling can watch the lightning safely from inside.
payload.explanation: Calm reassurance, factual explanation, and distraction are the kindest responses to thunder fear.

payload.snippet: Anna is in the garden when it starts raining and the garden gate blows open. The family dog immediately runs through it toward the road.
options: She calls the dog in a calm happy voice and moves toward the gate to close it gently.
She runs after the dog shouting its name as loudly as she can.
She slams the gate shut to block the road even though the dog is already through it.
She runs indoors and gets a treat to lure the dog back through the open gate.
payload.explanation: A calm happy call encourages the dog to return without making it run further away.

payload.snippet: Jake is on a nature walk when steady rain makes the path muddy. He sees a steep short-cut down a muddy bank that would save ten minutes.
options: He takes the longer safe path instead and arrives wet but uninjured.
He slides down the muddy bank on his boots as it looks fun and quick.
He asks the group to link hands and cross the muddy bank together for safety.
He sits at the top and waits for the rain to stop before descending.
payload.explanation: Avoiding a slippery muddy bank prevents a dangerous fall even if it takes longer.

payload.snippet: Clara is helping decorate for a garden party when the forecast changes to heavy rain all day.
options: She and the family move all the decorations inside and set up in the living room instead.
She puts waterproof bags over the decorations and leaves them in the garden.
She tells all the guests the party is cancelled and reschedules for next week.
She leaves the outdoor decorations up and lends guests umbrellas as they arrive.
payload.explanation: Moving a party indoors before heavy rain saves the decorations and keeps guests comfortable.

payload.snippet: Oliver notices a large puddle at the school gate entrance has blocked the only path to the main door, forcing children to step into the puddle.
options: He tells a teacher so the caretaker can lay a board over the puddle as a safe crossing.
He carries the smallest children across the puddle one by one before class.
He steps through the puddle himself and holds his hand out for others to balance.
He posts about the puddle in the school's parent chat so parents know to warn their children.
payload.explanation: Reporting a blocked path to staff ensures the correct fix — a board or alternative route — is implemented safely.

payload.snippet: Maya is making paper boats for her younger cousins to sail in puddles outside. The paper gets soggy and sinks within seconds each time.
options: She asks her mum for wax paper from the kitchen to make sturdier boats.
She makes the boats smaller so they weigh less and last longer in the water.
She dips each boat in cooking oil to make the paper water-resistant.
She wraps normal paper around a plastic bag to make a waterproof hull.
payload.explanation: Wax paper repels water and holds its shape much longer than regular paper in puddles.

payload.snippet: Ben is walking home from a friend's house in the rain when he slips on a wet metal drain cover and twists his ankle. He can still walk but it hurts.
options: He limps the last block home carefully, sitting down when he arrives, and tells a parent.
He runs the rest of the way home to get indoors faster and off the wet path.
He sits on the pavement and calls his friend to come back and help him.
He stamps his foot a few times to check if it is broken before walking on.
payload.explanation: Careful limping home and telling an adult is the correct response to a minor twisted ankle.

payload.snippet: It has been raining for three days and the small stream at the bottom of the park has flooded over the path.
options: Anna warns others not to cross and takes the long route around the park instead.
Anna wades through the flooded section as it only looks ankle deep.
Anna places stepping stones in the flood to create a path for other walkers.
Anna calls the park authorities and waits by the flooded area for them to arrive.
payload.explanation: Flooded paths can hide deep water or strong currents — go around and warn others.

payload.snippet: Oliver's cat has been outside for two hours in the rain and comes in shivering and very wet.
options: He dries the cat gently with a towel and puts it near a warm radiator.
He puts the cat in the bath and runs warm water to warm it up quickly.
He puts the cat outside again so it can dry naturally in the fresh air.
He uses a hairdryer on full heat to get the cat dry in under a minute.
payload.explanation: Towel drying and warmth near a radiator is the correct way to warm a wet shivering cat.

payload.snippet: Jake's new umbrella has a metal handle and he is walking near a road as a thunderstorm begins.
options: He puts the umbrella down and takes shelter in the nearest shop doorway.
He holds the umbrella higher to keep more rain off during the lightning.
He keeps the umbrella up but holds it by the fabric dome instead of the metal handle.
He hands the umbrella to a passing adult and runs under a tree for cover.
payload.explanation: Metal umbrella handles conduct electricity in a thunderstorm — sheltering indoors is the only safe option.

payload.snippet: A drain at the end of the street is blocked with autumn leaves and rainwater is rising fast across the road surface.
options: Clara calls the council's highways emergency line to report the blocked drain.
Clara clears the drain herself by pulling the leaves away with her hands.
Clara builds a barrier from her bag and coat to redirect the water away.
Clara waits to see if the water will drain on its own before taking any action.
payload.explanation: Blocked road drains are a council responsibility — report it; do not clear deep drains yourself.

payload.snippet: Tom is at the top of the climbing frame when he realises he is too scared to climb back down.
options: He calls for an adult to help him down safely.
He jumps straight down from where he is to the ground.
He lets go and slides down the pole to get down faster.
He closes his eyes and climbs down facing the wrong way.
payload.explanation: Calling an adult is the safest way to get down from a height when scared.

payload.snippet: Lily sees a younger child crying alone on a bench at the edge of the playground with no adult nearby.
options: She goes to the child and asks if she is okay and if she needs help finding her grown-up.
She leaves her alone because the grown-up is probably just nearby.
She tells the child to go and look for her mum by herself.
She waves to the child from a distance and carries on playing.
payload.explanation: Checking on an alone crying child and helping them find their carer is kind and correct.

payload.snippet: Sam is on the swing when the chain feels loose on one side and wobbles each time he swings higher.
options: He stops pumping, lets the swing slow down, and gets off to tell an adult.
He holds the loose chain tighter and swings even higher to test it.
He asks his friend to push him from the front while he holds the chain.
He moves to the other swing and leaves the broken one for someone else.
payload.explanation: A loose chain is a safety hazard — stop swinging and report it to an adult.

payload.snippet: Anna trips over a raised tree root on the path between the climbing frame and the slide and grazes her knee.
options: She finds the playground supervisor and shows them the graze and the root.
She puts dirt on the graze to stop it bleeding and carries on playing.
She covers the root with a pile of leaves so no one else trips on it.
She hops the rest of the way to the slide and checks her knee at home.
payload.explanation: Reporting both the injury and the hazard ensures she gets first aid and the root gets marked.

payload.snippet: Jack notices that someone has left a broken bottle near the edge of the sandbox and younger children are about to go and play there.
options: He stands near the glass to stop children approaching while he calls an adult to remove it.
