He puts the fire out since it is causing problems.
payload.explanation: Identifying the cause and asking for an appropriate fix is the correct practical response.

payload.snippet: Clara is packing away the campsite when she finds a used battery on the ground near the fire pit.
options: She picks it up carefully and places it in a separate waste bag to be recycled at an appropriate facility.
She throws it into the fire pit to get rid of it.
She leaves it since she did not drop it.
She puts it in the general rubbish bag.
payload.explanation: Batteries contain harmful chemicals — they must not go in general rubbish or be burned.

payload.snippet: Oliver is on a camping trip when he wakes up needing the toilet but the shared toilet block is a five-minute walk away and it is raining.
options: He gets dressed, puts on his rain jacket, and makes the walk.
He uses a corner of the campsite rather than walk in the rain.
He holds it until morning and hopes for the best.
He wakes his tent-mate to go with him.
payload.explanation: Using the designated toilet facilities, even inconveniently, is the respectful and hygienic choice.

payload.snippet: Anna is camping with her class when a classmate who is usually confident begins shaking and says she does not want to sleep in the tent because she is scared.
options: She sits with her classmate, listens without teasing, and suggests they tell a teacher so they can decide together what to do.
She tells her classmate to be brave since it is only one night.
She tells the rest of the group so everyone can help.
She offers to swap sleeping spots since she is less scared.
payload.explanation: Listening without teasing and involving a teacher to find a solution is the caring and practical response.

payload.snippet: Jake is helping cook on a camp stove when the flame goes out unexpectedly. He can smell gas.
options: He moves away from the stove immediately, does not relight it, and tells the adult in charge.
He tries to relight the stove straight away since the food is still cooking.
He checks under the stove to see what happened.
He opens the gas canister to check whether gas is flowing.
payload.explanation: A gas smell after flame-out is a safety emergency — do not relight and tell an adult immediately.

payload.snippet: Maya's sleeping bag gets wet from condensation during the night. She is cold and uncomfortable.
options: She tells her parent at first light and asks for a spare blanket or dry layer while the sleeping bag is aired.
She puts the sleeping bag in the direct sun without telling anyone, hoping it dries before tonight.
She says nothing and tries to sleep through the next night in the damp bag.
She turns the bag inside out and gets back in straight away.
payload.explanation: Reporting the wet bag and asking for a dry alternative ensures you stay warm — putting a damp bag in direct sun without adult awareness is not a reliable fix.

payload.snippet: Tom is walking a trail at the campsite when a sign says the path ahead is temporarily closed for conservation work.
options: He turns back and follows the alternative route marked on his map.
He continues on the closed path since he can see it is usable.
He looks for a way around the barriers.
He asks a passing walker to accompany him past the sign.
payload.explanation: Conservation closures must be respected — the path closure is for ecological, not purely physical, reasons.

payload.snippet: Clara is collecting firewood when she notices the wood pile contains several pieces with a bright orange fungal growth on them.
options: She tells the adult in charge and does not use the affected wood.
She uses the wood since fire will kill the fungus.
She uses the unaffected pieces from the same pile since the fungus only covers some of them.
She removes the fungal pieces and uses the rest without telling anyone.
payload.explanation: Infected or fungus-covered wood should be reported — burning it spreads spores and is not a safe solution.

payload.snippet: Oliver is at a family campsite when he notices a younger child from another pitch is eating berries they have picked from a bush near the treeline.
options: He tells a nearby adult from the child's family immediately.
He tells the child the berries might be poisonous.
He asks the child to show him the bush so he can check what kind they are.
He takes the berries away from the child.
payload.explanation: A young child eating unidentified berries is a safety emergency — the nearest responsible adult must be alerted immediately.

payload.snippet: Anna has forgotten her sunscreen on a sunny camping trip. There is one other bottle in the group.
options: She asks if she can borrow some, uses a small amount, and makes sure there is enough left for others.
She uses as much of the shared bottle as she normally would.
She stays in the shade all day without telling anyone why.
She asks her parent to drive to a shop during the trip to buy more.
payload.explanation: Using a sensible amount of shared resources and leaving enough for others is the considerate approach.

payload.snippet: Jake finds a bird that appears injured on the path near the campsite.
options: He keeps his distance, marks the spot, and tells the campsite warden.
He tries to pick up the bird and carry it to a safer place.
He stands guard over the bird until it recovers.
He leaves it and continues his walk without telling anyone.
payload.explanation: Injured wildlife should be reported to the warden — handling it may injure the bird further and handling wild birds is not safe.

payload.snippet: Maya's family is barbecuing when the charcoal takes a long time to light. Her brother suggests using petrol to speed it up.
options: She says she does not think that is safe and suggests asking a parent before trying anything.
She goes along with the idea since her brother is older.
She tries it herself since petrol is faster.
She lights more firelighters instead without saying anything.
payload.explanation: Petrol near a barbecue is a serious fire and explosion risk — stopping to ask an adult is the correct response.

payload.snippet: Tom wakes up and finds water pooling inside the bottom of the tent after heavy rain.
options: He wakes his parent, moves his sleeping bag and belongings off the wet groundsheet, and waits for adult guidance on next steps.
He tries to re-pitch the tent himself in the rain.
He soaks up the water with his sleeping bag.
He moves to the car without telling his parent.
payload.explanation: Waking the adult and moving belongings away from the water while waiting for guidance is the correct response.

payload.snippet: Clara is on a guided nature walk when the guide asks the group not to touch any plants they do not recognise.
options: She follows the instruction and asks the guide about any plant that interests her.
She touches a leaf of a plant she thinks she knows.
She asks another child what a plant is before touching it.
She waits until the guide's back is turned before examining an interesting plant.
payload.explanation: Following the guide's instruction and asking if curious is the safe and respectful approach.

payload.snippet: Oliver is at a campsite with rules about quiet time after 10pm. His family's neighbours are still playing music at 11pm.
options: His parent speaks politely to the neighbouring campers to let them know about the quiet time rule.
He goes and tells the neighbours himself to be quiet.
He turns up his own music to make a point.
He calls the campsite warden without first speaking to the neighbours.
payload.explanation: A polite word from an adult to the neighbouring campers is the proportionate first step — escalating to the warden comes if that fails.

payload.snippet: Anna's group loses signal on their phones during a walk and the map app stops loading.
options: She tells the group leader and suggests they follow the last saved map direction until signal is restored.
She keeps walking in the direction she thinks is correct.
She climbs a nearby hill to try to get a signal.
She tells the group they are lost and should call for help.
payload.explanation: Telling the group leader and using the last known information calmly is the correct response when technology fails on a walk.

payload.snippet: Jake notices the campfire has been left with glowing embers when everyone goes to sleep.
options: He wakes a parent and tells them the fire is not fully out.
He pours water on it himself.
He puts soil on top and goes back to sleep.
He leaves it since glowing embers are normal.
payload.explanation: An unextinguished campfire must be fully put out — waking an adult to do this correctly is the safe approach.

payload.snippet: Maya finds a tick attached to her leg during a camping trip.
options: She tells an adult immediately without trying to remove it herself.
She pulls it off with her fingers.
She burns it off with a match.
She covers it with Vaseline and waits.
payload.explanation: Ticks must be removed correctly with a special tool — improper removal increases infection risk.

payload.snippet: Tom's camping group is crossing a shallow stream when one child slips and gets completely soaked.
options: He helps the child to the bank and calls the group leader immediately.
He laughs and helps the child out without telling anyone.
He tells the child to walk quickly so they dry off faster.
He continues the walk and leaves the group leader to notice.
payload.explanation: A soaked child in outdoor conditions needs adult attention immediately for warmth and safety assessment.

payload.snippet: Clara is tidying her room when she finds a broken glass she did not know about under the bed.
options: She leaves it where it is and tells a parent immediately so they can clear it up safely.
She tries to pick it up with her hands.
She sweeps it away with her foot.
She covers it with a sock and ignores it.
payload.explanation: Broken glass is a safety hazard — an adult must be told so it can be cleared up correctly.

payload.snippet: Oliver is cleaning his room when he finds a library book that has been missing for a week.
options: He puts it aside to return to the library and checks whether any fine has accumulated.
He hides it under a new pile of clothes.
He returns it without telling his parent about the fine.
He leaves it where he found it since he has already given up on finding it.
payload.explanation: Finding an overdue library book means returning it promptly and being honest about any fine.

payload.snippet: Anna is asked to tidy her room before her friend arrives in an hour. The room is very messy.
options: She prioritises the areas her friend will see and sorts items quickly, leaving a deeper tidy for later.
She pushes everything under the bed and into the wardrobe.
She tells her friend her room is clean and blocks the door.
She cancels the visit since the room is too messy to fix in time.
payload.explanation: Prioritising key areas and planning a fuller tidy later is a practical and honest approach.

payload.snippet: Jake is organising his desk when he finds some homework he forgot to hand in last week.
options: He tells his teacher the next day, explains it was lost in a messy room, and hands it in.
He throws it away since it is too late to hand in.
He puts a different date on it and hands it in quietly.
He hides it again and hopes the teacher forgot to chase it.
payload.explanation: Being honest about late work — even when it is your own fault — is better than deception or avoidance.

payload.snippet: Maya is decluttering her room when she finds toys she no longer uses that are still in good condition.
options: She asks her parent if they can be donated to a charity or passed on to younger children.
She throws them in the bin since she does not want them anymore.
She keeps them all since she might want them later.
She sells them at school without telling her parent.
payload.explanation: Donating or passing on still-usable toys is a good way to declutter and help others.

payload.snippet: Tom's room has a very strong smell. He cannot find the source after a quick look.
options: He does a more thorough search including under the bed and behind the wardrobe.
He opens the window and ignores the smell.
He sprays air freshener and considers it handled.
He tells his parent the room smells but it is not his fault.
payload.explanation: A persistent smell requires a proper search — masking it with freshener does not solve the problem.

payload.snippet: Clara is cleaning her room with her music on loud when her sibling knocks and asks her to turn it down.
options: She turns it down or uses headphones and continues tidying.
She ignores the knocking.
She turns it up louder to show it is her room.
She opens the door and argues.
payload.explanation: Considering others in a shared home by adjusting your volume is considerate.

payload.snippet: Oliver is supposed to tidy his room but instead organises one small drawer for twenty minutes and declares the room tidy.
options: He recognises he is avoiding the harder work and makes a proper start on the rest of the room.
He tells his parent the room is done.
He takes a break and promises to do more later.
He tidies only the areas his parent checks.
payload.explanation: Avoiding the harder parts of a task while appearing productive is not the same as completing the task.

payload.snippet: Anna is cleaning her room and finds a friend's belonging she borrowed three months ago and forgot about.
options: She contacts her friend, apologises, and arranges to return it soon.
She keeps it since the friend has probably forgotten.
She hides it more carefully so the friend cannot ask for it.
She returns it without apologising.
payload.explanation: Returning a borrowed item promptly and apologising for the delay is the honest and respectful response.

payload.snippet: Jake tidies his room very quickly before a chore check and hides several items in his wardrobe without organising them.
options: He acknowledges to himself that the wardrobe still needs sorting and plans to do it properly when he has more time.
He tells his parent the room is fully tidy.
He locks the wardrobe so no one can check.
He forgets about the wardrobe and never returns to it.
payload.explanation: Acknowledging that a hidden mess is not truly tidy — and planning to address it — is honest self-awareness.

payload.snippet: Maya is asked to help clean a shared room but her sibling refuses to help and leaves Maya to do everything.
options: She does her share of the shared space and tells a parent that her sibling is not participating.
She refuses to clean anything until her sibling helps.
She does the whole room herself and says nothing.
She makes her sibling's area even messier in protest.
payload.explanation: Doing your share and involving a parent to address unequal participation is the fair response.

payload.snippet: Tom finds a bag of coins while tidying that he does not recognise. He thinks they might belong to his sibling.
options: He puts them somewhere safe and asks his sibling if they are theirs.
He keeps them since he found them in his room.
He puts them in his piggy bank before asking.
He spends them and hopes his sibling does not ask.
payload.explanation: Finding items that might belong to someone else requires checking before claiming them.

payload.snippet: Clara realises she has been putting off tidying her room for two weeks and it has become overwhelming.
options: She breaks the task into small sections — one area at a time — and starts with the easiest part.
She gives up since it is too much to do.
She asks her parent to do it for her.
She tidies the entire room in one go even if it takes the whole day.
payload.explanation: Breaking an overwhelming task into manageable sections is a practical and effective strategy.

payload.snippet: Oliver is tidying his room when he finds a gift he was given but never used and does not like.
options: He puts it away neatly and considers whether it could be donated without hurting the giver's feelings.
He throws it in the bin.
He gives it to a friend directly without asking his parent.
He leaves it out where the giver can see he has used it when they visit.
payload.explanation: Donating an unused gift thoughtfully — and with parental guidance — is kinder than throwing it away.

payload.snippet: Anna is cleaning and finds a note from a friend that she had kept but now wants to throw away.
options: She decides whether it holds personal value before putting it in the bin.
She leaves all notes everywhere in case they matter later.
She keeps every note without reading them.
She shows the note to her sibling before deciding.
payload.explanation: Deciding what has personal value before discarding notes is a good habit when decluttering.

payload.snippet: Jake is asked to tidy his room by a specific time. He does not finish in time.
options: He tells his parent honestly that he ran out of time and asks for a short extension.
He pretends he is finished when his parent checks.
He hides the remaining mess under the bed.
He blames his sibling for distracting him.
payload.explanation: Honest communication about not finishing — rather than hiding the mess — is the mature response.

payload.snippet: Maya finds her sister's toy in her room and realises she had borrowed it and forgotten to return it.
options: She returns it and apologises.
She puts it in the charity bag since she does not use it.
She denies knowing anything about it if asked.
She puts it back in her room but in a hidden place.
payload.explanation: Returning what you borrowed and apologising for not returning it sooner is the right thing to do.

payload.snippet: Tom is cleaning and finds some money on the floor — he is not sure if it is his.
options: He puts it in a safe place and asks the family if anyone is missing money.
He keeps it since he found it in his own room.
He puts it in a family pot without asking.
He spends it and tells no one.
payload.explanation: Even money found in your own room could belong to a visitor or sibling — checking first is honest.

payload.snippet: Clara is supposed to clean her room but asks her younger sibling to do it for her in exchange for a sweet.
options: She reconsiders and does her own room — it is her responsibility.
She lets the younger sibling do it and gives them the sweet.
She lets the sibling start and then takes over when her parent comes.
She pays the sibling but tells her parent she cleaned it herself.
payload.explanation: Your own chores are your own responsibility — using a younger sibling as a substitute is not fair.

payload.snippet: Oliver does a thorough tidy of his room and is proud of the result. His parent asks him to do it again the following week.
options: He maintains the standard he reached and starts the next week's tidy from a much easier starting point.
He is annoyed since it was already clean.
He tidies only the parts that got messy again.
He refuses since he just did it.
payload.explanation: Maintaining a clean room makes each subsequent tidy much easier.

payload.snippet: Clara is doing a homework project and realises she has copied a whole paragraph from a website without changing anything.
options: She rewrites the paragraph in her own words and cites the website as a source.
She submits the paragraph as written since she found the information herself.
She changes a few words so it looks different.
She deletes the paragraph and leaves that section blank.
payload.explanation: Rewriting in your own words and citing the source avoids plagiarism — minor word changes do not.

payload.snippet: Oliver has three pieces of homework due the same day. He leaves them all to the night before.
options: He works out which will take longest and starts with that one, completing as much as possible before bed.
He picks the easiest one and submits only that, hoping teachers forget the others.
He copies his friend's answers for the two he runs out of time for.
He stays up all night to finish everything.
payload.explanation: Prioritising by effort required and working through as much as possible is more effective than avoidance or copying.

payload.snippet: Anna is asked to research a topic for homework and the first website she finds has information that contradicts her textbook.
options: She checks two or three additional sources to see which version is supported by most reliable evidence.
She uses the website since it came up first in the search.
She uses the textbook since teachers provided it.
She includes both versions and lets the teacher decide which is correct.
payload.explanation: Cross-checking multiple sources is the correct research method when information conflicts.

payload.snippet: Jake has been given a reading homework but discovers he has left his reading book at school. The assignment is due tomorrow.
options: He emails his teacher that evening to explain and asks if there is a digital version available, or if he can complete it the next day.
He invents a summary of what he thinks the pages probably contain.
He copies a review of the book from online and submits it.
He tells the teacher he finished the reading, having not done it.
payload.explanation: Honest communication about a missing resource — with a request for an alternative or extension — is the correct response.

payload.snippet: Maya is given a maths homework sheet but half the questions seem to relate to content her class has not yet been taught.
options: She completes the questions she can, leaves the others blank, and notes for her teacher that she was not sure about those sections.
She guesses the answers for the unfamiliar questions.
She copies answers from an online homework helper site.
She asks her parent to complete the unfamiliar sections.
payload.explanation: Completing what you can and flagging confusion honestly is the correct response to homework beyond your current understanding.

payload.snippet: Tom has a homework deadline at 8am and at 7:30am he spots a significant error in his submitted work.
options: He sends a quick correction to his teacher explaining the error before the deadline if possible.
He says nothing and hopes the teacher marks it as correct.
He resubmits a new version without informing the teacher.
He deletes the submission and resubmits as if the error never existed.
payload.explanation: Proactively notifying a teacher of a spotted error — before or just after a deadline — demonstrates honesty and responsibility.

payload.snippet: Clara is given a homework extension by her teacher. She uses the extra time to do a much more thorough job than she would have done originally.
options: She submits the improved work and thanks the teacher for the extension.
She does only slightly more than she originally submitted.
She submits the same work she would have done anyway.
She asks for another extension since she wants to improve it further.
payload.explanation: Using extra time productively and acknowledging the teacher's flexibility is the mature and respectful response.

payload.snippet: Oliver's parent offers to check his homework and suggests significant changes to the answers.
options: He considers the suggestions but makes sure the submitted work reflects his own understanding rather than his parent's answers.
He copies all his parent's suggestions directly since they must be correct.
He ignores the suggestions to avoid getting help.
He thanks his parent but does not change anything regardless of whether the suggestions are useful.
payload.explanation: Using suggestions to understand — and then writing in your own words — is the right use of parental help.

payload.snippet: Anna has been ill for a week and comes back to school with several pieces of missed homework to catch up on alongside current work.
options: She talks to each teacher about what she missed and agrees a realistic catch-up schedule.
She does as much as she can without talking to teachers and hopes no one notices the gaps.
She prioritises only the subjects she likes and ignores the rest.
She asks her friends to summarise the missed content for her to save time.
payload.explanation: Communicating with teachers about illness-related missed work and agreeing a structured catch-up is the professional and effective approach.

payload.snippet: Jake is given a creative writing homework and is completely stuck on ideas.
options: He uses a simple brainstorm method — jotting random words and images until something sparks — before starting to write.
He submits a very short piece because he had no ideas.
He copies the plot of a book he has read recently.
He asks a parent or sibling to come up with the story idea for him.
payload.explanation: A brainstorm gives you a starting point even when you feel blank — using someone else's idea is not your own creative work.

payload.snippet: Maya has a long-term project due in three weeks. She plans to start in the final few days.
options: She reconsiders and sets a plan to do a small amount each day so she is not overwhelmed at the end.
She sticks to her original plan since the deadline is still far away.
She asks her teacher to extend the deadline in advance just in case.
She asks a friend to share their completed project so she can see how to structure it.
payload.explanation: Starting a long-term project in stages from the beginning produces better work and avoids last-minute stress.

payload.snippet: Tom receives back a graded homework with a low mark and comments he does not understand.
options: He asks the teacher after class to explain the comments so he knows how to improve.
He ignores the comments and moves on.
He argues with the teacher about the mark.
He asks his parent to email the teacher about the mark.
payload.explanation: Asking a teacher to explain feedback — rather than arguing or ignoring it — is the most useful response to a low mark.

payload.snippet: Clara is doing group homework online when she notices one member has been contributing very little while others do the majority of the work.
options: She mentions it to the group first, and if it continues, she tells the teacher about the contribution imbalance.
She does all the work herself to avoid the problem.
She removes the low-contributing member from the group without speaking to them.
She complains to the teacher immediately without speaking to the group first.
payload.explanation: Raising the issue within the group first — and escalating to the teacher if it continues — is the correct sequence.

payload.snippet: Oliver has a homework task that requires internet research but his home broadband is broken.
options: He visits the local library or uses his school's homework club to complete the task.
He submits the homework without the research section.
He uses his mobile data even though it will use up his allowance.
He tells the teacher he had no internet and hopes for an extension.
payload.explanation: Finding an alternative access point for research is more resourceful than skipping the task or requesting an extension without trying.

payload.snippet: Anna is checking her completed homework when she realises a question she answered confidently may actually have a different correct answer.
options: She rechecks the answer using another source before submitting.
She submits her original answer since she is probably right.
She asks a friend which answer they got and copies their version.
She removes the answer and leaves it blank to be safe.
payload.explanation: Rechecking a doubted answer with a reliable source before submission is good academic practice.

payload.snippet: Jake finishes his homework very quickly and thinks it might be too short.
options: He rereads the question to check whether he has met all the requirements and adds more if needed.
He submits it since he has answered the question.
He adds padding to make it look longer without adding content.
He asks a parent to write an extra paragraph for him.
payload.explanation: Checking the task requirements before submitting ensures you have not missed something — padding without content does not improve quality.

payload.snippet: Maya discovers that a classmate has been copying from her homework in several different subjects without her knowledge.
options: She tells a teacher privately rather than confronting the classmate alone.
She confronts the classmate in front of others.
She says nothing since it benefits her classmate and does not hurt her.
She deliberately puts wrong answers in future homework to stop the copying.
payload.explanation: Telling a teacher privately is the correct response — deliberate wrong answers could harm your own marks, and confrontation without teacher involvement escalates conflict.

payload.snippet: Tom is assigned a homework task he finds genuinely interesting and wants to spend a lot of extra time on it.
options: He completes the required task well and then develops his extra interest independently as a side project.
He submits an enormous extended version and asks his teacher for extra credit.
He focuses so much on the extended version that he neglects other homework.
He submits only his extended version without completing the core task.
payload.explanation: Completing the core task first and pursuing extra interest separately ensures no other responsibilities are neglected.

payload.snippet: Clara's parent corrects an incorrect answer on her homework before she submits it without asking her.
options: She explains to her parent that she needs to learn from her own mistakes and changes it back, or at least tells the teacher the answer was given by a parent.
She submits it with the parent's correction since it is now right.
She deletes the parent's correction and guesses a different answer herself.
She tells the teacher the answer was hers and hopes the teacher does not notice.
payload.explanation: Submitted homework should reflect your own understanding — submitting a parent's answer as your own is dishonest.

payload.snippet: Oliver is given a homework task but genuinely does not understand the topic at all, despite trying for over an hour.
options: He writes down what he tried and where he got stuck, and emails his teacher to ask for guidance.
He leaves the homework blank since trying seems pointless.
He copies from an online answer site since he has tried.
He asks his parent to explain it even though they do not know the subject well.
payload.explanation: Documenting your attempt and asking the teacher for guidance is better than blanking the work or using answer sites.

payload.snippet: Clara starts at a new school and her teacher asks her to introduce herself to the class.
options: She takes a deep breath, says her name, and shares one thing she enjoys.
She says nothing and looks at the floor.
She speaks so quietly no one can hear.
She refuses and sits down.
payload.explanation: A simple self-introduction — name and one interest — is enough to start making a good impression.

payload.snippet: Oliver meets a new classmate at lunch and realises they share a common interest.
options: He asks a follow-up question about the shared interest to keep the conversation going.
He talks only about his own version of the interest without asking about theirs.
He changes the subject to something he finds more interesting.
He nods politely but says nothing more.
payload.explanation: Following up with a question shows genuine interest and keeps a new friendship growing.

payload.snippet: Anna is trying to make friends with a new classmate but her attempts at conversation are not being returned warmly.
options: She gives the classmate some space and tries again another day.
She tells the whole class the new student is unfriendly.
She stops trying altogether and avoids the classmate.
She asks a teacher to make the classmate be her friend.
payload.explanation: Giving space and trying again later respects that not everyone warms up at the same pace.

payload.snippet: Jake's new friend group has an inside joke he does not understand yet.
options: He smiles and asks them to explain the joke when there is a natural pause.
He laughs along even though he has no idea what the joke is.
He tells them inside jokes are rude to outsiders.
He walks away since he feels excluded.
payload.explanation: Asking for an explanation in a relaxed way is more honest than faking understanding.

payload.snippet: Maya meets a new girl at an after-school club who is very different from her usual friends.
options: She gives the friendship a chance and looks for things they have in common.
She decides they are too different to be friends.
She is polite but avoids spending time with her.
She only talks to the new girl when her usual friends are not there.
payload.explanation: Giving a new friendship a genuine chance often reveals shared ground you would not expect.

payload.snippet: Tom's new friend cancels plans at the last minute for the second time in a row.
options: He tells his friend honestly that he was disappointed and asks if they can plan something they are both sure about.
He pretends it is fine and says nothing.
He stops inviting his friend to things.
He complains to other friends about how unreliable the new friend is.
payload.explanation: An honest but gentle conversation about disappointment gives a new friendship a better chance than silence or gossip.

payload.snippet: Clara is making a new friend but her existing best friend seems jealous and is being cold with her.
options: She speaks to her best friend privately and reassures her that the new friendship does not change things between them.
She stops spending time with the new friend to avoid conflict.
She tells the new friend about her best friend's jealousy.
She ignores her best friend's feelings and carries on.
payload.explanation: Reassuring an existing friend privately — rather than choosing sides or ignoring the tension — helps everyone feel secure.

payload.snippet: Oliver meets a new student who tells him some personal information in confidence on only their second meeting.
options: He listens respectfully and keeps the information to himself.
He tells another friend since it is interesting.
He brings it up again in front of others later.
He tells the new student they shared too much too soon.
payload.explanation: Respecting early confidences, even if you are surprised by them, builds trust in a new friendship.

payload.snippet: Anna's new friend has cultural traditions that are unfamiliar to her.
options: She asks genuine, respectful questions to learn more.
She tells her friend her traditions seem strange.
She avoids asking and makes assumptions instead.
She says her own traditions are better.
payload.explanation: Asking genuine respectful questions about unfamiliar traditions shows curiosity and respect.

payload.snippet: Jake tries to become part of a new social group at school but is left out of a group chat they all use.
options: He mentions it to one of the group members he is closest to and asks if he can be added.
He creates a competing group chat and invites only some of the group.
He acts upset and distant until someone notices.
He tells a teacher the group is excluding him.
payload.explanation: Directly and calmly asking to be included is the most straightforward and mature response.

payload.snippet: Maya's new friend asks her to keep a secret that makes Maya uncomfortable.
options: She tells her friend she is not comfortable keeping that kind of secret and explains why.
She agrees to keep the secret to avoid conflict.
She immediately tells someone else since it is not her secret anyway.
She stops being friends to avoid the situation.
payload.explanation: Being honest about what kind of secrets you can keep protects both you and the friendship.

payload.snippet: Tom moves to a new neighbourhood and wants to make friends with children he sees playing outside.
options: He goes outside and asks if he can join in.
He watches from his window hoping they will notice him.
He asks his parent to arrange playdates for him without meeting the children first.
He ignores the local children and hopes to meet friends at school instead.
payload.explanation: Going outside and asking directly is the most natural and effective way to start neighbourhood friendships.

payload.snippet: Clara is becoming close friends with someone new when she discovers they have a mutual friend who has said negative things about her.
options: She focuses on forming her own opinion of the new friend based on their direct interactions.
She tells the new friend what the mutual friend said.
She decides the new friend cannot be trusted since they know someone who dislikes her.
She asks the new friend to stop seeing the mutual friend.
payload.explanation: Forming your own opinion based on direct experience is more fair and accurate than reacting to second-hand information.

payload.snippet: Oliver is at a party where he knows no one. His host has not introduced him to anyone.
options: He approaches a small group and introduces himself.
He stands near the food and waits for someone to speak to him.
He leaves early since no one is talking to him.
He asks the host to stay with him all evening.
payload.explanation: Taking the initiative to introduce yourself at a social event is a learnable and valuable social skill.

payload.snippet: Anna's new friend asks a lot of personal questions very early in the friendship.
options: She answers what she is comfortable with and gently redirects questions she is not ready to answer.
She answers everything to seem open.
She stops the conversation abruptly.
She tells the friend they are being nosy.
payload.explanation: Setting comfortable boundaries early in a friendship — politely and without drama — is healthy and normal.

payload.snippet: Jake finds it very hard to make friends and feels lonely at his new school after two weeks.
options: He tells a trusted adult about how he is feeling and asks for any suggestions.
He pretends to be fine so no one worries.
He decides he will never make friends and gives up.
He tries to buy friendship by giving away his belongings.
payload.explanation: Asking a trusted adult for advice on loneliness is a brave and practical step.

payload.snippet: Maya discovers that a new friendship she was excited about has started to feel one-sided — she always reaches out first.
options: She gives it a little more time and then, if nothing changes, tells her friend she would like them both to initiate contact sometimes.
She immediately ends the friendship.
She matches the low effort and sees if the friendship fades.
She complains to mutual friends about the imbalance.
payload.explanation: Giving a direct, kind signal about imbalance gives the friendship a real chance to correct itself.

payload.snippet: Tom is making a new friend from a different cultural background and accidentally says something unintentionally offensive.
options: He apologises sincerely as soon as he realises, without over-explaining.
He defends himself since he did not mean to offend.
He laughs it off and moves on.
He avoids the friend afterwards out of embarrassment.
payload.explanation: A sincere apology without excessive defensiveness repairs the moment — avoidance makes it worse.

payload.snippet: Clara's new best friend asks to copy her homework because she did not do hers.
options: She declines and offers to help her friend understand the work instead.
She lets her copy since they are friends.
She lets her copy this once and tells her not to ask again.
She reports her friend to the teacher immediately.
payload.explanation: Helping a friend understand the work is more genuinely helpful than letting them copy — and protects both of you.

payload.snippet: Oliver has been making a new friend but notices his other friends are teasing the new student when he is not there.
options: He tells his friends privately that the teasing is not okay.
He joins in to avoid social pressure.
He says nothing since it is not happening in front of him.
He tells the new friend what his other friends have been saying.
payload.explanation: Speaking up against teasing privately and directly — before it escalates — is the right and courageous response.

payload.snippet: Clara loses her school reading record book in the final week of term. She is not sure if she left it at school or at home.
options: She searches thoroughly at home, then checks at school, and tells her teacher she is looking for it.
She tells the teacher she lost it only after the teacher asks where it is.
She borrows a friend's completed record and copies the entries.
She says she handed it in weeks ago when she did not.
payload.explanation: A thorough search and honest communication with the teacher is better than deception or delay.

payload.snippet: Oliver loses his phone at a shopping centre. He has borrowed his parent's phone.
options: He calls his own number and retraces his steps, then asks at the customer service desk.
He buys a new phone and does not tell his parent about the loss.
He tells his parent the phone was stolen to avoid being blamed for carelessness.
He checks social media to see if anyone has posted about finding a phone.
payload.explanation: Calling your own number and asking at customer service are the most effective immediate steps when a phone is lost in a public place.

payload.snippet: Anna leaves her musical instrument on the train. She realises at the next station.
options: She gets off at the next station and contacts the train operator's lost property service immediately.
She continues home and contacts lost property the next day.
She travels back on the same line hoping to spot it.
She says nothing and hopes someone returns it.
payload.explanation: Immediate contact with the operator's lost property service gives the best chance of recovery before the item is moved further.

payload.snippet: Jake finds a wallet in the park containing cash and cards.
options: He hands it in to the nearest police station or contacts the police non-emergency line.
He keeps the cash and hands in only the cards.
He uses the contact details in the wallet to contact the owner directly.
He leaves it on a nearby bench so the owner can find it.
payload.explanation: Handing a found wallet to the police — not keeping the cash or attempting private contact — is the legally and ethically correct response.

payload.snippet: Maya realises she left her bag containing her homework on the school bus.
options: She contacts the school bus company and tells her teacher that the homework is in the bag.
She tells the teacher she did the homework but forgot to bring it.
She recreates the homework from memory and submits it without explaining.
She says her bag was stolen.
payload.explanation: Contacting the bus company and being honest with the teacher is the correct response — recreating work without disclosure or lying about a theft both misrepresent the situation.

payload.snippet: Tom cannot find his library book anywhere at home and it is due today.
options: He returns to the library, explains the situation, and asks about the replacement cost.
He tells the librarian he has already returned it.
He borrows an identical copy from a friend and returns that one.
He ignores the due date and continues looking.
payload.explanation: Honesty about a genuinely lost library book — and asking about the cost — is better than deception or ignoring the due date.

payload.snippet: Clara finds a set of car keys in a supermarket car park.
options: She takes them to the supermarket customer service desk immediately.
She presses the key fob buttons to find the car and leaves the keys on the bonnet.
She keeps them in case the owner comes back while she is still shopping.
She puts them on a nearby wall so they are visible.
payload.explanation: The customer service desk is the correct place to hand in found keys — leaving them on the car or a wall leaves them vulnerable to theft.

payload.snippet: Oliver loses a borrowed item belonging to a friend.
options: He tells the friend honestly, apologises, and offers to replace it or pay for a replacement.
He tells his friend the item was accidentally broken.
He replaces it with a similar but cheaper item without telling the friend.
He avoids his friend until the item is forgotten.
payload.explanation: Honest disclosure and an offer to replace the item are both required when you lose something borrowed from a friend.

payload.snippet: Anna is convinced she left her jacket in a café. She calls them and they say they have not found it.
options: She visits the café in person and checks nearby areas in case it was moved or dropped between the café and the street.
She decides it is definitely gone and buys a replacement immediately.
She posts on local social media claiming the café lost it.
She calls the café again the next day demanding they look harder.
payload.explanation: A visit in person allows a more thorough check than a phone call — items are sometimes missed by staff on initial searches.

payload.snippet: Jake finds a toy in the park that has a child's name written on it.
options: He hands it in at the park keeper's office with the name visible.
He takes it home since it looks abandoned.
He calls out the name loudly hoping the child is nearby.
He puts it on a park bench with the name facing up.
payload.explanation: Handing in a named item to park staff gives the best chance of reuniting it with the owner.

payload.snippet: Maya loses a prescription medication during a trip. She does not have a spare.
options: She contacts her GP or pharmacist immediately to arrange an emergency prescription.
She manages without the medication until she is home.
She borrows similar medication from a friend who takes the same drug.
She waits until the following morning to contact anyone.
payload.explanation: Prescription medication cannot wait — an emergency prescription from a GP or pharmacist must be arranged immediately.

payload.snippet: Tom finds a set of house keys in the street with a supermarket loyalty card attached.
options: He takes them to the supermarket so staff can try to identify the owner via the loyalty card account.
He calls a locksmith and uses the loyalty card details to find the address.
He hangs them on a nearby fence in case the owner passes.
He takes them to the police station.
payload.explanation: The supermarket can use the loyalty card account to contact the owner — this is safer than trying to find the address yourself, and also correct compared to a police station which would also work but is less targeted.

payload.snippet: Clara discovers she has accidentally taken home a book belonging to a classmate mixed in with her own.
options: She contacts the classmate and returns it as soon as possible, apologising for the mix-up.
She waits until she sees the classmate at school naturally.
She returns it without acknowledging the mix-up.
She reads it first since she already has it.
payload.explanation: Contacting the classmate and returning the book promptly — with an apology — is the right response to an accidental take-home.

payload.snippet: Oliver thinks he may have lost his wallet at one of three places he visited today.
options: He calls each place starting with the last one he visited and working backwards.
He waits to see if someone contacts him before searching.
He cancels all his bank cards before checking if the wallet has been handed in.
He posts on social media asking if anyone has found a wallet.
payload.explanation: Working backwards through your day is the most systematic approach to tracing a lost item across multiple locations.

payload.snippet: Anna finds an expensive camera in a changing room at a leisure centre.
options: She hands it to the leisure centre reception with a description of where she found it.
She keeps it since someone clearly left it behind.
She checks inside the camera for clues about the owner and contacts them herself.
She leaves it where she found it in case the owner comes back.
payload.explanation: Handing found valuable items to reception is the correct step — self-initiated contact using the item's contents is not standard lost property process.

payload.snippet: Jake realises mid-journey that he has left his passport at home. His flight is in four hours.
options: He turns around immediately and asks someone at home to confirm the passport is there before he commits to the return journey.
He continues to the airport hoping he can travel on other ID.
He contacts the airline to explain and ask what to do.
He checks his bag again in the vehicle in case he missed it.
payload.explanation: Checking that the passport is definitely at home before turning back avoids a wasted journey — airline contact is a secondary step if the passport cannot be retrieved in time.

payload.snippet: Maya loses her earring in a hotel room during a trip and cannot find it.
options: She asks hotel housekeeping to look carefully when they clean the room, and leaves her contact details.
She turns the room completely upside down before checking out.
She extends her checkout time to continue searching.
She accepts it is gone and checks out on time.
payload.explanation: Asking housekeeping to look and leaving contact details is the practical and considerate approach.

payload.snippet: Tom finds a credit card on the floor in a supermarket.
options: He gives it immediately to a supermarket staff member.
He places it face-down on the nearest checkout desk.
He uses the name on the card to look the person up online.
He keeps it and calls the number on the back to return it himself.
payload.explanation: Giving a found credit card to a staff member immediately is the safest and correct step — self-initiated return calls or online searches are not standard lost property procedure.

payload.snippet: Clara has lost a sentimental item that is impossible to replace. She has searched everywhere.
options: She accepts she may not find it, processes the loss, and — if appropriate — tells the person who gave it to her honestly.
She keeps searching obsessively even after weeks.
She pretends she still has it to avoid upsetting the person who gave it.
She blames another person for losing it.
payload.explanation: Accepting genuine irretrievable loss — and being honest with those who matter — is healthier than prolonged searching or dishonesty.

payload.snippet: Oliver has found someone's lost passport inside a returned library book.
options: He hands it in at the library desk so it can be reported to the police or local authority.
He contacts the passport office directly using the details on the passport.
He posts it back to the address listed inside.
He keeps it safe at home in case the person comes looking.
payload.explanation: Found identity documents must be handled through official channels — mailing or keeping them at home are not secure or correct.

payload.snippet: Chloe accidentally sits on her favourite toy and cracks it. She feels upset.
options: She tells her parent and shows them the crack
She hides the toy so she won't get in trouble
She blames her baby brother
She glues it without asking
payload.explanation: Being honest about accidents is better than hiding them.

payload.snippet: Ryan's remote control car stops moving after he drives it into a wall. The shell is cracked.
options: He checks if batteries need replacing and then tells Mum
He throws the car against the wall again
He pretends the car still works
He blames his friend
payload.explanation: Checking batteries first is a sensible step before telling an adult.

payload.snippet: Ava's art set is left in the rain and the paints crack and dry out.
options: She tells Mum and asks if she can replace just the dried colours
She tries to add water and blend the cracked paints
She throws the whole set away
She blames whoever left it outside
payload.explanation: Being specific about what broke helps fix things cheaply.

payload.snippet: Josh's toy light-sabre stops lighting up. He loves it and is worried it's permanently broken.
options: He checks whether the batteries need changing
He hits it against the sofa trying to make it work
He tells Mum it is completely ruined
He throws it in the bin
payload.explanation: A battery check often solves electronic toy faults.

payload.snippet: Molly is at a friend's house and accidentally drops their board game box; all the pieces scatter and one card rips.
options: She apologises, picks up every piece, and tells her friend's parent what happened
She scoops pieces up quickly and says nothing about the rip
She blames the friend's little sibling
She pretends she did not notice the rip
payload.explanation: Admitting an accident to the responsible adult is the honest course.

payload.snippet: Oliver's toy train track breaks in the middle during play. His brother wants to keep going but the train can't run.
options: He tells his brother they need to stop and ask an adult to repair the track first
He keeps pushing the train over the gap anyway
He blames his brother for breaking it
He throws the broken section away
payload.explanation: Stopping play to fix a hazard prevents further damage.

payload.snippet: Daisy gets glue on her favourite plush toy while doing a craft project, making its fur stiff and matted.
options: She shows Mum right away; Mum trims the stiff fur so it is fluffy again
She hides the toy under her bed
She scrubs it with a wet cloth making it worse
She puts the toy in the bin and says it was already old
payload.explanation: Acting quickly with adult help often saves a toy that seems ruined.

payload.snippet: Theo's kite crashes into a tree and the fabric tears. He wants to fly it again next weekend.
options: He asks Dad if they can buy a repair patch to cover the tear
He yanks the kite so hard the fabric tears more
He decides the kite is too broken and throws it away
He hides the kite and pretends the trip never happened
payload.explanation: A repair patch can restore a kite for very little cost.

payload.snippet: Aria's snow globe leaks water onto her shelf and the mechanism inside stops playing music.
options: She tells Mum calmly and they clear up the water together
She shakes it harder hoping the music restarts
She hides the globe in a drawer
She puts it back and lets the shelf stay wet
payload.explanation: Addressing a spill promptly prevents damage to other belongings.

payload.snippet: Finn's brand-new birthday drone crashes on its first flight and one propeller breaks off. He feels sick with disappointment.
options: He tells Dad what happened and checks if spare propellers came in the box
He hides the broken propeller hoping Dad won't notice
He cries and refuses to touch the drone again
He blames the wind
payload.explanation: Spare propellers often come in the box; honest reporting lets adults help.

payload.snippet: Zara borrows a classmate's colouring pencils and snaps one by mistake. She still has the two pieces.
options: She tells her classmate straight away and apologises
She puts both pieces at the bottom of the pot hoping no one notices
She hides one piece so it looks like a small pencil
She says nothing and returns the set
payload.explanation: Owning up to accidental damage keeps trust in a friendship.

payload.snippet: Jake's toy xylophone loses two keys that rattle out. Without them it can't play a proper scale.
options: He picks up the loose keys and asks Mum if they can be refitted
He bangs the remaining keys harder trying to compensate
He throws the whole xylophone away
He hides the keys in his toy box
payload.explanation: Loose parts can often be refitted with adult help.

payload.snippet: Phoebe drops her telescope and the eyepiece cracks. She uses it for astronomy club.
options: She tells her parents so they can look into a replacement eyepiece
She tries to look through the cracked eyepiece and hurts her eye
She super-glues the crack and does not tell anyone
She stops going to astronomy club without explanation
payload.explanation: A cracked optical piece needs professional attention, not DIY glue.

payload.snippet: Tom has a toy construction set and one of the base plates snaps clean in two. His set is no longer complete.
options: He sorts through the set to see which builds still work without that plate
He throws the whole set away
He tries to tape the plate together with sellotape
He blames his sister for the broken plate
payload.explanation: Sorting out what still works makes the most of a partially broken set.

payload.snippet: Emma's bubble-blowing wand melts slightly after she leaves it near a sunny window. It no longer makes round bubbles.
options: She shows Mum and they look online for a replacement wand
She keeps blowing but gets frustrated when bubbles are misshapen
She throws the whole bottle of bubble solution away
She draws on the wand to make it look normal
payload.explanation: Replacing just a broken part saves having to buy a whole new set.

payload.snippet: Noah accidentally breaks a wheel off his skateboard while practising a trick. He cannot ride it safely.
options: He tells his dad and they take the board to a skate shop for repair
He rides the three-wheeled board slowly and hopes for the best
He hides the broken wheel
He blames the pavement for being uneven
payload.explanation: A damaged skateboard is a safety hazard — get it repaired before riding.

payload.snippet: Lily's jigsaw puzzle box gets soaked in a puddle and all the pieces are stuck together and damaged.
options: She lays the pieces out to dry and checks if any can be saved
She throws the whole puzzle away immediately
She tries to peel the pieces apart while wet, tearing them
She tells Mum the puzzle was already broken
payload.explanation: Drying puzzle pieces out first gives the best chance of saving them.

payload.snippet: Ben's toy bow-and-arrow string breaks and whips back at his hand. His hand stings.
options: He tells a parent his hand stings and shows them the broken string
He tries to retie the string himself
He hides the bow so he won't lose it
He blames the toy for being badly made
payload.explanation: Safety matters — a broken string on a toy bow must be fixed before further use.

payload.snippet: Cleo's musical jewellery box stops spinning when the lid is open. The ballerina just sits still.
options: She shows Grandma, who gently winds the mechanism more carefully
She forces the ballerina to spin with her finger
She bangs the box on her desk
She throws the box out, calling it boring
payload.explanation: Winding mechanisms need gentle care — an adult touch often fixes them.

payload.snippet: Oscar's LEGO model falls off the shelf and breaks into hundreds of pieces. He spent days building it.
options: He takes a photo of the model online for reference and starts rebuilding
He cries and refuses to rebuild it ever
He throws all the pieces in the bin
He blames whoever bumped the shelf
payload.explanation: A photo provides a blueprint to rebuild from, turning disaster into a fresh project.

payload.snippet: Jake's team does all the tidying while the other team just watches. He feels frustrated.
options: He tells the teacher that the work is not being shared fairly
He refuses to tidy anything
He tips the other team's work over
He tidies alone in silence all week
payload.explanation: Reporting an imbalance to a supervising adult is the correct response.

payload.snippet: Olivia always picks the game at break and her friends are getting bored of it.
options: Her friends ask if they can take turns choosing
They refuse to play and leave Olivia alone
They play Olivia's game but sulk loudly
They let Olivia always choose but feel resentful forever
payload.explanation: Calmly asking to rotate who chooses is the fair and direct solution.

payload.snippet: In a relay race, one team has five runners and the other has three, making the race unfair.
options: They agree to let two runners run twice to make it equal
The bigger team wins and takes the prize
The smaller team drops out
They abandon the race altogether
payload.explanation: Adjusting numbers so both sides are equal keeps competition fair.

payload.snippet: Riya always volunteers to read aloud and the shy students never get a chance.
options: The teacher starts calling on different students to give everyone a turn
Riya reads every session and other students never improve
The class tells Riya to stop volunteering
The shy students complain but nothing changes
payload.explanation: A teacher rotating participation ensures every student benefits.

payload.snippet: Two students work equally hard on a group project but only the louder one is praised by the teacher.
options: The quieter student tells the teacher they both contributed equally
The quieter student does all future projects alone
The quiet student lets it go every time
The loud student takes full credit on purpose
payload.explanation: Advocating for equal recognition, even quietly, is fair and right.

payload.snippet: Liam is given extra chores because he is older, even though he and his sibling make similar messes.
options: He calmly tells his parent the chores feel unequal and asks to share them more evenly
He refuses all chores in protest
He does his sibling's chores silently but builds up resentment
He leaves all chores undone hoping someone else does them
payload.explanation: Calmly raising perceived unfairness gives parents a chance to correct the balance.

payload.snippet: In a class vote, one group is allowed to vote twice by mistake.
options: The teacher discovers the error and runs the vote again fairly
The group who voted twice keeps their result
The teacher picks the result they preferred anyway
The losing group refuses to accept the result
payload.explanation: A procedural error in a vote invalidates the outcome — a re-run is the fair response.

payload.snippet: Emma's team has been practising for three weeks; the other team only joined yesterday but they both receive the same trophy.
options: Emma's coach explains to the group that participation trophies are about inclusion, not effort comparison
Emma's team demands bigger trophies for more effort
Emma's team refuses to let the new team take a trophy
Emma throws her trophy away in protest
payload.explanation: Participation awards celebrate involvement; different rewards exist for recognising greater effort.

payload.snippet: A teacher gives one student extra time on a test but doesn't explain why to the rest of the class.
options: The teacher explains that different students have different needs and all deserve a fair chance to show what they know
The other students refuse to take the test
The other students demand extra time too even without a need
The student with extra time is mocked for being unfair
payload.explanation: Reasonable adjustments ensure equal opportunity, not identical treatment — that is what fairness means.

payload.snippet: In a class talent show, judges score a popular student higher for the same quality act as a less popular classmate.
options: A teacher notices and reminds the judges to use the scoring criteria, not popularity
The popular student wins and nothing is said
The less popular student drops out of future activities

Stop watering to stress the plant into fruiting
payload.explanation: Runner beans stop producing when old pods are left to swell — picking triggers more.

payload.snippet: The bird netting over the strawberry bed has collapsed under the weight of last night's heavy rain.
options: Remove and prop the netting up on wire hoops
Throw the netting away
Let birds eat the crop
Move the strawberries inside the greenhouse
payload.explanation: Wire hoops hold netting above the fruit so birds cannot reach through it.

payload.snippet: The allotment has a serious dock-weed problem and pulling by hand keeps leaving root fragments that regrow.
options: Dig the full root out with a fork carefully
Spray the entire bed with salt water
Cut the tops weekly and hope
Cover with newspaper for a season
payload.explanation: Full root removal is the only reliable way to stop dock weeds regrowing.

payload.snippet: Aphids have colonised the broad bean tips at the top of every plant in the bed this week.
options: Pinch off the aphid-covered tips carefully
Spray each plant with diesel fuel
Cut all the bean plants down
Ignore them because the beans are almost mature
payload.explanation: Pinching off the tips removes the aphid colony and encourages the plant to pod up.

payload.snippet: The potting-shed bag of seed compost has got damp from a dripping roof and now feels clumpy.
options: Move the compost to a dry place and let it air out
Use the damp compost straight in seed trays
Bin the entire bag immediately
Freeze the compost to dry it out
payload.explanation: Compost stored damp grows mould that kills seedlings — drying saves the rest.

payload.snippet: The sweet peas planted in spring have flowered once but completely stopped even though the foliage looks fine.
options: Deadhead every spent flower to encourage new buds
Fertilise heavily with nitrogen feed
Cut the entire plant back to the ground
Add thick mulch around the roots
payload.explanation: Regular deadheading keeps sweet peas blooming throughout the whole season.

payload.snippet: The wildflower meadow patch has been overrun by thistles over the summer and is crowding out the smaller plants.
options: Dig out the thistles with gloves before they set seed
Cut the tops and let them regrow bigger
Water only the thistles to tire them
Sow more wildflower seeds on top
payload.explanation: Removing thistles before seeding stops them spreading across the whole patch.

payload.snippet: A large section of the garden fence has been blown over and is lying across the vegetable beds.
options: Prop the fence up and check the plants for damage
Throw the fence away
Replant everything in new beds
Water the crushed plants heavily
payload.explanation: Propping and assessing first — some crushed plants recover once the weight is off.

payload.snippet: The container herbs on the balcony are drying out within one day of watering during the recent heatwave.
options: Move them into partial shade during the afternoon
Water them with warm water only
Add more compost to the top
Squeeze all pots tightly together on the hot tile
payload.explanation: Afternoon shade reduces water demand significantly during a heatwave.

payload.snippet: The garlic planted in autumn has produced very small bulbs when lifted in June compared to last year.
options: Check if the spacing was too tight when planting
Add high-nitrogen feed next autumn
Water more during the green growth phase
Harvest later in July instead
payload.explanation: Tight spacing splits the available nutrients between too many competing bulbs.

payload.snippet: Heavy clay soil in the new garden is causing puddles to sit on the vegetable beds for days after rain.
options: Dig in grit and compost to improve drainage
Add more clay soil on top
Plant only water plants in the beds
Leave puddles to drain on their own each time
payload.explanation: Grit and compost open up clay soil so water moves through instead of sitting.

payload.snippet: The greenhouse tomatoes have developed blossom end rot on many of the developing fruits this week.
options: Water more consistently and add calcium to the soil
Pick off every affected fruit and discard
Add more nitrogen fertiliser immediately
Remove the entire plant and start again
payload.explanation: Consistent watering prevents the calcium lockout that causes blossom end rot.

payload.snippet: The supermarket has run out of the specific brand of baby formula the health visitor recommended and there is no substitution advice on the empty shelf.
options: Ask the pharmacist nearby for an appropriate safe alternative
Buy the cheapest formula on the shelf without advice
Order the exact brand online and wait several days
Mix adult powdered milk as a temporary fix
payload.explanation: Pharmacists are trained to advise on safe formula alternatives when a specific brand is unavailable.

payload.snippet: The automatic checkout has charged for five bags but the screen shows a ten-item limit error and the transaction is frozen midway.
options: Press the help button and wait for the assistant to fix it
Force the transaction through and leave quickly
Scan every item again from scratch at the same machine
Move to a different machine and start the whole scan over
payload.explanation: The help button calls someone trained to unfreeze checkout errors without losing the scan progress.

payload.snippet: The store manager has announced the shop will close in five minutes due to an emergency and you still have half your list to go.
options: Pay for what is already in the basket immediately
Ask the manager for five extra minutes to finish
Abandon the basket and leave with no items paid
Shop faster by running through the remaining aisles quickly
payload.explanation: Paying for the basket immediately is the only legal and sensible response to an emergency closure announcement.

payload.snippet: A fellow shopper has left their wallet on the shelf beside the yoghurt section and walked into the next aisle.
options: Call out to the shopper or hand the wallet to a staff member
Keep the wallet until they come back themselves
Take it to the till and hand it to the cashier there
Leave it on the shelf hoping they will return
payload.explanation: Calling out plus staff handover is the fastest and most trustworthy route to getting the wallet back to its owner.

payload.snippet: The online grocery order has arrived with three items missing and two items that were not ordered at all.
options: Contact customer services and report both issues for credit
Accept the swap items and forget about the missing ones
Return all items at the door immediately
Reorder the missing items at full price on a second order
payload.explanation: Customer services can credit missing items and arrange returns for wrongly sent substitutions on the same call.

payload.snippet: The checkout belt has stopped moving completely while your items are still in the basket.
options: Wait calmly while the cashier calls for technical help
Lift all your items manually over the belt by hand
Leave the shop without paying for anything
Move to a different cashier and start mid-scan there
payload.explanation: Waiting calmly while the cashier calls for technical help is the correct and legal response to a broken belt.

payload.snippet: The shop has substituted four key items with different brands that the family cannot eat due to an allergy saved in the account.
options: Reject all four substitutions at the door and request a refund
Accept the substitutions and return them inside later
Use the substitutions and manage the allergy carefully
Order from a different shop without reporting the issue
payload.explanation: Rejecting and requesting a refund at the door is both safe and your legal right when substitutions conflict with a saved allergy.

payload.snippet: A large shop sign has fallen and blocked the fire exit near the back of the store during your shopping trip.
options: Alert a staff member immediately and step back from the sign
Move the sign yourself to clear the exit
Photograph the sign and post it on social media
Continue shopping past the blocked exit as normal
payload.explanation: Only trained staff should move a fallen sign near a fire exit because the structure above may still be unstable.

payload.snippet: The hot food counter deli chicken at the back is priced before the fifteen-minute hold time warning printed on the label.
options: Ask for freshly cooked chicken from the next batch
Take the oldest item at the back because it is cheaper
Take two and reheat one safely at home later
Buy it and eat immediately at the store entrance
payload.explanation: Fresh hot food is worth the short wait compared to the safety risk from an item near its hold-time limit.

payload.snippet: The special-offer shelf-edge label says half price but the item scans at full price and there is a long queue behind you.
options: Ask the cashier to check the shelf-edge label before paying
Pay the full price to save time for everyone
Argue loudly about the price across the long queue
Step out of the queue and check the price yourself
payload.explanation: A quick cashier check is the right move — by law the advertised shelf price must be honoured.

payload.snippet: The shop has a buy-three-get-one-free deal but you only need two of the item for the week ahead.
options: Buy three to get the free one and use all four across the week
Skip the deal and pay full price for just two
Take one free without buying the required three
Ask the cashier to activate the deal for only two items
payload.explanation: Getting four while you use them all is better value than paying full price for just two.

payload.snippet: The receipt at the end of the big weekly shop is fifty pounds more than expected and you cannot spot why at the till.
options: Ask the cashier to scan the receipt while still at the till
Pay and check at home alone later
Leave the shopping and come back another day
Ask the person behind you to help spot the difference
payload.explanation: Cashier checks at the till can catch and void over-scans immediately before the transaction closes.

payload.snippet: The freezer aisle items packed at the start of the shop have been in the warm trolley for over forty minutes.
options: Pay first or put the frozen items in an insulated cool bag
Continue shopping for another hour with the frozen items still in
Refreeze the items once you get home
Put the frozen items back and choose fresh instead
payload.explanation: Frozen items warm to danger temperatures after thirty minutes — insulated bags or priority checkout protect them.

payload.snippet: Your parent has given you cash to pay but the machine only accepts contactless and you have no card.
options: Ask the cashier if they can take cash on the contactless till
Ask the next person in the queue to tap for you
Put the item back on the shelf and call home
Leave without buying the item at all
payload.explanation: Some shops can process cash on contactless-only tills — asking the cashier directly is the correct first move.

payload.snippet: The trolley coin has jammed in the coin slot at the supermarket entrance and you cannot get a trolley.
options: Tell the trolley supervisor immediately
Force the coin out with a sharp key
Buy a new coin from the kiosk nearby
Abandon your shopping plans for the day entirely
payload.explanation: The trolley supervisor has the right key to free a jammed coin without damaging the mechanism.

payload.snippet: A promotional sample stand is asking for your name and email to give you a free product.
options: Give only your first name or politely decline the data request
Give all your details happily for the free product
Give a fake email and made-up name
Ask a stranger next to you to give their details instead
payload.explanation: Personal data has real value — sharing only a first name or declining protects your privacy at a sample stand.

payload.snippet: Your teenage child has used the shared family supermarket account to add items to the basket and the final order has nearly sixty pounds of unrequested items.
options: Edit the order before the cut-off time and remove the unrequested items
Pay for everything and have the conversation after delivery
Cancel the entire order and reorder everything from scratch
Remove only the most expensive items and leave the rest
payload.explanation: Editing before the cut-off is the only way to avoid the overspend without cancelling the whole delivery.

payload.snippet: The online click-and-collect is ready but one heavy item was left out described as oversized for the bay with no prior notification.
options: Ask the service desk to arrange home delivery for the oversized item at no charge
Go home without the heavy item and reorder at full delivery price
Carry it yourself from the delivery bay without staff authorisation
Accept the loss and plan to buy it another day
payload.explanation: Same-day home delivery for the missing item is within the standard service commitment when size was not declared at ordering.

payload.snippet: The reduced yellow-sticker item you chose has a different product label stuck over the original price making the contents unclear.
options: Ask a staff member to confirm the product and its safety before buying
Buy it based on the outer visible label only
Assume it is the original product and use it at home
Remove the yellow sticker yourself to read the original label
payload.explanation: Staff can confirm whether the sticker placement was a pricing error or a genuine reduction and what is actually inside.

payload.snippet: The shop's budget range tinned tomatoes has doubled in price overnight and is now more expensive than the premium brand right next to it.
options: Check the premium brand size and unit price before choosing
Buy the budget tin anyway out of habit without checking
Write a complaint letter that evening about the price rise
Skip tinned tomatoes entirely this week
payload.explanation: Unit-price comparison is the correct move when a budget label becomes more expensive than its premium neighbour.

payload.snippet: Your child keeps getting out of bed every ten minutes asking for water, another story, and more cuddles after lights-out.
options: Set a firm lights-out routine with one final water and one story then stay consistent
Let them get up as many times as they like
Lock the bedroom door from the outside
Give a snack every time they get up
payload.explanation: A consistent boundary takes a few nights to settle but stops the repeated wake-ups.

payload.snippet: You have been struggling to fall asleep before midnight every night for two weeks despite going to bed at nine.
options: Switch off all screens an hour before bed and dim the room lights
Stay up until midnight every night to match your body clock
Take a long nap in the afternoon instead
Exercise hard right before lying down
payload.explanation: Screen light suppresses melatonin — cutting it an hour before bed shifts sleep onset earlier.

payload.snippet: Your six-year-old is terrified of monsters under the bed and checks under the bed every night before sleeping.
options: Do a calm monster check together and add a small nightlight
Tell them monsters are real but the light scares them off
Move the bed into the middle of the room
Take the bed apart so there is no under space
payload.explanation: Calm validation plus a nightlight addresses both the fear and the need for reassurance.

payload.snippet: The school has moved the start time to 8:15 and the whole family's bedtime routine is now running thirty minutes too late.
options: Move the entire evening routine thirty minutes earlier this week
Keep the old routine and just rush in the morning
Ask the school to push the start time back
Skip the morning shower to save thirty minutes
payload.explanation: Shifting the whole routine earlier preserves the sleep amount without morning panic.

payload.snippet: Your teenager insists on staying up until 1am on weekends and then struggles to wake on Monday morning.
options: Agree on a weekend bedtime no more than one hour later than weekday
Let them sleep until noon to compensate on Sunday
Wake them at 6am every weekend to keep the schedule
Allow the 1am bedtime because weekends are different
payload.explanation: A one-hour weekend shift avoids full social jet-lag on Monday.

payload.snippet: The family is on holiday in a different time zone and the children are waking at 3am and refusing to sleep.
options: Shift bedtime by one hour per day until it lines up with local time
Force the children into the local schedule on day one
Let them sleep whenever they naturally feel tired
Keep the home timezone throughout the holiday
