loads the shelf anyway and checks it regularly to see when it starts to loosen
leans the shelf against the wall as extra support and leaves the weak fixings
tells no one about the concern since the shelf seems fine for now
payload.explanation: Ensuring safety before loading the shelf prevents a future injury — fixing it now is the responsible action.

payload.snippet: Ava is part of a team building a set for the school play when the director wants the set to be taller than is safely possible with available materials.
options: explains the safety limit to the director and suggests a creative alternative
builds it to the unsafe height since the director has final authority
refuses to build anything taller at all and lets the project stop
builds it unsafely but adds extra backstage supports hoping they hold
payload.explanation: Explaining safety limits and offering a creative alternative is the professional and responsible approach.

payload.snippet: Ben finds that a large tree root is growing under the path in his garden and cracking the paving stones from below.

digs up the root himself using garden tools to remove the problem
breaks the cracked paving stones further to make them less of a trip hazard
lays new paving stones on top of the cracked ones to hide the problem
payload.explanation: Professional advice ensures the root is managed correctly without damaging the tree or causing further issues.

payload.snippet: Grace is working on a group building project when one team member insists on ignoring the safety briefing and working without protective equipment.
options: speaks to the team member directly and then asks the supervising adult to reinforce the rules
works alongside the team member hoping peer pressure encourages compliance
refuses to work until the team member puts on the correct equipment
takes photos as evidence in case an accident occurs later
payload.explanation: Speaking directly to the team member and then escalating to the supervising adult is the correct safety response.

payload.snippet: Max has designed a model structure but when it is built the real version has proportions that look very wrong compared to his drawings.

submits the model as built and adds a note that it differs from the plan
rebuilds the whole model from scratch with no explanation to his team
adjusts the drawings to match the model as built instead of the other way around
payload.explanation: Finding the scaling error in the measurements is the only way to understand and correct the design problem.

payload.snippet: Lily is helping build a treehouse when her dad wants to cut a large branch from the neighbour's tree to make space, without asking the neighbour.
options: tells her dad they should ask the neighbour's permission before cutting any part of their tree
says nothing since her dad is an adult and must know the property law on this
knocks on the neighbour's door herself to explain and ask permission for her dad
suggests her dad cut only the smallest branches since smaller cuts probably do not matter
payload.explanation: Permission must be sought before cutting branches from a neighbour's tree — it is a legal requirement in many places.

payload.snippet: Zoe notices that a newly built ramp at her school has been installed at too steep an angle for wheelchair users.

tries the ramp in a wheelchair herself to confirm whether it is a real problem
puts a sign on the ramp warning wheelchair users that it is steep
tells only her friends about the problem rather than reporting it officially
payload.explanation: Formally reporting an accessibility issue ensures it is assessed and corrected by the right people.

payload.snippet: Sam is building a model using hot glue and accidentally burns his finger on the glue gun.

puts butter on the burn since he heard it helps reduce the pain
ignores the burn and continues working so he does not fall behind
wraps the burn in sticky tape to protect it while he finishes the model
payload.explanation: Cool running water for ten minutes is the correct first aid for a burn — butter is harmful.

payload.snippet: Finn is designing a new layout for his bedroom and wants to knock down part of a wall to create more space.
options: asks his parents to consult a builder or architect about whether the wall is structural
knocks on the wall himself to decide whether it sounds hollow enough to remove
starts removing the wall before telling his parents since it is his own room
paints the wall a lighter colour to make the room feel bigger without knocking it down
payload.explanation: Consulting a professional before removing any wall is essential — structural walls support the building.

payload.snippet: Ruby is building a model city for a school geography project and her team cannot agree on the best layout for the road network.

lets the loudest team member decide so the argument ends quickly
builds two separate layouts and lets the teacher choose which one to display
presents a random layout and claims it represents an actual city's road network
payload.explanation: Research-based design is the most credible and educational approach for a school project.

payload.snippet: Owen is working on a renovation project and discovers asbestos-looking material in the ceiling while removing tiles.
options: stops work immediately and tells the adult in charge without touching the material
removes the suspect material himself wearing a dust mask he found in the shed
takes a sample of the material to identify it before deciding what to do
covers the area with new tiles since the material is safely enclosed now
payload.explanation: Asbestos is extremely hazardous — stopping work and alerting an adult immediately is the correct response.

payload.snippet: Sophie's class is building a model town and she notices that their bridge design will block access to the river for the model boats they are also building.
options: suggests modifying the bridge design to include a higher central arch
removes the bridge from the design entirely since the boats are more important
scales down all the boats to fit under the bridge as designed
leaves the conflict and lets the teacher decide which element should be changed
payload.explanation: Suggesting a modified design that solves both constraints shows creative problem-solving.

payload.snippet: Jake is building a scale model of a famous building from memory but keeps getting proportions wrong.
options: looks up reference photographs and dimensions to check his work
continues from memory since the model is his artistic interpretation
starts again from scratch each time he notices a proportion error
decides to build a fictional building so accuracy does not matter
payload.explanation: Using reference photographs and dimensions is the approach real architects use to model accurately.

payload.snippet: Chloe is painting a room and notices the first coat of paint has dripped and dried in streaks on the wall.
options: sands down the dried drips carefully before applying the second coat
paints the second coat over the dried drips hoping they become invisible
strips all the paint back to bare wall and starts the whole painting process again
tells her parents the room looks fine and the drips are barely visible
payload.explanation: Sanding down dried drips before a second coat gives a smooth professional finish.

payload.snippet: Ethan is participating in a design and build challenge when he discovers another team has copied his design directly.
options: speaks to the supervising teacher about what he has observed
tears up his own design so there is nothing left to copy from
accuses the other team loudly in front of everyone participating
redesigns his model completely in a different direction without telling anyone why
payload.explanation: Speaking to the supervising teacher is the fair and formal way to address design copying in a competition.

payload.snippet: Isla is building a model tower with a team when a disagreement about leadership causes the whole group to stop working.
options: suggests the group divide roles clearly so everyone has a specific responsibility
takes full leadership herself since someone needs to take charge now
tells the teacher the group is not functioning and asks for a new team
leaves the group to work alone even though this breaks the team assignment rules
payload.explanation: Dividing roles clearly reduces leadership conflict by giving everyone defined ownership.

payload.snippet: Leo's class is debating a book character's decision and he holds an opinion that is completely different from everyone else in the group.
options: explains his view calmly and with evidence from the text
stays quiet so he does not seem strange in front of everyone
changes his opinion to match the majority view without actually believing it
argues so forcefully that the debate stops being enjoyable for others
payload.explanation: Sharing a well-supported different opinion is exactly what book discussions are designed for.

payload.snippet: Mia discovers a book that has been officially removed from some school libraries and is very curious about why this was decided.
options: reads the book and then researches the reasons it was challenged or removed
reads it secretly to see if the content is as shocking as rumoured
refuses to read it since it must be wrong if schools removed it
asks a parent to explain the reasons without reading the book herself
payload.explanation: Reading the book and researching the context is the thoughtful and critical approach.

payload.snippet: Kai has been rereading the same comfort book every week for a whole year and a friend says he is missing out on many other great stories.
options: agrees to try one new book while still keeping the comfort book for certain moments
ignores the advice completely since the comfort book is his choice to make
gives up the comfort book entirely to prove he can move on from it
reads a new book but does not engage with it since he prefers his own
payload.explanation: Balancing comfort reading with new books is a healthy middle path.

payload.snippet: Nina has been asked to write a creative story for class and the assigned theme makes her personally uncomfortable.
options: asks the teacher privately if she can explore the theme in a different way
writes the story as assigned even though it causes her genuine distress
refuses to complete the assignment without explaining why to the teacher
writes a completely different story and hopes the teacher does not notice the theme change
payload.explanation: Asking the teacher privately is the mature and communicative way to handle a personally difficult assignment.

payload.snippet: Tom discovers his favourite author is coming to his school for a special talk but it is at the exact same time as his most important exam.
options: attends the exam and asks if notes or a recording from the talk can be shared later
skips the exam to attend the author talk since the chance is once in a lifetime
tries to do both by running between rooms every few minutes
tells the exam board the author visit was more important to his education
payload.explanation: Attending the exam is the responsible decision — a recording or notes can preserve much of the experience.

payload.snippet: Ava reads a library book and strongly disagrees with the values the story appears to be teaching its young readers.
options: writes a thoughtful review explaining her concerns about the values in the book
tears out the pages she most disagrees with to prevent others from reading them
tells the librarian the book should be banned immediately
says nothing since the book is published and her opinion will not matter
payload.explanation: A thoughtful written review is a legitimate and respectful way to express disagreement with a book's values.

payload.snippet: Ben is in a book club when one member dominates every discussion and talks over everyone else whenever they try to contribute.
options: suggests the group tries a format where each person speaks in turn with equal time
stops contributing since the dominant member always gets the final word
argues with the dominant member loudly to challenge their control of the discussion
leaves the book club without explaining why he is no longer attending
payload.explanation: Suggesting a structured taking-turns format is a constructive solution that helps everyone participate.

payload.snippet: Grace finds a handwritten note tucked inside a library book that appears to be a message from a previous reader in emotional distress.
options: shows the note to a trusted adult librarian or teacher immediately
keeps the note private since it is a personal message between readers
writes a reply note and tucks it back in the book hoping the same person finds it
posts a photo of the note online asking if anyone recognises the handwriting
payload.explanation: Showing the note to a trusted adult is the correct welfare response — the person may still need support.

payload.snippet: Max's school has decided to remove a book from the library that had a very meaningful impact on him personally.
options: asks a teacher to explain the decision and writes a respectful case for keeping the book
takes the book home before it is removed so at least one copy survives
organises a student petition to shame the school into reversing the decision publicly
accepts the decision since the school has authority over the library collection
payload.explanation: Asking for an explanation and writing a respectful case engages with the process constructively.

payload.snippet: Lily's book group assignment requires everyone to read a book she finds too upsetting and distressing to continue reading.
options: tells her teacher privately that she is finding the book difficult and asks for guidance
pushes through the whole book alone without telling anyone about her distress
refuses to complete the assignment and says nothing about why to the teacher
reads only a summary online and pretends she read the full book
payload.explanation: Telling the teacher privately allows for accommodation or support — no one should read in silence through genuine distress.

payload.snippet: Zoe is writing a story for a class project and realises partway through that she has included details clearly from her friend's private life without permission.
options: changes those details so the connection to her friend is no longer recognisable
continues writing since her friend will probably be flattered to be in a story
asks her friend permission after writing it rather than before
leaves the story as written but changes her friend's name only
payload.explanation: Changing the details before submission protects her friend's privacy and avoids future hurt.

payload.snippet: Sam realises halfway through writing his class story that the plot is almost identical to a famous published book he read last year.
options: acknowledges the influence, develops his own unique angle, and submits his version with a note
submits the story pretending it is entirely original since no one will check
scraps the whole story and starts again with a completely different idea
submits the story without acknowledging the influence and changes only the names
payload.explanation: Acknowledging an influence while adding your own angle is honest and shows literary self-awareness.

payload.snippet: Finn's story submitted for the school newsletter has been significantly edited by the teacher without his knowledge or permission.
options: asks the teacher politely why changes were made and whether he can discuss them
asks for his story to be withdrawn entirely if he cannot approve edits first
publicly objects to the changes at the next class and says his work was censored
accepts the edited version without comment since the teacher has authority
payload.explanation: Asking politely for an explanation is the mature and communicative response to unexpected editing.

payload.snippet: Ruby reads a published story where a character from her own cultural background is portrayed in a stereotyped and inaccurate way.
options: writes a review or letter explaining clearly how the portrayal is inaccurate and harmful
refuses to ever read that author's books again and tells everyone to do the same
tears out the pages in the book with the stereotyped portrayal
reports the book to the school library asking for its immediate removal
payload.explanation: Articulating why a portrayal is inaccurate and harmful creates productive understanding.

payload.snippet: Owen is asked to present his book review to the class but the book had a very sad and personal emotional impact on him that he is not sure he can talk about in front of everyone.
options: tells his teacher beforehand so they can consider an alternative or provide support
presents the review anyway without mentioning his personal connection to the themes
refuses to present without explaining his reason to the teacher
presents someone else's review of a different book hoping the teacher will not notice
payload.explanation: Telling the teacher beforehand allows an adult to offer support or a reasonable adjustment.

payload.snippet: Sophie discovers her class will perform a dramatisation of a story she finds extremely dull and does not want to participate in at all.
options: participates with her best effort even though it is not her favourite story
refuses to take part in the performance at all since she dislikes the story
participates but complains loudly throughout every rehearsal
tries to persuade the teacher to change the story to one she prefers
payload.explanation: Participating fully even in work you find unexciting is part of being a respectful and reliable team member.

payload.snippet: Jake writes a humorous story for class that accidentally reveals something quite embarrassing about himself that he did not intend to share.
options: edits the story to remove the personal detail before submitting or presenting it
submits the story anyway and hopes no one makes the connection
tells the class the story is pure fiction even though it is not fully true
withdraws the story entirely and submits nothing rather than editing it
payload.explanation: Editing before submission is the sensible solution — there is no need to withdraw the whole piece.

payload.snippet: Chloe discovers that her school's annual storytelling competition has been won by students from the same friendship group for the last four years running.
options: asks a teacher how entries are judged and whether the process is transparently fair
accuses the judging panel of favouritism without any evidence at all
decides not to enter since she assumes the competition is not fair regardless
enters and submits a great story, trusting the process while being observant
payload.explanation: Asking about the judging process is a fair and constructive question that a teacher can answer.

payload.snippet: Ethan reads a book that genuinely changes the way he thinks about something he has always believed without question.
options: thinks carefully about both his old belief and what the book says before deciding what he now thinks
immediately abandons everything he used to believe based on one book alone
refuses to accept the book's argument since he has always believed the opposite
tells everyone his beliefs have changed and they should all read the same book
payload.explanation: Thinking carefully about both perspectives before changing beliefs shows mature critical thinking.

payload.snippet: Isla's creative writing piece has been entered into a national competition by her teacher without asking her permission first.
options: asks her teacher to explain the decision and discusses whether she is comfortable proceeding
feels flattered and decides it is fine since it is a good opportunity
demands her entry be withdrawn immediately without discussing it first
contacts the competition organisers herself to withdraw without telling her teacher
payload.explanation: Asking for an explanation and discussing comfort is the mature way to handle this — it opens dialogue rather than creating conflict.

payload.snippet: Leo is on a supervised open water swim when he starts to feel sick and very nauseous halfway through the course.
options: signals to the safety kayak immediately and is helped out of the water
pushes through to the end since he has trained hard and does not want to give up
slows his pace right down and hopes the nausea passes before the finish
calls out to other swimmers near him to ask if they feel okay too
payload.explanation: Signalling to the safety kayak immediately is the correct response — nausea during open water swimming can escalate quickly.

payload.snippet: Mia witnesses a child fall into a deep part of the lake while on a nature walk and no adults are immediately visible.
options: shouts for adult help loudly and throws a floating object to the child if one is nearby
jumps into the lake herself to attempt a rescue
runs to find an adult but moves away from the lake where the child fell in
shouts instructions to the child about how to swim to safety
payload.explanation: Shouting for help and throwing a floating object is the correct approach — jumping in without training often results in two casualties.

payload.snippet: Kai discovers that a popular swimming spot near his town does not have any warning signs about strong underwater currents.
options: reports the absence of warning signs to the local council or water authority
tells his friends about the currents so they can be careful when swimming there
puts up his own handmade warning signs at the location himself
assumes the currents must not be that dangerous since no signs have been put up yet
payload.explanation: Reporting the absence of warning signs to the relevant authority triggers an official safety review.

payload.snippet: Nina is at a water park when a much younger child gets separated from their parent near a large wave pool.
options: holds the child's hand and takes them to the nearest lifeguard immediately
looks around the area for a parent and calls the child's name loudly
waits near the child while waving to get a lifeguard's attention from a distance
takes the child to the park information desk since it is further away but more official
payload.explanation: Taking the child directly to the nearest lifeguard is the fastest and most reliable course of action.

payload.snippet: Tom is kayaking with his school group when another student's kayak overturns and the student cannot right it despite trying several times.
options: paddles alongside and holds the upturned kayak steady while calling the instructor
tries to tip his own kayak to demonstrate how to right it for the student
paddles quickly to tell the instructor while leaving the student with the overturned kayak
helps the student climb onto the upturned kayak hull to wait for the instructor
payload.explanation: Paddling alongside, stabilising the kayak, and calling the instructor is the correct buddy response.

payload.snippet: Ava is at a public pool when she notices the water appears a different colour than usual and smells strange.
options: tells a pool staff member about what she has noticed before entering the water
gets into the water since the pool staff have presumably already checked it
touches the water and tastes a small amount to see if it is really different
tells other swimmers about the unusual water before telling any staff
payload.explanation: Telling pool staff immediately means they can check chemical levels before anyone swims in potentially unsafe water.

payload.snippet: Ben is at a beach resort when he sees a snorkeller in difficulty far from shore but lifeguards are not on duty.
options: calls the emergency services and throws a rope or float from shore if available
swims out to the snorkeller to help since no lifeguards are available
shouts to other beach visitors to ask if anyone is a trained lifeguard
waves to the snorkeller hoping they will swim to shore on their own
payload.explanation: Calling emergency services immediately and throwing equipment from shore is the correct non-swimming rescue approach.

payload.snippet: Grace is helping run a children's water sports day when she notices a child wearing an incorrectly fitted life jacket.
options: helps the child adjust the life jacket correctly before any activity begins
lets the child continue since the life jacket is at least being worn
asks the child's parent to check and adjust the jacket themselves
replaces the incorrectly fitted jacket with a larger one that will fit loosely
payload.explanation: Correctly fitting a life jacket before any activity is a non-negotiable safety requirement.

payload.snippet: Max is paddleboarding on a river when he hears a distress whistle from around a river bend and cannot see who blew it.
options: paddles toward the sound and calls out while preparing to assist safely
paddles away from the sound since the current around bends can be dangerous
blows his own whistle back to signal he has heard them and waits for them to come to him
gets out of the water on the bank and runs along the path toward the sound instead
payload.explanation: Paddling toward the sound while calling out and preparing to assist safely is the correct water rescue response.

payload.snippet: Lily is at a swimming competition when she realises another swimmer in her heat has started before the starting signal.
options: continues her own race from the official start and tells the official after the race
stops swimming to point out the false start to the race officials
speeds up immediately to catch up before the other swimmer gains more advantage
deliberately swims more slowly to protest the unfair advantage of the other swimmer
payload.explanation: Continuing her own race and telling an official after is the correct competitive response.

payload.snippet: Zoe's family is visiting a river when her father suggests swimming across it despite a visible strong current.
options: expresses her concern clearly and asks to check local conditions first
says nothing since her father is an adult and has presumably assessed the risk
refuses to watch and asks to wait somewhere else away from the river
agrees to swim if her father says it is safe since he is the adult
payload.explanation: Expressing concern and asking to check local conditions is the correct safety assertiveness response regardless of who is suggesting the swim.

payload.snippet: Sam's swimming club wants to organise a night swim in the sea and the proposal has no formal safety plan.
options: raises the need for a safety plan before agreeing to participate or recruiting others
declines to participate but says nothing about the absence of a safety plan
asks the club leader to add at least one person with a torch to the plan
participates since the other club members also seem unconcerned about safety
payload.explanation: Raising the need for a formal safety plan before any commitment is the responsible action.

payload.snippet: Finn is on a canal boat holiday when he accidentally falls overboard into the cold water.
options: treads water, calls for help, and swims toward the nearest bank calmly
swims after the moving boat since the bank is further away
dives under the water to find the boat's ladder from below
panics and thrashes toward the nearest person on the bank
payload.explanation: Treading water calmly, calling for help, and swimming to the bank is the correct cold water immersion response.

payload.snippet: Ruby's family is at a beach when her younger sibling complains of numbness and tingling in their legs after being in the cold sea for a long time.
options: takes the sibling out of the water and wraps them in warm towels immediately
assumes the numbness is from the cold and that it will pass when the sibling dries off
tells the sibling to move their legs more in the water to restore circulation
takes the sibling out and rubs their legs vigorously to warm them up quickly
payload.explanation: Removing from cold water and wrapping in towels is the correct hypothermia prevention response — vigorous rubbing can be harmful.

payload.snippet: Owen is on a boat trip when another passenger is sick over the side and begins to lean dangerously far over the edge.
options: holds the person's clothing gently and calls for the boat's crew to assist
tries to lift the sick person back upright by their shoulders
shouts to crew members who are at the other end of the boat
holds the railing with one hand and the person's arm with the other
payload.explanation: Holding clothing and calling for crew is the safest response — leaning over to assist someone leaning overboard is very dangerous.

payload.snippet: Sophie is at a lake when she sees two children arguing about who owns a watercraft and one child pushes the other off it into deep water.
options: tells a supervising adult immediately and monitors the child in the water
jumps in to help the child who is in the water
shouts at the child who pushed to get into the water and help
throws the child in the water a life ring from the shore
payload.explanation: Telling a supervising adult immediately while monitoring is the correct response — throwing a life ring is also a good secondary action.

payload.snippet: Jake is swimming at the pool and notices a child at the bottom of the pool who is not moving.
options: shouts for a lifeguard immediately and points to show exactly where the child is
dives in and attempts to bring the child to the surface himself
blows a poolside whistle and then dives in to assist
runs to find the lifeguard rather than alerting them from poolside
payload.explanation: Shouting for the lifeguard and pointing is faster than any alternative — trained lifeguards respond in seconds.

payload.snippet: Chloe is at a waterfall viewpoint when a tourist leans over a safety railing to take a photo and begins to slip.
options: shouts a clear warning and reaches out to help stabilise them if safe to do so
grabs the tourist forcefully to pull them back before they slip further
runs to get a park ranger since she should not intervene herself
shouts for everyone to move away in case the tourist falls
payload.explanation: Shouting a warning and offering stabilising help if safe is the correct immediate response.

payload.snippet: Ethan's school swimming gala team finishes third and his teammate is devastated and refuses to get out of the pool.
options: gets out himself and goes over to support his teammate kindly from poolside
stays in the pool with his teammate to show solidarity and comfort them
tells his teammate they need to get out of the pool before they cause an issue
tells the teacher the teammate is refusing to come out and needs help
payload.explanation: Getting out himself and offering poolside support is kind and appropriate without creating a pool safety issue.

payload.snippet: Isla is at an outdoor water park when lightning is spotted in the distance and the park starts to clear everyone from the water.
options: gets out immediately and moves to the indoor shelter area as directed
stays in the shallow toddler pool since lightning usually strikes the tallest things
argues that the lightning is far away and asks staff to let her finish her final ride
waits to see if other visitors get out before making her decision
payload.explanation: Getting out immediately when directed during a lightning warning is non-negotiable water safety.

payload.snippet: Tom is sledging down a steep hill when he notices a younger child standing at the bottom directly in his path.
options: He rolls sideways off the sledge into the snow to stop himself.
He shouts loudly and hopes the child moves in time.
He speeds up to fly over the child's head safely.
He pulls the rope hard so the sledge shoots forward faster.
payload.explanation: Rolling off is the fastest way to stop without hitting the child.

payload.snippet: Anna has been building a snow fort for an hour when she notices her fingertips have gone white and she cannot feel them.
options: She goes inside immediately and warms her hands slowly with cool water.
She rubs her fingertips together very hard to get the feeling back.
She holds her fingers over the hot tap to warm them quickly.
She puts her hands in her coat pockets and keeps building.
payload.explanation: White numb fingertips are a sign of frostnip requiring slow gentle rewarming.

payload.snippet: The family dog escapes through the garden gate into deep snow and will not come when called.
options: She gets a lead, coat, and her boots and fetches the dog calmly.
She chases the dog in her socks across the snowy garden.
She calls loudly from the door until the dog gets too cold.
She waits inside and hopes the dog finds its own way back.
payload.explanation: Calm retrieval with proper clothing is the safe way to get the dog.

payload.snippet: Jake notices the elderly neighbour's path is buried under thick snow and she is trying to chip at it herself.
options: He asks if she would like him to shovel it for her.
He watches from his window to see if she manages.
He tells his mum to call the council to send someone.
He waits until she finishes and then compliments the path.
payload.explanation: Offering to help an elderly neighbour is the neighbourly and safe response.

payload.snippet: The school bus skids on black ice and stops at an angle across the road, blocking both lanes.
options: The driver keeps everyone seated and calls for emergency assistance.
The driver opens the doors and tells children to walk to school.
The driver reverses quickly to try to straighten the bus.
The driver asks older children to push from outside to free it.
payload.explanation: Keeping passengers seated and calling emergency services is the correct bus incident response.

payload.snippet: Clara is ice skating for the first time and falls, scraping her palm on the rough ice surface.
options: She skates to the barrier, takes off her skate, and checks the wound.
She carries on skating and shows everyone her palm as proof.
She sits on the ice and waits for the session to end.
She takes off both skates and walks home in her socks.
payload.explanation: Getting off the ice to inspect an injury is the correct response.

payload.snippet: Oliver's friend suggests crossing a frozen lake as a shortcut to the other side of the park.
options: He refuses and says they should walk around the long way.
He tests the ice with his foot first and then crosses slowly.
He agrees but says they should hold hands while crossing.
He throws a stick to see if the ice can hold weight.
payload.explanation: Frozen lakes are unpredictable and should never be crossed for a shortcut.

payload.snippet: The electricity cuts out during a severe blizzard, leaving the house dark and the heating off.
options: Mum lights candles safely, wraps everyone in blankets, and turns the gas off at the meter.
Mum runs the car engine in the garage to use the car heater.
Mum opens the oven door to heat the kitchen overnight.
Mum turns on all electric heaters on extension leads just in case.
payload.explanation: Candles, blankets, and safe gas shutoff are correct blizzard power-cut responses.

payload.snippet: She is wearing ice skates and needs the toilet but cannot figure out how to walk across the rubber matting safely.
options: She takes small careful steps with her blade guards on.
She takes off her skates and runs to the toilet in her socks.
She asks a stranger to carry her across to the toilet.
She shuffles across on her heels with her toes in the air.
payload.explanation: Blade guards protect the surface and slow movement makes skates walkable.

payload.snippet: Ben's snowball fight gets out of hand when a ball with an ice core hits a friend in the face hard.
options: He stops the fight immediately and checks if his friend is hurt.
He apologises from a distance and keeps throwing softer balls.
He declares himself the winner and goes inside to celebrate.
He explains the ice core was an accident and blames the weather.
payload.explanation: Stopping and checking for injury is the first response when someone gets hurt.

payload.snippet: A fox appears in the snowy garden looking thin and unable to find food in the frozen ground.
options: She puts out some cooked chicken pieces well away from the house.
She tries to bring the fox inside to keep it warm overnight.
She shoos it away so it does not get used to people.
She pours out a big bowl of milk for the fox on the step.
payload.explanation: Putting appropriate food out at a distance helps wildlife without causing dependency.

payload.snippet: The pond where they usually feed ducks is frozen solid and the ducks are huddled at the edge.
options: They scatter duck pellets on a clear patch of ground near the bank.
They pour hot water on the pond to break a gap in the ice.
They chip at the ice with a stick to make a pool for the ducks.
They throw bread onto the ice so the ducks slide to reach it.
payload.explanation: Scattering pellets on ground near the bank feeds ducks safely in winter.

payload.snippet: Maya's class is doing a winter science project and she wants to measure the exact depth of the overnight snowfall.
options: She uses a ruler in three different spots and averages the readings.
She guesses by how deep her boot sinks when she stamps down.
She measures once from the deepest drift in the garden.
She asks the teacher what the weather forecast says for snowfall depth.
payload.explanation: Multiple measurements and averaging gives accurate snowfall depth data.

payload.snippet: A heavy snowfall has bent the greenhouse frame badly and the roof is close to collapsing.
options: Dad brushes snow off the roof before entering the greenhouse.
Dad goes inside the greenhouse to check the plants first.
Dad props the bent frame up with a garden chair from inside.
Dad waits until spring and orders a replacement greenhouse frame.
payload.explanation: Removing snow from outside prevents collapse before entering the structure.

payload.snippet: Jack slips on ice outside the supermarket and lands hard on his wrist, which is now very painful and swollen.
options: He goes inside and asks staff to call a first aider.
He flexes his wrist in circles to test if it is just bruised.
He holds snow against his wrist and walks slowly home.
He completes his shopping and goes to a doctor the following day.
payload.explanation: Swollen painful wrists after impact need professional first aid assessment.

payload.snippet: Lily finds the garden pond has frozen over completely and worries about the fish underneath.
options: She melts a small hole in the ice with a pan of hot water.
She breaks the ice with a heavy rock to free the fish.
She brings all the fish inside in a bucket of pond water.
She adds boiling water to the whole pond to melt the ice fast.
payload.explanation: Gentle hot water melts a breathing hole without shocking the fish.

payload.snippet: Tom is walking home through heavy snowfall when he realises he has taken a wrong turn and does not recognise the street.
options: He stops, stays calm, and calls home for directions.
He keeps walking quickly in the same direction hoping to find a landmark.
He knocks on a random door and asks to wait inside until the snow stops.
He retraces his steps at a run before his footprints fill in.
payload.explanation: Stopping and calling home is the safe response when lost in bad weather.

payload.snippet: The forecast warns of a severe blizzard tomorrow and grandma lives alone on a rural road.
options: The family drives to collect her and bring her to stay for the duration.
They call her daily and trust the council to check on her.
They send her a supply kit by courier and hope it arrives in time.
They wait until the blizzard starts to assess how bad it really is.
payload.explanation: Collecting a vulnerable person before a blizzard is the safest precaution.

payload.snippet: Oliver has been wearing wet gloves all afternoon and his hands are very cold, red, and painful.
options: He goes inside, removes the gloves, and warms his hands gently with warm water.
He keeps the wet gloves on because removing them would be colder.
He holds his hands over a direct flame to get the heat back quickly.
He runs his hands under the cold tap to wake the feeling up.
payload.explanation: Removing wet gloves and using warm (not hot) water is the correct cold-hand treatment.

payload.snippet: A blizzard starts while Clara's family is on a motorway far from any exit.
options: Dad slows right down, puts hazard lights on, and follows the vehicle ahead carefully.
Dad pulls fully off the road and turns the engine off to save fuel.
Dad accelerates to reach the next exit before the snow gets worse.
Dad reverses along the hard shoulder to the exit they already passed.
payload.explanation: Slowing, using hazards, and following the car ahead are correct blizzard-driving rules.

payload.snippet: Tom and his friends have been cycling in the summer heat for three hours without a break when one friend suddenly stops, says he feels sick and confused, and his skin feels very hot and dry.
options: Tom gets him into shade immediately, calls 999, and uses water to cool the back of his neck while they wait.
Tom pours cold water over his friend's head and tells him to lie in the sun to stay awake.
Tom gives him an energy drink and asks him to eat something quickly to raise his blood sugar.
Tom sits him upright against his bike, fans him with a map, and calls his parents.
payload.explanation: Hot dry skin with confusion signals heat stroke — 999, shade, and cool water to the neck are urgent.

payload.snippet: Anna is at an outdoor music festival when a friend who has been in the sun all day collapses. The friend is conscious but very pale, sweating heavily, and says her vision is going blurry.
options: Anna calls for the medical tent team, moves her friend into shade, lays her down with legs raised, and gives her water in small sips.
Anna fans her friend briskly, gives her all her remaining water, and calls her parents.
Anna walks her friend slowly to the medical tent, supporting her weight on one side.
Anna pours her friend's water bottle over her face and head to cool her down quickly.
payload.explanation: Pale sweating dizziness is heat exhaustion — lay down with legs raised, shade, small sips, and call medical staff.

payload.snippet: Jake is helping his neighbour paint the garden fence in direct sun when he notices the neighbour has stopped moving, is sitting slumped in the chair, and does not respond to his name.
options: Jake shouts for help, calls 999, tilts the neighbour's head back to open the airway, and checks for breathing.
Jake pats the neighbour's cheeks firmly and asks if he is okay before deciding what to do.
Jake runs inside the house to get water and a cool towel for the neighbour.
Jake calls the neighbour's wife first because she will know what medication he takes.
payload.explanation: Unresponsive means 999 first, then airway-check — not fetching water or calling family.

payload.snippet: Clara's family has parked their car and gone for a walk, accidentally leaving the windows up and her younger brother asleep in the back seat on a day that is now thirty-four degrees.
options: She tells her parents immediately, who run back and open the car doors at once and cool her brother with water.
She knocks on the window to wake her brother so he can attract attention.
She waits at the car while her parents carry on walking as her brother is asleep and calm.
She calls the ice cream van to park next to the car so the cold side keeps it cooler.
payload.explanation: A child locked in a hot car is a life-threatening emergency requiring immediate adult return and ventilation.

payload.snippet: Oliver is mowing the lawn in the summer heat and finds a young hedgehog lying still on its side in the open grass during daylight hours.
options: He leaves it in place, stops mowing that patch, places a box loosely over it, and calls a wildlife rescue line for advice.
He picks it up, brings it inside to a warm spot, and gives it bread and milk.
He moves it to a hedgerow with his gloved hands and checks on it later that evening.
He leaves it completely alone and resumes mowing around it carefully.
payload.explanation: Hedgehogs active in daylight and lying still are likely injured or ill — wildlife rescue advice is needed.

payload.snippet: Maya is in charge of five younger children at a summer party in the garden when she notices dark clouds rolling in rapidly and hears distant thunder.
options: She calmly leads all children inside the house and informs the hosting adult immediately.
She lets the children finish the current game and then brings them inside at its natural end.
She moves the children to a large tree at the garden edge for natural shelter.
She counts the seconds between lightning and thunder to judge if it is close enough to worry about.
payload.explanation: Thunder means lightning is present — all outdoor supervision responsibilities require immediate indoor evacuation.

payload.snippet: Ben is at the beach building sandcastles when his younger cousin digs a deep narrow trench nearby and then climbs inside to hide. The trench walls suddenly collapse inward covering the cousin's legs and waist.
options: Ben calls loudly for adults, kneels at the edge without going in, and begins carefully removing sand from around his cousin's waist while adults run over.
Ben jumps into the trench to pull his cousin free as quickly as possible.
Ben runs to the sea to get a bucket of water to make the sand softer and easier to remove.
Ben tells his cousin to push with his hands to free himself from the collapsed walls.
payload.explanation: Sand collapses can be deadly — calling adults, staying out of the trench, and careful sand removal are correct.

payload.snippet: The family's outdoor paddling pool has been sitting uncovered in the sun for five days and has developed green algae on the base.
options: Mum empties it completely, scrubs it with a diluted disinfectant, and rinses it thoroughly before refilling.
Mum adds extra pool chlorine tablets and lets the children play while the chemicals work.
Mum lets the sun kill the algae for another day as UV is a natural disinfectant.
Mum skims the visible algae off the top with a net and refills with clean water to dilute it.
payload.explanation: Algae in paddling pools require emptying, disinfection, and full rinse before refilling — not chemical top-ups.

payload.snippet: Tom is helping at the community summer fete when an elderly volunteer faint in the drinks queue on what is the hottest day of the year.
options: He lowers her gently to the ground, elevates her legs, calls for the first-aider, and keeps her cool with a wet cloth on her forehead.
He helps her to a chair and gets her a glass of cold water to drink straight away.
He fans her face vigorously and asks nearby people to help him walk her to the shade.
He lays her flat on her back, puts her arms by her sides, and calls for an ambulance.
payload.explanation: Fainting in heat requires: down to the ground, legs raised, first-aider called, cool compress — not sitting up.

payload.snippet: Anna is walking her dog at noon when it lies down suddenly on the path and refuses to move, panting rapidly.
options: She picks the dog up if she can, or sits with it in any available shade, pours water over its paws and head, and calls the vet.
She waits for the dog to recover and then continues the walk at a slower pace.
She tries to encourage it with a treat and walks it to the nearest water fountain.
She puts the lead down and jogs ahead to find the nearest shaded bench for it.
payload.explanation: A dog collapsing mid-walk in heat is a medical emergency — shade, cooling, and a vet call are urgent.

payload.snippet: Jake finds a dead bird near the garden bird bath on a very hot day and wonders if it was the water.
options: He empties and scrubs the bird bath and refills it with fresh cool water, then washes his hands thoroughly.
He covers the bird bath so other birds cannot drink from it until he checks.
He tips extra water in to dilute any contamination that might be in the bath.
He leaves everything as it is to avoid disturbing the scene before he does more research.
payload.explanation: Stagnant bird bath water breeds bacteria — cleaning and refilling prevents further harm to garden birds.

payload.snippet: Clara's younger sibling plays barefoot on the hot patio and comes inside crying with a blister forming on one foot.
options: Clara runs cool water over the blister gently, covers it with a clean dressing, and tells a parent.
Clara pops the blister with a clean pin and covers it with a plaster.
Clara applies butter from the kitchen to soothe the hot skin on the foot.
Clara puts ice from the freezer directly on the blister to cool it down fast.
payload.explanation: Cool water, not ice or butter, soothes a heat blister; do not pop it — cover and tell an adult.

payload.snippet: Ben's family is camping when they find an abandoned campfire left by a previous group that is still smouldering the next morning.
options: Dad douses it with water, stirs the ashes with a stick until no steam rises, and reports it to the campsite warden.
Dad covers the smouldering area with soil to smother it and leaves it to cool.
Dad leaves it alone as smouldering fires burn themselves out without causing a wildfire.
Dad uses a bucket of sand from the campfire kit to cover the hot embers.
payload.explanation: Full water dousing, stirring to ash, steam check, and reporting are the correct abandoned campfire steps.

payload.snippet: The class is on a summer trip to a nature reserve when a student is stung on the neck by an unknown insect and the sting site swells rapidly to twice the size of a normal sting.
options: The teacher calls 999, keeps the student calm and still, asks if she has an EpiPen, and loosens anything tight around the neck.
The teacher applies antihistamine cream from the first-aid kit and gives the student water.
The teacher takes a photo to show the doctor later and monitors the swelling carefully.
The teacher calls the school office for advice and asks a parent helper to drive the student to a walk-in centre.
payload.explanation: Rapid large-area swelling near the airway after a sting warrants 999 and airway monitoring — not cream or driving.

payload.snippet: Oliver is at an outdoor film screening when the grass fire alarm sounds. He can smell smoke but cannot see any flames from his position.
options: He gathers the people near him and walks calmly toward the nearest exit markers.
He waits to see flames before reacting so he does not cause unnecessary panic.
He climbs onto his picnic chair to look for the smoke source and assess the risk.
He asks the people around him to vote on whether to stay or go.
payload.explanation: Smoke without visible flames is still a fire alarm — immediate calm evacuation is always correct.

payload.snippet: Jake is mowing the sports-field grass when the mower kicks out a stone that shatters the glass panel of the groundskeeper's shed twelve metres away. No one is hurt but the broken glass has scattered across the footpath children use to reach the cricket nets.
options: He stops the mower, marks both ends of the glass-covered path with cones, and reports the damage and the hazard to the groundskeeper before resuming.
He sweeps the visible pieces off the path with his boot and carries on mowing.
He puts a sign saying 'watch your step' at one end of the path and continues his schedule.
He completes the mowing first so the field is safe and then reports the shed damage.
payload.explanation: Marking the glass hazard and reporting it before resuming work is the correct duty-of-care response.

payload.snippet: Clara is at an outdoor summer market when she notices an unattended backpack sitting under a stall table that no vendor or visitor has approached in over fifteen minutes.
options: She informs the nearest market steward or security officer immediately without touching the bag.
She opens the bag carefully to check if it belongs to anyone or contains anything harmful.
She picks it up and hands it to the nearest stall holder so it does not block the path.
She waits another fifteen minutes to see if an owner returns before doing anything.
payload.explanation: Unattended bags in a public place should be reported to security without being touched.

payload.snippet: Ben's younger sibling is playing in the paddling pool when she slips climbing out and scrapes her chin on the plastic edge, producing a small but freely bleeding cut.
options: Ben lifts her out, applies gentle pressure with a clean cloth, and tells a parent immediately.
Ben pours pool water over the cut to rinse it and tells her to press the edge herself.
Ben goes to get a plaster and leaves his sibling sitting on the wet pool edge alone.
Ben applies pressure with his hand and asks a neighbour to call an ambulance right away.
payload.explanation: Gentle pressure with a clean cloth controls small bleeding while an adult is summoned.

payload.snippet: Maya is helping organise a summer charity run when a participant returns early and reports a runner is lying by the path two kilometres out, conscious and confused, and very pale.
options: Maya calls 999 immediately, sends a marshal in a buggy to the location with a first-aid kit, and stops further runners from being dispatched until the situation is clear.
Maya asks the returned participant to run back to help while she finishes her route-marshal duties.
Maya drives the route herself to locate the runner and assess what first aid is needed.
Maya tells the race director and waits for his decision before acting.
payload.explanation: A collapsed runner with confusion is a 999-level emergency requiring immediate first-aid dispatch and a race pause.

payload.snippet: Oliver is doing a summer litter-pick in the park when he finds a used syringe half-hidden in a patch of grass near the children's play area.
options: He marks the spot with a stick, keeps others away, and calls the local council's sharps-collection line.
He picks it up carefully with a plastic bag over his hand and puts it in the nearest bin.
He uses tongs from his kit to move it into the hedgerow where children will not find it.
He photographs it and posts it to the council's social media page asking for urgent collection.
payload.explanation: Discarded syringes must be reported to a professional sharps-collection service — never handle them yourself.

payload.snippet: Tom is delivering newspapers on his bike when a flash downpour starts. He has twelve more streets to cover and the papers are in an open basket getting drenched.
options: He pulls under the nearest shelter, wraps the remaining papers in the plastic liners from the delivered ones, and continues delivering once the worst passes.
He delivers as fast as he can and apologises to each customer about the wet papers.
He abandons the remaining papers at a community noticeboard and heads home.
He phones the newsagent to ask whether he should continue or return with the wet papers.
payload.explanation: Protecting remaining stock and waiting for the worst to pass keeps the papers readable and the job done.

payload.snippet: Anna is leading a group of eight-year-olds on a nature walk when steady rain turns to a severe downpour with thunder. They are in an open field with no building in sight.
options: She moves the group to the lowest point in the field away from isolated trees and has them crouch low in a spread-out cluster, not touching each other.
She takes the group to the tall hedgerow at the field edge for maximum shelter.
She runs the group to the nearest large isolated oak tree to shelter underneath.
She tells the children to stand flat against each other under her waterproof cape.
payload.explanation: In an open field during lightning: avoid trees, move to low ground, spread out and crouch — tall objects attract strikes.

payload.snippet: Jake is camping when overnight rain makes the tent floor wet. He realises water is seeping in under the groundsheet and has soaked his sleeping bag.
options: He moves his sleeping bag to the dry end, uses clothes to soak up water at the entry point, and the next morning re-pitches the tent on higher ground.
He opens the tent door to let the water flow out through the front and then closes it.
He puts stones around the tent base to divert the water and stays in the wet sleeping bag.
He gets up and sits in the car for the rest of the night so the sleeping bag can dry.
payload.explanation: Stopping the water source, using clothes as temporary absorbent, and re-pitching higher prevents recurrence.

payload.snippet: Maya's grandmother's house has a flat roof extension and heavy rain is pouring through a section of ceiling in the kitchen. A patch of plaster is bulging visibly with trapped water above it.
options: Maya tells her grandmother not to go in the kitchen, places a bucket under the bulge, and calls a family member with the photos she takes.
Maya pushes a skewer through the bulge so the water drains through a small hole rather than in a burst.
Maya stacks towels on the counter under the bulge and goes to get a ladder to inspect the roof.
Maya tells her grandmother to phone the council for emergency repairs right away.
payload.explanation: Staying out, catching the water, and calling family for help is the correct response to an indoor ceiling flood.

payload.snippet: Oliver is playing in the garden when he finds his baby sibling has climbed out through the open back door and is sitting in a puddle in the rain in only a nappy.
options: He brings his sibling inside immediately, wraps them in a warm towel, and calls a parent.
He covers his sibling with a large leaf and runs inside to get a parent before picking them up.
He gives his sibling a drink of water to warm them up and calls for a parent to come outside.
He stays with the sibling in the garden and waits for a parent to notice they are missing.
payload.explanation: Wet babies lose heat fast — bringing the baby in and warming them before calling a parent is correct.

payload.snippet: Clara is in charge of a junior after-school film club in a temporary outdoor shelter when the weather forecast changes to a severe weather warning with risk of structural damage from wind and rain.
options: She calmly ends the session early, ensures every child is collected by a known adult, and stays with any remaining children inside the school building until all are accounted for.
She checks the shelter's stability and continues the session as the warning says risk not certainty.
She sends all children home on their own immediately so they reach safety before the storm arrives.
She calls a parent vote by text message on whether to continue or end the session.
payload.explanation: A structural-risk severe weather warning ends outdoor/temporary-shelter supervision — all children inside with known adults.

payload.snippet: Ben is fishing by a river when he notices the water level is rising rapidly and the bank he is sitting on is starting to feel soft and unstable underfoot.
options: He picks up his equipment and moves immediately to higher ground well back from the bank.
He casts further into the river to get ahead of the rising water before leaving.
He calls the Environment Agency to report the rising level before moving position.
He sits on a dry patch of bank three metres from the water and monitors the level.
payload.explanation: Rapidly rising water on a soft bank is a flash-flood warning — immediate retreat to high ground.

payload.snippet: Tom is supervising younger children at an indoor soft-play centre when the ceiling starts dripping and several large patches of water form on the play equipment after a burst pipe above.
options: He removes all children from the wet play areas immediately, reports to staff at the reception desk, and keeps children in the dry seating area.
He tells children to avoid the dripping patches and continues supervising their play.
He puts his coat over the wettest patch of equipment so the children can keep playing.
He takes the children outside while the roof leak is fixed by staff.
payload.explanation: Wet soft play equipment is a slip and electrical hazard — clear children immediately and report to staff.

payload.snippet: Anna's class is doing an outdoor science experiment recording rainfall over twenty-four hours when overnight heavy rain fills their rain gauge to overflowing, losing the true reading.
options: She notes the gauge overflowed, records the overflow as the minimum figure, and suggests repeating the experiment with a larger gauge or more frequent readings.
She estimates the extra rainfall from a neighbouring weather website and adds it to the reading.
She asks the class to accept the gauge maximum as the official reading for the experiment.
She empties the gauge and repeats only the final four hours of the experiment.
payload.explanation: Scientific integrity requires flagging measurement failure, noting the minimum bound, and improving methodology — not estimating or ignoring the error.

payload.snippet: Oliver walks into the school library and notices water pouring through a ceiling tile above a shelf of fragile reference books. Two books are already wet.
options: He moves the wet books to a dry surface, puts a bin under the drip, alerts the librarian, and helps lay the books flat open to dry.
He stacks the wet books tightly together to protect their spines while they dry.
He puts the wet books outside on the windowsill so the wind helps them dry faster.
He reports the leak to the office and leaves the books in place so the librarian can assess them.
payload.explanation: Moving wet books flat to dry and catching the drip limits damage while professional help is arranged.

payload.snippet: Maya is returning from a camping trip when a rainstorm floods the road she planned to drive home on. Her map shows an alternative route but it crosses a ford that may also be flooded.
options: The driver turns around and follows a diversion on higher ground roads, avoiding both the flooded road and the uncertain ford.
The driver tests the ford slowly in four-wheel drive to check whether it is passable.
The driver waits at the flooded road for thirty minutes to see if the level drops.
The driver takes the shortcut across a ploughed field beside the road to bypass the flood.
payload.explanation: Flooded roads and uncertain fords should both be avoided — a longer high-ground diversion is the only safe choice.

payload.snippet: Jake is standing at a bus stop in heavy rain when he notices a young woman who is soaking wet and shivering has been standing there for over half an hour and is not checking a phone or looking for a bus.
options: He asks if she is okay and whether she needs any help.
He moves to the other end of the bus shelter to give her space and privacy.
He calls 999 because she might be in some kind of danger.
He gives her his umbrella and walks away so she does not feel embarrassed.
payload.explanation: Checking in with someone visibly distressed in a public space is a compassionate and proportionate response.

payload.snippet: Clara is at a sports tournament being held on outdoor courts when the rain makes the surface dangerously slippery and a player slips and falls hard, winding herself badly.
options: Clara calls for the match referee to pause play, stays with the player, and supports her to sit up gently once she is breathing normally again.
Clara helps the player to her feet immediately and walks her to the sideline.
Clara pours water on the court surface where the player slipped to wash the mud away.
Clara shouts to the other players to keep playing while she checks on the fallen player.
payload.explanation: Pausing play for safety and supporting a winded player calmly are the correct match-official and bystander responses.

payload.snippet: Ben is walking home in rain when he trips on a broken paving slab and grazes both palms on the wet ground. His hands are bleeding and dirty.
options: He cleans his hands as best he can with the water bottle in his bag, holds a clean tissue over the worst graze, and walks the rest of the way home to clean it properly.
He puts his hands in a puddle of rainwater to wash the grazes with fresh clean water.
He wraps his school scarf tightly around both hands and runs the rest of the way home.
He knocks on the nearest house and asks the occupant for antiseptic cream.
payload.explanation: Bottled water and a clean tissue are the best immediate first-aid tools when grazes occur outdoors.

payload.snippet: Tom is helping his dad unload shopping from the car in heavy rain when one carrier bag splits, spilling a dozen loose eggs across the wet driveway.
options: Tom gathers the unbroken eggs by hand into another bag and leaves the broken ones for his dad to clean once they are inside.
Tom picks all the eggs up as fast as he can, cracked and whole, and carries them to the kitchen.
Tom stamps on the remaining cracked eggs to prevent them being stepped on later.
Tom takes off his coat to carry all the eggs at once so they stay drier.
payload.explanation: Salvaging unbroken eggs and leaving the messy cleanup for later is the sensible priority in the rain.

payload.snippet: It has been raining for three days and the small stream at the bottom of the park has flooded over the path. Anna wants to cross to reach the picnic area on the other side.
options: Anna warns others not to cross and takes the long route around the park instead.
Anna wades through the flooded section as it only looks ankle deep.
Anna places stepping stones in the flood to create a path for other walkers.
Anna calls the park authorities and waits by the flooded area for them to arrive.
payload.explanation: Flooded paths can hide deep water or strong currents — go around and warn others.

payload.snippet: Jake's new umbrella has a metal handle and he is walking near a road as a thunderstorm begins.
options: He puts the umbrella down and takes shelter in the nearest shop doorway.
He holds the umbrella higher to keep more rain off during the lightning.
He keeps the umbrella up but holds it by the fabric dome instead of the metal handle.
He hands the umbrella to a passing adult and runs under a tree for cover.
payload.explanation: Metal umbrella handles conduct electricity in a thunderstorm — sheltering indoors is the only safe option.

payload.snippet: Oliver is doing a summer litter-pick in the park when he finds a used syringe half-hidden in a patch of grass near the children's play area.
options: He marks the spot with a stick, keeps others away, and calls the local council's sharps-collection line.
He picks it up carefully with a plastic bag over his hand and puts it in the nearest bin.
He uses tongs from his kit to move it into the hedgerow where children will not find it.
He photographs it and posts it to the council's social media page asking for urgent collection.
payload.explanation: Discarded syringes must be reported to a professional sharps-collection service — never handle them yourself.

payload.snippet: Clara is at a sports tournament being held on outdoor courts when the rain makes the surface dangerously slippery and a player slips and falls hard, winding herself badly.
options: Clara calls for the match referee to pause play, stays with the player, and supports her to sit up gently once she is breathing normally again.
Clara helps the player to her feet immediately and walks her to the sideline.
Clara pours water on the court surface where the player slipped to wash the mud away.
Clara shouts to the other players to keep playing while she checks on the fallen player.
payload.explanation: Pausing play for safety and supporting a winded player calmly are the correct match-official and bystander responses.

payload.snippet: Maya is returning from a camping trip when a rainstorm floods the road she planned to drive home on. Her map shows an alternative route but it crosses a ford that may also be flooded.
options: The driver turns around and follows a diversion on higher ground roads, avoiding both the flooded road and the uncertain ford.
The driver tests the ford slowly in four-wheel drive to check whether it is passable.
The driver waits at the flooded road for thirty minutes to see if the level drops.
The driver takes the shortcut across a ploughed field beside the road to bypass the flood.
payload.explanation: Flooded roads and uncertain fords should both be avoided — a longer high-ground diversion is the only safe choice.

payload.snippet: Tom is supervising his younger siblings on the playground when he notices the bolts on the bottom of the slide ladder have come loose and the whole structure wobbles when touched.
options: He tells his siblings to stay off the slide, marks the area with his bag, and tells the nearest adult immediately.
He tightens the bolts himself with a coin from his pocket and tests the structure carefully.
He helps his siblings down the slide one at a time watching closely for any wobble.
He tells his siblings to use it but to hold the sides very tightly at all times.
payload.explanation: A structurally unsafe piece of equipment must be kept clear and reported — never attempt DIY repairs.

payload.snippet: Anna is at the park with a group of friends when one friend tries to show off by standing up on the moving roundabout and loses his balance, hitting the ground hard and holding his wrist.
options: She calls for an adult, keeps her friend still, and checks if he can move his wrist without rushing him.
She helps him to his feet and asks him to flex his wrist to check it is just a sprain.
She continues turning the roundabout slowly while she assesses the injury.
She asks the group to form a circle around him so she can assess the injury privately.
payload.explanation: After a fall with a wrist impact, keeping the person still and calling for an adult is correct — do not force movement.

payload.snippet: Jake is playing in the park when a stranger approaches the playground and starts asking the children where their parents are and offering to show them something on his phone.
options: Jake moves toward the group of children near the main gate and calls out for the adults sitting on the nearby benches.
Jake tells the stranger that the adults are watching and asks him what he wants to show them.
Jake runs to the opposite corner of the park and hopes the adults notice the stranger.
Jake asks the stranger politely to leave before running to get an adult.
payload.explanation: Moving children to safety and alerting adults without confronting the stranger is the correct safeguarding response.

payload.snippet: Clara has been playing on the zip wire for twenty minutes when a younger child with a disability comes over and asks for a go but cannot reach the handle by themselves.
options: Clara helps the child reach the handle and stays nearby while they have a go.
Clara tells the child the zip wire is for older children and suggests the swings instead.
Clara asks her friends to watch so they are ready if the child falls.
Clara lifts the child onto the zip wire and pushes them gently to get them started.
payload.explanation: Helping the child access the equipment safely and supervising closely is inclusive and kind.

payload.snippet: Oliver is running across a wet wooden bridge in the playground when he slips and lands on his back, knocking the wind out of him. He cannot breathe for about ten seconds.
options: He stays still until his breathing comes back, then sits up slowly and tells an adult.
He gets straight back up and carries on playing so his friends do not worry.
He asks a friend to perform the Heimlich manoeuvre on him right away.
He panics and tries to breathe faster to replace the air he lost quickly.
payload.explanation: Getting winded needs calm stillness until breathing returns — then tell an adult to confirm you are okay.

payload.snippet: Maya watches as two older children start throwing woodchip pieces at each other from the play area and one piece hits a toddler in the face nearby.
options: She immediately picks up the toddler and checks their face, then calls for the nearest adult.
She shouts at the older children to stop and then assesses the toddler herself.
She moves the toddler away and watches to see if the children stop on their own.
She photographs the older children and sends the photo to the park's Facebook page.
payload.explanation: Protecting the vulnerable child first and calling an adult are the correct immediate priorities.

payload.snippet: Ben is playing on the high climbing net when he hears a ripping sound and notices the net has torn loose from one of its fixings directly above where younger children are climbing below.
options: He calls down to the children to move away from the net immediately and shouts for an adult.
He climbs down and tries to reattach the net to the fixing with a knot.
He tells the children to avoid that section but finishes his climb first.
He climbs to the broken fixing and holds it in place until an adult arrives.
payload.explanation: Warning children below and calling an adult without touching a broken piece of equipment is the correct response.

payload.snippet: Anna is playing in the park when she sees a toddler fall face-first off a low step and not move for several seconds. The toddler's parent runs over but is panicking.
options: Anna stays calm, tells the parent the toddler needs to be checked gently, and offers to call 999 if the parent is too distressed to dial.
Anna picks up the toddler and places her on the nearby bench so the parent can see her better.
Anna asks the parent to turn the toddler over quickly to check her face.
Anna runs to the café in the park to call for a first aider instead.
payload.explanation: A child not moving after a fall needs gentle assessment — staying calm and offering to call 999 supports the distressed parent.

payload.snippet: Jake is at the skate park attached to the playground when he sees a younger child on a scooter heading straight toward the deep bowl section without a helmet or any protective gear.
options: He stands at the edge of the bowl to block the child's path and asks the child to stop.
He shouts a warning and steps back so the child can make their own choice.
He lets the child go as the bowl is only two metres deep and they will be fine.
He chases the child and grabs their scooter to stop them, causing the child to fall sideways.
payload.explanation: Physically blocking the route is the fastest safe way to prevent a helmetless child entering a deep skate bowl.

payload.snippet: Clara is in a playground next to a main road when a ball goes over the fence and lands on the pavement on the other side.
options: She asks an adult to retrieve the ball rather than climbing the fence herself.
She climbs the fence quickly and picks up the ball before any cars come.
She asks a friend to hold her legs while she leans over the fence to grab it.
She leaves the ball and tells the owner to ask their parents to get it later.
payload.explanation: Retrieving a ball near a main road is a task for an adult, not a child alone.

payload.snippet: Oliver notices a child on the seesaw who has been bumping the seat hard on the ground repeatedly and now shows a graze on their coccyx area and is starting to cry.
options: He offers to help the child to the bench and tells the playground supervisor what happened.
He asks the child to sit on the seesaw more gently from now on and checks on them later.
He tells the child that hurting themselves was their own fault for bumping the seesaw.
He finishes his current game before checking on the child.
payload.explanation: Helping an injured child to safety and reporting to the supervisor is the correct caring response.

payload.snippet: Maya is on the trampoline in the park when she bounces into the air and lands awkwardly on her ankle, which twists under her. She can feel it swelling already.
options: She sits on the edge of the trampoline, avoids putting weight on the ankle, and calls for an adult.
She bounces gently a few more times to loosen the joint and see if it improves.
She gets off the trampoline and walks around on it to test whether it is a sprain.
She lies flat on the trampoline to rest and waits for the swelling to go down.
payload.explanation: A swelling ankle after a twist needs to be rested immediately and shown to an adult.

payload.snippet: Ben is playing in the park on a hot day when he notices another child who has been sitting alone on a bench in full sun for a long time and is very red in the face and not moving much.
options: He goes over to check on the child, asks if they are okay, and calls for an adult if the child seems unwell.
He offers his water bottle to the child from across the path.
He tells a nearby adult that the child looks hot and then leaves them to it.
He asks his friends if they know the child before approaching.
payload.explanation: Directly checking on a child showing signs of heat exhaustion and calling for help is the caring and correct response.

payload.snippet: Anna is helping run a holiday club in a playground when a thunderstorm begins. She counts five children spread across different pieces of equipment.
options: She calls all five children in by name, counts them, and leads them as a group to the nearest indoor building.
She shouts for all children to go inside and then runs in herself before they all arrive.
She uses the buddy system and pairs children to run to cover in twos.
She takes the three closest children inside first and then runs back for the remaining two.
payload.explanation: All children must be counted and moved as one group to indoor safety during a lightning risk.

payload.snippet: Jake finds a wallet on the ground near the park entrance with cards and cash inside it.
options: He hands it in to the park warden's office without looking through the contents.
He looks through it to find the owner's name and then calls out across the park.
He puts it in his bag to hand to his parents who can deal with it at home.
He leaves it on the nearby bench where the owner is more likely to find it.
payload.explanation: Handing a found wallet to a park warden intact is the correct lost-property procedure.

payload.snippet: Ben is at an outdoor playground when he sees a water feature has a pump making a loud grinding noise and has a visible electrical cable lying across the wet ground near the splash area where young children are playing.
options: He moves all children away from the wet area immediately, calls for the park warden, and makes sure no one touches the cable or the water until the warden arrives.
He asks a child to hold the cable off the ground so it does not touch the water.
He switches the pump off at the power button on the unit to remove the electrical hazard.
He tells children to step over the cable carefully and continues watching the area.
payload.explanation: A wet cable near an electrical pump with children present is a live electrical hazard — clear the area immediately and call a warden.

payload.snippet: Jake finds a wallet on the ground near the park entrance with cards and cash inside it.
options: He hands it in to the park warden's office without looking through the contents.

He puts it in his bag to hand to his parents who can deal with it at home.
He leaves it on the nearby bench where the owner is more likely to find it.
payload.explanation: Handing a found wallet to a park warden intact is the correct lost-property procedure.
