She climbs the fence quickly and picks up the ball before any cars come.
She asks a friend to hold her legs while she leans over the fence to grab it.
She leaves the ball and tells the owner to ask their parents to get it later.
payload.explanation: Retrieving a ball near a main road is a task for an adult, not a child alone.

payload.snippet: Tom is leading an after-school art club when he notices a student mixing two chemicals from the school's printmaking supplies together in a jar. The mixture immediately starts fizzing and producing a sharp smell.
options: He evacuates everyone from the room, opens windows if safe to do so, and calls for the science or health and safety lead immediately.
He takes the jar from the student and pours the mixture down the sink right away.
He puts the jar outside the classroom window and carries on with the session.
He asks the student what they mixed and looks up the chemicals on his phone.
payload.explanation: Unknown chemical reactions in a classroom require evacuation and specialist response — do not handle the mixture.

payload.snippet: Anna is photographing her art project for a portfolio submission when she realises the photos are needed in an hour and her camera memory card is corrupted, losing all the images she had already taken.
options: She sets up the lighting as best she can, re-photographs all available work quickly, and notifies the submission coordinator about the technical issue.
She borrows a classmate's photos of a similar project to submit in place of her own.
She submits the portfolio without photos and explains what happened in a cover note.
She asks the art teacher to give her extra time by claiming a personal illness caused the delay.
payload.explanation: Re-photographing and transparently communicating the technical problem is the honest and practical response.

payload.snippet: Jake is screen-printing t-shirts for a school fundraiser when the squeegee handle breaks mid-run, leaving twenty incomplete prints with wet ink on them.
options: He lays all twenty prints flat to protect the wet ink, asks the teacher for a replacement squeegee, and then completes the prints once he has one.
He uses his hand to complete the remaining prints, spreading the ink as evenly as he can.
He abandons the batch and starts over when the new squeegee arrives.
He completes the prints using the broken handle by pressing harder with both thumbs.
payload.explanation: Protecting wet prints and waiting for the right tool ensures all twenty are completed correctly.

payload.snippet: Clara is working on a clay kiln project and notices a classmate has placed a sealed hollow clay form in the kiln before firing — it has no air holes.
options: She tells the teacher before the kiln is switched on, because a sealed hollow form can explode in the kiln.
She pokes an air hole in the piece herself to solve the problem quickly.
She tells the classmate quietly and lets them decide whether to remove the piece.
She removes the piece herself while the classmate is not looking to prevent an argument.
payload.explanation: Sealed hollow clay explodes in a kiln — tell the teacher before firing so the piece can be corrected or removed.

payload.snippet: Oliver is painting a large landscape outdoors when a gust of wind blows his wet canvas face-first onto the grass, embedding grass and dirt into the paint surface.
options: He carefully removes the largest debris with a palette knife, lets it dry, and then assesses whether to incorporate the texture or scrape and repaint.
He wipes the canvas clean with a wet cloth while the paint is still wet.
He discards the canvas and starts fresh, as the grass-embedded surface cannot be recovered.
He adds more paint immediately on top of the contamination to cover it up.
payload.explanation: Letting an accidental texture dry and then deciding how to respond is the correct approach for wet canvas damage.

payload.snippet: Maya is doing a photography project in a public space when a member of public approaches and objects to being in the background of her shots and asks her to delete any images with him in them.
options: She apologises, confirms whether he is identifiable in any images, deletes those where he clearly appears, and thanks him for letting her know.
She explains she has the legal right to photograph in a public space and does not need to delete anything.
She agrees to crop him out of the images but keeps the originals for her portfolio.
She moves to a different location immediately without showing him which images have him in them.
payload.explanation: Respecting an objection to being photographed and deleting identifiable images is the ethical and courteous response.

payload.snippet: Ben is building a papier mâché balloon sculpture for a school exhibition when he notices the balloon inside has deflated before the final layers have dried, causing the shape to sag and deform.
options: He inflates a new balloon inside carefully through a small opening and reinforces the structure with fresh layers.
He fills the sagging form with expanding foam to restore the shape quickly.
He props the sculpture with rolled paper from the inside to maintain the shape while it dries.
He accepts the sagged shape as a creative outcome and redesigns the piece around the new form.
payload.explanation: Re-inflating carefully and adding fresh layers is the correct repair for a deflated papier mâché armature.

payload.snippet: Anna is using a band saw for a woodcarving sculpture in design technology when the blade starts vibrating noticeably more than usual and the cut becomes irregular.
options: She switches the machine off immediately and tells the teacher before resuming.
She slows her feed rate and presses the wood more firmly against the fence to reduce vibration.
She checks the blade tension herself by flicking it and adjusting the tension knob.
She finishes the current cut quickly and then reports the vibration at the end of the lesson.
payload.explanation: Unusual machine vibration means stop immediately and report — do not try to compensate with technique.

payload.snippet: Jake is working on a multi-media project that uses copyright music as its soundtrack. His teacher has asked him to find a legal audio track for the school presentation.
options: He searches for Creative Commons or royalty-free music sites and finds a track with the right licence for school use.
He downloads his favourite song from a streaming service as the quality is much better.
He records himself humming the tune of the song he wants so it technically is not the original.
He uses the copyrighted track and credits the artist in his presentation notes.
payload.explanation: Creative Commons and royalty-free sources provide legal music for school presentations — crediting a copyrighted track does not make it legal.

payload.snippet: Clara is applying gold leaf to a final piece using size adhesive when she reaches the last section and realises she does not have enough gold leaf to complete it. The adhesive is already applied and will become too dry to work with if she does not act in the next thirty minutes.
options: She asks the teacher if there are more gold leaf sheets, and if not, adapts the design by incorporating a different metallic finish for the final section.
She applies a second layer of size over the tacky section to buy more time while she finds gold leaf.
She cuts the remaining sheets into very small pieces and tries to tile the whole area with minimal overlap.
She leaves the adhesive section ungilded and presents the piece as an intentional incomplete artwork.
payload.explanation: Asking for more materials first and adapting creatively if none are available is the professional response to a supply shortfall mid-process.

payload.snippet: Oliver is leading an art workshop when he notices that one of the participants is becoming increasingly distressed while painting — the subject matter on their canvas is getting darker and more disturbing with each layer.
options: He checks in gently with the participant after the session, notes his concern, and mentions it to the session coordinator or safeguarding lead.
He stops the participant mid-session and asks what the dark images mean.
He moves the participant to a different table and gives them a different subject to paint.
He monitors the participant without raising the concern, as art is a personal expression.
payload.explanation: Unusual distress signals in creative work warrant a gentle post-session check-in and safeguarding notification — not mid-session confrontation or ignoring the signal.

payload.snippet: Maya is doing an outdoor mural commission on a community wall when she realises the wall surface is still wet from recent rain and the exterior paint she is using is refusing to adhere properly.
options: She waits for the wall surface to dry fully before continuing, even if it means returning on a different day.
She applies the paint more thickly to compensate for the poor adhesion on the wet surface.
She uses a hair dryer to dry the wall surface section by section as she paints.
She adds water to the paint to thin it so it absorbs better into the damp wall.
payload.explanation: Exterior paint applied to a wet surface will peel — waiting for full drying is the only correct approach for a permanent commission.

payload.snippet: Ben is running a screen-printing business from home and discovers that the chemicals he uses to reclaim screens are classified as hazardous waste that cannot be poured down the drain.
options: He contacts the local council to find out the correct hazardous waste disposal procedure and makes arrangements accordingly.
He dilutes the chemicals heavily with water before pouring them down the drain to reduce concentration.
He pours the chemicals into sealed containers and puts them in the regular household waste collection.
He asks a neighbouring print studio if they can take his waste chemicals when they dispose of theirs.
payload.explanation: Hazardous chemicals must be disposed of through the correct council channels — diluting or hiding them in household waste is illegal.

payload.snippet: Anna is photographing a classmate for a portrait project. Reviewing the images later she realises one shows the classmate in an unflattering and vulnerable moment they were unaware of.
options: She does not use the image in any form and deletes it, then tells her classmate she has done so.
She uses the image in her portfolio as it shows genuine emotion and is artistically strong.
She crops the image heavily so the moment is less obvious and uses it in her private portfolio.
She asks her classmate which images they are happy with and lets them choose from the full set.
payload.explanation: Photographing someone in an unaware vulnerable moment and using it without consent is an ethical violation — delete and inform.

payload.snippet: Jake is painting a community portrait project when he realises the preliminary sketch he transferred onto the canvas has an anatomical error — the proportions of one figure's arms are clearly wrong after scaling up.
options: He corrects the drawing with charcoal over the transferred lines before applying any paint.
He paints the first layers and hopes the painting will draw attention away from the arm proportions.
He adds extra objects to the composition near the figure to obscure the arm area.
He re-scales the entire canvas transfer to get the proportions right before painting.
payload.explanation: Correcting a proportional error in charcoal before painting is the most efficient and cleanest fix.

payload.snippet: Jake is working on a commission for a local authority public sculpture. During fabrication he discovers the structural steel was a lighter gauge than the specification, meaning the finished piece may not be safe for public interaction.
options: He stops fabrication, documents the discrepancy, contacts the supplier and the commissioning authority, and will not proceed until correctly specified materials are provided and an engineer signs off.
He reinforces the lighter steel by welding additional internal supports so the piece meets the load requirement.
He proceeds with fabrication and discloses the material substitution in the installation documentation.
He contacts the commissioning authority but continues fabrication to avoid missing the installation deadline.
payload.explanation: A safety-critical material substitution in public art requires a full stop, documented disclosure, and engineering sign-off before proceeding.

payload.snippet: Anna is finalising a documentary photography project about a vulnerable community when she realises one of her most powerful images inadvertently identifies a person who had only consented to appear in anonymous form.
options: She excludes the image from all exhibitions and publications, contacts the subject to inform them, and re-examines all other images for similar consent issues before publishing.
She crops the image to obscure the identifying features and uses it in the exhibition.
She uses the image only in her private portfolio since it will not be seen publicly.
She includes the image and credits the subject by their chosen alias to satisfy the consent requirement.
payload.explanation: Consent to appear anonymously must be fully honoured — exclude, inform the subject, and audit all remaining images.

payload.snippet: Oliver is running a community print workshop when a participant with severe colour blindness arrives and struggles to distinguish between the colours needed for the layered registration process.
options: He modifies the registration markers to high-contrast black-and-white patterns and provides verbal guidance for each layer.
He assigns another participant to guide the colour-blind person through the session.
He suggests the participant do a mono-colour single-layer print instead.
He provides a printed colour chart and asks the participant to reference it for each step.
payload.explanation: Adapting the environment with high-contrast markers gives the participant full independent access to the process.

payload.snippet: Maya is exhibiting at a major graduate show when she learns the day before opening that the lighting rig above her work is flickering, which may trigger photosensitive epilepsy in visitors.
options: She reports it to the gallery's technical team immediately and requests the flickering light be replaced or her piece be moved before opening.
She places a warning sign in front of her piece and leaves the decision to visitors.
She tells the gallery team at the opening so they are aware during the show.
She turns off the light above her piece and uses natural light from the window instead.
payload.explanation: A flicker that may trigger epilepsy is a safeguarding issue requiring a technical fix or relocation before public access — a warning sign is insufficient.

payload.snippet: Ben is working on a multi-media project that uses copyright music as its soundtrack. His teacher has asked him to find a legal audio track for the school presentation.
options: He searches for Creative Commons or royalty-free music sites and finds a track with the right licence for school use.
He downloads his favourite song from a streaming service as the quality is much better.
He records himself humming the tune of the song he wants so it technically is not the original.
He uses the copyrighted track and credits the artist in his presentation notes.
payload.explanation: Creative Commons and royalty-free sources provide legal music for school presentations — crediting a copyrighted track does not make it legal.

payload.snippet: Tom is performing his first public piano recital when he notices halfway through the piece that the piano's sustain pedal is not working, significantly changing the sound of the music.
options: He adapts his finger technique to hold notes longer manually and completes the performance professionally.
He stops, announces the problem to the audience, and asks for the piece to restart.
He plays so fast that the missing sustain is not noticeable to the audience.
He leaves the stage and asks the teacher to play instead.
payload.explanation: A professional adapts to equipment failure mid-performance rather than stopping — the audience barely knows the intended sound.

payload.snippet: Anna is leading a junior music group when one child becomes distressed and starts crying during a free improvisation exercise. When asked, the child says the sound reminds them of something sad.
options: She gently redirects the group to a different, brighter activity and checks in with the distressed child quietly afterwards.
She asks the child to share what memory the music triggered with the whole group.
She stops the improvisation entirely and ends the session early to protect the child.
She continues the improvisation and asks the group to play more cheerfully.
payload.explanation: Gently redirecting and checking in privately respects the child's feelings without making them the centre of attention.

payload.snippet: Jake is playing the acoustic guitar at a community event when he hears a faint buzzing from the guitar body every time he plays a specific note.
options: He identifies which fret is causing the buzz, avoids that position where possible, and reports the issue to be fixed after the event.
He presses down harder on that note to eliminate the buzz regardless of how much it hurts his fingertip.
He stops playing and announces there is a problem with his guitar to the audience.
He detunes the affected string slightly so the note is not played in that position.
payload.explanation: Identifying and working around a buzz mid-performance, then reporting it afterwards, is the professional approach.

payload.snippet: Clara is a student music teacher running her first lesson when the pupil refuses to put down their phone and keeps playing games during the lesson.
options: She calmly asks the phone to be placed face-down on the piano, explains why focus is needed, and continues the lesson.
She takes the phone from the pupil and locks it in the piano bench for the lesson.
She gives the pupil a five-minute free time on the phone at the end if they focus now.
She texts the pupil's parents during the lesson to inform them of the behaviour.
payload.explanation: A calm direct request with a brief explanation is the appropriate first response to distracted behaviour in a lesson.

payload.snippet: Oliver is the lead singer in a band and the bassist shows up to rehearsal visibly upset and not focused, making repeated mistakes throughout the session.
options: He pauses the rehearsal, checks in with the bassist one-to-one, and adjusts the session to run-through pieces the bassist knows well today.
He tells the bassist that personal problems should stay at the door and continues.
He asks the bassist to sit out this rehearsal and watch instead.
He replaces the bassist with a stand-in for the rehearsal and says nothing more about it.
payload.explanation: Checking in and adjusting the session shows care and keeps the rehearsal productive despite a difficult day.

payload.snippet: Maya is practising for her grade five violin exam when she pulls a muscle in her bow arm and it is sore and swollen the day before the examination.
options: She rests the arm completely, applies ice, and calls the examination board to ask about a medical postponement if it does not improve overnight.
She practises at half speed to keep her skills sharp without straining the arm further.
She performs the exam the next day and relies on adrenaline to push through the pain.
She cancels the exam immediately and rebooks without asking about a medical postponement option.
payload.explanation: Rest, ice, and asking about medical postponement are the correct responses to a pre-exam injury — practising through injury worsens it.

payload.snippet: Ben is running a community choir when two members with strong voices are persistently singing louder than everyone else and drowning out the sopranos.
options: He addresses the group as a whole about balance, using a general note rather than singling the two members out, then follows up individually if the imbalance continues.
He moves the two loud members to the back of the choir so their volume is absorbed by the group.
He asks the other members to project more to compensate for the imbalance.
He tells the two members directly in front of the whole choir that they need to reduce their volume.
payload.explanation: A general note addresses the issue without humiliating individuals — individual follow-up is reserved if the problem continues.

payload.snippet: Anna is teaching a music lesson when she notices that one pupil is consistently producing a strained sound on the flute and appears to be in mild discomfort around the jaw.
options: She stops the pupil, gently corrects the embouchure, and asks if the pupil has been experiencing jaw pain.
She continues the lesson and notes to mention the embouchure at the end.
She asks the pupil to rest while the others continue, to avoid reinforcing a bad habit.
She passes the pupil on to a specialist teacher without discussing it first.
payload.explanation: Immediately correcting a technically poor embouchure prevents physical injury and bad habits from developing.

payload.snippet: Jake finds a rare vintage guitar at a car boot sale for ten pounds. When he gets it home he realises it may be a historically significant instrument worth considerably more.
options: He has it assessed by a reputable musical instrument dealer before doing anything else.
He sells it online immediately for fifty pounds to make a quick profit before someone claims it.
He takes it apart to check for hidden serial numbers that might confirm its value.
He uses it for daily practice because it sounds exceptional and he owns it legally.
payload.explanation: Getting a professional assessment before any sale, modification, or extended use is the responsible step with a potentially valuable instrument.

payload.snippet: Clara is rehearsing for a school concert when the accompanist makes repeated errors in the same place, and the rehearsal time is running short.
options: She adjusts the tempo slightly to give the accompanist more time in the difficult passage and continues without making the errors a big deal.
She asks the accompanist to practise the section alone at home and moves on without them for now.
She plays through the section herself on the piano to show the accompanist how it should sound.
She tells the music teacher that the accompanist is not ready for the concert.
payload.explanation: Adjusting tempo to support a struggling accompanist during limited rehearsal time is collaborative and constructive.

payload.snippet: Oliver is recording a demo at a home studio when he notices that the recording contains a clearly audible click at the beginning of every bar, which he eventually traces to the CPU fan on his laptop.
options: He moves the laptop further from the microphone and uses a noise gate plugin before recording the final takes.
He re-records everything at twice the speed so the fan noise is less noticeable per second.
He accepts the clicks as background ambience and submits the demo as is.
He edits out every click manually in the waveform editor before submission.
payload.explanation: Physical separation and a noise gate address the source and the symptom of laptop fan interference in recording.

payload.snippet: Maya is in a music exam when she realises thirty seconds in that she has memorised the wrong piece and is playing a different one than the examiner is following.
options: She stops, tells the examiner politely, and asks to restart with the correct piece.
She continues playing the piece she knows and hopes the examiner will mark her on what she plays.
She tries to transition from her memorised piece to the correct one mid-performance.
She plays the wrong piece to the end and then explains the mistake in her written feedback form.
payload.explanation: Stopping and asking to restart is the only correct response when you realise you are playing the wrong piece in a formal examination.

payload.snippet: Ben is performing at an open-mic night when a drunk heckler in the audience interrupts his song twice.
options: He pauses briefly, says something lighthearted, and resumes performing without engaging in a back-and-forth.
He stops the song and asks the venue staff to remove the heckler before he will continue.
He responds directly to the heckler with a cutting remark to assert control of the room.
He plays louder to drown out the heckler for the remainder of his set.
payload.explanation: A brief lighthearted response followed by resuming the performance keeps control of the room without escalating.

payload.snippet: Anna is teaching a pupil who is technically talented but refuses to practise scales, claiming they are boring and pointless.
options: She explains the specific technique each scale builds and ties it to a passage in a piece the pupil loves.
She removes scales from the lesson until the pupil agrees to practise them at home.
She tells the pupil that scales are required for their grade exam and leaves it at that.
She finds a different teacher who uses a methodology without technical exercises.
payload.explanation: Connecting scales to music the pupil loves makes the purpose concrete and motivates practice.

payload.snippet: Jake is part of a school band that is supposed to perform at an assembly in an hour when the keyboard player does not arrive and is not answering their phone.
options: He informs the music teacher immediately and they together decide whether to perform without keyboard or replace with a simpler arrangement.
He starts trying to learn the keyboard part himself on his instrument in the remaining time.
He tells the rest of the band the performance is cancelled and they should go back to class.
He calls all the keyboard player's friends in the school to track them down.
payload.explanation: Immediate teacher notification when a performer goes missing allows a decision to be made with enough time to adapt.

payload.snippet: Clara overhears two members of her choir gossiping about a third member's voice quality in a way that would be hurtful if overheard.
options: She speaks to the two members privately and asks them to keep choir feedback constructive and within the group's values.
She tells the choir director so the two members can be formally warned.
She stands near the person being gossiped about to make sure they do not overhear.
She says nothing because gossip is not her responsibility to manage.
payload.explanation: Addressing gossip privately and reinforcing group values is the proportionate first response before escalating to a director.

payload.snippet: Oliver is playing in an exam when he notices a parallel melody piece that sounds very similar to a copyrighted pop song he has been asked to arrange for a competition.
options: He checks the competition rules about copyright, substitutes the problematic passage with an original bridge, and discloses the similarity to the competition organiser.
He submits the arrangement and notes in the submission form that it was inspired by the pop song.
He changes the key and rhythm of the similar passage so it no longer sounds obviously related.
He withdraws the arrangement entirely and submits a completely different piece instead.
payload.explanation: Copyright in competition arrangements requires rule-checking, modification, and organiser disclosure — not relying on inspiration as a defence.

payload.snippet: Maya is a student composer who submits a piece for a local prize and wins, but later discovers she accidentally included eight bars that are near-identical to a published work she had studied closely.
options: She contacts the prize organisers immediately, discloses the similarity, and offers to withdraw if the committee deems it appropriate.
She keeps the prize and resolves to be more careful in future compositions.
She contacts only the original composer to apologise rather than the prize organisers.
She revises the work and resubmits the corrected version without mentioning the original submission.
payload.explanation: Accidental musical plagiarism in a prize entry requires immediate disclosure to the organisers — keeping the prize while knowing about the similarity is dishonest.

payload.snippet: Ben is asked to play the organ at a friend's wedding service. During the ceremony he loses his place in the hymn and plays three bars of silence while flicking through his score.
options: He finds his place and re-enters on the next strong beat as smoothly as possible.
He plays whatever notes come to mind to fill the silence while he searches the score.
He stops playing and signals to the congregation to continue unaccompanied.
He closes the score and plays the melody from memory, hoping his version is close enough.
payload.explanation: Finding your place and re-entering on a strong beat is the most seamless recovery from a lost page mid-ceremony.

payload.snippet: Anna discovers that her music-streaming playlist used for a warm-up class contains a track with explicit lyrics she was not aware of, and the class includes young children.
options: She skips the track immediately, apologises to any parents present, and audits her playlist before the next session.
She turns the volume down so the lyrics are less intelligible and finishes the warm-up.
She keeps the track running and tells the children not to listen to the words.
She ends the warm-up early to avoid playing any more of the unreviewed playlist.
payload.explanation: Skipping immediately, apologising, and auditing the playlist before next use is the correct response.

payload.snippet: Tom is refereeing a youth football match when both team coaches simultaneously start shouting contradictory instructions to their players from the sideline, making it impossible for the players to hear each other or focus.
options: He stops play, walks to the touchline, and calmly reminds both coaches of the sideline conduct expectations before restarting.
He ignores the shouting and lets the coaches manage their own sidelines during play.
He issues both coaches a yellow card from the touch line without stopping play.
He asks the team captains to go and tell their coaches to be quiet.
payload.explanation: Stopping play and directly addressing the coaches is the only way to restore a focused playing environment.

payload.snippet: Anna is a sports coach when one of her athletes discloses that a coach at their previous club used to make them train through pain they had reported, leading to a stress fracture that took six months to heal.
options: She listens fully, thanks the athlete for sharing, and explains that her approach here is always to refer to the medical team when an athlete reports pain.
She reassures the athlete that she is different and moves on to the training session.
She contacts the previous club to inform them of the disclosure.
She asks the athlete to write down the details and submit them to the club as a formal complaint.
payload.explanation: Listening, validating, and explaining the current safe practice address both the athlete's concern and the culture going forward.

payload.snippet: Jake is a young cricket player on a school tour abroad when a teammate who has been struggling with the trip says he wants to go home early and stops speaking to others in the group.
options: Jake tells the tour manager privately about the teammate's withdrawal, while continuing to include the teammate in normal group activities.
Jake reassures the teammate himself and promises to keep it private without telling any adults.
Jake posts in the group chat asking everyone to be nice to the teammate who is having a hard time.
Jake gives the teammate some space for the rest of the tour and checks in again on the last day.
payload.explanation: Reporting withdrawal to the tour manager ensures adult support while private inclusion maintains dignity.

payload.snippet: Clara is a gymnastics coach when a gymnast achieves a personal best vault on a surface she used without permission because the official surface was occupied. The unofficial surface has no edge safety mat.
options: She praises the vault performance and separately addresses the safety boundary that was crossed — using any equipment without permission or proper safety matting is non-negotiable.
She validates the personal best fully and notes the safety issue in her session plan for later.
She tells the gymnast the vault does not count because it was on the wrong surface.
She completes the session normally and adds safety rules to the next session's briefing instead.
payload.explanation: Performance and safety must both be addressed — one does not override the other.

payload.snippet: Oliver is the team manager for a junior rugby club when he discovers that one of the volunteer coaches has been giving under-sixteen players supplements he describes as 'protein boosters' without parental consent or medical advice.
options: He removes the coach from all contact with players immediately, informs the parents of all players who may have received supplements, and reports the incident to the national governing body's safeguarding team.
He speaks to the coach privately and warns him never to give supplements again.
He contacts the supplement supplier to confirm the product is safe for minors before deciding on next steps.
He sends a general note to parents about club supplement policy without identifying the specific incident.
payload.explanation: Unsolicited supplement use with minors is a safeguarding matter requiring immediate removal, parent notification, and NGB reporting.

payload.snippet: Maya is a PE teacher when a student refuses to participate in the swimming lesson because they are embarrassed about wearing a swimsuit in front of their classmates.
options: She speaks to the student privately, acknowledges the concern without judgment, and explores whether a different swimwear option or a private changing arrangement would help.
She marks the student as absent for the lesson and does not raise the issue further.
She asks the class to focus on their own swimming so the student has less pressure.
She tells the student that swimming is mandatory and they must participate regardless.
payload.explanation: Addressing body image concerns privately and adapting where possible is the inclusive and respectful response.

payload.snippet: Ben is a sports journalist attending an international athletics event when he witnesses a competitor collapse just after crossing the finish line in first place. Medical staff rush onto the track.
options: He continues reporting the event but contacts his editor immediately to flag the developing situation rather than assuming the collapse is minor.
He approaches the medical team to ask for an update on the athlete's condition for his report.
He publishes a brief update on social media stating the athlete has collapsed before any medical information is confirmed.
He waits until after the medal ceremony to mention the collapse in his full match report.
payload.explanation: A journalist should flag a developing medical situation to their editor immediately without speculating on severity or seeking medical information at the scene.

payload.snippet: Anna is the manager of a junior sports team when she learns that a parent has been sending intimidating messages to a teenage player on the opposing team after a cup match because they disagreed with a foul call.
options: She contacts the parent immediately to make clear this behaviour is unacceptable, informs the league's disciplinary officer, and checks on the wellbeing of the targeted player.
She contacts the other team's manager to apologise and hopes the issue resolves informally.
She warns the parent at the next training session in front of other parents to set a clear example.
She waits to see whether the targeted player or their parents make a formal complaint before acting.
payload.explanation: Parent online intimidation of a player requires immediate parental contact, league disciplinary reporting, and player welfare check — not waiting for a complaint.

payload.snippet: Jake is a swimming club coach when he notices one of his fastest swimmers has lost a significant amount of weight in a short period and is performing worse despite increasing training. The swimmer has become withdrawn.
options: He speaks to the swimmer privately after training, checks in on their wellbeing without mentioning weight directly, and follows the club's safeguarding protocol to report his concern.
He reduces the swimmer's training load and monitors their performance over the next month.
He asks other swimmers if they have noticed anything different about their teammate.
He contacts the swimmer's parents to discuss the weight loss before following any formal protocol.
payload.explanation: Performance decline combined with weight loss and withdrawal signals a potential eating disorder — safeguarding protocol, not parent contact by the coach, is the correct response.

payload.snippet: Clara is playing in a school cross-country team and notices the planned route takes runners across a wooden bridge that has a large crack down its centre plank after heavy rain.
options: She tells the PE teacher before the race that the bridge looks unsafe.
She crosses the bridge herself to test it before deciding whether to tell the teacher.
She tells other runners to jump over the cracked plank as they cross.
She avoids the bridge herself and takes an unofficial diversion without telling anyone.
payload.explanation: Reporting a structural concern before a race allows the teacher to make a safety decision — individual workarounds leave other runners at risk.

payload.snippet: Oliver is competing in a martial arts tournament when he delivers a technique that scores a point, but the opponent immediately says they were injured by the strike and calls for medical attention.
options: He steps back, bows respectfully, and waits quietly while the medical team assesses his opponent.
He argues that the technique was legal and the injury claim looks exaggerated.
He continues the round as the referee has not called time.
He helps his opponent to the side himself rather than waiting for the medical team.
payload.explanation: Stepping back, bowing, and waiting for medical assessment is the correct martial arts sportsmanship response.

payload.snippet: Maya is participating in a sailing regatta when she sees a competitor capsize in a strong gust some distance away. The competitor is visible but does not appear to be righting the boat.
options: She alters course toward the capsized boat, assesses whether the competitor needs assistance, and alerts the safety boat by radio.
She continues racing as the safety boat will have seen the capsize on their radar.
She calls out to the competitor from a distance to check if they are okay before deciding.
She drops her sails and paddles toward the competitor to help them right the boat herself.
payload.explanation: Sailing safety rules require investigating a capsize and alerting the safety boat — continuing racing is not acceptable when a competitor may need help.

payload.snippet: Ben is a youth football coach when his team wins a match after a controversial penalty decision that even his own players agree looked wrong.
options: He acknowledges privately to his players that the decision was questionable and focuses the post-match debrief on their own performance rather than the result.
He celebrates the win fully with his team and does not raise doubts about the referee decision.
He approaches the referee after the match to ask whether they are confident in the penalty call.
He files a sportsmanship report with the league acknowledging the questionable decision.
payload.explanation: Acknowledging a questionable decision privately while focusing the debrief on performance teaches honesty and separates individual effort from luck.

payload.snippet: Anna is a PE teacher whose class is doing trampolining when a pupil attempts a back somersault unsupported — a skill not yet approved in their progression plan.
options: She stops the lesson immediately, checks the pupil for injury, and restates the safety progression framework to the whole class before resuming.
She lets the successful attempt stand as evidence the pupil is ready to progress their plan.
She completes the lesson and updates the pupil's progression plan retroactively.
She asks the pupil to demonstrate the skill again with spotters to make the progression official.
payload.explanation: Unapproved trampolining skills are a serious safety breach requiring a full stop, injury check, and reinforced framework — not retroactive sign-off.

payload.snippet: Jake is a marathon runner who overtakes an athlete near the finish when that athlete stumbles and grabs Jake's arm for support before regaining their footing.
options: He steadies them for a moment and then resumes his own race.
He slows down to run alongside the athlete in case they stumble again.
He uses the stumble to surge past the athlete and does not look back.
He stops his own race to help the athlete reach the finish line safely.
payload.explanation: A brief stabilising support followed by resuming the race respects the other athlete's dignity and autonomy.

payload.snippet: Maya is playing her first competitive tennis match when she realises mid-set that her racket tension is too low and her shots are landing long. She has no second racket.
options: She adjusts her swing technique to generate less power, accepts the limitation, and focuses on placement over pace.
She calls a medical timeout to request her coach brings a replacement racket from home.
She tells the umpire the racket is faulty and asks to replay the game.
She keeps playing the same way and hopes her opponent makes more errors.
payload.explanation: Adapting your game to equipment limitations is standard match play — timeouts and replays are not available for personal equipment issues.

payload.snippet: Tom is on a school cross-country team when he passes a runner from another school who is crouched over and has clearly twisted their ankle badly. The runner is alone with no coach nearby.
options: He stops, checks on the runner, and flags down a marshal or official before continuing.
He shouts encouragement and keeps running to avoid losing his race time.
He stops and stays with the runner until a marshal arrives even if it means not finishing.
He tells the next runner he passes to check on the injured athlete.
payload.explanation: Flagging a marshal and briefly checking safety is the minimum duty of care — staying indefinitely or ignoring are both wrong.

payload.snippet: Clara is a school PE teacher whose class is playing a contact sport when a pupil suddenly removes their protective mouth guard and pockets it halfway through the game.
options: She stops the activity immediately, explains the safety rule, and does not allow the pupil to return to play without the mouth guard in place.
She allows the pupil to continue as long as they are not involved in heavy contact.
She tells the pupil to put it back in and continues play without pausing.
She waits until the end of the game to address the issue to avoid disrupting the session.
payload.explanation: Safety equipment must be worn during play — stopping immediately sends the right message and prevents injury.

payload.snippet: Anna is a junior swimmer who has just set a new personal best time and her coach says it is because the lane rope was slightly lower on that side, giving her a small advantage.
options: She acknowledges the condition, asks whether the time can be officially recorded with a note, and accepts the coach's guidance on whether it counts.
She insists the time should stand because she swam her best and the lane rope is not her responsibility.
She asks the timekeeper to record the faster time without mentioning the lane rope.
She immediately asks the event organiser to invalidate the result.
payload.explanation: Questioning whether an environmental factor affects official validity is the right sporting response — the coach and officials decide, not the swimmer.

payload.snippet: Jake is coaching a junior football team and notices one player has been deliberately standing offside repeatedly to waste time when his team is winning in the final minutes.
options: He calls the player to the touchline, explains clearly that deliberate tactical offside is unsporting, and tells him it will not happen again.
He praises the player quietly for gamesmanship that is technically within the rules.
He ignores it because the referee is managing the offside calls.
He substitutes the player off without explanation to avoid rewarding the behaviour.
payload.explanation: Coaching against unsporting tactical play is the team coach's responsibility regardless of whether it is technically legal.

payload.snippet: Clara is a school librarian who discovers that a student has been photocopying entire textbook chapters for the whole class rather than purchasing or borrowing the books, citing the cost.
options: She speaks to the student, explains the copyright restrictions on bulk copying, and works with the school to identify a legitimate access solution such as a class set loan.
She allows the photocopying to continue since the school cannot afford the books.
She confiscates the photocopies and reports the student to the head teacher immediately.
She tells the student to stop and leaves finding an alternative to them.
payload.explanation: Copyright law restricts bulk copying — the librarian's role is to explain the rules and help find a legal access route.

payload.snippet: Oliver is borrowing library books on behalf of his housebound grandmother when the librarian tells him her card has expired and she must come in person to renew it.
options: He explains his grandmother's situation and asks whether there is a housebound borrower scheme or an alternative renewal process.
He renews the card himself using his grandmother's details online without telling her.
He uses his own card to borrow the books under a different account.
He argues that the rule is unfair and demands the librarian make an exception.
payload.explanation: Many libraries have housebound schemes — asking about an accessible alternative is the correct first step.

payload.snippet: Anna is using the library's quiet study room when a group enters and starts a loud video call despite a 'no calls' sign on the door.
options: She politely points out the sign and asks them to take the call outside, and if they refuse, she lets library staff know.
She turns up her own audio to block out the noise.
She immediately complains to the librarian without speaking to the group first.
She leaves the room without saying anything and uses the noisy general area instead.
payload.explanation: Addressing the issue directly first is the correct step before escalating to staff.

payload.snippet: Jake is researching a sensitive personal topic at a library computer when he realises the person next to him can clearly see his screen.
options: He uses the privacy screen filter available at the desk or repositions his seating to reduce visibility, and continues his research.
He stops researching entirely and waits until he is at home.
He asks the librarian to move the other person.
He uses a smaller font so the content is harder to read from a distance.
payload.explanation: Using available privacy tools or repositioning are the practical responses to unwanted screen visibility.

payload.snippet: Maya discovers that a popular book she has reserved has been withdrawn from the library collection due to a damage assessment, and she has been waiting three weeks.
options: She asks the librarian whether a replacement copy is on order or whether an interlibrary loan can be arranged.
She asks the librarian to source a second-hand copy from a charity shop.
She buys the book herself and asks the library to reimburse her.
She disputes the damage decision and asks to inspect the book herself.
payload.explanation: Interlibrary loan or enquiring about a replacement order are the correct routes when a reserved book is withdrawn.

payload.snippet: Tom is a library volunteer who is reshelving returned books when he finds a book that has been incorrectly classified and has been in the wrong section for years.
options: He brings it to the librarian with the correct classification details and lets them decide whether to reclassify it officially.
He moves the book to what he believes is the right section without telling anyone.
He adds a sticky note to the spine with the correct number and leaves it in the wrong section.
He sets it aside as a curiosity and shows other volunteers without raising it formally.
payload.explanation: Reclassification is a cataloguing decision for the librarian — volunteers flag, not fix.

payload.snippet: Clara finds a note tucked inside a returned library book that contains what appears to be a detailed description of self-harm. The note is unsigned.
options: She preserves the note and immediately brings it to the library manager, who follows the library's safeguarding protocol.
She reads the note carefully to decide whether it is serious before escalating.
She discretely scans the library to see if anyone looks distressed before deciding what to do.
She throws the note away to protect the privacy of whoever wrote it.
payload.explanation: A note describing self-harm inside a returned book is a safeguarding concern — immediate escalation to the manager is required.

payload.snippet: Oliver borrows an audiobook on CD from the library and discovers when he gets home that one of the discs is scratched and skips badly.
options: He returns the audiobook and reports the damage, asking whether there is a working replacement copy or a digital version available.
He tries to polish the disc himself before returning it.
He returns the disc and says nothing about the damage.
He asks the librarian to waive the final disc since he has already started listening.
payload.explanation: Reporting pre-existing damage on return protects the borrower from liability and helps the library update its stock.

payload.snippet: Anna is researching a school project at the library when she finds a Wikipedia article that directly contradicts what her teacher's source says. She is unsure which is correct.
options: She searches for a peer-reviewed or library-database source to verify which claim is supported by reliable evidence.
She uses the Wikipedia article because it is more recent.
She uses the teacher's source because the teacher is more trustworthy.
She includes both versions in her project and lets the reader decide.
payload.explanation: Verifying claims using authoritative library resources is the correct research response to conflicting information.

payload.snippet: Jake is at the library when an elderly borrower struggles to use the self-service checkout machine and the queue behind them is growing.
options: He quietly offers to help the borrower with the machine while the queue waits a moment.
He goes to the front of the queue himself since he knows how to use the machine.
He asks the librarian to open another checkout so the queue moves faster.
He loudly suggests the elderly person uses the staffed desk to speed things up.
payload.explanation: Offering quiet, direct help to the struggling borrower is the most respectful and practical response.

payload.snippet: Maya is on the library committee when a committee member proposes removing all physical books in a subject area to free up space, arguing that digital access covers the need.
options: She raises concerns about digital access inequality and proposes a usage audit before any withdrawal decision is made.
She agrees with the proposal since physical books take up space and cost more to maintain.
She proposes keeping one copy of each title and withdrawing duplicates only.
She blocks the proposal entirely, arguing that all physical books must always be kept.
payload.explanation: A usage audit before withdrawal decisions protects equitable access and is based on actual need rather than assumption.

payload.snippet: Tom is borrowing a rare local history book that the library marks as reference-only when the librarian steps away and leaves the desk unattended for several minutes.
options: He waits for the librarian to return and explains that he would like to view the reference book at a table within the library.
He takes the book to a table since the librarian is not watching.
He photographs all the pages quickly while the desk is unattended.
He asks another member of the public at the desk if they can check the book out for him.
payload.explanation: Reference-only books must be used within the library under normal supervision — the librarian's absence does not change the rule.

payload.snippet: Clara notices that the library's computer filter blocks access to a legitimate government health website she needs for research, while similar sites are accessible.
options: She asks the librarian to report the incorrect block to the IT team and explains what site she needs and why.
She uses a VPN on the library computer to bypass the filter.
She gives up and uses an unfiltered source she found elsewhere that is less authoritative.
She uses her mobile phone's data to access the site while sitting at the library computer.
payload.explanation: Reporting an incorrect filter block to the librarian is the correct first step — bypass tools are not permitted on library systems.

payload.snippet: Oliver discovers that the library's online catalogue shows a book as available on the shelf but it is not there when he looks.
options: He reports the discrepancy at the desk so the librarian can check whether the book is misshelved, lost, or recorded incorrectly.
He searches all adjacent shelves for twenty minutes before giving up.
He assumes it is borrowed and places a reservation on the catalogue.
He marks it as missing himself on the public catalogue system.
payload.explanation: Reporting a catalogue discrepancy to the librarian is the fastest way to resolve a misshelved or missing book.

payload.snippet: Anna is running a book group at the library when a participant begins aggressively criticising another participant's literary interpretation in a way that becomes personal.
options: She redirects the discussion to the text and, if needed, reminds the group of the respect guidelines agreed at the start.
She tells the aggressive participant to leave the group immediately.
She pauses the session and asks everyone to take five minutes outside.
She asks the targeted participant if they want to respond before she intervenes.
payload.explanation: Redirecting to the text and restating group norms are the correct facilitator responses to interpersonal conflict in a book group.

payload.snippet: Jake is a library assistant when a member asks him for advice on which book to read next based on a genre she enjoys, but he personally dislikes that genre and has not read it.
options: He is honest that the genre is not his own reading area and asks her what she has enjoyed recently so he can use the library's recommendation system or ask a colleague.
He recommends the most popular book in the genre he knows of without disclosing that he has not read it.
He tells her he cannot help and directs her to browse the section herself.
He recommends a different genre he does know well, explaining she might enjoy it more.
payload.explanation: Honest acknowledgement of the limits of your knowledge and using available tools is better than a guess or an unsolicited genre redirect.

payload.snippet: Tom is a secondary school librarian who discovers that several students have been using the library computers to access an AI writing tool to complete their essays entirely, submitting the output as their own work.
options: He raises the issue with the head of year and the relevant subject teachers, sharing the evidence he has observed, and asks for clarification on the school's academic integrity policy regarding AI tools.
He speaks to the students himself and warns them to stop before raising it with teachers.
He blocks the AI tool's website from the library computers without informing staff.
He monitors the situation for two more weeks to gather further examples before acting.
payload.explanation: The librarian's role is to raise the observed pattern to the relevant academic staff — unilateral blocking or direct student confrontation are outside the correct process.

payload.snippet: Clara is cataloguing a donated collection and finds that some titles were published by an extremist organisation, although the content itself is historical and factually informative.
options: She consults the library's collection development policy and brings the titles to the library director for a decision on whether to include them with appropriate context notes.
She adds the titles to the collection since historical material should be accessible.
She discards the titles since they were published by an extremist organisation.
She catalogues the books but does not list the publisher in the record.
payload.explanation: Titles with extremist origins require a policy-based decision by the appropriate authority — unilateral acceptance or disposal both bypass correct governance.

payload.snippet: Oliver is a library volunteer who notices a patron regularly photographing other patrons without their knowledge, apparently for artistic purposes.
options: He reports what he has observed to the librarian so the library can address it under its photography and privacy policy.
He approaches the patron himself and asks them to stop.
He asks the patron what they are photographing before deciding whether to raise it.
He ignores it since the photos are being taken in a public space.
payload.explanation: Photographing people without consent in a semi-public space like a library is a privacy concern — reporting to the librarian is the correct first step.

payload.snippet: Anna is a library manager when a visiting group books the meeting room and uses it for what turns out to be a private recruitment event for a multi-level marketing company.
options: She speaks to the group, clarifies the room's permitted uses under the library's booking policy, and ends the booking if it falls outside permitted uses.
She allows the event to continue since the room was booked under general community use.
She asks the group to move outside since commercial events are not covered by the booking.
She calls the police since an unauthorised commercial event is taking place on library premises.
payload.explanation: Enforcing room-use policy directly and politely is the librarian's responsibility — police involvement is not warranted for a booking misuse.

payload.snippet: Tom is a dental nurse when a patient undergoing a routine filling says they can feel pain despite having been given local anaesthetic. The dentist has already started drilling.
options: She signals the dentist immediately so the procedure can be paused and the patient's anaesthesia reassessed.
She tells the patient to be brave since the drilling is nearly finished.
She notes the patient's discomfort on the record but waits for the dentist to notice.
She asks the patient to describe the pain more clearly before stopping the procedure.
payload.explanation: Any reported pain during a procedure under local anaesthetic requires an immediate pause and reassessment — continuing is not acceptable.

payload.snippet: Clara is a dental receptionist when a patient calls to ask for the results of their recent X-ray. The practice has a policy that clinical results must be communicated by the clinician.
options: She explains the policy, takes a message, and arranges for the dentist to call the patient back.
She reads the X-ray notes from the record to the patient since they are already in the system.
She tells the patient there is nothing concerning since the dentist did not contact them.
She transfers the patient directly to the dentist's mobile without checking availability first.
payload.explanation: Clinical results must be communicated by the treating clinician — administrative staff should not interpret or relay them.

payload.snippet: Oliver is a dental hygienist who notices during a scale-and-polish that a patient has what appears to be an oral lesion that was not present at the last appointment.
options: He stops the clean, notes the finding, and refers the patient to the dentist for examination before continuing.
He completes the clean and adds the lesion observation to the notes for the dentist to review next time.
He photographs the lesion for his own reference and continues the appointment.
He tells the patient he has seen something and asks them to book a separate appointment.
payload.explanation: An unexpected oral lesion requires immediate referral to the dentist within the same appointment — continuing without assessment delays potentially important diagnosis.

payload.snippet: Anna is a dentist who is running forty minutes late due to a complex emergency procedure. The waiting room has several patients who have not been informed of the delay.
options: She asks her receptionist to inform all waiting patients of the delay, give an approximate revised wait time, and offer to reschedule anyone who cannot wait.
She continues working as fast as possible and relies on patients understanding that emergencies happen.
She sends the receptionist to apologise but does not offer rescheduling since that would create further gaps in the diary.
She finishes the emergency, then addresses the waiting patients herself mid-session.
payload.explanation: Informing waiting patients promptly, giving revised timings, and offering rescheduling are the correct responses to an unforeseeable clinical delay.

payload.snippet: Jake is a dental student on placement when his supervising dentist asks him to complete a procedure Jake does not feel competent to perform unsupervised.
options: He tells the supervising dentist honestly that he is not confident in that procedure at this stage and asks for closer supervision or a demonstration before he attempts it.
He attempts the procedure since the dentist must know his skill level and has approved it.
He starts the procedure and stops partway through if he encounters difficulty.
He asks another dental student to swap the procedure without telling the supervising dentist.
payload.explanation: Disclosing a competency gap before attempting a procedure is a patient safety obligation — starting and stopping mid-way is more harmful than declining in advance.

payload.snippet: Maya is a dentist who realises during a filling that she has inadvertently drilled deeper than intended and may have entered the pulp chamber of the tooth.
options: She stops, reassesses the situation, explains to the patient what has happened, and discusses the now-likely need for root canal treatment.
She completes the filling and monitors the tooth at the next appointment to see if symptoms develop.
She applies a protective dressing and tells the patient the filling was routine.
She refers the patient immediately to an endodontist without explaining what happened.
payload.explanation: An inadvertent pulp exposure requires immediate honest disclosure to the patient and discussion of the treatment implications.

payload.snippet: Tom is a dentist whose patient discloses in the chair that they have recently started taking a new medication. Tom does not recognise the drug name and is unsure of its interactions with the local anaesthetic he is about to use.
options: He tells the patient he needs to check the interaction before proceeding, looks up the drug in his reference tool, and only continues when he has confirmed safety.
He proceeds since the patient's GP would have flagged any dental interactions.
He uses a lower dose of anaesthetic as a precaution and continues.
He completes the examination first and checks the interaction before prescribing or injecting.
payload.explanation: Unknown medication interactions with anaesthetics must be verified before administration — proceeding on assumption or reduced dose are not safe alternatives.

payload.snippet: Clara is a dental practice manager who discovers that two dentists at her practice have been prescribing antibiotics for dental pain at a rate significantly above national guidelines, without recording the clinical justification.
options: She raises the issue with both dentists, reviews the clinical records for the relevant cases, and reports the prescribing pattern to the clinical governance lead.
She asks both dentists to add retrospective justifications to the records before reporting.
She sends an email reminding all clinical staff of the antibiotic prescribing guidelines.
She monitors the pattern for one more month to establish whether it is a genuine trend.
payload.explanation: Above-guideline antibiotic prescribing without recorded justification is a clinical governance concern requiring immediate escalation, not observation or retrospective record amendment.

payload.snippet: Oliver is a dental nurse when a parent asks to remain in the surgery while their ten-year-old child has treatment, but the child has privately told the dentist they do not want the parent present.
options: She supports the dentist in honouring the child's expressed preference, explaining to the parent that the child has asked for privacy in the surgery.
She allows the parent to remain since parental presence generally aids a child's compliance.
She asks the child to reconsider since the parent is worried.
She compromises by having the parent stand in the doorway rather than at the chair.
payload.explanation: A ten-year-old's expressed preference about their own healthcare setting should be respected — the child's autonomy takes precedence over assumed parental benefit.

payload.snippet: Anna is a dentist who sees a patient for the first time and notices significant dental decay consistent with long-term neglect. The patient, an adult, has said they are embarrassed and reluctant to discuss their history.
options: She acknowledges their feelings without judgement, focuses on what can be done now, and develops a treatment plan that prioritises urgent pain relief before addressing the wider decay.
She tells the patient the state of their teeth is a serious concern and asks directly about their past dental habits.
She proceeds with a full assessment and treatment plan without acknowledging the patient's embarrassment.
She focuses on a general health discussion first, delaying the clinical assessment to build trust.
payload.explanation: Acknowledging feelings without judgement and prioritising urgent needs first is the correct patient-centred approach to reluctant patients with complex decay.

payload.snippet: Jake is a dental practice manager when a patient complains formally that they were charged for a treatment they had not consented to, following an appointment they attended for a different procedure.
options: He acknowledges the complaint in writing, reviews the clinical notes and consent record for that appointment, and arranges for the patient to speak with the treating dentist before any refund decision.
He issues a full refund immediately to resolve the complaint without a clinical review.
He tells the patient the dentist must have had a clinical reason and asks them to contact the GDC if they are unhappy.
He asks the treating dentist to confirm verbally that consent was given and closes the complaint based on that confirmation.
payload.explanation: A consent complaint requires review of written records — verbal confirmation from the treating dentist alone or a refund without review are both insufficient responses.

payload.snippet: Maya is a dental hygienist working with a patient with severe dental anxiety who begins hyperventilating on the chair before treatment has started.
options: She stops all preparation, speaks calmly and slowly, and offers the patient the opportunity to sit up and breathe before deciding whether to continue.
She reassures the patient verbally and begins treatment since starting quickly will make it shorter.
She calls the dentist in immediately since a hyperventilating patient is a medical emergency.
She tells the patient she will just do the minimum today and proceeds with a basic scale.
payload.explanation: Pausing, sitting the patient up, and letting them recover before making any decision is the correct response to pre-procedural hyperventilation.

payload.snippet: Tom is a newly qualified dentist who is asked by a more senior colleague to sign off a clinical note for a procedure the senior colleague performed unsupervised after Tom had left for the day.
options: He refuses to sign off a procedure he did not witness, explains this to the colleague, and advises the colleague to sign their own notes.
He signs the note since the senior colleague is experienced and he trusts them.
He asks the colleague to describe the procedure in detail so he can sign it in good conscience.
He consults his defence organisation before responding, to understand the legal implications.
payload.explanation: Signing clinical notes for procedures you did not witness is fraud regardless of the colleague's seniority — the correct response is immediate refusal.

payload.snippet: Clara is a dental practice manager when a new patient's previous dental records, requested by the practice, arrive containing sensitive mental health disclosures from a previous clinical note.
options: She ensures the records are stored securely, confirms the treating dentist has access to the relevant clinical information, and does not discuss or share the mental health content beyond what is clinically necessary.
She reads the notes to prepare a welcome briefing for the whole clinical team.
She redacts the mental health content before passing the records to the dentist to protect the patient's privacy.
She asks the patient at their first appointment whether they are comfortable with the team having access to the records.
payload.explanation: Mental health information in clinical records is shared only on a need-to-know clinical basis — briefings or redaction without patient consent both handle it incorrectly.

payload.snippet: Oliver is a dentist whose patient repeatedly cancels and rebooks their appointment for a necessary extraction. He suspects dental anxiety is the cause but the patient has not disclosed it.
options: He calls the patient directly to ask whether there is anything they are worried about and whether any adjustments would help them attend.
He sends a letter warning the patient that further cancellations will result in removal from the practice list.
He asks the receptionist to note the patient as an unreliable attender on the system.
He waits until the patient next attends and addresses the cancellation pattern during the appointment.
payload.explanation: Proactively calling to explore barriers to attendance is a patient-centred response to repeated cancellations — warning letters penalise anxiety rather than addressing it.

payload.snippet: Anna is a senior dental nurse who observes a junior colleague using an instrument that should have been sterilised but has a visible protein deposit indicating the cycle may not have completed correctly.
options: She stops the procedure immediately, removes the instrument, and reports the decontamination breach to the infection control lead.
She wipes the instrument with an alcohol swab and allows the procedure to continue.
She waits until the procedure is finished before raising the decontamination concern.
She tells the junior colleague quietly and asks them to resterilise the instrument before the next patient.
payload.explanation: A potentially unsterilised instrument must be removed immediately and the breach reported — continuing or delaying risks cross-infection.

payload.snippet: Maya is a dentist who reviews a new patient's intake form and notices the patient has listed no allergies, but on closer inspection, a previous note from their GP record mentions a penicillin allergy.
options: She raises the discrepancy with the patient before any treatment or prescription, asks them to confirm their allergy status, and updates the record accordingly.
She proceeds based on the intake form since the GP note is old and the allergy may have resolved.
She adds the penicillin allergy from the GP note to the record without checking with the patient.
She does not prescribe any antibiotics at this visit and monitors the situation at the next appointment.
payload.explanation: Contradictory allergy information requires patient verification before treatment — acting on either record without confirming is unsafe.

payload.snippet: Tom is a dental practice manager who reviews the annual equipment maintenance schedule and finds that the practice's amalgam separator has not been serviced in over a year, which is outside the required maintenance interval.
options: He arranges the service immediately, checks whether any environmental compliance reports need to be updated, and reviews whether other equipment is approaching its maintenance deadline.
He schedules the service for the next available slot in three weeks and continues operations in the meantime.
He checks whether the separator is functioning visibly and only books a service if there are signs of a problem.
He notifies the practice owner and waits for their approval before booking the service.
payload.explanation: An overdue amalgam separator service is an environmental compliance issue — it requires immediate action, not a wait-and-see or approval delay.

payload.snippet: Clara is a dental nurse who notices that the patient's radiograph requested by the dentist is missing from the records for today's appointment. A new X-ray would mean additional radiation exposure.
options: She raises the missing radiograph with the dentist before the appointment proceeds, so the dentist can decide whether to re-take or check whether the image was filed elsewhere.
She takes the new radiograph since the dentist has requested it and the missing one may be lost.
She tells the patient the X-ray is missing and asks whether they have a copy at home.
She proceeds with the appointment and adds a note to the record that the previous X-ray was missing.
payload.explanation: A missing radiograph should be identified to the clinician before re-imaging — the dentist determines whether re-taking is clinically justified given the additional exposure.

payload.snippet: Oliver is a dental associate reviewing a patient who presents with significant dental anxiety and asks to discuss sedation options. Oliver is not qualified to provide sedation.
options: He explains his own scope of practice, discusses what sedation options are available through the practice or a referral, and involves the practice principal in the next steps.
He explains the sedation options in full and tells the patient to let him know if they want a referral.
He tells the patient that sedation is not available at this practice.
He assures the patient that most anxious patients manage without sedation and tries to treat them without exploring alternatives.
payload.explanation: When a treatment request falls outside your competence, the patient must be told about options available through referral — dismissing the need or implying a preference for no referral are both inappropriate.

payload.snippet: Anna is organising a milestone birthday party for her grandmother when she discovers two family members who are estranged have both been invited without being told the other is coming.
options: She calls each family member separately to let them know, and asks whether they are comfortable attending or need to discuss the situation.
She tells neither of them and hopes it goes smoothly on the day.
She uninvites one without telling the other why.
She tells her grandmother about the conflict and asks her to resolve it.
payload.explanation: Informing both parties of the situation before the event is the respectful and practical approach — surprises can turn a celebration into a confrontation.

payload.snippet: Jake is helping plan a class birthday event when he realises the venue chosen is not wheelchair accessible and one classmate uses a wheelchair.
options: He raises the accessibility issue with the teacher before the booking is confirmed and suggests looking for an accessible alternative.
He waits to see if the wheelchair user mentions it themselves before raising it.
He tells the wheelchair user the venue is already booked and they can plan something separate.
He suggests the wheelchair user can attend the part of the event held outside the inaccessible area.
payload.explanation: Accessibility must be considered before bookings are finalised — waiting for the affected person to raise it or offering partial inclusion are not adequate.

payload.snippet: Maya is throwing her own birthday party when a close friend unexpectedly bursts into tears during the celebration due to personal problems they have not shared yet.
options: She steps aside with her friend, gives them a moment, and checks if they need anything — then lets the friend decide whether to stay or go.
She asks her friend to hold their feelings until after the party is over.
She tells the group what has upset her friend so everyone understands.
She asks the friend to go home so the mood of the party is not affected.
payload.explanation: Making space for your distressed friend to decide their own next step is empathetic — sending them away or publicising their emotions are both wrong.

payload.snippet: Tom is blowing up balloons for his sister's party when he notices the balloon pump has a small crack that could cause it to break under pressure.
options: He stops using the pump and tells his parent so a replacement can be found before the children arrive.
He continues pumping carefully since the crack looks small.
He uses his hands to inflate the rest of the balloons.
He hides the pump and inflates only a few balloons without explaining why.
payload.explanation: A cracked pump under pressure is a safety risk — stopping and telling a parent immediately is the right response.

payload.snippet: Clara is at a friend's birthday party when the birthday child's parent begins serving alcohol-laced punch at a party where some guests are minors and adults are not clearly labelled.
options: She tells the parent she noticed the punch is alcoholic and that younger guests need a clearly separated non-alcoholic option.
She quietly tells the other teenagers to avoid the punch.
She drinks some herself but says nothing since the hosts are responsible.
She calls her own parent immediately to come and collect her.
payload.explanation: Directly alerting the adult host to the labelling issue is the appropriate first step — it addresses the problem at the source.

payload.snippet: Oliver is celebrating his birthday at a go-kart venue when the instructor gives a safety briefing he cannot hear clearly because of background noise.
options: He asks the instructor to repeat the parts he missed before getting into the kart.
He listens to what he can hear and assumes the rest is standard.
He asks a friend next to him what the instructor said.
He gets into the kart and drives at reduced speed in case he missed something important.
