payload.explanation: Abandon the bike, use the wall for support, and move diagonally with the current to exit — do not fight moving floodwater.

payload.snippet: Clara is responsible for a group of six children at an outdoor birthday party in a public park. While she is counting, she realises one five-year-old is missing. The last time she saw the child he was near the pond at the bottom of the slope.
options: She calls loudly, assigns one adult to stay with the other five, and runs directly to the pond to check before expanding the search.
She assigns all adults to search different sections of the park simultaneously.
She calls the child's parents immediately and asks them to come to the park.
She tells the remaining children to spread out and look for their friend.
payload.explanation: When a child near water is missing, the water hazard must be checked first — always.

payload.snippet: Tom is a volunteer at a school sports day helping to supervise the climbing wall activity when a nine-year-old reaches the top but the belayer's hand slips and the child drops two metres before the system catches them with a jolt. The child is dangling and crying.
options: He calls for the trained climbing instructor immediately, keeps the child calm and still while suspended, and does not attempt to lower the child himself.
He reaches up and unclips the child's harness so they can climb down the rope themselves.
He asks the belayer to slowly lower the child while he steadies the child from below.
He tells the child to let go of the wall and lower themselves hand-over-hand down the rope.
payload.explanation: Suspending a frightened child after a drop requires a trained instructor — keep them calm and do not improvise a lowering.

payload.snippet: Anna is at an outdoor play area when she witnesses an older child systematically intimidating and threatening younger children to stay off the equipment, making several of them cry. The child's parent is present and watching but not intervening.
options: She calmly speaks to the park warden or reports to the supervisor and does not confront the parent directly.
She directly challenges the older child in front of their parent to make the situation stop.
She takes the younger children to the far side of the park and calls the park closed for the area.
She tells the older child loudly that their behaviour is wrong so other parents can hear.
payload.explanation: Reporting to a park authority rather than confronting the parent avoids escalation and ensures proper handling.

payload.snippet: Oliver is leading a junior ranger forest-school session at a woodland playground when a child climbs a dead tree at the edge of the site. The tree visibly sways and the bark crumbles under the child's grip.
options: He calls the child down in a calm steady voice, moves the group away from the tree, and marks it for removal.
He has two other children hold the base of the tree while the climbing child descends.
He climbs the tree himself to assess whether it is structurally safe enough for play.
He waits until the child reaches a low branch before giving instructions, to avoid startling them.
payload.explanation: A dead swaying tree is a structural hazard — calm retrieval and marking are required immediately.

payload.snippet: Maya is working as a playground supervisor when she observes a new child join the group who appears to have fresh bruising on both forearms in a pattern inconsistent with playground falls — multiple circular marks in a line.
options: She documents what she sees accurately, does not question the child directly, and reports immediately to the school's designated safeguarding lead.
She asks the child in private what caused the bruises to understand what happened.
She photographs the bruises for the record and then monitors the child for the rest of the session.
She calls the child's parents to report the bruising pattern and see if they can explain it.
payload.explanation: Patterned bruising requires safeguarding reporting — do not interrogate the child or contact parents.

payload.snippet: Ben is helping install a new outdoor play structure at a community centre when he notices the ground anchors provided are a different specification than the drawing shows. He raises this with the site manager who tells him to fit them anyway and sign off the installation.
options: He refuses to sign off on the incorrect specification and asks the site manager to put the instruction in writing before he proceeds.
He fits the anchors as instructed and notes his concern in a site diary in case something goes wrong.
He installs the anchors as told, planning to replace them at the next inspection.
He calls the manufacturer directly and asks whether the alternative anchors are actually safe to use.
payload.explanation: Installing incorrect safety-critical anchors and signing off creates personal liability — require written instruction and refuse sign-off.

payload.snippet: Jake is supervising children at an adventure playground when one child starts a dare game that has escalated to jumping from a platform two metres high onto the grass below. Three children have already jumped before he notices.
options: He stops the game immediately, checks each child who jumped for injury, fills in an incident report, and informs the parents of all three.
He stops the next child from jumping and monitors the three who already jumped for the rest of the session.
He finishes supervising and completes an incident report at the end of the session.
He ends the session early and asks the children to wait for parents without explaining why.
payload.explanation: Immediate stop, injury checks for all participants, incident report, and parent notification are all required.

payload.snippet: Clara is running an after-school playground session when it starts raining heavily and the wooden decking on the assault course becomes extremely slippery. One child has already fallen.
options: She closes the wooden section immediately, moves children to the covered area, and files an incident report about the fall.
She tells children to remove their shoes to get better grip on the wet wood.
She keeps the session going but positions herself at the wet section to catch anyone who slips.
She ends the session and waits for the rain to stop before anyone continues playing.
payload.explanation: A wet wooden surface with a known fall requires immediate closure of that section and an incident report.

payload.snippet: Tom is playing at a skate park when he sees a child he knows from school sitting alone behind the toilet block looking distressed, with their phone lit up in their hand. When he asks, the child says an older person keeps messaging them asking them to meet.
options: He sits with the child, looks at the message if the child shows him, and walks with the child to tell a trusted adult immediately.
He tells the child to block the number and not to reply, then leaves them alone.
He tells the child to meet the person in a public place so they can see who it is.
He takes a photo of the screen for evidence and reports it to the police app on his own phone.
payload.explanation: An adult soliciting a child online for a meeting is a safeguarding matter — accompany the child and tell a trusted adult immediately.

payload.snippet: Oliver is at a community playground when he sees a child have a seizure lasting about forty-five seconds near the swings. The child comes round and seems confused and tired. No adult is immediately visible.
options: He keeps bystanders back, notes the duration, keeps the child in the recovery position if needed, calls 999, and stays with the child until an adult arrives.
He helps the child to the bench and gives them water while waiting for them to recover.
He runs to find the child's parent before calling 999 so they can authorise medical help.
He puts the child in the recovery position, waits for five minutes, and calls 999 only if there is another seizure.
payload.explanation: A first seizure in a child requires 999 regardless of apparent recovery — do not delay for parental authorisation.

payload.snippet: Maya discovers that the protective rubber surfacing under the climbing frame has been partially lifted at one corner, exposing a concrete edge that children could fall onto.
options: She stands near the hazard to redirect children away from it and calls the park authority to report the exposed concrete.
She pushes the rubber surfacing back down and stomps on it to reattach it temporarily.
She places a warning cone over the lifted section and hopes the park authority will notice it.
She redirects children verbally and sends a photo to the park's social media page.
payload.explanation: A supervisor must physically block access to an exposed hard surface and report it officially — DIY repairs to safety surfaces create liability.

payload.snippet: Ben is at an outdoor playground when he notices a water feature has a pump that is making a loud grinding noise and has a visible electrical cable lying across the wet ground near the splash area, where young children are playing.
options: He moves all children away from the wet area immediately, calls for the park warden, and makes sure no one touches the cable or the water until the warden arrives.
He asks a child to hold the cable off the ground so it does not touch the water.
He switches the pump off at the power button on the unit to remove the electrical hazard.
He tells children to step over the cable carefully and continues watching the area.
payload.explanation: A wet cable near an electrical pump with children present is a live electrical hazard — clear the area immediately and call a warden.

She helps him to his feet and asks him to flex his wrist to check if it is just a sprain.
She continues turning the roundabout slowly to let the rest of the group finish their turns.
She asks the group to form a circle around him so she can assess the injury privately.
payload.explanation: After a fall with a wrist impact, keep the person still and call for an adult — do not force movement.

She opens the exhibition as planned and speaks to the ceramics artist after the opening to avoid a scene.
payload.explanation: Honesty with the artist, documentation for insurance, and process improvement for future events are all required.

payload.snippet: Tom is a graphic design student working on a live client brief for a real small business when he realises he has accidentally deleted the master project file and the auto-backup failed. The client presentation is in forty-eight hours.
options: He contacts the client immediately, explains the situation, reconstructs as much as possible from exported files and screen recordings, and works extended hours to deliver the best version possible by the deadline.
He creates a completely new design that is significantly simpler to produce in the time available and presents it as an evolution of the original concept.
He asks the client for a one-week extension without explaining what happened, blaming a personal emergency.
He submits the previous version's rough draft and tells the client it is still in progress to buy time.
payload.explanation: Transparency with the client, recovery using available assets, and maximum effort to meet the deadline are the professional responses.

payload.snippet: Anna is a final-year art student whose major exhibition piece is a large oil painting that another student has accidentally walked through, leaving a footprint-shaped hole in the centre of the canvas.
options: She documents the damage, consults a canvas conservation resource, repairs the canvas from behind with a patch, and inpaints the damaged area, while reporting the incident to the department.
She repaints the entire piece from scratch as the damage is too severe to repair convincingly.
She frames the damaged canvas with the hole visible and presents it as a commentary on fragility.
She accepts compensation from the other student and withdraws the piece from the exhibition.
payload.explanation: Documentation, conservation repair, inpainting, and official reporting are the correct responses to accidental major artwork damage.

payload.snippet: Oliver is teaching an after-school pottery class when a student's kiln piece explodes during firing, damaging two adjacent student pieces. The explosion appears to have been caused by air pockets in the clay that were not properly worked out.
options: He runs through proper wedging and air-pocket checking technique with the whole group, documents the incident, contacts the students whose pieces were damaged, and checks whether the kiln itself was damaged before the next firing.
He tells the students whose pieces were damaged to redo their work and takes no further steps.
He checks the kiln briefly, runs the next firing, and teaches wedging technique at a later session.
He uses the damaged pieces as discussion examples but does not formally inspect the kiln.
payload.explanation: Kiln explosions require kiln inspection, incident documentation, affected student contact, and group technique reinforcement.

payload.snippet: Maya is a professional mural artist who has been commissioned to paint a large exterior mural on a community centre. Halfway through, the building owner asks her to change the subject matter in a way that significantly compromises the artwork's integrity and contradicts the brief she was given in writing.
options: She politely but firmly refers to the signed brief, explains how the requested change contradicts it, offers a limited modification that respects both her vision and the owner's concern, and documents all communication in writing.
She agrees to the changes to protect the client relationship and repaints the relevant sections.
She ignores the request and continues with the original design, trusting the building owner will be satisfied when it is finished.
She stops work on the mural until a revised contract is agreed, regardless of the impact on the timeline.
payload.explanation: Referring to the signed brief, proposing a compromise, and documenting all communication are the professional responses to a mid-commission scope change.

payload.snippet: Ben is photographing an outdoor public art piece when he discovers the artist has died recently and the copyright situation is unclear. A gallery wants to use one of his images for a commercial print run.
options: He advises the gallery to seek legal advice on the copyright status of both the artwork and his photograph before proceeding.
He licenses his photograph to the gallery as he owns the copyright to the photograph regardless of the artwork.
He contacts the deceased artist's family for permission even though he cannot establish whether they own the rights.
He withdraws from the project entirely as the legal complexity makes it too risky to proceed.
payload.explanation: Photographs of copyrighted artworks create dual copyright issues — legal advice before commercial use is the only safe approach.

payload.snippet: Jake is an art teacher when a student submits a portfolio piece for external assessment that he strongly suspects has been substantially created by an AI image generator rather than the student, despite the student's claim it was hand-drawn.
options: He speaks to the student privately, asks them to walk him through their process, and if still unconvinced, follows the school's academic integrity policy.
He accepts the portfolio entry and notes his suspicion in his own records in case it becomes an issue later.
He fails the student immediately and refers it to the head of department without speaking to the student first.
He asks the student to recreate a smaller version of the piece in class as a test without explaining why.
payload.explanation: Academic integrity concerns require private process questioning followed by policy compliance — not unilateral action or covert testing.

payload.snippet: Clara is coordinating a student art auction for charity when she discovers that one piece submitted for auction was copied directly from a known artist's work without attribution or transformation.
options: She contacts the submitting student privately, explains the issue, removes the piece from the auction, and replaces it with an alternative to avoid embarrassment while maintaining the integrity of the event.
She displays the piece with a note explaining it was inspired by the original artist as a compromise.
She accepts the piece as the student's artistic choice and lets bidders decide its value.
She withdraws the entire auction until all pieces can be verified as original work.
payload.explanation: Removing a plagiarised piece privately and replacing it maintains event integrity without public shaming the student.

payload.snippet: Tom is working on a commission for a local authority public sculpture. During fabrication he discovers the structural steel he was supplied was a lighter gauge than the specification required, meaning the finished piece may not be safe for public interaction.
options: He stops fabrication, documents the discrepancy, contacts the supplier and the commissioning authority, and will not proceed until correctly specified materials are provided and an engineer signs off the design.
He reinforces the lighter steel by welding additional supports internally so the finished piece meets the load requirement.
He proceeds with fabrication and discloses the material substitution in the installation documentation.
He contacts the commissioning authority but continues fabrication so as not to miss the installation deadline.
payload.explanation: A safety-critical material substitution in public art requires a full stop, documented disclosure, and professional engineering sign-off before proceeding.

payload.snippet: Anna is finalising a documentary photography project about a vulnerable community when she realises that one of her most powerful images inadvertently identifies a person who had only consented to appear in anonymous form.
options: She excludes the image from all exhibitions and publications, contacts the subject to inform them, and re-examines all other images for similar consent issues before publishing.
She crops the image to obscure the identifying features and uses it in the exhibition.
She uses the image only in her private portfolio since it will not be seen publicly.
She includes the image and credits the subject by their chosen alias to satisfy the consent requirement.
payload.explanation: Consent to appear anonymously must be fully honoured — exclude, inform the subject, and audit all remaining images.

payload.snippet: Oliver is running a community print workshop when a participant with severe colour blindness arrives and struggles to distinguish between the colours needed for the layered registration process.
options: He modifies the registration markers to high-contrast black and white patterns and provides verbal guidance for each layer.
He assigns another participant to guide the colour-blind person through the session.
He suggests the colour-blind participant do a mono-colour single-layer print instead.
He provides a printed colour chart and asks the participant to reference it for each step.
payload.explanation: Adapting the environment — high contrast markers — gives the participant full independent access to the process.

payload.snippet: Maya is exhibiting at a major graduate show when she learns the day before opening that the lighting rig above her work is flickering, which may trigger photosensitive epilepsy in some visitors.
options: She reports it to the gallery's technical team immediately and requests the flickering light be replaced or her piece be moved before opening.
She places a warning sign in front of her piece and leaves the decision to visitors.
She tells the gallery team at the opening so they are aware during the show.
She turns off the light above her piece and uses natural light from the window instead.
payload.explanation: A flicker that may trigger epilepsy is a safeguarding issue requiring technical fix or relocation before public access — a warning sign is insufficient.

payload.snippet: Clara is a student gallery coordinator when she discovers that two artists' pieces were hung at the wrong height and a fragile ceramics installation was partially damaged by a volunteer.
options: She adjusts the hung pieces that evening, photographs the damaged installation for the insurance record, contacts the ceramics artist to discuss the damage, and ensures volunteers receive handling instructions for future events.
She hides the damaged piece in the stockroom and tells the ceramics artist it could not be included due to space.
She asks the volunteers to reassemble the damaged installation as best they can before the opening.
She opens the exhibition as planned and speaks to the ceramics artist after the opening to avoid a scene.
payload.explanation: Honesty with the artist, documentation for insurance, and process improvement for future events are all required.

payload.snippet: Clara is a music teacher when a fifteen-year-old student begins using song lyrics during a lesson to express themes of self-harm in a way that feels personal rather than analytical. The student has also been increasingly withdrawn over recent weeks.
options: She does not address the lyrics directly in that moment, ends the lesson naturally, stays behind to check in gently with the student, and follows the school's safeguarding protocol by reporting to the designated safeguarding lead.
She analyses the lyrics with the student academically and asks what draws them to this type of music.
She calls the student's parents immediately from the music room to inform them of the concerning lyrics.
She tells the student that the chosen lyrics are not suitable for class and asks them to choose different material.
payload.explanation: Safeguarding concern from a vulnerable student's art requires a gentle check-in and DSL report — not in-lesson confrontation or direct parent contact by the teacher.

payload.snippet: Oliver is conducting a youth orchestra rehearsal when two section leaders have a heated argument in front of the rest of the orchestra about the correct interpretation of a passage.
options: He calmly stops the rehearsal, thanks both for their passion, proposes a short break, and speaks to each section leader privately before resuming.
He publicly sides with one section leader to resolve the debate quickly and move on.
He lets the argument continue until one section leader concedes, maintaining authority through non-intervention.
He removes both section leaders from the rehearsal to avoid the disruption continuing.
payload.explanation: A calm break and private conversations preserve both the rehearsal dynamic and each leader's dignity.

payload.snippet: Maya is a newly qualified music therapist working with a child with autism who becomes suddenly distressed during a session — throwing the instrument and covering her ears. The music had been gentle and familiar up to this point.
options: She stops the music immediately, sits calmly and quietly at a distance, and allows the child to self-regulate without adding further sensory input.
She continues playing very softly to help the child re-regulate through the familiar sound.
She holds the child gently to prevent further instrument throwing and reassures them verbally.
She ends the session and writes a detailed incident report, leaving the child alone in the room.
payload.explanation: Sensory overload in autism therapy requires immediate cessation of all stimuli and patient quiet presence — touch and continued sound worsen the response.

payload.snippet: Ben is performing in a professional chamber ensemble when a fellow musician makes a significant wrong entry three bars early in the final movement of a public concert. The entry disrupts the ensemble and confuses three other players.
options: He continues playing his own part clearly and confidently, providing a secure reference point for others to find their way back.
He stops playing to allow the others to sort out the confusion before he re-enters.
He plays a supporting harmony louder to try to pull the group back into the correct section.
He glances at the offending musician to signal that they must stop immediately.
payload.explanation: Continuing securely provides the stable rhythmic and harmonic anchor others need to re-orient — stopping makes the confusion worse.

payload.snippet: Tom is a school music technician setting up the PA system for a major concert when he discovers that the main power supply has a ground loop producing a hum through every speaker in the venue. The concert starts in ninety minutes.
options: He identifies the ground loop source, breaks the loop using a DI box on the most likely offender, retests, and has the system clean well before the concert.
He turns the master volume down so the hum is below audible at normal listening distance.
He removes all instruments from the PA chain and runs the concert through monitors only.
He switches to a different venue amp that was not part of the original spec.
payload.explanation: Ground loop diagnosis and DI box interruption is the standard technical fix — reducing volume masks the problem and monitors-only is unworkable for a major concert.

payload.snippet: Anna is leading an inclusive music workshop that includes a participant who is profoundly Deaf. The session is centred on rhythm but has no provision for tactile or visual rhythm feedback.
options: She introduces tactile elements — a drum pad placed on the table, balloons to feel bass frequencies — and ensures visual cues accompany every rhythmic instruction.
She asks the participant to observe rather than participate since they cannot hear the rhythm.
She speaks very loudly and clearly so the participant can lip-read all instructions.
She pairs the participant with a hearing partner who taps the rhythm on their shoulder.
payload.explanation: Tactile and visual adaptations give a Deaf participant full independent access to a rhythm workshop.

payload.snippet: Jake is a session musician hired to record a guitar track for an album. On hearing the playback, he realises the producer has requested a tone and style he has never used before and his recorded take sounds poor.
options: He tells the producer honestly, asks to hear reference tracks for the desired tone, and offers to redo the take once he understands the target sound.
He submits the take and hopes the producer will process it in the mix to achieve the desired sound.
He adjusts the EQ and overdrive settings himself before submitting the take without telling the producer.
He tells the producer the requested style is outside his skill set and asks to be paid for the session regardless.
payload.explanation: Transparency, reference listening, and offering a redo are the professional responses to a misaligned studio take.

payload.snippet: Clara is a choral director and one member of the choir persistently sings slightly sharp, pulling neighbouring singers off pitch. She has raised it in group feedback twice without improvement.
options: She works one-to-one with the member, uses a pitch drone to help them hear the target note, and explores whether there is a technical cause.
She moves the member to a less prominent position so their sharpness has less influence on others.
She asks the member to sing more quietly so the pitch deviation is less audible to the ensemble.
She removes the member from the choir for the coming concert and explains it is about performance quality.
payload.explanation: Individual work with a pitch drone identifies and corrects the technical cause — repositioning or silencing avoids the root cause.

payload.snippet: Oliver is teaching A-level music and marking a student's composition when he notices it appears to be substantially copied from a less-known published work that the student almost certainly has access to.
options: He asks the student to attend a brief viva discussion about their compositional choices, noting the specific musical features he wants to understand, before making any formal allegation.
He immediately reports the suspected plagiarism to the examination board before speaking to the student.
He awards the piece low marks without explanation and moves on without raising the issue.
He tells the student he suspects plagiarism and gives them twenty-four hours to produce evidence of original working.
payload.explanation: A viva to explore compositional thinking is the correct academic integrity step — it confirms or disproves copying before any formal report.

payload.snippet: Maya is a recording studio engineer when a band arrives for a six-hour session but the lead vocalist has acute laryngitis and can barely speak, let alone sing.
options: She suggests recording all instrumental tracks and overdubs first to maximise the paid session time, and rebooks the vocal session.
She tells the band the session must be cancelled as there is nothing useful to record without the vocalist.
She runs the vocalist through the parts at a whisper to preserve the emotional feel of the session.
She asks the vocalist to push through a few takes now and use vocal processing to fix it in the mix.
payload.explanation: Recording all non-vocal parts first maximises the session cost and a rebooked vocal date completes the project properly.

payload.snippet: Tom is a music journalist who has been given early access to an album under an embargo agreement. He receives an offer from a rival outlet to publish his review early for a significant fee.
options: He declines, honours the embargo, and publishes on the agreed date.
He publishes early and refunds the original outlet's access fee as compensation.
He writes a vague opinion piece that hints at the album's content without technically reviewing it.
He asks the original outlet to release him from the embargo so he can publish early legitimately.
payload.explanation: Embargo agreements are professional contracts — breaking them for financial gain is a serious breach of journalistic integrity.

payload.snippet: Anna is a piano examiner who has just failed a candidate for a grade eight exam. The candidate's parent approaches her aggressively after the session, demanding to know the result and threatening to report her.
options: She remains calm, explains that results are communicated officially by the exam board rather than the examiner, and does not disclose the assessment.
She tells the parent the candidate will need to work harder next time without confirming the result.
She shows the parent her marking sheet so they can see the scores for themselves.
She calls the exam board immediately from the venue to report the parent's behaviour.
payload.explanation: Examiners do not disclose results — citing official process and remaining calm is the correct response to post-exam parent pressure.

payload.snippet: Jake is a music producer who is asked by an artist to reproduce the feel of a very well-known copyrighted song closely for a commercial release.
options: He explains the legal risks of derivative work, suggests creating something inspired by the elements that cannot be copyrighted (feel, tempo, genre), and recommends the artist seek legal advice before release.
He produces the track as requested and advises the artist to change the title to differentiate it.
He adds enough original elements that he is confident no court would find it infringing.
He declines the project entirely to avoid any legal exposure on his part.
payload.explanation: Advising on copyright risk, offering a legal creative approach, and recommending formal legal review is the professional music producer's responsibility.

payload.snippet: Clara is a physical education teacher when a sixteen-year-old student with a known cardiac condition collapses during a fitness test. The student is unresponsive and not breathing. The school defibrillator is in the main office one floor up.
options: She begins CPR immediately, sends a student at a run for the defibrillator and to call 999, and does not stop CPR until the AED arrives or the student starts breathing.
She stops CPR to run for the defibrillator herself so she can be sure it is brought quickly.
She checks the student's pulse for sixty seconds to confirm CPR is needed before starting.
She sends two students for the defibrillator and waits with the student until it arrives.
payload.explanation: CPR must begin immediately and not stop — send others for the AED and to call 999 while CPR continues.

payload.snippet: Oliver is a junior rugby coach when he notices that one of his players winces every time he makes physical contact and has been avoiding tackles for two weeks. The player denies any injury when asked.
options: He removes the player from contact training immediately, informs the player's parents, and requires a medical clearance before the player can return to contact.
He reduces the player's contact exposure and monitors for another two weeks before making a decision.
He accepts the denial and continues normal training while watching the player more closely.
He asks the team physiotherapist to assess the player during the next match as a cover.
payload.explanation: Persistent pain signals in a contact sport require removal, parent notification, and medical clearance — not monitoring through discomfort.

payload.snippet: Maya is the team manager of a semi-professional football club when she discovers that three players have been falsifying their COVID vaccination certificates to comply with a competition requirement that was still in effect at the time.
options: She reports the falsification to the competition authority, suspends the three players pending a disciplinary hearing, and cooperates fully with any competition investigation.
She speaks to the players privately and gives them the opportunity to get properly vaccinated before the next match.
She quietly removes the players from the eligible squad list without reporting the falsification.
She notifies the club's legal team only and waits for their advice before taking any action.
payload.explanation: Falsified health documents for competition entry require immediate competition authority report, player suspension, and full cooperation — not informal correction.

payload.snippet: Ben is a certified first aider at a triathlon event when a competitor exits the water in distress, collapses on the beach, and shows signs of secondary drowning — coughing, low oxygen saturation on his pulse oximeter, and increasing confusion.
options: He calls 999 immediately, administers oxygen from the event's first-aid kit, keeps the competitor lying down, and does not allow the competitor to sign a self-discharge.
He gives the competitor ten minutes to recover and reassesses before calling 999.
He helps the competitor to the medical tent in a wheelchair and monitors them there.
He calls 999 but allows the competitor to sit upright because lying down makes the breathing harder.
payload.explanation: Secondary drowning is a life-threatening respiratory emergency — 999, oxygen, lying down, and no self-discharge are mandatory.

payload.snippet: Tom is a sports physiotherapist at a county athletics training camp when an athlete pushes through a session ignoring his advice to rest a stress-reaction injury in her foot. She completes the session and says she is fine.
options: He documents the non-compliance formally, refers her to the team doctor for imaging, and informs the head coach that she has trained against medical advice.
He accepts her self-assessment since she completed the session without visible distress.
He increases the frequency of his assessments and monitors the injury at every future session.
He keeps the non-compliance in his notes privately and waits to see whether symptoms worsen.
payload.explanation: Documented non-compliance, medical referral, and coach notification protect both the athlete's health and the physiotherapist's professional duty of care.

payload.snippet: Anna is the safeguarding officer for a county swimming club when a parent volunteers a piece of information during a casual conversation — their child mentioned that a senior coach 'always hugs goodbye' and that sometimes it feels uncomfortable.
options: She thanks the parent, listens without pressing for more detail, records the disclosure carefully, and reports it to the NGB's safeguarding team on the same day.
She tells the parent she will raise the general topic of appropriate physical contact in the next coaches' meeting.
She watches the coach's behaviour closely at the next session before deciding whether to escalate.
She asks the child directly what they mean by 'uncomfortable' to get clearer information.
payload.explanation: An informal disclosure involving inappropriate physical contact with a child requires same-day NGB safeguarding report — not investigation or observation by the club officer.

payload.snippet: Jake is a professional cyclist when his power meter data shows a suspicious spike in his teammate's performance output that correlates with a period when the teammate was out of the testing pool. He cannot be certain the data is evidence of anything.
options: He does not report the data alone, but when his teammate asks him to collaborate on a practice plan that relies on continued improved outputs, he declines to facilitate and instead discusses his concern honestly with the teammate.
He reports the suspicious data to anti-doping authorities immediately as potential evidence of a violation.
He accepts the data as evidence of natural improvement and supports the teammate's new training plan.
He says nothing, but begins quietly collecting further data to build a stronger case before acting.
payload.explanation: Uncertain performance data is not reportable alone — honest direct conversation with the teammate is the proportionate first step.

payload.snippet: Clara is a gymnastics judge at a regional competition when she scores a routine that she believes deserves an 8.4. The chief judge collects the scores and announces a panel average of 8.0 — noticeably lower — without explaining which judges were closest.
options: She raises her scoring concern privately with the chief judge after the session and asks whether her score was included in the panel average correctly.
She changes her scoring sheet to match the average so there is no discrepancy in the official records.
She announces her own score to the audience to show she judged the routine more highly.
She accepts the panel average as the correct outcome of collegial judging and does not raise it.
payload.explanation: Querying a scoring discrepancy privately with the chief judge is the correct procedural step — changing records or public announcements are not acceptable.

payload.snippet: Oliver is a sports psychologist working with an elite sprinter who has begun to show signs of overtraining syndrome — persistent fatigue, mood changes, and declining performance despite increased volume. The athlete's personal coach is resistant to reducing the training load.
options: He presents his clinical assessment to the performance director and recommends a formal multi-disciplinary review of the athlete's programme.
He speaks to the athlete alone and advises them to reduce their own training volume without informing the coach.
He respects the coach's programme because the coach has final authority over training decisions.
He arranges a conversation between himself and the coach and hopes the coach will accept the recommendation.
payload.explanation: A clinical finding in conflict with a coach's programme requires escalation to the performance director and a formal MDT review — not unilateral athlete advice or one-to-one hope.

payload.snippet: Maya is a football association official reviewing a match report when she notices the home team's starting lineup included a player who was under a three-match ban at the time. The match has already been played and the home team won.
options: She opens a formal investigation, notifies both clubs, and begins the process for a replay or points deduction under competition rules.
She contacts the home club to ask whether the lineup error was intentional before deciding on a course of action.
She notes the irregularity in the system and waits for either club to raise a formal objection.
She issues a fine to the home club but allows the result to stand given it is an administrative error.
payload.explanation: Fielding a suspended player is a competition rules violation requiring formal investigation and result remedy — intent is irrelevant to the procedure.

payload.snippet: Tom is a junior athletics coach when a female athlete discloses between training sessions that her parents are planning to remove her from school to train full time, a decision she is deeply unhappy about and did not agree to.
options: He listens fully, acknowledges her feelings, explains that he cannot intervene in family decisions, but follows the safeguarding protocol to report the concern about potential educational neglect.
He speaks to her parents at the next competition to explain how important continued education is for long-term athlete development.
He consults with the head of the athletics club and decides to monitor the situation informally first.
He tells her that her parents know best and encourages her to focus on her training.
payload.explanation: A child's objection to being removed from education triggers a safeguarding consideration for educational neglect — parent persuasion by the coach is not the correct response.

payload.snippet: Ben is managing a youth rowing club when the cox in the club's top crew is diagnosed with anorexia and the club's lightweight policy permits coxes at the athlete's current weight.
options: He removes the lightweight policy requirement for the cox immediately and arranges for the athlete to receive support from the club's sports welfare officer.
He maintains the lightweight policy but waits until the athlete has completed treatment before enforcing it.
He asks the crew's coach whether the cox's performance has been affected before making any policy changes.
He speaks to the cox privately and recommends they speak to a doctor, taking no action on the lightweight policy.
payload.explanation: A lightweight policy that intersects with a diagnosed eating disorder must be suspended immediately and welfare support activated — performance considerations are irrelevant.

payload.snippet: Oliver is a youth athletics coach when an athlete's parent approaches him after training to demand he moves their child into the senior group, citing a time that the parent has calculated using their own stopwatch rather than the official timer.
options: He explains that group placement decisions are made using official competition times only, offers to review the athlete's progress at the next scheduled assessment, and does not accept the parent's stopwatch time as evidence.
He agrees to trial the athlete in the senior group for one session to avoid a conflict with the parent.
He tells the parent their child's official times will be reviewed at the end of the season.
He explains that the athlete needs to work harder before a group change can be considered.
payload.explanation: Official times only are used for group placement — parent-measured times and pressure do not override the assessment process.

payload.snippet: Maya is a junior tennis player who wins a match when her opponent clearly clips the line on a shot that Maya called out. Her opponent disputes it but there was no line judge.
options: She offers to replay the point, acknowledging she is not certain the call was correct.
She upholds the call because line calls are the player's responsibility in her favour.
She concedes the point to her opponent to avoid any doubt.
She asks a spectator who was watching to confirm which way the call should go.
payload.explanation: When a player is genuinely uncertain about a line call with no official, replaying the point is the fairest resolution.

payload.snippet: Tom is a youth football coach whose team is losing 3-0 at half-time. One parent on the touchline has been shouting aggressive criticism at the opposing team's players.
options: He speaks directly to the parent during the break, explains that abusive touchline behaviour reflects on the whole club, and makes clear it must stop. If it continues, he will ask the match official to have the parent removed.
He ignores the parent because his priority at half-time is his players' performance.
He tells his team captain to walk near the parent and ask them to calm down.
He reports the parent's behaviour to the club committee after the match.
payload.explanation: A coach has a direct responsibility to address abusive touchline conduct in the moment — a post-match report does not protect the targeted players.

payload.snippet: Clara is a school PE head who discovers one of her department's teachers has been timing pupils' runs using an old stopwatch that loses five seconds per minute, meaning the school records for the past two years may be inaccurate.
options: She recalibrates all department timers, flags the affected records with a notation, and runs re-tests for any pupils whose times are close to the school record thresholds.
She replaces the timer and uses corrected records going forward without retesting.
She checks whether the error affected school records and only retests if a record is within five seconds of the original time.
She removes all records from the past two years from the board and starts fresh.
payload.explanation: Equipment failure affecting official records requires re-testing near-threshold athletes and annotating affected results — simply going forward is not sufficient.

payload.snippet: Anna is refereeing a high-stakes junior swimming relay when she notices after the final split-touch that one swimmer appeared to complete a two-hand touch with one hand slightly behind the other.
options: She reviews the touch with the second official and makes a joint decision before announcing it, following the competition rules on ambiguous touch calls.
She disqualifies the team immediately since the touch was clearly not simultaneous from her angle.
She awards the result to the team and does not raise the touch in case she was wrong.
She asks the team's coach to review the video from poolside before she makes a call.
payload.explanation: Ambiguous officiating calls in high-stakes events require second-official review — solo disqualification or poolside video review are both incorrect.

payload.snippet: Jake is a youth cricket club chairman when he learns that an away club has been systematically recording incorrect scores in their home match scorebooks, resulting in their players gaining higher batting and bowling averages than their actual performance.
options: He reports the discrepancy to the league governing body with documented evidence and requests an official review of the relevant results.
He tells the away club's chairman informally to correct their scorebooks going forward.
He adjusts his own club's records to compensate for the average inflation.
He waits for the end of the season and raises it at the annual general meeting.
payload.explanation: Systematic scorebook falsification is a league integrity issue — it requires a formal report to the governing body with evidence, not an informal conversation.

payload.snippet: Oliver is a gymnastics judge at a junior regional competition when he suspects a fellow judge has awarded a score that significantly exceeds what the code of points allows for the routine performed.
options: He raises a formal inquiry with the head judge after the rotation, citing the specific element scores he believes are inconsistent with the code.
He averages his score with the outlier to reduce its effect on the final result.
He approaches the fellow judge privately after the session to discuss the scoring difference.
He accepts that judges differ in interpretation and does not raise it.
payload.explanation: A materially inconsistent score in competition gymnastics requires a formal inquiry — private conversation or score averaging are not the correct channels.

payload.snippet: Maya is a triathlete who crosses the finish line in second place and then sees that the athlete who finished first was given a course cut by a marshal who directed them the wrong way, saving approximately two minutes.
options: She reports what she observed to the race director immediately after finishing, provides details of where she witnessed the course cut, and asks for an official review.
She accepts the result because the first-placed athlete may not have known they were directed incorrectly.
She posts about the incident on social media while waiting for the results to be official.
She waits to see if the race director notices independently before saying anything.
payload.explanation: Witnessing a course cut affecting results requires an immediate report to the race director — social media or waiting are not the correct responses.

payload.snippet: Maya is a public librarian when a patron requests access to a large collection of historical newspaper archives that are not digitised. Digitising them would cost more than the annual acquisitions budget.
options: She explains the current access limitations, checks whether a heritage digitisation grant or partnership programme might cover the cost, and offers the patron access to the physical archives in a supervised reading room.
She tells the patron the archives are not accessible and suggests they try the national library.
She applies for a digitisation grant without informing her manager of the budget implications.
She photocopies the most relevant sections herself over several days as a compromise.
payload.explanation: Explaining current limitations, exploring grant options, and offering supervised physical access are all appropriate responses to an underfunded digitisation need.

payload.snippet: Tom is a children's librarian who notices a regular young patron visiting daily and staying until closing, always alone and always reluctant to leave.
options: He creates a warm but non-intrusive relationship with the child over time, and discusses with his safeguarding lead whether the pattern warrants a gentle welfare check.
He speaks to the child directly and asks whether everything is alright at home.
He contacts the child's school directly to report his observations.
He informs the child's parent when they next appear that the child is spending a lot of time alone in the library.
payload.explanation: Patterns suggesting a child may be using the library as a refuge should be escalated to the safeguarding lead — direct questioning or contacting the school bypass the correct process.

payload.snippet: Clara is a library manager when a local political group requests a display promoting their campaign materials in the library's community notice board space.
options: She declines, citing the library's political neutrality policy, and offers the group the same access to the notice board space that any community group receives for non-partisan materials.
She allows the display since the library serves all community groups equally.
She consults the council before responding, delaying the decision by several weeks.
She allows the display on the condition that opposing parties are given equal space.
payload.explanation: Libraries maintain political neutrality — campaign material is not equivalent to community information and should be declined under neutrality policy.

payload.snippet: Oliver is a library archivist handling a family's donation of nineteenth-century letters when he discovers one letter describes what appears to be a serious historical injustice against an identifiable living family.
options: He consults the library's collections policy, flags the letter to his manager, and considers whether restricted access or a delay in catalogue publication is appropriate while taking legal advice.
He digitises and publishes all letters as received since they are of historical value.
He removes the letter from the donation without informing the family.
He contacts the identifiable living family to ask how they would like the letter handled.
payload.explanation: Sensitive archival material with potential impact on living people requires managerial consultation, policy review, and legal advice before publication.

payload.snippet: Anna is a school librarian who is asked by a teacher to remove a book from the library collection because the teacher considers some of its content inappropriate for the age group.
options: She reviews the book against the library's collection development policy and brings the challenge to the library committee rather than removing the book unilaterally.
She removes the book immediately since the teacher has a duty of care for students.
She moves the book to a restricted access section without consulting the committee.
She disagrees and tells the teacher that librarians, not teachers, make collection decisions.
payload.explanation: Book challenges should be handled through the formal review process — unilateral removal or dismissal both bypass the correct procedure.

payload.snippet: Jake is a librarian who discovers that a patron has been systematically photographing the full contents of several academic reference books over multiple visits, appearing to be building a private digital library for commercial use.
options: He explains the library's copyright policy to the patron, notes that commercial reproduction is not permitted under personal use exceptions, and asks them to cease the systematic copying.
He confiscates the patron's phone and deletes the photographs.
He bans the patron from the library immediately.
He says nothing since photographing within the library is not technically prohibited by posted rules.
payload.explanation: Explaining copyright policy and asking the patron to stop is the correct first step — immediate banning or confiscation are disproportionate.

payload.snippet: Maya is a library director when the local council proposes cutting the library's opening hours by forty percent to save costs. A community petition against the cuts has gathered two thousand signatures.
options: She prepares a data-led report on library usage, economic impact, and social value, presents it to the council, and engages the community petition in a formal consultation response.
She publicly campaigns against the council's decision using the library's social media accounts.
She reduces opening hours before the decision is formalised to demonstrate willingness to compromise.
She asks the petition organiser to attend the council meeting in place of a formal library response.
payload.explanation: A data-led case and formal consultation response are the professional routes — campaigning on official accounts or pre-emptive cuts both misuse her position.

payload.snippet: Tom is cataloguing a donated private book collection when he discovers several volumes contain handwritten dedications suggesting they belonged to a Holocaust survivor whose family was killed. The donor does not know the provenance.
options: He documents the provenance clues carefully, informs his manager, and consults with a heritage provenance organisation before accepting the donation into the permanent collection.
He accepts the books into the collection since they were donated in good faith.
He contacts the donor and asks them to take the books back until the provenance is resolved.
He photographs the dedications and adds them to a public online database of found Holocaust material.
payload.explanation: Provenance research and specialist consultation are required before incorporating potentially looted heritage items into a collection.

payload.snippet: Clara is a public librarian when a patron requests detailed information on how to access dark web forums. The patron says it is for journalism research.
options: She provides factual information on internet safety and anonymity tools from published sources while noting she cannot verify the stated purpose, and directs the patron to digital literacy resources and journalistic guidance organisations.
She provides detailed instructions since the patron has given a legitimate reason.
She refuses to engage with the question and asks the patron to leave.
She reports the request to the police as suspicious.
payload.explanation: Providing published factual resources while noting limitations is appropriate — unsupported escalation to police or refusal to engage are both disproportionate for a stated research purpose.

payload.snippet: Oliver is a library trustee when an audit reveals the library director has been approving personal taxi fares to and from the library as business expenses.
options: He brings the findings to the full board of trustees, ensures the director is suspended from approving their own expenses pending a formal review, and commissions an independent audit of all director-approved claims.
He speaks to the director privately and asks for repayment before raising it with the board.
He passes the matter to the library's accountant and does not involve the full board.
He resigns from the board rather than be involved in a process against a colleague he respects.
payload.explanation: Trustee financial misconduct requires full board involvement, suspension of self-approval authority, and independent audit — private repayment requests or passing to a single accountant are insufficient.

payload.snippet: Anna is a university librarian when a professor requests that she increase the borrowing limits for their research students beyond the standard policy limit, citing the volume of research the course demands.
options: She reviews the library's collections data on the relevant titles, assesses whether the demand can be met within existing stock, and brings a proposal for a tiered postgraduate limit to the library committee for a policy decision.
She increases the limit informally for that professor's students only without changing the policy.
She declines because policy changes require formal approval and she cannot expedite the process.
She purchases more copies of the relevant titles and increases the limit for all students without committee approval.
payload.explanation: Policy changes for borrowing limits require a formal committee process — informal exceptions and unilateral stock increases both bypass governance.

payload.snippet: Jake is a librarian in a small rural community library when he discovers that half of the children who use the after-school homework club have no internet access at home, meaning they cannot complete online assignments.
options: He works with his manager to extend the library's evening opening hours and explores whether the library can apply for connectivity or device loan funding to support those children.
He tells the children's teachers about the issue and leaves the solution to the school.
He gives the affected children his personal mobile hotspot password to use at home.
He asks the children's parents to apply for a commercial broadband package and suggests a budget provider.
payload.explanation: Extending access hours and pursuing funding are the librarian's proper levers — delegating to schools or sharing personal credentials are not appropriate solutions.

payload.snippet: Jake is a public librarian in a diverse urban area when a community group requests a display of materials that promote cultural practices another regular patron group has previously complained about as offensive.
options: He reviews the display request against the library's display policy, which supports representing diverse communities, and approves it on those grounds while ensuring the display does not contain material that breaches community standards.
He declines the display to avoid community conflict.
He approves the display but removes specific items the complaining group found offensive.
He holds a community consultation before approving or declining the request.
payload.explanation: Display policy, not community pressure, is the basis for display decisions — approvals or refusals driven by prior complaints rather than policy breach the principle of equitable access.

payload.snippet: Maya is a library director when a local councillor requests that she provide data on how many people from a specific ethnic group are library members, citing a community engagement initiative.
options: She declines to provide membership data segmented by ethnicity, explains that such data is not collected or held in that form, and offers to share general usage statistics that do not identify individuals by protected characteristics.
She provides the requested data since the councillor is a legitimate public official.
She tells the councillor the data is available but they need a formal data request.
She checks with her DPO and provides aggregated data that she believes cannot identify individuals.
payload.explanation: Membership data segmented by ethnicity is sensitive personal data — it requires a lawful basis the council engagement initiative does not provide, and sharing anonymised data requires DPO confirmation, not assumption.

payload.snippet: Tom is a school librarian who receives a list of books the head teacher wants removed from the school library ahead of an Ofsted inspection, with no educational justification given.
options: He asks the head teacher for the educational basis for the removal, explains the school's collection development and review procedure, and does not remove books without a documented rationale.
He removes the books as requested since the head teacher has ultimate responsibility for the school.
He removes the books but keeps a personal record of the titles in case they are needed later.
He tells the head teacher the request must go through the governors before any removal.
payload.explanation: Book removals from a school library require documented educational justification and proper process — compliance without justification or escalation to governors without first discussing it undermine the librarian's professional role.

payload.snippet: Clara is a community library manager when the building's landlord announces plans to convert the upper floor into private flats, removing the library's community reading garden that is used by over three hundred people weekly.
options: She formally objects to the change via the lease terms and council planning process, gathers evidence of community usage, and presents the case through official channels.
She negotiates directly with the landlord and accepts reduced garden access in exchange for lower rent.
She organises a public petition before exhausting the formal lease and planning route.
She accepts the change since the landlord has the legal authority to convert the space.
payload.explanation: A lease or planning challenge is the correct formal route before any negotiation or public campaign — accepting or negotiating before exhausting formal options forfeits rights unnecessarily.

payload.snippet: Oliver is a library acquisitions manager who discovers that a supplier has been double-invoicing the library for a significant number of orders over twelve months, resulting in overpayments of several thousand pounds.
options: He documents the double invoicing with records, reports it to his finance director, and requests a full reconciliation and refund from the supplier.
He issues a stop-payment on future invoices and deducts the overpayment amount from the next order.
He contacts the supplier informally and accepts their assurance that it was a system error.
He raises it at the next quarterly finance review meeting.
payload.explanation: A supplier double-invoicing pattern is a finance integrity issue requiring formal documentation, finance director escalation, and a formal refund request — informal resolution or self-deduction are not appropriate.

payload.snippet: Anna is a head librarian when a significant bequest of rare books arrives and a specialist dealer approaches her privately, offering to purchase several items at well above market value before they are formally catalogued.
options: She declines any private transaction, informs her director and the trustees of the approach, and ensures all items are fully catalogued and assessed before any disposal decision is made.
She accepts the offer since the price is well above market and the funds would benefit the library.
She declines the specific items requested but invites the dealer to bid once the items are catalogued.
She asks the dealer to put the offer in writing before deciding whether to present it to the trustees.
payload.explanation: Pre-cataloguing private purchase offers for donated heritage items bypass governance — any disposal requires formal trustee decision after full cataloguing.

payload.snippet: Jake is a library manager when a journalist requests access to the library's CCTV footage of a specific day, citing a public interest investigation.
options: He declines to share the footage without a legal order, explains the library's data retention and access policy to the journalist, and notes that CCTV disclosure to third parties requires either consent or a court order.
He views the footage himself and shares a verbal description of what it shows without releasing the recording.
He shares the footage since a public interest investigation is a legitimate justification under data protection law.
He asks his manager whether a public interest exemption applies before responding to the journalist.
payload.explanation: CCTV footage is personal data — disclosure to a journalist without a legal order is not permitted under public interest alone; seeking managerial advice does not change the legal position.

payload.snippet: Maya is a public library manager whose library runs a reading programme for adults with low literacy. She is approached by a local newspaper that wants to profile a participant as a human interest story.
options: She explains the request to the participant in plain language, ensures they understand fully what the story involves, and only facilitates the interview if the participant gives clear, voluntary, and informed consent.
She facilitates the interview since the participant is an adult and can decide for themselves.
She declines on the participant's behalf since the literacy programme is confidential.
She asks the participant's support worker to decide whether the interview is in the participant's best interest.
payload.explanation: Informed consent for a vulnerable participant must be confirmed directly with that person — facilitation without full understanding or proxy consent from a support worker are both inadequate.

payload.snippet: Maya is a dentist who reviews her morning schedule and finds she has been booked for twelve patients in a four-hour session, which is two more than her standard safe number. Her practice manager has added the extras to meet revenue targets.
options: She speaks to the practice manager before the session begins, explains her safe clinical capacity, and agrees a revised schedule that removes the additional patients.
She completes the session at pace since she does not want to turn away patients who need treatment.
She raises the scheduling issue at the next staff meeting rather than on the day.
She accepts the schedule but works faster on simpler cases to balance the time.
payload.explanation: Safe clinical capacity is a patient safety issue — it must be addressed before the session begins, not raised retrospectively or compensated for with speed.

payload.snippet: Tom is a dental surgeon who, during an extraction, breaks an instrument tip inside the socket. The patient is under local anaesthetic and unaware.
options: He stops, assesses the situation, decides whether retrieval is safe given the tip's size and position, and informs the patient honestly before completing the procedure or making an onward referral.
He completes the extraction and documents the fragment in the notes without disclosing it to the patient until they ask.
He attempts to retrieve the fragment without reassessing the risk, since leaving it is worse.
He closes the socket and plans to disclose at the follow-up appointment when he has more information.
payload.explanation: An instrument fracture is a clinical incident requiring immediate honest disclosure to the patient — delayed disclosure or undisclosed documentation are both failures of duty of candour.

payload.snippet: Clara is a dental hygienist when a patient tells her they have been taking a herbal supplement their dentist does not know about. She recognises it as something that may cause excessive bleeding during scaling.
options: She delays the scale, documents the supplement, and contacts the treating dentist to advise before proceeding.
She proceeds cautiously and applies extra haemostatic pressure if needed during scaling.
She tells the patient to inform their dentist at the next check-up but continues the treatment today.
She refuses to treat the patient until they stop taking the supplement for two weeks.
payload.explanation: A supplement with known bleeding implications must be flagged to the treating dentist before any scaling procedure — proceeding or deferring disclosure are both unsafe.

payload.snippet: Oliver is a dentist who recognises signs of domestic abuse in a patient's presentation — patterned facial injuries, a minimising explanation, and a partner who insists on accompanying them into the surgery.
options: He creates a moment alone with the patient, uses a validated clinical question to explore safety, documents his observations accurately, and follows his practice's safeguarding protocol.
He speaks to the accompanying partner to gather a more complete history.
He completes the clinical treatment without raising the issue, to avoid endangering the patient.
He asks the patient directly whether their partner is hurting them during the clinical examination.
payload.explanation: Safeguarding suspicion in adults requires a private assessment opportunity, validated inquiry, accurate documentation, and protocol adherence — questioning the partner or direct blunt questioning in a non-private setting can increase risk.

payload.snippet: Anna is a dental practice owner who discovers that a self-employed associate at her practice has been providing treatments she has not authorised and that fall outside the scope of the practice's insurance policy.
options: She immediately suspends the associate's access to the practice systems and list, notifies her indemnity insurer, and meets with the associate to address the contract breach before any resumption of work.
She asks the associate to cease the unapproved treatments and monitors their compliance over the next month.
She updates the practice insurance to cover the additional treatments retrospectively.
She speaks to the associate informally and documents the conversation as a verbal warning.
payload.explanation: Unauthorised treatments outside insurance scope are both a patient safety and legal exposure issue requiring immediate suspension, insurer notification, and formal process.

payload.snippet: Jake is a dental nurse who is asked by the dentist to prepare a higher-than-standard dose of local anaesthetic for a particularly anxious patient. Jake believes the dose exceeds safe limits.
options: He queries the requested dose with the dentist before preparing it, citing the safe limit he is aware of.
He prepares the dose as requested since the dentist has clinical responsibility.
He prepares the standard dose without telling the dentist and notes the discrepancy in his own record.
He refuses to prepare any dose until a second dentist confirms the request is safe.
payload.explanation: Questioning a clinical instruction you believe is unsafe is a duty — preparing it unchallenged or refusing without raising the concern are both wrong.

payload.snippet: Maya is a dentist who identifies a lesion in a patient's mouth that she suspects may be oral cancer. The patient is visibly distressed by previous bad news in their life and Maya is concerned about causing further distress.
options: She sensitively but clearly explains that she has seen something that needs urgent specialist review, refers the patient through the two-week wait pathway, and ensures the patient understands the importance of attending.
She refers the patient but describes the lesion as a minor irregularity to avoid causing alarm.
She waits for the patient to return for a routine appointment in three months before deciding whether to refer.
She asks the patient's GP to break the news so the patient has a familiar clinician to support them.
payload.explanation: Suspected oral cancer requires an honest explanation and urgent referral — downplaying the finding or delaying referral to manage distress risks the patient's outcome.

payload.snippet: Tom is a locum dentist who arrives at a new practice and finds that the sterilisation equipment has not been serviced within its recommended maintenance window and the log shows no record of the last cycle completing correctly.
options: He raises the issue with the practice manager before beginning his session and does not treat patients until the equipment is verified safe or replaced for the day.
He proceeds with the session and documents his concern in his own notes for indemnity purposes.
He calls the equipment supplier directly to ask whether the equipment is still safe to use.
He requests that used instruments be double-cleaned with an alcohol wipe before use today.
payload.explanation: Unverified sterilisation equipment is a patient safety issue — a locum clinician has the same duty as any other to refuse to treat until safety is established.

payload.snippet: Clara is a dental practice manager when a patient complains that the dentist made a discriminatory comment during their appointment. The dentist is the practice owner's relative.
options: She acknowledges the complaint formally, records it, and follows the practice's complaint procedure, treating the complaint on its merits regardless of the dentist's relationship to the owner.
She speaks to the practice owner informally before formally acknowledging the complaint.
She tells the patient the dentist is a relative of the owner and suggests they complain to the GDC instead.
She investigates the complaint herself by speaking to the dentist and closes it based on the dentist's account.
payload.explanation: Complaints must be handled through the formal procedure regardless of the respondent's relationship to management — informal handling or deflection to the regulator both undermine the process.

payload.snippet: Oliver is a dentist who realises mid-treatment that he has been treating the wrong tooth. The patient had a routine filling on the upper left first molar but Oliver has started drilling the upper left second molar.
options: He stops immediately, explains honestly to the patient what has happened, and decides next steps with the patient — including whether to complete the unintended preparation in a way that minimises harm and schedule the correct tooth separately.
He completes the filling on the wrong tooth and treats the correct tooth in the same session without disclosing the error.
He stops and tells the patient the tooth required treatment as well, so it was a clinical decision.
He completes the drilling, does not disclose, and monitors the mistakenly drilled tooth for symptoms.
payload.explanation: Wrong-tooth treatment is a clinical incident — immediate honest disclosure, patient involvement in deciding next steps, and incident reporting are all required.

payload.snippet: Anna is a dental nurse who observes that a colleague nurse has been accessing patient records out of hours without a clinical reason. She suspects the colleague knows one of the patients personally.
options: She reports her observation to the practice manager and data protection lead without first confronting the colleague.
She asks the colleague directly whether they know the patient before raising it formally.
She monitors the pattern for another week to confirm her suspicion before reporting.
She speaks to the patient to ask if they have given consent for a friend to view their records.
payload.explanation: Unauthorised access to patient records is a data protection breach — it must be reported immediately without prior confrontation of the person suspected.

payload.snippet: Jake is an orthodontist who reviews a referred patient's records and suspects the referring dentist has misdiagnosed the case in a way that led to premature extraction of two teeth that were not needed. The patient is fourteen.
options: He discusses his clinical assessment with the patient and their parent, explains that the extractions may not have been necessary based on his review, and completes a formal referral record that accurately reflects his findings.
He treats the case based on the current presentation without raising his concerns about the prior treatment to avoid undermining the referring dentist.
He contacts the referring dentist informally to discuss the case before noting any concerns in the records.
He advises the patient's parent to make a formal complaint against the referring dentist before he proceeds with treatment.
payload.explanation: Clinical concerns about a prior treatment must be recorded accurately and the patient informed — avoiding documentation to protect a colleague or advising immediate complaint both fail the patient.

payload.snippet: Anna is a dentist whose patient is a twelve-year-old who discloses during an examination that they have been using a vaping device regularly. The parent is in the waiting room.
options: She thanks the child for sharing this, explains the oral and general health risks clearly, documents the disclosure, and discusses with the child's permission whether they are comfortable with the dentist sharing this with their parent.
She calls the parent in immediately and informs them of the disclosure since the child's health is at risk.
She notes the disclosure in the record and does not raise it further since the child is old enough to make some decisions.
She tells the child she must tell their parent, then goes out and informs the parent without the child's involvement.
payload.explanation: A twelve-year-old's disclosure of vaping requires a health discussion, documentation, and a conversation about whether they consent to parental disclosure — informing the parent without the child's involvement breaches the duty to consider the child's developing autonomy.

payload.snippet: Jake is a dental surgeon who performs a tooth extraction and then discovers the following day that the post-operative instructions given to the patient contained an error — the patient was told they could rinse vigorously on the day of the procedure, which risks dislodging the blood clot.
options: He contacts the patient the same day to explain the error in the instructions, advise them on the correct aftercare, and ask whether they have already rinsed vigorously and whether they have any pain or symptoms.
He waits to see whether the patient calls with a complication before deciding whether to reach out proactively.
He updates the practice's post-operative instruction template and raises the error at the next clinical governance meeting.
He calls the patient, explains there was a printing error, and advises the correct aftercare without specifying what the wrong instruction said.
