payload.snippet: An incident commander is managing flooding in a city centre after a Victorian sewer system collapses under a main shopping street. Raw sewage is mixing with floodwater at the surface, two hundred shoppers are trapped inside a large department store, and the electricity substation serving the street is submerged.
options: She immediately requests the electricity network to cut power to the substation, cordons the affected street for a hundred-metre radius to prevent public contact with sewage-contaminated water, and coordinates evacuation of the store via the rear delivery entrance onto a clear street.
She evacuates the shoppers through the main front entrance using raised boards over the contaminated floodwater.
She focuses on the electricity substation risk first and holds the store evacuation until power is confirmed off.
She cordons the street and waits for the sewage authority to confirm the collapse extent before evacuating the store.
payload.explanation: Sewage flooding with a submerged electrical substation requires simultaneous power cut, contamination cordon, and safe rear evacuation — front-entry evacuation through sewage water is not acceptable.

payload.snippet: A search-and-rescue drone operator is deployed over a flash-flooded valley to locate and guide rescuers to survivors. His thermal camera identifies eight heat signatures in a flooded farmhouse but the access road is completely submerged. Two rescue boats are available, one with an outboard motor and one paddle-powered. The current is strong and the water is cold.
options: He uses the drone to map the fastest safe water route to the farmhouse, guides the motorised boat as the lead rescue craft while the paddle boat follows closely, and maintains a continuous live feed to the incident commander to track the operation.
He guides both boats simultaneously on different routes to reach survivors faster.
He lands the drone to conserve battery and gives the boat crews a single set of verbal directions.
He guides the paddle boat as lead because it is quieter and will not disturb the structure of the flooded farmhouse.
payload.explanation: Drone-guided rescue: map the route first, lead with the motorised boat, maintain live command feed — do not split guidance between two boats.

payload.snippet: A water-safety charity director is preparing testimony for a parliamentary inquiry into drowning deaths during rainy-season flash floods. Data show that sixty-three percent of drowning deaths occur within five metres of a safe bank, and sixty percent of victims were attempting to rescue others. She has three minutes to make a single most-impactful recommendation.
options: She recommends mandatory throw-line installation at all publicly-accessible water edges above a risk threshold, as the data show victims are close to the bank and a reach or throw aid would have prevented the majority of deaths.
She recommends a national public information campaign about the dangers of entering water to rescue others.
She recommends swimming proficiency testing be made a school-leaving requirement to reduce the number of non-swimmers who attempt water entry.
She recommends emergency services response-time targets be reduced for water incidents so professionals arrive before bystanders attempt self-rescue.
payload.explanation: Proximity data points to a structural intervention — throw-lines at the bank prevent both the primary and secondary drowning — campaigns and standards take years and do not change the physical environment.

payload.snippet: A flash flood has swept a woman and her young son into a storm drain channel with steep concrete walls. The mother is holding the child above water and is stationary against a support pillar, but the current is strong and her grip is weakening. Three bystanders are present, one with a ten-metre rope. Emergency services are six minutes away.
options: One bystander anchors themselves and holds one end of the rope, a second person holds the middle as a belay, and the third throws the weighted free end to the woman while calling her name clearly. They talk her through clipping it under the child's arms first, then her own.
All three bystanders enter the channel together to physically support the woman and child.
The bystander with the rope throws it directly to the woman without anchoring it first.
The bystanders form a human chain from the channel edge, with the last person lowering themselves into the water to reach the woman.
payload.explanation: Rope rescue: anchor first, belay the middle, throw to casualty — child before adult when both need the same line; never enter a fast-current channel as a bystander.

payload.snippet: A civil engineer reviewing flood-modelling data for a coastal town's sea-defence upgrade discovers that the current model was calibrated on historical storm-surge data but does not account for a one-metre sea-level rise projected over thirty years. The proposed new defences are designed to last sixty years. The upgrade is already approved and construction is due to start in four months.
options: She formally notifies the project client in writing with her modelling analysis, recommends halting construction until the defence design is reassessed against the thirty-year projections, and escalates to the Environment Agency if the client does not act within two weeks.
She raises the concern informally with the project lead and monitors whether the design team revise the model before construction starts.
She documents her concern in the project risk register and continues with her assigned engineering work.
She redesigns the affected sections herself using the updated sea-level data and presents the revised drawings to the client.
payload.explanation: A safety-critical design flaw in long-life flood infrastructure requires formal written notification, a construction hold request, and regulatory escalation if not acted upon — informal flagging is insufficient.

payload.snippet: A hydrologist monitoring a catchment during sustained heavy rain detects that two river gauges upstream of a residential valley show a flow increase of four hundred percent in ninety minutes — a rate consistent with a dam failure or a catastrophic lateral inflow upstream. She cannot confirm the cause remotely. Emergency services have been alerted but will take twenty minutes to reach the valley.
options: She immediately issues a self-initiated evacuation advisory through the local authority's emergency broadcast system citing the gauge data and the unconfirmed but plausible dam-failure risk, then continues monitoring to update the advisory in real time.
She waits for emergency services to arrive and confirm the upstream cause before issuing any public advisory.
She advises the local authority to issue a precautionary advisory while she takes another thirty minutes to investigate the cause.
She calls the dam operator to confirm status before issuing any advisory that could cause panic if the dam is intact.
payload.explanation: A four-hundred-percent flow surge with an unconfirmed dam-failure hypothesis and a twenty-minute emergency-services lag requires immediate public advisory on available data — waiting for confirmation costs lives.

payload.snippet: A community resilience officer conducting post-flood analysis discovers that a care home operator failed to execute their flood evacuation plan during a recent event, leaving twelve residents in a ground-floor room as water entered the building. Staff lacked training and the plan had not been tested in three years. No residents were seriously harmed but the outcome was very close.
options: She files a formal Duty of Care concern with the Care Quality Commission, supports the care home in immediately arranging an emergency drill, requires the operator to submit a revised tested plan within thirty days, and includes the incident in the local multi-agency flood debrief.
She notes the near-miss in her report and recommends the care home review their plan at the next annual staff training cycle.
She contacts the care home manager informally and agrees to revisit the plan with them at the next quarterly resilience meeting.
She focuses the debrief on what went right rather than the near-miss to maintain staff morale and cooperation.
payload.explanation: A near-miss safeguarding failure in a regulated care setting requires CQC notification, immediate drill, a mandatory revised plan, and multi-agency learning — not informal advice.

payload.snippet: A playground equipment manufacturer's safety manager receives a report that three serious injuries — one critical — have occurred at different local authorities using the same model of climbing frame within six months. Her own company's records show that a batch of connecting brackets was produced with undersized threading due to a machining error, and the affected serial numbers were distributed to forty-seven sites across the country.
options: She immediately issues a mandatory recall and out-of-service notice to all forty-seven sites, notifies the Health and Safety Executive, cooperates fully with the investigation, and arranges emergency inspection of all affected equipment.
She contacts the three affected sites first and waits for their technical reports before deciding whether a wider recall is necessary.
She arranges independent testing of ten random brackets from the batch before issuing any recall that could expose the company to legal liability.
She issues a precautionary advisory to all sites to inspect their brackets visually while allowing them to remain in service.
payload.explanation: Three serious injuries linked to a known manufacturing defect require immediate mandatory recall, HSE notification, and full cooperation — independent testing before action is not acceptable.

payload.snippet: A local authority play space manager discovers during a routine inspection that a contractor has installed a zip wire with a stopping mechanism that fails at loads above fifty kilograms. The site has been open for six weeks and has had several hundred users. No reported injuries yet, but a child weighing fifty-five kilograms would impact the end post at significant speed.
options: She closes the zip wire immediately, erects barriers, contacts the contractor for emergency remediation, notifies the local authority's risk management team, and checks incident logs from all six weeks of operation.
She places a weight limit sign at the zip wire and monitors it for the remainder of the day before closing it.
She allows use of the zip wire with a spotter to catch users before they hit the end post until a fix is arranged.
She closes the zip wire and reports the contractor to the council's procurement team for the next contract review.
payload.explanation: A weight-dependent safety failure on public equipment requires immediate closure, contractor notification, risk management escalation, and retrospective incident review.

payload.snippet: A child protection expert reviewing serious case reviews from the past decade notes a recurring pattern: abuse occurring in unmonitored areas of public playgrounds, typically behind toilet blocks or within dense play structures. She has been asked to present recommendations to a national play safety body.
options: She recommends sightline audits for all new and existing playground designs, mandatory reporting requirements for operators when abuse is suspected in their facility, and integrated safeguarding training for all play supervisors.
She recommends installation of CCTV in all areas of public playgrounds to eliminate all unmonitored zones.
She recommends that all public playgrounds require adult supervision of children at all times to remove the opportunity for abuse.
She recommends reducing the physical complexity of play structures to eliminate the possibility of children being out of sightlines.
payload.explanation: Safeguarding in play spaces requires sightline design, operator training, and reporting mandates — not blanket surveillance or design impoverishment that reduces play value.

payload.snippet: An outdoor play area operator is notified that ground contamination from a former industrial site was found in soil samples taken from outside the play area boundary. Subsequent testing of soil within the play boundary shows trace levels of a heavy metal at seven percent above the safe threshold for children's play areas. Forty children use the facility daily.
options: She closes the facility immediately, notifies the local authority's environmental health team, arranges further multi-point sampling to map the extent of contamination, and contacts the families of regular users through the centre's records.
She restricts children from digging or touching the soil surface and allows the facility to remain open with increased supervision.
She waits for the environmental health team to advise her before closing, as she is not qualified to assess the risk independently.
She closes the facility for the weekend while further sampling is arranged and opens it again on Monday pending results.
payload.explanation: A confirmed above-threshold heavy-metal reading in a children's play area requires immediate closure, authority notification, contamination mapping, and family contact — not operational modification.

payload.snippet: A school adventure playground coordinator discovers that unsupervised evening use by teenagers has led to significant structural damage — multiple welds cracked, one platform rope support frayed to thirty percent of its original diameter — on equipment that will be used by primary children the following morning. It is now 10pm and the playground opens at 8am.
options: She declares the entire adventure playground out of service, arranges emergency signage and locking, contacts the headteacher, and calls the equipment supplier's emergency inspection line to arrange a morning visit before the playground can reopen.
She takes the damaged equipment out of service and allows the rest of the playground to open as normal in the morning.
She photographs all damage, shares it with the site manager, and waits for a decision from senior management in the morning.
She repairs the visibly frayed rope herself using a splice technique she has used before and opens the playground with close supervision.
payload.explanation: Multiple structural failures on children's equipment require full closure, emergency signage, management notification, and professional inspection before any reopening.

payload.snippet: An occupational therapist working in a specialist play development programme notices that the only fully accessible piece of equipment in the district's twenty public playgrounds is a single swing with a supportive seat. Children with mobility impairments who visit other playgrounds have no equipment they can use independently. She has been given a seat on the new district play strategy board.
options: She presents evidence on the developmental and social harms of inaccessible playgrounds, proposes accessible equipment standards for all new installations, and recommends an audit of existing facilities against the Equality Act duty with a costed remediation schedule.
She recommends installing one accessible swing at every playground as a cost-effective first step toward inclusion.
She focuses her strategy input on the highest-footfall playgrounds only, as they affect the most children.
She recommends allocating the entire play budget to a single exemplary fully accessible flagship playground.
payload.explanation: Systemic inaccessibility requires an evidence-based standard for all installations, a legal audit, and a phased remediation plan — not token additions or flagship-only solutions.

payload.snippet: A senior parks manager is presented with a planning application for a large commercial adventure playground on green belt land adjacent to an existing public playground. The commercial operator has proposed a twelve-metre aerial ropes course with a risk assessment signed off by a private safety consultant they appointed themselves.
options: She commissions an independent third-party safety audit of the risk assessment, reviews the consultant's qualifications and independence, and requires the operator to address all findings before granting approval.
She accepts the risk assessment on the basis that the consultant is professionally qualified and the applicant is financially accountable.
She approves the application subject to a council safety inspection in the first three months of operation.
She requests that the operator reduce the maximum height to eight metres to bring it within the standard reference for supervised adventure play.
payload.explanation: Self-commissioned risk assessments for novel high-risk play structures require independent audit and qualification verification before planning approval.

payload.snippet: A forensic investigator is called to a public playground where a child has suffered a serious injury after a swing chain broke. Her task is to determine whether the failure was due to manufacturer defect, installation error, or maintenance negligence. She has access to the broken chain link, the installer's records, the manufacturer's maintenance specification, and the local authority's maintenance logs.
options: She analyses metal fatigue patterns on the fracture face, cross-references the chain replacement interval in the specification against the log dates, checks the installer's torque records against the manufacturer's specification, and documents a chain of custody for all physical evidence.
She interviews the maintenance team first to establish their recollection before examining the physical evidence.
She focuses her investigation on the most recent maintenance visit as the most likely proximate cause.
She examines the physical evidence and issues a preliminary finding within twenty-four hours to support the family's legal claim.
payload.explanation: Forensic investigation of a playground injury follows physical evidence first, systematic cross-referencing, and chain of custody — not interview-led or premature preliminary findings.

payload.snippet: A school adventure playground coordinator discovers that unsupervised evening use by teenagers has caused significant structural damage — multiple cracked welds and a frayed rope support at thirty percent capacity — on equipment opening the following morning at 8am. It is now 10pm.
options: She declares the entire adventure playground out of service, arranges emergency signage and locking, contacts the headteacher, and calls the equipment supplier's emergency line for a morning inspection.
She takes the damaged equipment out of service and allows the rest of the playground to open normally.
She photographs all damage, shares it with the site manager, and waits for a management decision in the morning.
She repairs the frayed rope herself using a splice technique and opens the playground with close supervision.
payload.explanation: Multiple structural failures require full closure, emergency signage, management notification, and professional inspection before any reopening.

She allows use with a spotter stationed at the end post until a fix is arranged.
She closes the zip wire and reports the contractor to the procurement team for the next contract review.
payload.explanation: A weight-dependent safety failure on public equipment requires immediate closure, contractor notification, risk management escalation, and retrospective incident review.

She recommends allocating the full play budget to a single fully accessible flagship playground.

options: She immediately issues a mandatory recall and out-of-service notice to all forty-seven sites, notifies the Health and Safety Executive, and cooperates fully with the investigation.
She contacts the three affected sites first and waits for their technical reports before deciding on a wider recall.
She arranges independent testing of ten random brackets before issuing any recall that could expose the company to legal liability.
She issues a precautionary advisory asking all sites to inspect their brackets visually while remaining in service.

Subsequent testing within the boundary shows trace heavy metals at seven percent above the safe threshold for children's play areas. Forty children use the facility daily.
options: She closes the facility immediately, notifies the environmental health team, arranges multi-point sampling to map the extent of contamination, and contacts families of regular users through the centre's records.
She restricts children from digging or touching the soil surface and allows the facility to remain open with increased supervision.
She waits for the environmental health team to advise her before closing, as she is not qualified to assess the risk independently.
She closes the facility for the weekend while sampling is arranged and opens again on Monday pending results.
payload.explanation: A confirmed above-threshold heavy-metal reading in a children's play area requires immediate closure, authority notification, contamination mapping, and family contact.

payload.snippet: A play development researcher is presenting to a government taskforce on the declining rate of outdoor unsupervised play among children in the UK over thirty years. She has data showing a correlation between restricted outdoor play and increased rates of childhood anxiety, reduced risk assessment competence, and poor motor development.
options: She recommends graduated autonomy policies in schools and local authorities, design standards that build in child-led risk assessment opportunities, and public education campaigns reframing acceptable risk in play.
She recommends removing all physical risk from play environments as the primary policy goal to address the safety concerns that drive parental restriction.
She recommends mandatory outdoor play quotas in school timetables as the single most evidence-based intervention.
She recommends a media campaign targeting overprotective parents as the root cause of declining outdoor play.
payload.explanation: Play deprivation policy requires systemic change across autonomy, design, and public framing — not single-lever interventions or parent-blaming.

payload.snippet: A parks director is reviewing the aftermath of a serious incident in which a child was abducted from a public park for two hours before being found. The park had no operational supervision, broken gate latches, and no sightline from the gate to the main play area. She must present a safeguarding improvement plan to the council.
options: She proposes a sightline redesign for the main entrance, a funded part-time park warden for peak hours, a gate latching specification upgrade across all parks, a public reporting QR code system for hazards, and community liaison sessions with local primary schools.
She proposes installing perimeter fencing around all parks to limit access points to monitored entrances.
She proposes a closed-time policy for all parks after 3pm when most incidents occur.
She proposes a phone-in registration system for parents allowing children to enter only after adult registration.
payload.explanation: Public park safeguarding requires layered environmental design, proportionate supervision, technical standards, and community engagement — not access restriction that defeats the purpose of public open space.

payload.snippet: A secondary school is considering removing its outdoor adventure play area after a series of minor injuries. The school's health and safety officer argues for removal; the PE head argues that the physical and psychological development benefits outweigh the managed risk. The headteacher must decide.
options: The headteacher commissions an independent risk-benefit assessment, reviews injury rates against national benchmarks, consults both the H&S officer and the PE head, and reviews the risk-management protocols before making a final decision based on evidence.
The headteacher defers to the health and safety officer as the designated risk authority on site.
The headteacher removes the adventure play area to eliminate all liability exposure.
The headteacher retains the play area and asks the PE department to manage all risk independently from the H&S officer.
payload.explanation: A risk-benefit decision on valued play infrastructure requires an independent assessment, national benchmarking, and evidence-based judgement — not unilateral deference to either safety or programme advocates.

payload.snippet: A charity that manages a network of thirty inner-city adventure playgrounds receives notification that its public liability insurer is withdrawing cover due to increasing claims from a specific style of rope-based play feature that appears across twelve of its sites. Without cover, all twelve sites must close, affecting eight hundred children weekly.
options: The charity commissions a structural safety review of all twelve rope features to separate high-risk from acceptable risk, negotiates with the insurer using the review findings, applies for emergency bridge funding to cover retrofits, and publicly campaigns for play insurance reform.
The charity closes all twelve sites immediately and replaces all rope features with low-risk equipment to regain insurability.
The charity disputes the insurer's decision legally while keeping all twelve sites open on a risk-accepted basis.
The charity closes only the three sites with the highest historical claims and accepts reduced provision as the pragmatic outcome.
payload.explanation: Insurance-driven play closure requires a risk-stratified response, evidence-based negotiation, retrofit funding, and systemic advocacy — not blanket closure or legally contested continued operation.

payload.snippet: A museum conservator is examining a seventeenth-century oil painting scheduled for international loan when she discovers a previously unrecorded network of microfractures in the paint layer that suggests the work is at risk of significant surface loss during transportation. The receiving institution has planned a major exhibition around the painting and tickets are already sold.
options: She documents the condition report in full, advises against transportation in the current state, recommends stabilisation treatment before any decision is made, and communicates her finding to the lending institution's director and the receiving curator.
She clears the painting for transport because the microfractures have likely been stable for many years.
She applies a consolidant to the most vulnerable sections and approves transport with enhanced packaging.
She completes the condition report but defers to the director's commercial judgement on whether to proceed.
payload.explanation: A conservator's professional duty requires full documentation and clear technical advice against transportation — not accommodation of commercial pressure.

payload.snippet: An art authentication expert is asked to verify a painting attributed to a major twentieth-century artist that has appeared on the market with questionable provenance documentation. The painting has already been sold for twelve million pounds. She has spectroscopic analysis showing a synthetic pigment that was not commercially available until twenty years after the artist's death.
options: She issues her written opinion that the attribution is untenable given the pigment evidence, advises the current owner of her findings, and reports her concern to the relevant art fraud authority.
She issues a qualified opinion noting the pigment anomaly but leaves the attribution open pending further investigation.
She advises the owner privately and waits for the market to respond before making any public statement.
She revisits the date of the pigment's commercial availability to see if any other explanation could account for its presence.
payload.explanation: Spectroscopic evidence of an anachronistic pigment is definitive authentication failure — a written opinion, owner notification, and fraud authority report are required.

payload.snippet: A public art commission manager is overseeing the installation of a monumental steel sculpture when the installation team discovers that the sub-surface conditions are significantly different from the geotechnical survey, making the planned foundation inadequate for the sculpture's weight. Installation day has arrived, the crane is hired, and the artist is present.
options: She stops the installation, sends the crane away, commissions a revised geotechnical assessment, and notifies all parties of the delay and its reason.
She has the installation team dig a deeper footing by hand to increase the stability before proceeding.
She proceeds with installation but accepts the artist's suggestion of adding a secondary anchor chain to nearby infrastructure.
She installs the sculpture on the day and commissions a geotechnical review to confirm post-installation stability within thirty days.
payload.explanation: Inadequate foundations for a monumental sculpture are a public-safety risk — stop, reassess, and do not install regardless of cost or schedule pressure.

payload.snippet: A graphic novelist discovers that a publisher has included her work in an anthology without permission and has commercially distributed it, but the cover letter she received twelve months ago contained ambiguous phrasing that the publisher claims constitutes consent. She has retained the original letter.
options: She consults an intellectual property lawyer, requests a formal written account from the publisher, and pursues compensation for unauthorised commercial use through the appropriate channel.
She accepts the publisher's interpretation and negotiates a royalty for future editions.
She publishes the original letter online to let her audience judge whether consent was given.
She requests her work be removed from the anthology and takes no further action on past commercial losses.
payload.explanation: Ambiguous commercial consent requires legal advice, formal documentation request, and compensation pursuit — not public appeals or accepting the unauthorised party's interpretation.

payload.snippet: A digital artist discovers that her generative artworks have been used without permission to train a commercial AI image model. The company claims that publicly posted images are legally usable for training. Her images carry a Creative Commons non-commercial licence.
options: She documents the infringement evidence, consults a specialist IP lawyer on whether the non-commercial licence was breached, joins an industry collective action, and updates her publication terms to make training exclusion explicit.
She watermarks all future works prominently to deter further scraping and accepts the existing use as irreversible.
She sends a cease-and-desist letter herself citing the non-commercial licence breach.
She removes all her work from public platforms to prevent further training-data use.
payload.explanation: AI training-data infringement requires evidence documentation, specialist IP advice, collective action, and terms hardening — not self-issued legal letters or platform withdrawal.

payload.snippet: A conservation team leader at a national gallery discovers that a restoration treatment applied to a major work by a previous conservator twenty years ago used a material now known to be causing long-term damage to the original paint layer. The previous treatment is documented and the previous conservator is alive and respected in the field.
options: She presents the findings to the gallery's conservation committee, recommends a priority examination of all works treated with the same material, and commissions a specialist to advise on stabilisation without attributing blame to the previous conservator.
She contacts the previous conservator first to give them the opportunity to advise before raising the matter with the gallery.
She treats only the specific painting identified and documents the current condition without raising the broader question.
She flags the material concern in the treatment report but does not recommend a wider audit to avoid alarm.
payload.explanation: A newly identified harmful restoration material requires systemic audit, specialist intervention, and committee escalation — individual treatment and blame avoidance are not sufficient.

payload.snippet: A street artist is invited by a property developer to create a mural on a building scheduled for demolition in two years. A month after completion, the mural receives international media attention and the artist learns the developer has applied for planning permission to convert the building permanently, effectively monetising the artwork without any agreement on residual rights or compensation.
options: She takes legal advice on moral rights in relation to public artworks, documents the original agreement, and negotiates with the developer for recognition, compensation, or a transfer of rights appropriate to the new circumstances.
She accepts that the developer owns the building and therefore controls all decisions about works on its surface.
She publicly campaigns for the building's demolition to proceed as originally agreed to reclaim her rights.
She requests the mural be photographically archived and removes herself from association with the project.
payload.explanation: Moral rights in an unexpectedly monetised public artwork require legal advice, documentation of the original agreement, and negotiation — not acceptance of the property owner's unilateral position.

payload.snippet: An art school's foundation course director is reviewing applications and discovers that a portfolio submitted by an applicant from a disadvantaged background is significantly stronger than any other application but includes a hand-drawn copy of a well-known painting presented without attribution. All other work is demonstrably original.
options: She interviews the applicant directly about the copied work, assesses whether it was presented as original or as a study piece, and makes an offer conditional on a clear policy briefing if the intent was not to deceive.
She rejects the application immediately as portfolio integrity is non-negotiable regardless of circumstance.
She accepts the application without raising the issue to avoid penalising a disadvantaged applicant for a likely oversight.
She accepts the application and notes the concern in the student's file for the faculty to monitor.
payload.explanation: A single ambiguous attribution in an otherwise strong application warrants a direct interview to establish intent before making a conditional offer — neither blanket rejection nor unaddressed acceptance is appropriate.

payload.snippet: A museum conservator examining a seventeenth-century oil painting scheduled for international loan discovers a previously unrecorded network of microfractures suggesting the work is at risk of significant surface loss during transportation. Tickets are already sold for the receiving institution's major exhibition.
options: She documents the condition report in full, advises against transportation in the current state, recommends stabilisation treatment before any decision is made, and communicates her finding to the lending institution's director and the receiving curator.
She clears the painting for transport because the microfractures have likely been stable for many years.
She applies a consolidant to the most vulnerable sections and approves transport with enhanced packaging.
She completes the condition report but defers to the director's commercial judgement on whether to proceed.
payload.explanation: A conservator's professional duty requires full documentation and clear technical advice against transportation — not accommodation of commercial pressure.

payload.snippet: An art authentication expert is asked to verify a painting attributed to a major twentieth-century artist. Spectroscopic analysis shows a synthetic pigment that was not commercially available until twenty years after the artist's death. The painting has already been sold for twelve million pounds.
options: She issues her written opinion that the attribution is untenable given the pigment evidence, advises the current owner of her findings, and reports her concern to the relevant art fraud authority.
She issues a qualified opinion noting the pigment anomaly but leaves the attribution open pending further investigation.
She advises the owner privately and waits for the market to respond before making any public statement.
She revisits the date of the pigment's commercial availability to see if any other explanation could account for its presence.
payload.explanation: Spectroscopic evidence of an anachronistic pigment is definitive authentication failure — a written opinion, owner notification, and fraud authority report are required.

payload.snippet: A public art commission manager is overseeing installation of a monumental steel sculpture when the team discovers that sub-surface conditions are significantly different from the geotechnical survey, making the planned foundation inadequate for the sculpture's weight. The crane is hired and the artist is present.
options: She stops the installation, sends the crane away, commissions a revised geotechnical assessment, and notifies all parties of the delay and its reason.
She has the installation team dig a deeper footing by hand to increase stability before proceeding.
She proceeds with installation but accepts the artist's suggestion of adding a secondary anchor chain to nearby infrastructure.
She installs the sculpture and commissions a post-installation geotechnical review within thirty days.
payload.explanation: Inadequate foundations for a monumental sculpture are a public-safety risk — stop, reassess, and do not install regardless of cost or schedule pressure.

payload.snippet: A graphic novelist discovers that a publisher included her work in an anthology without permission and has commercially distributed it, but the publisher claims ambiguous phrasing in a cover letter twelve months ago constitutes consent. She has retained the original letter.
options: She consults an intellectual property lawyer, requests a formal written account from the publisher, and pursues compensation for unauthorised commercial use through the appropriate channel.
She accepts the publisher's interpretation and negotiates a royalty for future editions.
She publishes the original letter online to let her audience judge whether consent was given.
She requests her work be removed from the anthology and takes no further action on past commercial losses.
payload.explanation: Ambiguous commercial consent requires legal advice, formal documentation request, and compensation pursuit — not accepting the unauthorised party's interpretation.

payload.snippet: A digital artist discovers her generative artworks have been used without permission to train a commercial AI image model. The company claims publicly posted images are legally usable for training. Her images carry a Creative Commons non-commercial licence.
options: She documents the infringement evidence, consults a specialist IP lawyer on whether the non-commercial licence was breached, joins an industry collective action, and updates her publication terms to make training exclusion explicit.
She watermarks all future works prominently to deter further scraping and accepts the existing use as irreversible.
She sends a cease-and-desist letter herself citing the non-commercial licence breach.
She removes all her work from public platforms to prevent further training-data use.
payload.explanation: AI training-data infringement requires evidence documentation, specialist IP advice, collective action, and terms hardening — not self-issued legal letters or platform withdrawal.

payload.snippet: A charity managing a network of thirty inner-city art studios receives notification that its public liability insurer is withdrawing cover due to increasing claims from a specific type of kiln equipment across twelve sites. Without cover, all twelve studios must close, affecting eight hundred young people weekly.
options: The charity commissions a safety review of all twelve kilns to separate high-risk from acceptable risk, negotiates with the insurer using the review findings, applies for emergency bridge funding to cover retrofits, and publicly campaigns for accessible arts insurance reform.
The charity closes all twelve sites and replaces all kilns with lower-risk equipment to regain insurability.
The charity disputes the insurer's decision legally while keeping all twelve sites open on a risk-accepted basis.
The charity closes only the three sites with the highest historical claims and accepts reduced provision as the pragmatic outcome.
payload.explanation: Insurance-driven arts closure requires a risk-stratified response, evidence-based negotiation, retrofit funding, and systemic advocacy — not blanket closure or legally contested continued operation.

payload.snippet: A public gallery director is approached by a major corporate sponsor who insists that a specific artist — whose work critically depicts the corporation's industry — be removed from the upcoming exhibition as a condition of a significant donation.
options: She declines the condition, documents the approach, consults the gallery's board, and seeks alternative funding sources to maintain the exhibition's artistic integrity.
She removes the artist's work to secure the donation and commissions a replacement piece with a neutral subject.
She accepts the condition privately and tells the artist the piece was withdrawn for curatorial reasons.
She accepts the donation and includes the artist's work anyway, judging the sponsor will not follow through on their threat.
payload.explanation: Accepting editorial conditions attached to sponsorship compromises institutional integrity — decline, document, inform the board, and seek alternative funding.

payload.snippet: A government arts funding body receives evidence that a major arts organisation it funds has been systematically misrepresenting its diversity statistics in grant applications over five years to appear more compliant with funding criteria than it actually is.
options: She commissions an independent audit, requires the organisation to suspend further applications pending the audit outcome, claws back any grant money obtained through misrepresentation, and updates application verification processes to prevent recurrence.
She meets with the organisation's director privately and allows them to self-correct their next application.
She reduces the organisation's next grant by a fixed penalty but continues the funding relationship.
She publishes the evidence immediately and lets the sector respond before deciding on a formal response.
payload.explanation: Systematic grant misrepresentation requires independent audit, application suspension, clawback, and process reform — not private correction or partial penalty.

payload.snippet: An independent art critic reviews a major exhibition and writes a strongly negative assessment. Three days later she receives a legal letter from the artist's gallery claiming the review constitutes defamation and demanding a public retraction.
options: She seeks independent legal advice, reviews her published text for any factual errors, corrects any genuine factual mistakes while standing by her critical judgements, and consults the publication's legal team.
She retracts the review immediately to avoid the expense and reputational risk of legal action.
She ignores the letter as criticism of art is clearly protected free speech and requires no response.
She publishes a response explaining why she stands by her review without taking legal advice.
payload.explanation: A legal threat against criticism requires legal advice, factual accuracy review, correction of genuine errors, and standing by legitimate critical opinion — not retraction or dismissal.

payload.snippet: A music conservatoire admissions panel is reviewing applications and discovers that a candidate has submitted fabricated masterclass certificates from a prestigious institution to bolster their portfolio. The candidate is a genuinely exceptional musician whose live audition was among the highest-scoring of the year.
options: The panel disqualifies the application for misrepresentation, notifies the institution whose name was used, and offers the candidate the opportunity to reapply in the following cycle with a verified portfolio.
The panel accepts the application based on the audition score and notes the fabrication internally.
The panel confronts the candidate immediately during the audition week about the falsified documents.
The panel reduces the candidate's overall score to reflect the integrity breach and considers them against that adjusted score.
payload.explanation: Fabricated credentials disqualify an application regardless of talent — contacting the named institution and offering a fresh cycle is the correct and fair response.

payload.snippet: A professional orchestra's music director discovers one week before the premiere that the commission they agreed to perform contains extensive unattributed quotation from a lesser-known twentieth-century composer's unpublished work. The composer's estate is known to be litigious.
options: She contacts the commissioning composer immediately, requests that proper attribution be added to the programme notes, informs the orchestra's legal team, and asks the estate's representative whether performance can proceed with attribution.
She proceeds with the premiere and adds a general acknowledgement of twentieth-century influences to the programme.
She cancels the premiere and commissions a replacement work for the remaining week.
She performs the work and waits to see whether the estate makes a claim after the fact.
payload.explanation: Unattributed quotation from a living estate requires legal team involvement, attribution negotiation, and estate permission before performance.

payload.snippet: A music streaming platform's content team receives a report that an algorithm used to curate playlists for children has been including songs with subtly hidden adult content that passes automated keyword filters. Fifty thousand children's accounts have been exposed over three months.
options: The team immediately suspends the algorithm, manually audits all affected playlists, removes flagged content, notifies affected account holders, and commissions an independent audit of the filter system before redeployment.
The team patches the keyword filter and redeploys the algorithm with the updated rules.
The team removes the specific songs that have been reported and monitors for further complaints.
The team notifies the platform's press team to prepare a statement and waits for the technical audit before taking action.
payload.explanation: Children's content exposure requires immediate algorithm suspension, full manual audit, account notification, and independent review before redeployment.

payload.snippet: A nationally recognised music therapist is asked to testify as an expert witness that a specific type of music can be used as a psychological influence tool based on unpublished preliminary research. The case has significant legal implications for the defendant.
options: She declines to testify beyond what the published peer-reviewed evidence supports, explains the limitations of preliminary research in formal testimony, and offers to testify only to what is scientifically established.
She testifies to the preliminary findings with appropriate caveats, judging the case important enough to share emerging research.
She declines the case entirely to avoid the professional risk of giving contested testimony.
She testifies to the established research and includes a brief reference to preliminary findings as supporting context.
payload.explanation: Expert testimony must be strictly limited to established peer-reviewed evidence — preliminary research cannot be presented as reliable in a legal setting.

payload.snippet: A major music festival discovers two days before opening that the main stage's acoustic design creates a dangerous standing-wave resonance at certain bass frequencies that could exceed safe exposure limits for extended listening, based on a last-minute acoustical assessment.
options: The festival director commissions an immediate acoustic engineer review, limits bass frequencies in the sound check, repositions the main speaker clusters to disrupt the resonance pattern, and consults an audiologist on the residual risk before opening.
The festival director limits the main stage's bass frequency during the opening night only and reassesses between acts.
The festival director proceeds as planned, trusting that audience movement and natural variation will disrupt the resonance.
The festival director closes the main stage and moves all acts to a secondary stage.
payload.explanation: A confirmed resonance risk at unsafe levels requires engineering mitigation, frequency limiting, speaker repositioning, and audiological review — not avoidance or assumption of natural disruption.

payload.snippet: A composer discovers that an AI tool she used to generate harmonic suggestions during a compositional process has drawn on a dataset that included copyrighted scores without licence. Her completed symphony is already accepted for a world premiere.
options: She discloses the AI tool's use and its dataset provenance to the commissioning body and her legal team, and requests a formal assessment of whether the generated elements constitute infringement before the premiere proceeds.
She does not disclose the AI tool's involvement since the final compositional decisions were entirely her own.
She replaces the AI-generated harmonic passages with original alternatives before the premiere without disclosing the issue.
She checks whether any of the AI suggestions are recognisably similar to specific copyrighted works and only discloses if they are.
payload.explanation: AI-assisted composition using an unlicensed training dataset requires proactive disclosure, legal assessment, and commissioning body notification before premiere.

payload.snippet: A music education researcher publishes a study claiming that a specific pedagogical method improves child literacy outcomes by thirty percent based on twelve months of data. Two years later she finds an error in her original analysis that reduces the effect size to eight percent. The study has been cited in national curriculum policy.
options: She publishes a formal correction in the original journal, notifies all citing parties she can identify, and contacts the relevant curriculum policy team directly.
She publishes a new study with the corrected methodology and relies on the academic record to update naturally.
She notes the correction in her next paper's literature review and considers the matter addressed.
She consults her institution and waits for their guidance before publishing any correction.
payload.explanation: A curriculum-influencing analytical error requires a formal journal correction, direct citing-party notification, and policy-team contact — passive correction is not sufficient given the scale of impact.

payload.snippet: A sound engineer is working on a live broadcast when she discovers that a microphone feed from a private backstage conversation between an artist and their manager — containing sensitive personal disclosures — has been accidentally fed into the broadcast mix for approximately forty seconds before she catches it.
options: She immediately removes the feed, flags it to the broadcast director, records the technical incident, and the broadcast team issues an appropriate statement to acknowledge the accidental transmission.
She removes the feed and says nothing, hoping the broadcast audience was not paying attention.
She removes the feed and overwrites the broadcast archive of those forty seconds to prevent further spread.
She flags it to the director after the show ends to avoid disrupting the live broadcast flow.
payload.explanation: An accidental private broadcast requires immediate removal, director notification, incident logging, and a public statement — overwriting records or silence are not acceptable.

payload.snippet: A record label executive discovers that a subsidiary producer has been using a royalty-split agreement that systematically underpays artists signed to the label by using an incorrect baseline calculation that has gone undetected for three years.
options: She halts all royalty payments pending a full audit, notifies the affected artists and their managers in writing, arranges correction of the calculation methodology, and repays all underpaid amounts with interest.
She corrects the calculation going forward and applies the fix to new payments without addressing the historical shortfall.
She offers affected artists a bonus on their next project as goodwill compensation for the past underpayment.
She consults the label's lawyers to determine whether the underpayment technically constitutes a breach before notifying artists.
payload.explanation: Systematic underpayment requires payment halt, full audit, artist notification, methodology correction, and back-payment with interest — not prospective-only fixes.

payload.snippet: A music school principal discovers that one of her most popular tutors has been accepting private students who he met through the school's booking system and charging them at lower rates without the school's knowledge, breaching his employment contract.
options: She meets with the tutor privately, presents the evidence, suspends him pending a formal disciplinary hearing, and informs affected families of the contractual situation.
She gives the tutor a formal written warning and asks him to stop immediately without further action.
She reduces the tutor's school rate to match the private rate to remove his incentive for the arrangement.
She monitors the situation for one more month to gather further evidence before raising it formally.
payload.explanation: Contract breach by an employee requires suspension, formal disciplinary process, and family notification — informal warnings or rate adjustments do not address the breach.

payload.snippet: A music charity that runs free instrument tuition for children in deprived areas discovers that its lead programme officer has been inflating participant numbers in grant reports by approximately thirty percent over two years to secure continued funding.
options: The board immediately places the programme officer on administrative leave, conducts an internal investigation with external auditors, notifies the funders proactively, and repays any overfunded amounts.
The board corrects the next grant report and does not disclose the historical inflation to avoid losing the funding relationship.
The board gives the programme officer the opportunity to correct the past reports themselves before taking any formal action.
The board notifies the funders only after the internal investigation is complete to ensure accuracy.
payload.explanation: Grant fraud by a charity staff member requires immediate leave, external audit, proactive funder notification, and repayment — waiting for investigation completion before notifying funders is not acceptable.

payload.snippet: A conservatoire professor is asked to write a reference letter for a former student applying for a prestigious fellowship. He remembers the student as talented but recalls a serious plagiarism incident that was handled internally and never formally recorded.
options: He writes an honest reference that reflects the student's strengths and discloses his concern about academic integrity based on his direct experience, making clear this is his professional judgement.
He writes a glowing reference and omits the plagiarism concern, judging it was handled internally.
He declines to write the reference without explaining why, to avoid harming the student's prospects.
He contacts the student first to discuss whether they want him to write the reference given what he knows.
payload.explanation: A reference letter must reflect the writer's honest professional assessment — omitting a direct integrity concern is misleading to the fellowship committee.

payload.snippet: A national anti-doping agency analyst receives a urine sample from a high-profile athlete at a major championship that tests positive for a prohibited substance. The athlete claims the positive was caused by a contaminated supplement they purchased legally. The substance is known to appear in some contaminated sports products. The analyst must decide how to handle the preliminary finding.
options: She proceeds with the full standard testing protocol, requests a B-sample analysis, documents the chain of custody meticulously, and refers the case to the athlete biological passport team for context before the result is communicated to any party.
She contacts the athlete's management immediately to inform them privately before the official process begins.
She runs an accelerated process given the championship context and notifies the governing body on the same day.
She searches the supplement database for a contamination match and if one is found, dismisses the positive as a likely contaminant.
payload.explanation: Anti-doping positives must follow the full standard protocol — B sample, chain-of-custody documentation, and biological passport context — before any communication.

payload.snippet: A sports club's board of directors discovers that the head coach of their elite junior programme has been privately receiving payment from a sports agency to recommend specific agents to promising young athletes without the athletes' or parents' knowledge.
options: The board suspends the coach immediately, informs all affected athletes and their families, reports the conduct to the national governing body and relevant sports agent regulatory body, and reviews all agent introductions made in the past three years.
The board gives the coach the opportunity to resign quietly and terminate the agency relationship to avoid reputational damage to the club.
The board suspends the coach and notifies only the most recent cases, as earlier cases may be too old to affect.
The board consults legal counsel before taking any action, as the financial arrangement may be legal depending on the contract.
payload.explanation: Undisclosed inducements involving minors require immediate suspension, full affected-party notification, regulatory reporting, and retrospective case review.

payload.snippet: A sports scientist advising a national athletics federation publishes a peer-reviewed study suggesting that a specific altitude training protocol produces a physiological adaptation that is indistinguishable from blood doping under current testing methods. The federation's performance director asks her to keep the findings confidential to protect competitive advantage.
options: She refuses to suppress the research, explains that the scientific and ethical obligation to publish is not negotiable, and notifies the World Anti-Doping Agency of the finding so testing methods can be updated.
She agrees to a one-year embargo on the publication while the federation prepares a response.
She publishes only in a lower-impact journal where the findings are less likely to be widely read.
She shares the findings only with other altitude training nations so the advantage is distributed rather than exclusive.
payload.explanation: A finding that undermines testing integrity must be published and reported to WADA — suppressing it for competitive advantage is a scientific and ethical violation.

payload.snippet: A sports television broadcaster discovers mid-broadcast that footage being used in a documentary about an athlete's childhood was obtained by a journalist who impersonated a family member to access private records. The broadcast is thirty minutes from the end.
options: She halts the broadcast of the implicated footage immediately, issues an on-air acknowledgement, and commissions an urgent internal review before any further use of the journalist's materials.
She completes the broadcast and publishes a correction statement the following day after the full review.
She removes only the specific footage in question and continues the remainder of the documentary.
She pauses the broadcast for thirty minutes while she determines the full extent of the journalist's access methods.
payload.explanation: Fraudulently obtained broadcast footage requires immediate withdrawal, on-air acknowledgement, and full material review — completing the broadcast first is not acceptable.

payload.snippet: A sports governing body receives credible evidence from a whistleblower that a member of the selection panel for the national team has been awarding selection to athletes represented by an agency in which they have an undisclosed financial interest.
options: The governing body removes the panel member from the selection process immediately, appoints an independent review panel to assess all recent selections, discloses the investigation publicly, and refers the matter to the relevant sports integrity organisation.
The governing body asks the panel member to recuse themselves from future decisions involving the agency while an informal investigation is conducted.
The governing body waits for legal advice before removing the panel member, to avoid an unfair dismissal claim.
The governing body investigates internally and discloses the outcome only if the independent review finds wrongdoing.
payload.explanation: Undisclosed financial conflicts in selection require immediate removal, independent review of all affected selections, public disclosure, and integrity organisation referral.

payload.snippet: A sports medicine physician working with a national team discovers that a colleague has been administering injections to athletes described in their medical records as 'vitamin supplements' but which contain unlabelled compounds not approved for sport use.
options: She escalates immediately to the team's chief medical officer, reports the administering colleague to the NGB's medical panel and to WADA, and ensures all affected athletes receive independent blood screening.
She confronts her colleague directly and asks them to stop the injections before escalating further.
She documents the injections and reports only to the NGB's medical panel, deferring to them on whether to contact WADA.
She requests an urgent lab analysis of the injection contents before reporting, to ensure her concern is substantiated.
payload.explanation: Unlabelled injections given to athletes are a doping and patient-safety emergency requiring immediate chief medical officer escalation, NGB and WADA reporting, and athlete screening.

payload.snippet: A professional sports club's data analyst discovers that their opposition analysis platform has been obtained by an unauthorised third party who has shared detailed proprietary tactical reports with the media. An investigation reveals the breach came from within the club.
options: She immediately revokes access to all current tactical data, initiates a full IT forensic investigation to identify the source, reports the data breach to the relevant data protection authority, and informs the club's leadership.
She changes all access passwords and monitors user activity logs for the next two weeks before deciding whether to report externally.
She identifies the most likely internal suspect and removes their access pending a quiet internal disciplinary process.
She reports the breach to the media proactively to control the narrative before the leaked reports are published.
payload.explanation: A data breach involving proprietary sports data requires immediate access revocation, IT forensic investigation, data protection authority notification, and leadership reporting — not targeted suspicion before investigation.

payload.snippet: A national football association's integrity team receives a report that a referee who officiated a high-profile match has placed bets on the match outcome through a family member's account in a jurisdiction where this is technically legal but prohibited under the association's code of conduct.
options: The association opens a formal investigation, suspends the referee from officiating pending the investigation, notifies the relevant betting integrity authority, and cooperates with any cross-border legal inquiry.
The association notes the breach and issues a formal warning given the legality of the bet in the jurisdiction concerned.
The association investigates privately and only takes action if the referee cannot demonstrate the bet was not a conflict of interest.
The association waits for the betting integrity authority to approach them before opening its own investigation.
payload.explanation: Betting on own-sport matches through proxies is a code-of-conduct violation regardless of jurisdiction — suspension, formal investigation, and betting authority notification are required.

payload.snippet: A junior athletics team discovers the day before a major relay championship that one team member has been recording false qualifying times in the registration system by entering an older sibling's times. Without that athlete, the relay team cannot legally compete.
options: The team manager reports the falsification to the event organiser immediately, withdraws the affected relay entry, and does not allow the athlete to compete under the false qualification.
The team manager enters the athlete under the correct times and accepts disqualification risk on the day.
The team manager asks the athlete to confess directly to the event organiser and waits to see what decision is made.
The team manager substitutes a qualified reserve athlete into the relay without disclosing the falsification.
payload.explanation: Falsified qualification data requires immediate organiser notification and withdrawal — competing with a false entry, even under corrected times, is still a fraudulent entry.

payload.snippet: A professional football club's youth academy director discovers that two of her coaches have been giving advanced training sessions off-site to selected academy players and charging the players' families privately, in breach of the academy's equal-access policy.
options: She suspends both coaches pending a formal disciplinary investigation, notifies the families of all affected and unaffected players of the equity breach, and reviews whether any official academy decisions were influenced by the off-site sessions.
She gives both coaches a final warning and requires them to cease the private sessions immediately.
She formalises the off-site sessions as an optional paid add-on available to all academy families.
She notifies the families involved but not the wider group, to avoid causing concern among parents whose children were not selected.
payload.explanation: Private paid coaching by academy staff creates a systemic equity breach — suspension, investigation, full family notification, and conflict-of-interest review are all required.

payload.snippet: A national sports governing body's anti-doping officer receives a credible anonymous tip that a senior athlete under their jurisdiction has been microdosing a banned substance for three months but is cycling it to avoid detection windows.
options: She escalates the tip to the independent anti-doping panel, documents the intelligence formally, and recommends a no-advance-notice test outside normal scheduling to increase detection probability.
She schedules a standard test under normal protocols and monitors whether the athlete's times improve further.
She confronts the athlete directly to give them an opportunity to come forward voluntarily before formal action.
She requests a test immediately under standard advance-notice timelines while keeping the tip confidential.
payload.explanation: Credible doping intelligence requires independent panel escalation, formal documentation, and no-advance-notice testing — standard protocols and athlete confrontation both compromise the investigation.

payload.snippet: A sports broadcaster holds exclusive rights to air a national team's qualifying matches. A volunteer fan group begins livestreaming matches on a social platform, reaching two hundred thousand viewers, arguing that broadcast exclusivity for national team sport in the home nation is against the public interest.
options: The broadcaster issues a formal cease-and-desist to the fan group, escalates the rights infringement to the platform, and initiates a legal review of whether their contract includes any public-interest carve-outs.
The broadcaster ignores the fan stream since the audience overlap does not affect their paid subscriber numbers significantly.
The broadcaster issues a public statement criticising the fan group and relies on reputational pressure to stop the stream.
The broadcaster contacts the national sports federation to request they ask the fan group to stop as a less adversarial first step.
payload.explanation: Rights infringement at scale requires formal legal action regardless of the fan group's public-interest argument — the broadcaster must also check whether their contract contains carve-outs that may legitimise it.

payload.snippet: A sports physiotherapist working at a major tournament discovers that a team doctor has been administering a substance to players via IV that is not on the banned list but has no documented therapeutic justification and has not been consented to individually by each player.
options: She documents what she has observed, raises it privately with the team doctor requesting explanation and consent documentation, and if no satisfactory explanation is given, reports it to the tournament's chief medical officer.
She reports the issue directly to the media to ensure public accountability for player health.
She advises players individually that they should ask the team doctor what they are being given.
She raises it only with the team's head coach and leaves the final decision with them.
payload.explanation: Undocumented, unconsented medical administration requires documentation, immediate internal escalation to the doctor, and if unresolved, formal escalation to the tournament medical authority.

payload.snippet: A rowing club's selection committee is about to confirm selections for a national competition when one member privately discloses to the chair that two of the athletes being selected are in a romantic relationship that the committee was not aware of — potentially affecting race dynamics and seating decisions.
options: The chair thanks the member for the disclosure, ensures the selection decision is based only on performance criteria, and asks the athletes directly whether the relationship would affect their performance or boat placement preferences.
The chair immediately substitutes one of the athletes to remove any relational dynamic from the boat.
The chair asks the disclosing committee member to keep the information private and proceeds with the selection as planned.
The chair defers the selection to the national federation to avoid any appearance of bias.
payload.explanation: Relationship disclosures in selection contexts require direct athlete consultation and performance-only criteria — substitution without consultation or concealment are both wrong.

payload.snippet: A marathon race director is informed by police two hours before the start that a credible security threat has been made against a specific high-profile athlete entered in the race. The threat cannot be immediately verified.
options: She immediately contacts the athlete and their team, arranges a police briefing, offers the option to withdraw or race with a security escort, and does not proceed without the athlete's informed consent.
She proceeds with the race as planned and asks police to monitor the route without telling the athlete.
She withdraws the athlete from the race unilaterally to eliminate the risk without disclosing the threat.
She announces the threat publicly so spectators can make their own safety decision.
payload.explanation: An unverified security threat affecting a specific athlete requires immediate disclosure to that athlete, police coordination, and their informed choice — covert monitoring, unilateral withdrawal, and public announcement are all wrong.

payload.snippet: A youth sports club's safeguarding officer receives a complaint from a parent that a coach has been taking individual photos of children during training and sending them privately to the children via a messaging app rather than through the club's official communication channel.
options: She immediately suspends the coach from all contact with children pending investigation, notifies the county FA safeguarding team and the statutory child protection authority, and preserves all available evidence.
She asks the coach to delete the photos and messaging thread and gives them a formal written warning.
She speaks to the children individually to assess whether they felt uncomfortable before deciding on further action.
She reviews the photos herself to assess whether the content is harmful before reporting to external agencies.
payload.explanation: Private photo-sharing with children by a coach is a safeguarding breach requiring immediate suspension, statutory authority notification, and evidence preservation — self-assessed reviews and informal warnings are not acceptable responses.

payload.snippet: A major sports league discovers that a club has been systematically filing false player injury reports to regulatory bodies over two seasons to conceal the use of performance-enhancing recovery protocols that sit in a grey area of the rules.
options: The league launches a formal investigation with access to the club's full medical records, suspends the club's chief medical officer pending findings, and publishes a timeline of the false reports and investigation to the regulatory body.
The league issues a points deduction for the current season and asks the club to revise its medical reporting procedures.
The league requests the club conduct an internal review and submit findings within thirty days.
The league contacts the club chairman privately to request an explanation before any formal action.
payload.explanation: Systematic false regulatory filings require a formal independent investigation, suspension of the responsible officer, and transparent regulatory notification — private conversations or internal reviews do not have the authority to address systematic deception.

payload.snippet: A sports journalist is given off-the-record information by a national team coach that the team's star player is dealing with a severe mental health crisis and will likely miss the upcoming tournament. The coach asks for confidentiality to protect the player.
options: She honours the off-the-record agreement, does not publish the mental health information, but may report factually that the player is absent from selection when this becomes public.
She publishes a carefully worded piece that implies a personal issue without naming mental health specifically.
She contacts the player's management to offer them the chance to publish their own version before she publishes.
She informs her editor of the information so the outlet can decide collectively whether public interest overrides confidentiality.
payload.explanation: Off-the-record mental health disclosures must be honoured — partial disclosure, management contact, or editorial escalation all breach the agreement.

payload.snippet: A national Paralympic committee receives credible evidence that a rival nation's athletes competing in a classification-dependent category have been deliberately underperforming during classification assessments — a practice known as intentional misrepresentation.
options: The committee submits a formal protest to the international Paralympic classification authority with the evidence, requests reclassification hearings for the athletes in question, and does not publicly name the athletes before the hearing.
The committee publishes the evidence to apply public pressure on the international authority to act faster.
The committee raises the concern informally with the rival nation's team management at the next meeting.
The committee files the protest but names the athletes publicly so the competitive field is aware.
payload.explanation: Classification integrity protests require formal submission to the governing authority with evidence, without premature public identification — public pressure campaigns and informal diplomacy both undermine due process.

payload.snippet: A sports sponsorship manager discovers that a sponsor's activation team has been paying young fans at events to hold their brand signs on camera without disclosing to the fans or their parents that this constitutes paid promotion under advertising standards rules.
options: She halts all activations immediately, notifies the sponsor's legal team and the advertising standards authority proactively, and ensures all future fan activations include full disclosure and parental consent for minors.
She adds disclosure text to future activations and does not report historical breaches since they involved minors informally.
She asks the activation team to stop paying fans and relies on organic brand-holding going forward.
She consults the sponsor's legal team before notifying the advertising standards authority to understand the club's liability first.
payload.explanation: Undisclosed paid promotion to minors requires immediate halt, proactive regulatory notification, and full consent and disclosure frameworks — legal consultation before regulatory disclosure is a delay tactic that compounds the breach.

payload.snippet: A public library is given a collection of privately-held documents by a descendant of a local industrialist. After cataloguing, the archivist discovers the collection includes evidence that the industrialist bribed local officials to approve a scheme that displaced a working-class community in the 1930s. The industrialist's family is still prominent locally.
options: The archivist documents the collection fully, informs the library director, and follows the institution's policy on sensitive or controversial provenance materials, which may include restricted access and notification of relevant community history organisations.
The archivist returns the most sensitive documents to the family before cataloguing them publicly.
The archivist publishes a press release immediately to ensure the historical record is public.
The archivist seeks legal advice to determine whether the documents expose the library to defamation risk before proceeding.
payload.explanation: Sensitive provenance material must be handled through institutional policy channels, with community history organisations consulted — neither suppression nor premature publication is appropriate.

payload.snippet: A national library is approached by a government department requesting access to the borrowing records of a named individual as part of an investigation. No court order has been presented.
options: The library director refuses to provide records without a valid court order, consults the institution's legal team, and notifies the professional body to ensure the request is on record.
The director provides a summary of the person's borrowing history while withholding personally identifiable details.
