options: The most capable participant takes a calm leadership role, makes the guide comfortable, keeps the group together, follows the known trail back toward the trailhead, and deploys any visual signal means available — mirror, whistle, or bright clothing — to attract attention.
The group leaves the guide in a secure location and moves faster to get help independently.
The group stays in place indefinitely since moving without full navigation expertise is more dangerous.
The group divides into two — one to stay with the guide and one to go for help.
payload.explanation: An incapacitated guide in a remote area requires group cohesion, trail-back movement, guide care, and signal deployment — leaving the guide, staying indefinitely, or splitting the group all increase overall risk.

payload.snippet: An outdoor education operator is informed by a participant's parent that the participant has been posting social media content showing campsite location, route details, and group member identities throughout a remote expedition, in violation of the pre-trip safety briefing.
options: The operator contacts the participant's supervising adult on the trip, has the posts removed from public view if possible, reviews the group's current safety exposure, and updates the consent and briefing process to prevent future breaches.
The operator tells the participant to stop posting but takes no further action since no immediate harm has occurred.
The operator ends the participant's place on the expedition immediately for breaching the safety agreement.
The operator reviews the posts and decides whether to act based on how much identifying information they contain.
payload.explanation: Publicly posted route and location data during a remote expedition is a live safety risk — immediate removal, on-trip supervisor notification, exposure assessment, and process review are all required.

payload.snippet: A teenager discovers during a room clear that they have been living with a small gas leak from a portable heater they have been using in their room for several months. The smell had become normalised.
options: They immediately open the window, turn off the heater, leave the room, and tell a parent or responsible adult so the heater can be checked by a qualified engineer.
They carry on as normal since they have been fine for months.
They throw the heater away and buy a new one.
They open the window and assume the problem is solved.
payload.explanation: A gas-smelling heater must be turned off and checked by a qualified engineer — normalised exposure and self-fixing are both dangerous.

payload.snippet: A student doing a deep room clean discovers that a private message conversation on an old device reveals their close friend has been sharing the student's personal secrets with others for over a year.
options: They process their feelings before acting, and have a direct, private conversation with the friend about what they found.
They immediately post publicly about the betrayal.
They confront the friend in front of their mutual group.
They end the friendship without explaining why.
payload.explanation: Processing emotions before acting, and having a private direct conversation, is the most constructive response to a discovered betrayal.

payload.snippet: A teenager finds a significant amount of cash hidden in their room that they do not recognise and cannot account for. The amount suggests it did not come from their own savings.
options: They tell a parent immediately and do not spend any of it until its origin is established.
They keep it since it is in their room.
They tell no one and spend it gradually.
They assume a relative must have given it to them and keep it.
payload.explanation: Unexplained significant cash requires immediate disclosure to a parent — spending it before establishing its origin could involve receiving stolen goods.

payload.snippet: A young adult is clearing their childhood bedroom at home and discovers a collection of items that, on reflection, they took from shops without paying when they were younger.
options: They reflect on the behaviour honestly, speak to a trusted adult, and decide how to make it right — whether through donation to charity or another appropriate act of restitution.
They throw the items away to destroy the evidence.
They return the items to the shops, which are no longer able to accept returns.
They keep the items since they were taken years ago and cannot be undone.
payload.explanation: Honest reflection on past behaviour and taking a meaningful restitutive action — even if the original wrong cannot be fully reversed — is the mature response.

payload.snippet: A teenager doing an overdue room clean discovers that the mess has been covering a significant structural problem in the floor — soft boards that suggest rot or water damage.
options: They tell their parent or landlord immediately and do not walk on the affected area until it has been assessed.
They cover the soft boards with a rug and mention it casually later.
They check online for how to repair it themselves.
They keep it hidden until they are ready to move out.
payload.explanation: Structural floor damage is a safety and property issue requiring immediate disclosure to a parent or landlord — self-repair or concealment both risk harm.

payload.snippet: A student who moved into their first flat clears their room after several months of very heavy study and discovers that mail has been accumulating unread, including several letters from their bank, a council tax notice, and a letter from the university.
options: They read all the letters immediately, assess what requires urgent action, and deal with each one in priority order — contacting relevant parties if deadlines have passed.
They throw the letters away since the deadlines have passed.
They read only the bank letters and ignore the others.
They put them in a pile to read later.
payload.explanation: Accumulated unread mail requires immediate sorting and urgent action on time-sensitive items — deferring again or discarding compounds the problem.

payload.snippet: A teenager finds a stash of their own childhood drawings and letters in a room clear, including a distressing letter they wrote to themselves at a very difficult time in their life.
options: They reflect on the letter, consider speaking to a trusted adult or counsellor about the feelings it brings up, and decide whether to keep, share, or dispose of it.
They post it publicly as a 'throwback' without considering the content.
They throw it away immediately to avoid thinking about it.
They show it to friends as an interesting artefact.
payload.explanation: Old material reflecting a past period of distress deserves private, thoughtful consideration — not public sharing or avoidance.

payload.snippet: A young person clearing their room discovers that a significant quantity of recyclable and general waste has built up due to a period of depression during which they were unable to manage self-care. The build-up has caused a minor pest problem.
options: They ask a trusted adult for help addressing the waste and pest problem, and speak to their GP or a mental health service about the underlying difficulty.
They deal with the waste alone and say nothing about how it occurred.
They move out of the room and avoid the problem.
They request pest control without addressing the waste that caused it.
payload.explanation: The physical problem and the mental health context both require addressing — involving a trusted adult and seeking support are both important.

payload.snippet: A teenager's room clear reveals that they have accumulated hundreds of packages of delivered items over two years, most unopened, as part of a compulsive buying habit they have kept hidden.
options: They tell a parent or trusted adult about the extent of the habit, seek help in understanding its cause, and make a plan for returning, donating, or disposing of the items.
They return what they can quietly and throw away the rest without telling anyone.
They hide the worst of it before showing the parent only part of the problem.
They sell the items online and use the money to buy more things.
payload.explanation: A hidden compulsive buying habit requires honest disclosure to a trusted adult and help addressing the underlying cause — concealment or returning the symptom without addressing the cause are both inadequate.

payload.snippet: An adult child helping clear out a deceased parent's home discovers the room contains a substantial quantity of hoarded medication, some of which is controlled prescription drugs.
options: They contact a pharmacist or the police (if the controlled drugs are significant in quantity) to arrange safe disposal, and do not attempt to use, sell, or simply discard the medication.
They bin all of it since it is past the expiry dates.
They keep the controlled drugs in case they are useful for their own health later.
They ask their GP to prescribe the same drugs for them instead of disposing of them.
payload.explanation: Controlled drugs found during estate clearances must be handled through proper disposal channels — a pharmacist or, for significant quantities, the police.

payload.snippet: A teenager discovers that a slow, creeping accumulation of clutter and unprocessed belongings in their room has become so severe that a fire exit route is now compromised.
options: They clear the fire exit route immediately without waiting, then work with a parent to address the broader clutter systematically.
They add it to a mental list of things to sort at the next big tidy.
They tell their parent but do not clear it immediately since a fire is unlikely.
They move some items to the exit route and consider the problem reduced enough.
payload.explanation: A blocked fire exit requires immediate clearance — probability of fire is irrelevant to the obligation to keep exits clear.

payload.snippet: A student clearing their room discovers that a trusted friend has been storing items in their room without permission, some of which appear to be expensive electronics the friend cannot otherwise account for.
options: They ask the friend to remove the items immediately and explain that they cannot store items they are not able to account for — and if the friend's explanation is not credible, they tell a parent or trusted adult.
They store the items as a favour since they trust their friend.
They return the items to the friend without asking any questions.
They call the police immediately since the items might be stolen.
payload.explanation: Unexplained expensive items stored by a friend require an honest explanation before any agreement to store them — credibility determines whether further escalation is needed.

payload.snippet: A social worker visits a family home and is concerned about the state of a teenager's room, which has accumulated significant mess and waste. The teenager is unresponsive to previous requests to address it.
options: The social worker raises the specific concerns with the family, provides information about support services if the issue is linked to a mental health or developmental need, and creates a plan with the family.
The social worker removes the teenager from the home pending resolution.
The social worker gives the parents a formal warning and leaves resolution entirely to them.
The social worker documents the concern and schedules a return visit without engaging the teenager directly.
payload.explanation: Room-related welfare concerns require family engagement, support service signposting, and a shared plan — removal or purely documentary responses miss the underlying need.

payload.snippet: A landlord conducting a routine property inspection discovers a tenant's room has caused significant structural damage through sustained neglect and has created a pest problem that is spreading to neighbouring flats.
options: The landlord serves formal notice, arranges professional pest control and structural assessment, bills the tenant for damage costs within the terms of the tenancy agreement, and considers whether to begin eviction proceedings.
The landlord cleans the room themselves and adds the cost to next month's rent without formal notice.
The landlord contacts the neighbouring tenants and asks them to wait while the situation is informally resolved.
The landlord monitors the situation for another month before acting formally.
payload.explanation: Structural damage and pest infestation affecting neighbours require formal notice, professional intervention, and tenancy enforcement — informal handling or delay worsen the situation for all tenants.

payload.snippet: A teacher notices a student consistently arrives at school with dirty or unwashed clothes and belongings in very poor condition. The student has mentioned their room at home being unliveable.
options: The teacher reports the welfare concern to the school's designated safeguarding lead, who initiates the appropriate child welfare referral.
The teacher gives the student clean clothes from lost property and organises a school locker for their belongings.
The teacher speaks to the student's parent directly about the home conditions.
The teacher monitors the situation for another two weeks before deciding whether to report.
payload.explanation: Signs of neglect — including poor home conditions disclosed by a student — are safeguarding concerns requiring DSL referral, not informal teacher-managed solutions.

payload.snippet: A fire safety inspection of a student accommodation block finds that several rooms have been used to store flammable materials and the corridor is partially blocked, creating a fire risk for the whole building.
options: The accommodation manager requires immediate removal of the materials and clearing of the corridor, arranges fire safety training for all residents, and issues formal warnings to those responsible.
The accommodation manager asks the responsible residents to deal with it and checks again in a week.
The accommodation manager clears only the corridor and leaves the individual rooms to the residents.
The accommodation manager bans the residents immediately without giving them an opportunity to correct the hazard.
payload.explanation: A confirmed fire risk in student accommodation requires immediate action, mandatory training, and formal warnings — neither a grace period nor immediate expulsion without correction opportunity is appropriate.

payload.snippet: A hoarder's room in a shared family home has become so severe that it is affecting the structural integrity of the floor and creating health risks for other family members.
options: The family arranges a professional hoarding support assessment, involves the local council environmental health team if needed, and supports the affected family member with a structured plan — prioritising safety first.
The family forcibly clears the room while the family member is away.
The family ignores the issue to avoid conflict with the affected member.
The family reduces the possessions gradually without informing environmental health.
payload.explanation: Severe hoarding with structural and health implications requires professional support, environmental health involvement, and a structured plan — forced clearing or avoidance both worsen the situation.

payload.snippet: A property manager discovers that the previous tenant left behind a room full of items including documents with personal information, medical supplies, and items of apparent personal value.
options: The manager secures the items, attempts to contact the previous tenant through their last known details, and if they cannot be reached, disposes of the items according to the law on abandoned goods.
The manager throws everything away since the tenancy has ended.
The manager keeps the valuables for themselves and disposes of the rest.
The manager leaves the items in the room until the next tenant is placed.
payload.explanation: Abandoned tenant belongings must be secured, the tenant contacted, and only disposed of through proper legal process — taking valuables or immediate disposal are both unlawful.

payload.snippet: A university student's accumulating mess has been a source of ongoing conflict with their housemates, who have repeatedly asked them to address their shared spaces. The student continues to promise and not follow through.
options: The housemates agree on a shared house meeting to formalise expectations with specific agreed standards and consequences, and involve the letting agent if the situation does not improve.
The housemates throw the student's belongings into their room to clean the shared space themselves.
The housemates stop speaking to the student and create separate household areas.
The housemates post about the situation on social media to apply social pressure.
payload.explanation: A structured house meeting with agreed standards and a clear escalation path is the correct response to repeated non-compliance — retaliation, isolation, and social media pressure all escalate conflict without resolving it.

payload.snippet: A teenage student with undiagnosed ADHD has a room that is chronically disorganised despite repeated attempts to address it, causing significant stress and conflict with their parents.
options: The parents arrange an assessment with the GP or a specialist, seek advice on ADHD-compatible organisation strategies, and stop treating the disorganisation as wilful behaviour.
The parents implement stricter consequences for ongoing mess.
The parents hire a professional organiser without investigating the underlying cause.
The parents accept the situation permanently and stop engaging with it.
payload.explanation: Chronic disorganisation despite genuine effort may indicate an underlying condition — an assessment and adapted strategies address the cause rather than the symptom.

payload.snippet: A student with dyslexia has been completing significantly more work than her classmates to achieve the same standard, and is burning out. Her school knows about her diagnosis but has not provided formal accommodations.
options: She and her parent formally request an Education, Health and Care plan review or a specific accommodations assessment with the school's SENCO, and document the current workload impact.
She continues managing alone to avoid being seen as making excuses.
She reduces her homework to a manageable level without notifying the school.
She asks a classmate to help her complete the work regularly to manage the load.
payload.explanation: A formal accommodations review through the SENCO is the correct process — managing silently or reducing work without notification both fail to address the systemic gap.

payload.snippet: A teacher discovers that a student's consistently excellent homework has a markedly different writing style from their in-class work, suggesting the homework may not be the student's own.
options: The teacher has a private conversation with the student, asks them to explain their approach and reasoning for a specific piece of homework, and makes an assessment based on that conversation before any formal action.
The teacher immediately reports the student to the head of year for academic dishonesty.
The teacher ignores the discrepancy and gives the student the benefit of the doubt.
The teacher sets a deliberately harder homework to test whether the quality drops.
payload.explanation: A private conversation to assess understanding before any formal action is the correct and fair response to a suspected academic integrity concern.

payload.snippet: A student receives a university-level scholarship based partly on exceptional homework grades. It later emerges that a parent with subject expertise substantially completed many of those assignments.
options: The student comes forward honestly to the scholarship body, explains the circumstances, and accepts any consequence — understanding that the scholarship was awarded based on a misrepresentation.
The student says nothing since the scholarship has already been awarded.
The student tells only their parent and asks them to stop helping, without disclosing to the scholarship body.
The student blames their parent and lets the scholarship body investigate independently.
payload.explanation: Honest self-disclosure to the awarding body is the only academically and ethically correct response — silence, partial disclosure, or blame all leave the misrepresentation in place.

payload.snippet: A secondary school discovers that a homework help website popular with students actually writes complete custom essays for a fee, and several students across the year group have been using it for assessed coursework.
options: The school informs affected students and parents of the academic integrity breach, conducts individual assessments to determine the extent of each student's involvement, and reports the website to the relevant authorities.
The school issues a general warning to all students and does not investigate individual use to avoid widespread consequences.
The school only investigates the students who were reported by peers.
The school informs parents but allows students to resubmit their work without any further consequence.
payload.explanation: A systemic academic integrity breach requires individual assessment of all affected students, parental notification, and reporting of the service — a general warning or resubmission without consequence do not address the breach.

payload.snippet: A homework marking system used by a school is found to have a significant algorithmic bias that consistently undermarks work by students whose first language is not English, resulting in lower academic records for those students over three years.
options: The school commissions an independent audit of the affected results, notifies all affected students and families, corrects the historical records, and discontinues the biased marking tool.
The school discontinues the tool and applies the correction going forward without adjusting historical grades.
The school investigates only the most recent year of affected results.
The school informs affected students informally without formally correcting their academic records.
payload.explanation: A systemic bias affecting historical records requires retroactive correction, full notification, and official record amendment — forward-only fixes or informal notification leave the historical harm unaddressed.

payload.snippet: A student who has been struggling with mental health challenges submits homework that contains a hidden message suggesting they are in serious distress. The subject teacher notices it while marking.
options: The teacher reports it to the designated safeguarding lead immediately and ensures the student is supported before the next school day.
The teacher speaks to the student personally before involving any other adults.
The teacher adds a supportive comment to the homework and monitors the situation over the following week.
The teacher calls the student's parent directly without going through the school's safeguarding process.
payload.explanation: A hidden distress message in student work is a safeguarding concern requiring immediate DSL referral — personal teacher intervention or monitoring without escalation could miss a serious risk.

payload.snippet: A student completing an online national assessment discovers a significant security vulnerability in the exam platform that could allow any student to access the questions and answers before the test.
options: They close the vulnerability from their end, do not exploit it or share it, report it to their teacher immediately, and advise the teacher to report it to the exam board.
They exploit the vulnerability to get the answers since finding it was a skill in itself.
They tell a friend so they can both benefit, swearing them to secrecy.
They do nothing since it is the exam board's responsibility to find their own vulnerabilities.
payload.explanation: Discovering and responsibly reporting a security vulnerability — without exploiting it — is the correct ethical and practical response.

payload.snippet: A student discovers that a homework assignment that their teacher marked as original was actually taken verbatim from an obscure academic paper by the teacher themselves, presented to students as if it were an original teacher-written task.
options: They raise the observation tactfully and privately with the teacher, or if uncomfortable, with a head of department.
They expose it publicly in front of the class.
They say nothing since the teacher has authority and it was probably an oversight.
They use the discovery to argue their own plagiarised work should also be overlooked.
payload.explanation: A tactful private approach — to the teacher or head of department — is the correct response to a possible academic integrity oversight by a teacher.

payload.snippet: A student is completing an international competition homework submission when they realise the project they are entering closely mirrors an entry that won the same competition two years ago, which they had studied as an example.
options: They revise the project significantly to distinguish their own approach, even if it means a weaker entry, and disclose the similarity to their supervising teacher.
They submit the original version since the competition year is different and judges may not notice.
They change the title and presentation only.
They ask their teacher to assess whether the similarity is close enough to be a problem.
payload.explanation: Significant revision and disclosure to the supervising teacher are both required — the competition judges and integrity standards apply regardless of whether the prior entry would be seen.

payload.snippet: A student receives their homework grade and suspects the teacher has misread or misunderstood a key part of their answer, resulting in an incorrect mark being applied.
options: They raise it politely with the teacher, citing the specific part of the answer and the mark scheme if available, and accept the teacher's final decision after review.
They appeal directly to the head of department without speaking to the teacher first.
They accept the mark since they are not sure enough to challenge it.
They change the original homework retroactively and present the changed version as evidence.
payload.explanation: Raising a potential marking error directly with the teacher — citing evidence — is the correct first step before any escalation, and accepting the reviewed decision closes the matter.

payload.snippet: A homework submission platform used by a class is found to have logged and stored all student draft submissions, including incomplete and abandoned work, in a format accessible to all class members.
options: The student who discovers it reports it to their teacher immediately and does not access any other students' drafts.
They look at a classmate's draft before reporting the issue.
They report it to the teacher but only after checking whether their own drafts are accessible.
They take screenshots of the vulnerability as evidence before reporting.
payload.explanation: Reporting a data exposure immediately without accessing other students' private work is the correct response — any access before reporting, even well-intentioned, violates other students' privacy.

payload.snippet: A high-achieving student who relies on homework grades for a scholarship realises they have become dependent on a study group that effectively completes their homework collectively, blurring the line between collaboration and academic dishonesty.
options: They withdraw from the collaborative completion practice and begin doing their individual homework independently, accepting the potential grade impact honestly.
They continue the practice since it has not been formally flagged as dishonest.
They ask the scholarship body whether collaborative homework is permissible.
They do individual homework only for the subjects that contribute to the scholarship criteria.
payload.explanation: Recognising that collaborative completion crosses into dishonesty — and withdrawing from it regardless of the grade impact — is an act of academic integrity.

payload.snippet: A student who has been bullied is given a homework task to write an essay on a topic that directly maps onto their bullying experience, which they find deeply distressing.
options: They speak to their teacher or form tutor privately about the distress the topic causes and ask whether an alternative topic is possible.
They write the essay and do not tell anyone it caused them distress.
They refuse to submit the homework without explanation.
They submit a homework complaint to the school governors.
payload.explanation: A private conversation with the teacher about a topic's personal impact — and requesting an alternative — is the correct first step before any formal escalation.

payload.snippet: A school discovers that an AI tutoring service it endorsed has been providing students with complete, ready-to-submit homework answers rather than explanations, and that a significant portion of the current year's homework marks are therefore invalid.
options: The school informs all affected students and parents, resets the relevant homework marks, and arranges assessed in-class alternatives to re-establish genuine attainment records.
The school withdraws its endorsement of the service but does not inform students or parents of the marking implications.
The school investigates individual use patterns and penalises only students with the highest suspiciously similar scores.
The school moves all homework to a different platform without resetting the affected marks.
payload.explanation: Invalid homework marks require transparent stakeholder notification, mark resets, and a verified replacement assessment — platform changes or selective investigation both fail to address the systemic problem.

payload.snippet: A university student submits a thesis chapter that a plagiarism detection tool flags as thirty percent matching an obscure foreign-language academic paper. The student translated and paraphrased sections without citation.
options: The student discloses to their supervisor that they used the foreign-language source extensively without proper citation, rewrites the relevant sections with accurate citation, and accepts any academic penalty.
The student argues the tool is wrong since they paraphrased rather than copied.
The student adds a citation to the source but does not rewrite the paraphrased sections.
The student asks the supervisor to interpret the match as a tool error.
payload.explanation: Paraphrasing without citation is plagiarism regardless of language or tool accuracy — disclosure, rewriting, and proper citation are all required.

payload.snippet: A student with serious exam anxiety has been using a private tutor who has gradually shifted from teaching to completing the student's assessed coursework, with the student's tacit consent.
options: The student ends the practice, tells their parent and school what has been happening, and accepts any academic consequence — then engages legitimate support for their anxiety.
The student ends the practice quietly without telling anyone, hoping the coursework already submitted will stand.
The student tells the tutor to reduce involvement gradually rather than stopping immediately.
The student submits all remaining coursework independently and considers the matter closed.
payload.explanation: Coursework completed by a tutor is fraudulent academic work — disclosure, consequence acceptance, and legitimate anxiety support are all required responses.

payload.snippet: A school identifies that a student has submitted homework using AI-generated content across twelve subjects over a full year. The student has learning difficulties that were not adequately supported.
options: The school investigates both the academic integrity breach and the adequacy of the student's learning support, provides appropriate remediation, and reviews whether the lack of support contributed to the reliance on AI.
The school addresses only the academic integrity breach and sets the student back a year.
The school accepts the AI use as an unofficial accommodation for the learning difficulty.
The school dismisses the student for dishonesty without reviewing the support failure.
payload.explanation: A pattern of AI use linked to inadequate support requires addressing both the integrity breach and the underlying support failure — either alone is an incomplete response.

payload.snippet: A student discovers that their parent has been impersonating them in online homework forums, asking subject questions and submitting the forum answers as the student's own work, believing it to be helping.
options: The student tells their parent clearly that this is academic dishonesty, takes over managing their own academic queries, and — if assessed work is affected — tells their teacher what happened.
The student says nothing since the parent means well.
The student lets the parent continue since the marks are improving.
The student tells the school before speaking to their parent.
payload.explanation: Academic dishonesty by a well-meaning parent still has consequences for the student — a clear conversation stopping the practice and disclosure of affected work are both required.

payload.snippet: A homework submission system is found to have been automatically grading and recording AI-generated content submitted by students as highly positive, creating inflated academic records for hundreds of students over two terms.
options: The school commissions an independent audit of affected records, notifies students and parents of the AI detection failure, resets implicated grades, and replaces the system with one that meets academic integrity standards.
The school patches the system to detect AI going forward and does not reset historical grades.
The school informs only those students whose scores were most implausibly high.
The school suspends use of the system but keeps the historical grades as they were recorded.
payload.explanation: Systemically inflated grades due to a tool failure require full retroactive audit, transparent notification, grade resets, and system replacement — partial or forward-only fixes leave the false records in place.

payload.snippet: A student who is a refugee with interrupted schooling submits a homework essay that is excellent but in a style significantly more advanced than their class performance would suggest. The teacher suspects AI use.
options: The teacher arranges a private conversation to understand the student's background and, if the work reflects genuine ability, recalibrates their assessment baseline rather than assuming AI use.
The teacher immediately reports the work for academic integrity review without speaking to the student.
The teacher gives the student a lower mark reflecting their class performance rather than the essay.
The teacher asks the student to resubmit the essay under timed supervised conditions.
payload.explanation: A significant gap between homework and class performance may reflect hidden ability, interrupted schooling, or AI use — a private conversation to understand context must precede any formal action.

payload.snippet: A teenager befriends an online acquaintance who gradually becomes very emotionally dependent on them — messaging constantly, expressing feelings of worthlessness when the teenager cannot respond, and warning about self-harm if the friendship ends.
options: The teenager tells a trusted adult about the situation immediately, does not engage with self-harm threats as though they are persuasion tactics, and supports the adult in ensuring the acquaintance receives proper help.
The teenager stays constantly available to prevent the threatened self-harm.
The teenager blocks the acquaintance immediately and does not tell anyone.
The teenager gradually reduces contact to test whether the threats are genuine before deciding what to do.
payload.explanation: Emotional dependency and self-harm threats in a new relationship require adult involvement — a teenager cannot safely manage that responsibility alone.

payload.snippet: A student who moved countries for family reasons finds that cultural miscommunications are repeatedly damaging new friendships before they begin, despite her genuine efforts.
options: She speaks to a school counsellor or cultural liaison about specific miscommunication patterns, and considers whether there are community groups where she can build friendships with shared cultural understanding.
She abandons any attempts to adapt to the new culture and socialises only with others from her home country.
She suppresses all aspects of her own culture to remove the source of friction.
She concludes that she will never make friends in the new country and stops trying.
payload.explanation: Targeted support for specific miscommunication patterns — and community groups with shared understanding — are more sustainable than cultural suppression or giving up.

payload.snippet: A new student at school discovers that the friendship group she has joined has an initiation that involves mildly humiliating a newer member as a condition of acceptance.
options: She declines to participate in the initiation, explains that she is not comfortable with it, and decides whether the group is one she still wants to be part of.
She goes through the initiation to gain acceptance and plans to refuse if asked to inflict it on someone else.
She reports the group's initiation to a teacher immediately.
She goes through it and then humiliates the next new member as she was humiliated.
payload.explanation: Declining an initiation on principle — and reassessing whether this is a group worth belonging to — is more integrity-preserving than compliance with future intentions to reform.

payload.snippet: A teenager's new friend group turns out to be involved in minor criminal activity that escalates over several months. The teenager has not participated but has been aware.
options: He tells a trusted adult about what he knows and understands that his silence — even without participation — has been problematic.
He continues to not participate but maintains the friendships since he has done nothing wrong.
He leaves the group and tells no one since the crimes are minor.
He confronts the group directly and tells them he is going to report them.
payload.explanation: Informing a trusted adult about known criminal activity — and acknowledging that silent complicity is not neutral — is the correct and courageous response.

payload.snippet: A young person moves to a new school following a period of severe mental health difficulties that were publicly known in their previous school. They want to form genuine new friendships without their history defining them.
options: They focus on building friendships gradually and authentically, share their history only when they feel ready and trust is established, and seek support from a counsellor for managing the social anxiety this involves.
They proactively tell everyone their history to control the narrative before others find out.
They hide their history entirely and live in constant fear of being found out.
They avoid all close friendships to prevent the history from mattering.
payload.explanation: Gradually building trust and sharing personal history when ready — with professional support — is the most sustainable approach to starting fresh.

payload.snippet: A student who is neurodivergent finds that they form intense attachments to new friends quickly, which has repeatedly led to mismatched expectations and friendship endings.
options: They work with a therapist or support worker on understanding their attachment patterns and how to communicate their friendship style clearly to potential new friends.
They suppress their natural attachment style entirely to appear more normative.
They stop seeking new friendships to avoid further pain.
They test new friends' loyalty early by creating situations that require it.
payload.explanation: Understanding your own relational patterns and communicating them openly — with professional support — is more effective than suppression or testing.

payload.snippet: A teenager discovers that a new friend who they have trusted deeply has been sharing their private conversations with a larger group as entertainment.
options: They confront the friend directly and privately with the specific evidence they have, explain the impact of the betrayal, and decide based on the friend's response whether to continue the friendship.
They immediately share the evidence publicly to expose the friend.
They say nothing but make sure every secret they tell from now on is false.
They cut off the friend and warn every mutual contact about what they did.
payload.explanation: A direct confrontation with evidence — giving the friend a chance to respond — is more honourable than public exposure or ongoing deception.

payload.snippet: A young person who grew up with no close friendships due to bullying is now in a new environment where people are genuinely trying to befriend them, but their defence mechanisms are pushing people away.
options: They work with a therapist on identifying and gradually adjusting the defence patterns, and communicate honestly with potential friends when they notice themselves withdrawing.
They ignore the problem since they have always been alone and that is just how they are.
They force themselves to accept all social invitations regardless of their comfort level.
They warn new potential friends about their patterns before any relationship has formed.
payload.explanation: Professional support and honest communication about withdrawal patterns — rather than resignation or forced compliance — give genuine friendships the best chance.

payload.snippet: A new student is befriended very intensively by an older student who wants to introduce them to social situations involving alcohol and substances.
options: They tell a trusted adult about the pressure they are experiencing and limit contact with the older student.
They accept the social invitations since the older student is well-connected and the friendship has social benefits.
They refuse individually but maintain the friendship to avoid social consequences.
They report the older student to the school immediately before speaking to their own parent.
payload.explanation: Telling a trusted adult and limiting contact are the correct responses to adult-facilitated substance pressure — maintaining a risky friendship for social capital is not safe.

payload.snippet: A teenager's new friend is consistently let down by adults in their life and has started treating the teenager as a parental substitute — seeking guidance, stability, and decision-making support beyond what a peer relationship can provide.
options: They tell their friend with compassion that they care about them but are not in a position to be their primary support, and involve a trusted adult to help connect their friend to appropriate services.
They step into the parental role since their friend needs it.
They abruptly end the friendship to protect their own wellbeing.
They encourage their friend to simply need less from people.
payload.explanation: A compassionate boundary — paired with connecting your friend to appropriate adult support — is healthier for both people than assuming a parental role.

payload.snippet: A student makes a new friend from a different background and discovers that their families have a historical conflict that the families have maintained for a generation.
options: They decide to form and maintain the friendship based on their own values and direct experience, and handle family tension by choosing not to escalate it.
They end the friendship to respect the family's historical position.
They immediately challenge both families to resolve their conflict.
They maintain the friendship secretly to avoid the family tension.
payload.explanation: Forming a friendship based on your own direct experience — and not escalating family conflict while being honest about the friendship — is the mature and independent approach.

payload.snippet: A teenager forms an intense online friendship that feels more meaningful than any in-person relationship they have had, and they begin withdrawing from real-world social activities.
options: They continue the online friendship while consciously maintaining real-world relationships, and speak to a trusted adult if they notice the pattern affecting their broader life.
They fully prioritise the online friendship since it meets their needs better.
They end the online friendship since it is clearly more important than it should be.
They introduce the online friend to their real-world social circle to bridge the two.
payload.explanation: Maintaining both connections — with adult oversight if real-world withdrawal is significant — is healthier than either extreme.

payload.snippet: Kieran has social anxiety and starting secondary school feels overwhelming; on his first day he has a panic attack in the hallway. A sixth-former named Ash spots him, crouches down, and speaks quietly.
options: Ash stays calm, reassures Kieran, and walks him to the school counsellor
Ash tells everyone in the hallway to move along and leaves Kieran alone
Ash pulls out his phone to record the incident
Ash tries to make Kieran stand up quickly so he is less embarrassed
payload.explanation: A calm, compassionate response during a mental-health episode can make a school feel safe.

payload.snippet: Imogen and her new friend Petra have been inseparable for three months when a girl from Imogen's old friend group starts messaging Imogen, pressuring her to exclude Petra from their plans.
options: Imogen refuses to exclude Petra and tells the girl her behaviour is unkind
Imogen gradually starts leaving Petra out to avoid conflict
Imogen forwards the messages to Petra to warn her
Imogen blocks both girls to avoid the whole situation
payload.explanation: Loyalty in a new friendship means standing up to manipulation even when it is uncomfortable.

payload.snippet: Two students from rival schools, Jordan and Blake, are placed on the same team for a regional science competition. They have heard rumours about each other and start the project in silence.
options: Jordan breaks the ice by suggesting they list what each of them is good at
Blake refuses to cooperate and tells the teacher he wants a different partner
Jordan does all the research so he gets credit if they win
They divide the project so they never have to speak
payload.explanation: Identifying complementary strengths turns a forced partnership into genuine collaboration.

payload.snippet: Anya moves to a small rural town from a big city. The local kids think she is arrogant because she mentions her old life often; Anya does not realise how it sounds until her new friend Tom tells her honestly.
options: Anya thanks Tom for telling her and makes a conscious effort to ask about others' lives
Anya is upset that Tom criticised her and stops talking to him
Tom keeps the observation to himself so Anya does not feel bad
Anya argues that city life genuinely is more interesting
payload.explanation: Honest feedback from a new friend, received with grace, accelerates social adjustment.

payload.snippet: Leo and his new friend Dani are walking home when Dani reveals something deeply personal she has never told anyone. Leo does not know what to say but can see Dani is relieved to have shared it.
options: Leo tells Dani he is glad she trusted him and will keep it private
Leo changes the subject because the conversation makes him uncomfortable
Leo tells one mutual friend because he thinks Dani needs more support
Leo asks lots of probing questions to understand every detail
payload.explanation: Honouring a friend's trust by listening and keeping confidence deepens the relationship.

payload.snippet: Sam is the first openly non-binary student in their school. A new classmate, Quinn, asks direct questions without knowing some are considered intrusive. Sam feels uncomfortable but can see Quinn means well.
options: Sam calmly explains which questions feel personal and suggests better ways to learn
Sam reports Quinn to the headteacher for harassment
Quinn apologises and decides never to ask any questions again
Sam ignores Quinn hoping the questions stop
payload.explanation: Educating someone who is curious but clumsy, rather than shutting down, is how understanding grows.

payload.snippet: Priya's new friend Jade always wants to make plans but cancels at the last minute, leaving Priya disappointed three times in a row. Priya enjoys Jade's company when they do meet.
options: Priya tells Jade gently that last-minute cancellations hurt and asks if everything is okay
Priya stops making plans with Jade without explaining why
Priya vents about Jade to other friends instead of addressing it
Priya books non-refundable tickets so Jade cannot cancel
payload.explanation: Raising a pattern issue kindly and early protects the friendship from quietly eroding.

payload.snippet: Felix and his online pen pal Marco have chatted for a year and finally meet in person. Felix is shocked that Marco seems much quieter in real life and wonders if their friendship was just words on a screen.
options: Felix gives Marco time to warm up and they find the same connection once the awkwardness fades
Felix says he expected Marco to be more like his messages
Felix makes an excuse to cut the visit short
Marco apologies for being different in person and says they should not meet again
payload.explanation: Allowing a friendship time to translate from online to in-person respects the reality of social nerves.

payload.snippet: A hiker goes missing in a national park after separating from their group. They have no phone signal and their companions do not know which direction they went.
options: The group contacts mountain rescue immediately, stays at the last known location as a reference point, and provides rescuers with a detailed account of the missing person's last known direction and clothing.
The group splits up to search the most likely areas before calling mountain rescue.
The group waits for two hours to see if the hiker returns before escalating.
The group follows the most likely trail in the hope of finding the hiker before rescue arrives.
payload.explanation: Mountain rescue must be contacted immediately when someone is missing in remote terrain — splitting the group or delaying the call reduces both the search effectiveness and the group's own safety.

payload.snippet: A care home discovers that a resident with dementia has gone missing from the building. CCTV shows they left through a fire exit thirty minutes ago.
options: Staff call the police immediately, check the immediate vicinity in teams without leaving the building unstaffed, and notify the resident's next of kin.
Staff search the building fully before contacting police, in case the resident is hiding inside.
Staff wait to notify next of kin until the resident is found to avoid causing unnecessary distress.
Staff contact the resident's GP before calling police to check whether the resident has wandered before.
payload.explanation: A vulnerable adult missing from a care home requires immediate police contact, simultaneous external search without depleting building staff, and immediate next-of-kin notification.

payload.snippet: A shipping company discovers that a container holding personal effects for a family emigrating abroad has been loaded onto the wrong vessel and is now en route to a different continent.
options: The company contacts the ship's operator immediately to arrange interception or return at the next port, notifies the affected family honestly and fully, and activates their liability insurance.
The company waits until the container reaches the wrong destination and then arranges onward shipping.
The company tells the family there has been an administrative delay without disclosing the true situation.
The company contacts the family only after a solution has been arranged to avoid unnecessary distress.
payload.explanation: Immediate interception attempt, full honest disclosure, and insurance activation are all required simultaneously — delayed or partial disclosure compounds the breach of trust.

payload.snippet: A museum discovers that a significant artefact from its permanent collection is missing after a large public event. The item may have been taken or may have been moved during setup.
options: The museum director locks down the building to prevent any further movement of items, initiates a full inventory of the relevant section, and contacts the police before drawing any conclusions.
The museum completes a full internal search before contacting the police, to avoid public embarrassment if the item is simply misplaced.
The museum contacts its insurers first to understand its liability before deciding whether to notify police.
The museum reviews CCTV footage internally before deciding whether to contact police.
payload.explanation: A missing artefact from a permanent collection requires immediate lockdown, inventory, and police contact — internal investigation before police notification can compromise evidence.

payload.snippet: A hospital discovers that a patient's medical records have been lost during a system migration, and the patient is scheduled for surgery the following morning.
options: The hospital notifies the patient immediately, postpones the surgery if the missing records cannot be reconstructed in time, and sources emergency records from the patient's GP and previous providers.
The hospital proceeds with surgery using the operating surgeon's direct assessment, without the patient's full history.
The hospital reconstructs the records from memory of the treating team's conversations with the patient.
The hospital performs the surgery with a qualified second surgeon present in case complications arise from unknown patient history.
payload.explanation: Missing medical records before surgery require postponement if they cannot be sourced — proceeding without the full history risks patient safety regardless of additional safeguards.

payload.snippet: A solicitor's office discovers that the original will of a recently deceased client is missing from their files. The estate is in dispute between claimants.
options: The firm immediately notifies all parties and the probate court of the missing document, searches for any certified copies, and commences an investigation into where the original was last recorded as held.
The firm uses the most recent draft version of the will as a substitute for probate.
The firm delays notifying the parties until the internal investigation is complete.
The firm notifies only the main beneficiary and asks them to consent to using an earlier version.
payload.explanation: A missing will must be reported to all parties and the court immediately — using a draft, delaying notification, or selective disclosure all undermine the probate process.

payload.snippet: A school discovers during a safeguarding audit that the DBS check records for three members of staff are missing from files and cannot be verified from any backup.
options: The school immediately places the three staff members on supervised duties only, contacts the DBS to verify the original checks, and commences urgent reverification if no record exists.
The school asks the three staff members to self-certify that they hold valid DBS clearance.
The school waits for the next annual audit to address the missing records in the correct administrative cycle.
The school commences reverification but allows the staff to continue normal duties in the meantime.
payload.explanation: Missing DBS records require immediate restricted duties and urgent official verification — self-certification or normal duties pending verification both compromise safeguarding.

payload.snippet: A commercial airline discovers during a pre-flight check that the load manifest does not account for several pallets of cargo. The aircraft is already boarded.
options: The airline grounds the aircraft until the manifest is reconciled and the unaccounted cargo is located and verified.
The airline proceeds with the flight since the unaccounted pallets are likely a paperwork error.
The airline offloads only the cargo that cannot be identified as pre-screened.
The airline delays only long enough to add an approximated weight estimate to the manifest.
payload.explanation: An unreconciled cargo manifest is a flight safety issue — the aircraft cannot depart until the load is fully accounted for.

payload.snippet: A researcher discovers that several years of field data stored on a remote server has been deleted due to a misconfigured backup system, and no verified backup exists.
options: They report the data loss to their institution immediately, attempt data recovery through a specialist service, and assess the impact on any publications or ongoing work that relied on the data.
They reconstruct the data from memory and partial notes, presenting it as the original dataset.
They delay reporting the loss until they have assessed whether recovery is possible.
They continue the research project as if the data still exists and plan to collect replacement data silently.
payload.explanation: Immediate institutional reporting, professional recovery attempts, and impact assessment are all required — reconstructed or replacement data presented as original constitutes research fraud.

payload.snippet: A company's payroll system failure has resulted in thousands of employees not being paid on their expected date. The cause is a technical error that may take several days to resolve.
options: The payroll director notifies all employees immediately with a transparent explanation, arranges emergency advance payments for those who request them, and provides a firm corrected payment date.
The payroll director waits until a solution is imminent before notifying employees to avoid alarm.
The payroll director notifies only those employees who contact HR to ask why they have not been paid.
The payroll director sends a general message saying there has been a 'delay' without specifying the cause or timeline.
payload.explanation: A payroll failure affecting many employees requires immediate transparent disclosure, emergency support for those in need, and a firm corrected date — vague or delayed communication leaves employees unable to plan.

payload.snippet: A national library discovers that an entire category of rare book records was incorrectly purged from its digital catalogue during a database migration three months ago, affecting over four thousand records.
options: The library director notifies researchers and institutions who have referenced those records, initiates a manual re-entry process from physical records, and files a formal incident report with their technical and governance teams.
The library rebuilds the catalogue silently over several months before notifying anyone.
The library notifies only researchers who have made enquiries about those specific records.
The library sends a general notice to all catalogue users without specifying which records were affected.
payload.explanation: A catalogue purge affecting four thousand records requires proactive notification to known users of those records, active reconstruction, and formal incident reporting — silent rebuilding or vague notices both leave affected researchers uninformed.

payload.snippet: A police evidence locker is found during an audit to be missing items tagged to an active criminal case. The trial is scheduled to begin in two weeks.
options: The custody sergeant notifies the prosecutor, the defendant's legal team, and the court immediately, initiates a full evidence audit, and preserves all remaining chain of custody documentation.
The custody sergeant completes the internal investigation before notifying the court, to avoid disrupting the trial schedule unnecessarily.
The custody sergeant notifies only the prosecutor and relies on them to decide what to disclose to the defence.
The custody sergeant replaces the missing items with identical substitutes from other cases.
payload.explanation: Missing evidence in an active criminal case requires immediate disclosure to all legal parties and the court — delay, selective disclosure, or substitution all compromise the trial and defendants' rights.

payload.snippet: An archivist at a museum discovers that a rare 17th-century manuscript, on loan from a private collector, has gone missing from its display case two days before the loan period ends. CCTV footage is inconclusive.
options: The archivist immediately notifies museum security, the collector, and local police without disturbing the display case further
The archivist conducts their own investigation for 24 hours before notifying anyone
The archivist replaces the manuscript with a replica to buy time
The archivist waits until the loan period ends hoping it reappears
payload.explanation: Rapid multi-agency notification preserves evidence and maximises recovery time for a stolen heritage item.

payload.snippet: A financial analyst notices that a critical data file containing six months of transaction records has been deleted from the shared drive, apparently by accident, one hour before an audit begins.
options: The analyst contacts IT immediately to restore from backup before the audit and informs the audit lead of the delay
The analyst reconstructs the data from memory and presents it without disclosure
The analyst postpones the audit without explanation
The analyst blames a colleague to avoid personal consequences
payload.explanation: Prompt escalation to IT and transparent communication with the auditor is the only ethical and practical response.

payload.snippet: A film production team realises the only hard drive containing two weeks of raw footage has been left in a hire car that has already been returned and re-hired by another customer.
options: The producer calls the hire company immediately, explains the urgency, and asks them to contact the new hirer to locate the drive
The producer assumes the footage is gone and begins reshooting
The producer drives to the hire lot and searches the car fleet unannounced
The producer waits until the new hirer returns the car
payload.explanation: Time-critical escalation through official channels is faster than self-directed searching for an item in a controlled system.

payload.snippet: A hiker leading a group in a national park loses the GPS device and paper map on a river crossing. The group is four hours from the trailhead and weather is deteriorating.
options: The hiker activates the emergency PLB beacon, keeps the group together on the trail, and uses landscape features to navigate toward the trailhead
The hiker splits the group to cover ground faster
The hiker retraces the entire river section searching for the device
The hiker waits at the river crossing hoping a ranger passes
payload.explanation: When navigation tools are lost in deteriorating backcountry conditions, activating an emergency beacon takes priority over searching.

payload.snippet: A nurse realises that a controlled medication key has gone missing during a busy ward shift. The medications cabinet cannot be opened and patients have doses due in thirty minutes.
options: The nurse immediately reports the missing key to the charge nurse, triggers the lost-key protocol, and requests emergency authorisation to access a backup cabinet
The nurse searches the ward alone for fifteen minutes before telling anyone
The nurse asks a colleague to pick the lock to avoid delaying patient doses
The nurse documents the loss and delays the doses until the key is found
payload.explanation: Healthcare safety protocols exist precisely for this scenario — immediate escalation protects patients without compromising security.

payload.snippet: During a diplomatic summit, an official's briefcase containing confidential treaty drafts is misplaced between sessions. It was last seen in a shared green room with delegates from multiple nations.
options: The official notifies security immediately and requests a discreet search of the green room and surrounding corridors
The official re-enters the green room unannounced and searches other delegates' belongings
The official reconstructs the documents from memory to continue negotiations
The official waits until the end of the day to report the loss
payload.explanation: Immediate security escalation for lost classified documents follows international protocol and prevents a potential diplomatic incident.

payload.snippet: A teenager discovers that the family dog has slipped out of the gate and is missing. The dog is elderly, has a heart condition, and the neighbourhood has a busy road nearby.
options: The teenager alerts the family, starts a systematic street search, posts on local social media, and calls the vet clinic in case the dog has been brought in
The teenager searches alone for two hours before telling parents
The teenager waits by the gate in case the dog returns on its own
The teenager calls the dog by name from the front door
payload.explanation: A fast, coordinated multi-channel search gives a vulnerable pet the best chance of being found safely.

payload.snippet: A student submits an online exam and receives a confirmation number, but the university portal shows no record of the submission. The submission deadline passed twenty minutes ago.
options: The student emails the module coordinator immediately with the confirmation number as evidence and contacts IT support
The student resubmits the exam hoping the portal accepts it after the deadline
The student waits for the grade to appear, assuming a glitch will resolve itself
The student posts on the student forum asking if others had the same problem
payload.explanation: Providing timestamped confirmation evidence through official channels is the correct response to a disputed digital submission.

payload.snippet: A teenager rebuilds a vintage motorcycle with a parent. Near completion, she realises she has over-torqued the wheel bearing, causing a hairline crack in the hub. Road-testing it could be catastrophic.
options: She tells her parent immediately and they take the wheel to a machinist to assess whether the hub can be repaired or needs replacement
She road-tests it at low speed on a private road to see if the crack worsens
She re-torques the opposite side to balance the stress
She coats the crack with JB Weld epoxy and does not mention it
payload.explanation: A cracked wheel hub is a catastrophic failure risk — transparency with an expert is non-negotiable.

payload.snippet: A secondary-school student is using the school's laser cutter unsupervised after being trained. She burns through a piece of work and the bed sheet underneath; the extraction fan also stops during the cut.
options: She turns off the machine immediately, leaves the room for fresh air, and reports both the damaged material and the fan fault to the technician
She fans away the smoke and finishes the cut to meet the deadline
She reports only the damaged work, hoping the fan fault goes unnoticed
She turns the extraction fan off and on hoping it resets
payload.explanation: A failed extraction fan in a laser-cutter room creates toxic fume risk — stopping immediately and reporting the fault prevents serious harm.

payload.snippet: An engineering student on a school placement accidentally shears a bolt while over-torquing a car suspension component. The engineer overseeing her has stepped away.
options: She stops work, marks the area as unsafe, and waits to tell the engineer as soon as they return
She replaces the sheared bolt herself with one from the spares bin
She marks the component as complete to avoid appearing incompetent
She continues with other components and mentions the issue at the end of the day
payload.explanation: A sheared suspension bolt compromises road safety — only the supervising engineer can decide whether the component is safe to use.

payload.snippet: A young programmer builds a home automation script that accidentally bricks the smart-home hub by sending malformed firmware. The household's heating, alarm, and locks are all offline.
options: She tells her parents immediately and contacts the manufacturer's support line with the device model and what happened
She keeps trying different firmware files hoping one reverts the device
She tells her parents the hub must have broken on its own
She resets the router assuming it is a network issue
payload.explanation: Admitting the cause immediately is the only way to get the right technical support; the manufacturer's team can often recover bricked devices.

payload.snippet: A student volunteers at a community makerspace and snaps the only available drill press chuck key by applying lateral force. Without it, no one can use the drill press.
options: She tells the makerspace coordinator straight away, apologises, and offers to source a replacement online that day
She hides the broken key in the toolbox hoping someone else finds it
She improvises a grip using pliers and continues using the drill press
She leaves the makerspace without telling anyone
payload.explanation: A communal tool affects every other user — immediate disclosure and a replacement offer is the responsible course.

payload.snippet: A teenager's chemistry homework experiment produces an unexpected exothermic reaction that scorches the kitchen worktop. The house smells of burnt material.
options: She turns off the heat source, ventilates the kitchen, and tells her parents honestly what experiment she was running
She scrubs the scorch mark and sprays air freshener before her parents return
She tells her parents the mark was already there
She continues the experiment in a different room
payload.explanation: Transparency about a chemical incident is a safety imperative — parents need to know the substance involved.

payload.snippet: A teenager borrows the family's expensive DSLR camera for a school project and drops it on concrete, shattering the UV filter and cracking the lens barrel.
options: She tells her parents the same day with the full details, so they can assess repair costs against insurance
She buys a new UV filter online and pretends that is all that broke
She puts the camera back in the bag without mentioning the crack
She tells them the camera slipped off a surface on its own
payload.explanation: Insurance claims for accidental damage require honest disclosure; attempting to hide a crack often makes repair impossible.

payload.snippet: A student working in a school greenhouse accidentally snaps the irrigation control lever; water begins flowing continuously into all beds, risking flood damage and plant root rot.
options: She finds the manual shutoff valve, closes it to stop the flow, and immediately tells the science technician
She props the lever in position with a stick and hopes it holds
She leaves the water running and reports it at the end of the day
She turns off the power to the greenhouse to stop the pump
payload.explanation: Knowing where a manual shutoff valve is and using it is the correct emergency response to runaway irrigation.

payload.snippet: A student's robotics team relies on a custom-built arm prototype for a regional competition in four days. She drops it during a practice run and the servo gearbox cracks.
options: She immediately tells the team, assesses whether a spare gearbox can be sourced or 3D-printed, and adjusts the competition strategy if not
She epoxies the crack and does not tell the team, hoping it holds during competition
She blames the floor surface for the drop
She withdraws the team from the competition without consulting anyone
payload.explanation: Transparent communication within a team allows for rapid problem-solving under a deadline.

payload.snippet: A teenager helping at a relative's jewellery workshop accidentally drops a customer's antique brooch into the ultrasonic cleaner with a flawed setting, and the vibration dislodges a small gemstone.
options: She stops the machine, retrieves both the brooch and the gemstone, and immediately tells the jeweller what happened
She glues the gemstone back in herself and says nothing
She puts the brooch back as-is and tells no one, hoping the customer won't notice
She blames the brooch for having a pre-existing weak setting
payload.explanation: Customer property with loose stones must be disclosed immediately — a jeweller can re-set it professionally; amateur repair risks further loss.

payload.snippet: A student intern at a video production company accidentally deletes a client's footage directory instead of a temp folder. There is no recycle bin on the edit server.
options: She tells her supervisor immediately and asks IT to attempt a file-system recovery before any new data is written to the drive
She runs her own recovery software to attempt restoration, potentially overwriting data
She recreates file names and structure hoping no one checks the metadata
She waits until end of day to tell anyone
payload.explanation: Every second of new disk writes reduces recovery chances — immediate escalation to IT is the only correct first step.

payload.snippet: A teenager fixes a family friend's old clock and, misreading the diagrams, winds the mainspring too tight, causing the gear train to strip. The clock was a family heirloom.
options: She tells her parents and the family friend honestly, explains her mistake, and researches specialist horological repair services
She reassembles the clock with the stripped gears and returns it, saying it runs a little slow now
She orders a replacement movement online and swaps it without disclosure
She tells the family friend the clock was already damaged when she opened it
payload.explanation: Admitting a misread instruction and seeking specialist repair is the only way to preserve both the object and the relationship.

payload.snippet: A student working in a school metalwork room accidentally breaks the chuck key for the metal lathe, leaving no way to change lathe tools during the session.
options: She stops the lathe, tells the technician immediately, and secures the lathe so no one else uses it until a replacement chuck key is sourced
She improvises a grip with pliers on the hot lathe
She leaves the broken key in the lathe drawer without reporting it
She finishes her work with the existing tool and reports at the end of the day
payload.explanation: A missing lathe chuck key must be reported immediately — using a lathe with improvised grips creates catastrophic entanglement risk.

payload.snippet: A teenager is servicing his own bicycle and overtightens the carbon fibre seatpost clamp, causing a hairline crack in the frame.
options: He stops riding, has the frame inspected by a professional bike shop before further use, and tells his parents honestly
He rides gently and checks the crack each day
He covers the crack with a carbon repair wrap and keeps riding
He returns the bicycle to the rack without telling anyone about the crack
payload.explanation: A cracked carbon fibre frame can fail catastrophically without warning — professional inspection before riding is non-negotiable.

payload.snippet: A student intern at a pottery studio accidentally drops and breaks a customer's finished glazed piece the day before collection.
options: She tells the studio manager immediately, helps the studio manager contact the customer with a sincere apology, and asks what she can do to make it right
She reconstructs the piece from similar stock and substitutes it without disclosure
She tells the manager the piece broke in the kiln
She leaves work early to avoid the conversation
payload.explanation: Honest disclosure is the only ethical response when someone else's property is damaged in a professional setting.

payload.snippet: A student volunteer at a charity hardware repair cafe strips a screw thread on an elderly visitor's radio while attempting a repair, making it impossible to reassemble.
options: She tells the visitor honestly, apologises, and asks the lead volunteer whether the component can be sourced for a proper repair
She forces the screw back in stripped and reassembles the radio hoping it holds
She tells the visitor the radio was beyond repair when it arrived
She leaves the disassembled radio on the table without explanation
payload.explanation: Volunteers have a duty of honesty to the people they serve — disclosing a repair mistake maintains trust in the repair service.

payload.snippet: A teenage sailing student accidentally jibes unexpectedly, and the boom breaks when it strikes the mast fitting. The boat is now unsafe to sail.
options: She secures the broken boom, signals to the safety boat, and reports the damage to the instructor on returning to shore
She tries to sail back to shore with the broken boom hanging loose
She anchors the boat and swims back without notifying anyone
She tells the instructor another boat hit her
payload.explanation: A broken spar makes a boat unsafe — signalling immediately and reporting honestly protects both the sailor and other water users.

payload.snippet: A student's ambitious trebuchet for physics class flings a stone that cracks a school window during an outdoor demonstration. The whole class saw it happen.
options: She tells the teacher immediately, takes responsibility, and offers to help arrange the repair through the school's administration
She blames the trebuchet design for not predicting the range correctly
She waits to see if anyone else reports it first
She tells the teacher a random stone flew up from the ground
payload.explanation: Taking immediate responsibility in front of witnesses is the only credible course; attempting to deflect is transparent and damages trust further.

payload.snippet: A teenager uses a friend's expensive vinyl cutter to make stickers. The blade holder breaks mid-job after she sets the force too high, ruining the head.
options: She stops immediately, tells her friend honestly what happened, and researches the replacement part cost
She resets the machine and keeps cutting on the damaged head hoping the output looks fine
She puts the machine back without mentioning the break
She tells her friend the machine must have had a faulty head
payload.explanation: Replacing or contributing to the cost of a broken borrowed tool is a basic responsibility of borrowing.

payload.snippet: A student restoring a vintage clock winds the mainspring beyond its limit and it fractures, spraying small metal fragments inside the movement.
options: She stops immediately without disturbing the movement further, covers the clock, and tells her parents so they can arrange a professional horologist to assess the damage
She picks out the fragments with tweezers and reassembles the movement
She tells her parents the clock stopped on its own
She throws the clock away to avoid explaining the damage
payload.explanation: Fractured mainsprings release stored energy unpredictably and leave sharp metal debris — only a professional horologist should open the movement after such a failure.

payload.snippet: A school introduces a merit badge system. Students from wealthier families consistently earn more badges because they can afford extracurricular activities that generate badge criteria. Students from poorer families fall behind socially.
options: The school audits which badge criteria require out-of-school spending and replaces them with in-school alternatives that are accessible to all
