The school keeps the system arguing it mirrors real-world meritocracy
The school abolishes all badges so nobody benefits
The school offers loans for extracurriculars, placing financial burden on poorer families
payload.explanation: Incentive systems should be audited for structural exclusion; replacing inaccessible criteria preserves the motivational benefit while removing inequality.

payload.snippet: A regional sports academy selects young athletes partly based on physical maturity. Children born early in the school year are consistently more physically developed and are over-represented, creating a long-term talent pipeline that excludes late-birthday athletes.
options: The academy introduces age-adjusted assessments and tracks late-birthday athletes separately to correct for relative-age bias
The academy keeps the system arguing early developers are simply better
The academy randomises selections to avoid all bias, regardless of ability
The academy abandons talent identification altogether
payload.explanation: Relative-age effect is a documented systemic bias in youth sport; correcting for it recovers talent that would otherwise be systematically discarded.

payload.snippet: A school assigns homework tasks that assume home computers and broadband access. Students without these resources consistently submit lower-quality work and fall behind, even when equally capable.
options: The school audits all homework for digital-access assumptions and provides lunchtime computer lab sessions and USB-based alternatives
The school continues assigning digital tasks and blames underperformance on lack of effort
The school eliminates all homework to make it equal
The school tells disadvantaged students to use the library without checking its hours
payload.explanation: Structurally unequal homework assignments entrench inequality of outcome — auditing for access and providing compensatory time restores fairness.

payload.snippet: In a school mock trial exercise, the prosecution team is given three weeks of preparation and the defence team is given one week, making the outcome predetermined.
options: Before the exercise, both teams raise that unequal preparation time makes the exercise educationally meaningless and ask for equal time
The prosecution wins every year and the exercise is considered a success
The defence refuses to participate and the exercise collapses
The teacher extends only the defence time but does not tell the prosecution
payload.explanation: A structured exercise designed to teach critical thinking must have structurally equal conditions; raising it before the exercise rather than after is the productive intervention.

payload.snippet: A school's gifted and talented programme is open by teacher nomination only. Research shows teachers systematically under-nominate students from minority ethnic backgrounds and those who are quieter.
options: The school replaces sole nomination with an open application process that includes blind-reviewed written and practical assessments
The school keeps the nomination system since teachers know their students best
The school reserves a fixed percentage of places regardless of performance
The school abolishes the programme to avoid any appearance of elitism
payload.explanation: Open, multi-method, blind assessment processes are the most reliable way to reduce nomination bias in talent identification.

payload.snippet: Two students co-author an academic paper as part of a school science project. When the paper is entered into a regional competition, the supervising teacher adds their own name as lead author without contributing any written work.
options: The students politely but directly inform the competition organisers of the actual authorship and ask their school's academic integrity coordinator to clarify the school's policy
The students accept the teacher's name to avoid conflict
The students withdraw the paper in protest
The students resubmit the paper independently under their own names without notifying the school
payload.explanation: Academic authorship must reflect actual intellectual contribution; using school channels before external ones is the appropriate escalation path.

payload.snippet: A class fundraiser uses a prize raffle. Wealthier students buy many tickets; poorer students buy one or none. The prizes go almost exclusively to students with more tickets, and the event generates resentment rather than community.
options: The organiser redesigns the event as a skills challenge where entry is free and prizes are determined by a fair competition rather than purchasing power
The raffle proceeds unchanged the following year
The event is cancelled because it caused resentment
All prize money is donated to charity so nobody wins individually
payload.explanation: When fundraising mechanisms generate inequity among the very community being built, redesigning the format serves both fairness and cohesion better than cancellation.

payload.snippet: A school's house points system rewards public speaking, sporting achievement, and leadership — all areas where extroverted, physically able students naturally dominate. Introverted or disabled students rarely accumulate points regardless of their effort.
options: The student council proposes expanding the criteria to include academic improvement, creative contribution, and community support, which are assessed by multiple staff members
The school keeps the existing system as it is traditional
The school abolishes house points to avoid any perceived hierarchy
The school adds one new category but does not change how contributions are assessed
payload.explanation: Recognition systems that systematically exclude large groups of students fail their motivational and community-building purpose — broadening and diversifying criteria is the structural fix.

payload.snippet: A scholarship is awarded to one student from an underfunded school, but the selection committee's unconscious bias means they consistently rank students who present in a confident, middle-class speech register higher, even when the written work is equal.
options: The committee introduces anonymous written assessment scored by independent reviewers before any interview stage, reducing presentation-style bias in the first round
The committee denies that any bias exists and continues the current process
The committee removes the interview stage entirely so all decisions are anonymous
The committee adds more diverse members but does not change the assessment method
payload.explanation: Blind written assessment as a first-round filter is a structural fix that reduces presentation-based bias without removing human judgement from the final round.

payload.snippet: A school's behavioural reward chart is visible to all students. Children who receive more detentions — often those with undiagnosed learning needs or difficult home lives — are publicly identifiable on the chart, adding shame to pre-existing disadvantage.
options: The school transitions to individual progress charts visible only to the student and their teacher, measuring personal improvement rather than absolute compliance
The school keeps the public chart as it encourages competition
The school removes the chart for every student including those thriving under it
The school asks parents whether their child's data can be displayed
payload.explanation: Behaviour systems should support progress, not publicise disadvantage; individual charts preserve motivation without using shame.

payload.snippet: A university entrance mock interview scheme is run by volunteers who are all alumni of elite schools. Feedback consistently praises students who speak and dress like the volunteers, and underrates equally-qualified students from state schools.
options: The scheme coordinator diversifies the volunteer pool and introduces a structured rubric that assesses specific interview competencies rather than general impression
The coordinator thanks all volunteers and makes no structural changes
The scheme is closed to avoid further bias
Students from state schools are given extra coaching to present more like the volunteers
payload.explanation: Diversifying assessors and standardising rubrics corrects for volunteer-pool homogeneity; coaching students to perform a particular class register is not a structural solution.

payload.snippet: A student council election in a large school allows candidates to campaign freely. Students with more social media followers, wealthier families, and more time outside class dominate the campaign, drowning out equally-capable candidates with fewer resources.
options: The school introduces a structured campaign format — equal poster allocation, equal speaking time at an assembly, and no social media campaigning during the election period
The school lets the election proceed and accepts that popular students win
The school cancels student elections and appoints a council by staff selection
The school gives disadvantaged candidates extra campaign funding but no structural rules
payload.explanation: Equal-format elections reduce campaign-resource advantages and return the selection to policy and personality rather than reach and wealth.

payload.snippet: A school's selection process for a prestigious international exchange programme is limited to students whose parents can pay a programme fee. Academically stronger students from lower-income families are ineligible.
options: The school sets up a bursary fund and applies to the exchange organiser for fee waivers, making selection based on merit not means
The school accepts that only wealthier families can access the programme
The school cancels its participation to avoid inequality
The school offers a domestic trip to poorer students as an alternative
payload.explanation: Prestigious development opportunities funded by families create structural inequity — bursary mechanisms restore merit-based selection.

payload.snippet: A school introduces a 'student of the month' award. Analysis over a year shows it has gone exclusively to white and East Asian students, despite a demographically diverse school.
options: The school's equity lead audits the nomination criteria and process, introduces anonymised submissions, and diversifies the judging panel
The school continues the award arguing nominees are simply the highest achievers
The school rotates the award alphabetically to guarantee diversity
The school cancels the award to avoid scrutiny
payload.explanation: An award with systematic demographic exclusion has a structural problem, not a talent one — anonymisation and diverse judging are the evidence-based fixes.

payload.snippet: In a school's house system, houses are named after historical figures who are now recognised as deeply problematic. Students from certain backgrounds feel excluded by the celebration of these figures.
options: The school convenes a student and staff working group to review the naming, consult the community, and propose alternatives that all students can feel proud of
The school keeps the names arguing historical context matters
The school renames all houses immediately without consultation
The school removes all naming and numbering houses instead
payload.explanation: Renaming community symbols requires genuine consultation to build ownership; both ignoring the issue and acting unilaterally undermine inclusion.

payload.snippet: A school's music department heavily subsidises lessons for students in the school orchestra while students who play genres outside the classical tradition receive no support.
options: The music coordinator expands subsidised lesson access to include all instrument types and genres, and audits the programme annually for equitable distribution
Classical music funding continues as it is a measurable academic pathway
The school removes orchestral subsidies to make the policy equal
Other genres receive a single annual workshop as a token recognition
payload.explanation: Musical genre hierarchies in subsidy decisions replicate cultural and class bias — equitable access requires removing the genre distinction from funding criteria.

payload.snippet: A student advocacy group publishes data showing that students with behavioural support needs receive less classroom support from teaching assistants than students whose difficulties are easier to manage.
options: The SENCO reviews allocation data, rebalances teaching assistant deployment based on documented need, and monitors outcomes quarterly
The school continues existing deployment since TAs are assigned by class, not individual need
The school adds more TAs without reviewing how current ones are deployed
The school tells students with behavioural needs to self-manage more
payload.explanation: Support resource allocation must be based on documented need; publishing allocation data and reviewing it quarterly creates structural accountability.

payload.snippet: A school anti-bullying policy is applied consistently to student-on-student bullying but teachers who bully students through sarcasm and public humiliation face no consequences.
options: The student council raises the inconsistency with the headteacher and asks for the policy to explicitly apply to all adults in the school community
The policy continues applying only to students
The council posts anonymously online about the bullying teachers
The council asks affected students to ignore teacher comments
payload.explanation: Anti-bullying policies that exempt adults create a protected class — extending the policy to all community members is the only logically consistent application.

payload.snippet: A school's grading system applies strict late-submission penalties regardless of reason, resulting in students with chronic illness or caring responsibilities systematically receiving lower grades than their attainment merits.
options: The school introduces a medical and personal-circumstance extension policy with a simple, private application process
The school applies equal rules to everyone arguing life skills require meeting deadlines
The school removes all deadlines to avoid penalising anyone
The school tells affected students to work harder to meet deadlines like everyone else
payload.explanation: Equal rules that produce structurally unequal outcomes are not fair; a private extension process maintains standards while accommodating genuine barriers.

payload.snippet: A secondary school's academic prize-giving ceremony recognises only academic achievement, leaving students who contribute enormously to school life through volunteering, peer mentoring, and community support without any recognition.
options: The school adds a community contribution award category with publicly stated, transparent criteria so all forms of school citizenship are valued
The school argues academic prizes are the only measurable outcome worth rewarding
The school adds informal mentions from the headteacher to avoid formal recognition
The school gives every student a participation certificate instead of distinct awards
payload.explanation: Recognising only academic achievement in a diverse school signals that only one form of excellence has value — expanding award categories accurately reflects the school's stated values.
